Minimalist logo design has been getting some stick in recent years. Simplicity in visual branding often makes a lot of sense. A clean, uncomplicated logo can be more memorable, it looks more modern and it's easier to use across different media, but then came anti-design and the backlash to what some see as a trend towards homogeneity in branding, or 'blanding', as it was dubbed.

Some argue that minimalist redesigns can strip a logo of its character, and we've seen the complaint everywhere from the great Cracker Barrel outrage to the new Harry Potter logos.

The new Sunlife logo is unlikely to end the debate. It might be one of the most dramatically simplified logo redesigns yet. The Canadian financial services company has eliminated the space from its name and all detail from its mark.

Sunlife, now one word, says its new logo is intended to bring its identity in line with the evolution of its business. While the design had barely changed in 25 years, the company has expanded from life insurance into services in health, asset management and other types of insurance.

There's also a new tagline, 'Making life brighter'. This is intended to connect to Sunlife's purpose of "helping clients build lifetime financial security and lead healthier lives".

"Together, the changes create a more modern, distinctive and consistent expression of Sunlife around the world," the company says.

"A great brand isn't defined by a logo. It's defined by the experiences it creates," said Linda Dougherty, Executive Vice-President, Chief Client and Strategy Officer, Sunlife. "Making life brighter captures what we want every Sunlife experience to deliver for Clients: greater clarity, confidence and connection. Our new identity gives us a powerful, consistent way to bring that commitment to life around the world."

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

The modernised, simplified logo, was "optimised for a digital world", the company says.

The old design was very much giving the corporate vibe of an insurance company from 25 years ago. The new symbol keeps the sun, or a weather forecast-like ultra simplification of it, and keeps the colour, while stripping out the fat. The wordmark, meanwhile, continues to use a serif font, but it feels slimmer, lighter and more contemporary.

The simplicity of the mark has sparked some bemused responses on social media, from people who think it's taken minimalism too far. "Is this satire," one person asks on X.

We have seen comparable designs to the yellow disc coming in other colours. Sunlife's compatriots the Green Party of Canada rebranded last year as the green dot emoji with the logic that it would help to have an easily shareable logo for social campaigns. There's also USA Today with its blue disc logo.

I think that with the serif wordmark, the overall design looks distinctive and a lot less dated. The combination of Sunlife into one word reads much better, and makes more sense now the company's no longer primarily a life insurance provider – the 'life' no longer makes you immediately think of death, which is probably a good thing for most brands.

#2. Live From the Lavender Lake

Dispatches from open studios events across town and the Tompkins Square Dog Halloween Parade.

I generally spend a decent amount of time in Gowanus, but weaving through the neighborhood’s streets and buildings for Open Studios on Saturday really demonstrated how the stretch of water has shed its sardonic designation of “Lavender Lake” and turned into a bizarro landscape of glimmering apartment buildings. The canalside Whole Foods is one thing, but the “luxury” high-rises boasting an “iconic” view of the waterfront in its funky fluorescence are still a head-scratcher for me.

Now, I’m neither a chemist, an architect, nor a physician, but I’m willing to bet that everyone probably would have benefitted from waiting for water remediation and sewage overflow prevention efforts to be completed instead of developers speedrunning the area’s sublimation from a Superfund site with a petering industrial profile to a bunch of towers offering studio apartments starting at $3,200/month.

Unless there’s a large band of civilians seeking front-row seats to Gowanus’s next poonami … Because they’re literally installing permanent picnic tables and reclining deck chairs along the banks of the canal.

At landscape painter Elizabeth O’Reilly’s studio on Union Street, I commented that she and a few other artists I’d dropped in on were kind for drawing inspiration from the neighborhood as it is. I find it endearing that they’re able to extrapolate beauty at both ends of the spectrum of devastating human impact — from a life-threateningly toxic pollution hub to a shiny new playground for gentrification to mall-ify eventually — and help others appreciate the importance of archiving it.

Keeping things coastal, contributor Aaron Short dropped in on the open studios programming in Red Hook and Sunset Park respectively. Short reports that Red Hook’s creative community barrels forward unabated 13 months after a five-alarm fire tore through a historic warehouse filled with converted artist studios, and that spaces in Sunset Park are somehow still affordable. On the other end of the borough, local artist Jazmine Hayes details the historical, spiritual, and environmental symbolism throughout her Percent for Art commission at the new Brownsville Multi-Service Center.

Since we’re talking about the environment, let’s add some animals to the mix, too. Those who foolishly missed the annual Tompkins Square Dog Halloween Parade can peruse some highlights courtesy of staff writer Anna Lee, who dropped to ankle level for Pup Leo and Santa Paws, among other costumed canines. There are also only a few days left to catch Cannupa Hanska Luger’s American Traditional, which is closing on the 24th at Garth Greenan Gallery’s new location on Greene Street. The show was highlighted in our round-up of New York exhibitions embodying Indigenous survivance, and Editor-at-Large and Co-Founder Hrag Vartanian attests that it’s Luger’s “strongest work yet.”

Lastly, take a glance at our “What Else is Happening?” section — I’ve got some neat stuff lined up for you.

While I can't promise it'll hold a candle to the Dog Parade, Hyperallergic's own Halloween Party next Wednesday is just the place for your niche, art-world costume to shine during an open bar. Calling all Kusama pumpkins and Magritte apple-faced individuals to the fore! (Discounted tickets available for members. RSVP here!)

I’ve never put much thought into how I want to be portrayed after I die. Perhaps I’d opt to be plastered on Etsy mugs, tea sets, and journal covers, à la Frida Kahlo (though I doubt I’d have many buyers, or that Kahlo would’ve enjoyed how her self-image is often nowadays detached from the politics and life behind it), or I would begin things early by enlisting an artist to paint their best guess at my posthumous body. Maybe I’d like to be dipped in ink and stamped onto rice paper, as Molly Tenzer does with the roadkill she finds on New York City streets. The lineup at this year’s DOC NYC, which returns to venues throughout the city from November 11 through November 29, offers many reflections on this question. | Anna Lee Read More

#3. Hundreds protest far-right government's removal of objects from Colombia's national museum

Colombia's government has removed more than 30 works from the permanent displays of the Museo Nacional de Colombia in Bogotá—including materials related to feminist and LGBTQ+ movements, and the country's 2016 peace agreement—citing "political indoctrination".

The decision sparked protests outside the museum over the weekend and prompted six other museums to issue a joint statement calling for the measure to be reconsidered. The case also reached the courts on Monday (19 October), when a judge ordered that the museum halt any further removals without formal justification.

Among the items taken down from the permanent galleries “Hacer sociedad” (Building society) and “Memoria y Nación” (Memory and Nation) were a pride flag belonging to the activist Elizabeth Castillo; campaign posters for the presidential candidates Bernardo Jaramillo Ossa and Carlos Pizarro, both assassinated in 1990; and a poster for the International Day for the Elimination of Violence Against Women.

Empty spaces where items were removed from the museum walls Courtesy Colombia Diversa

The move came as President Abelardo de la Espriella announced plans to rename the Ministerio de las Culturas, las Artes y los Saberes (Ministry of Cultures, Arts and Knowledge) as the Ministerio de Cultura y Patrimonio (Ministry of Culture and Heritage). The president said recently that the ministry “must return to its proper name”, adding: “The explicit inclusion of the word patrimonio is a direct blow to ‘wokeism’ and the ideologisation of culture, which is exactly what we are fighting.”

Culture Minister Paola Holguín defended the government’s removal of objects in a post on X, saying the museum's institutional role “is not to serve as an instrument of political indoctrination or a platform for spreading biased versions of our history”. She also said the museum cannot become a place for “glorification of crime or revictimisation”. Holguín added: “The museology and curatorial practices of the various spaces overseen by the ministry are being reviewed and redesigned.”

Over the weekend, hundreds of people gathered outside the Museo Nacional on Carrera Séptima—one of Bogotá's main thoroughfares—to protest censorship at the museum. Some protesters reproduced the works that had been taken down and pasted the images onto an art installation outside the building. Others held signs reading "Museo Nazional” (a reference to Nazism) and “La memoria no se borra” (Memory cannot be erased). On both Saturday and Sunday (17 and 18 October), riot police dispersed the crowds using tear gas, stun grenades and water cannons.

The dispute reached the courts on Monday, when a Bogotá judge ordered the museum to preserve the works already taken down and halt any further removals based on their content without formal justification. The temporary order followed a constitutional-rights case filed by representatives of LGBTQ+ groups. The judge, César Osorio Ortiz, also asked the cultural ministry to explain the legal basis for its actions.

Meanwhile, six Colombian museums—including the Museo de Arte Moderno de Bogotá and the Museo de Arte Moderno de Medellín—issued a joint statement expressing “deep concern” and calling for the protection of museums' professional autonomy.

“No government should decide which parts of our history we can see based on its political preferences, or impose one version that suppresses all others,” the museums said in the statement addressed to Holguín. The statement calls for a public review of the decision to remove works from the Museo Nacional.

For now, the pieces remain off display; the courts have yet to rule on the case itself.

Founded in 1823, the Museo Nacional is one of the oldest museums in the Americas. It has been without a permanent director since Liliana Angulo Cortés died in February. During her tenure, Angulo helped bring more diverse perspectives to the museum's curatorial approach.

Angulo’s work was devoted to decolonising the museum, anti-racism and reparation with a special focus on diversifying narratives to include more Black and Indigenous voices

#4. temporary pleasure: john leo gillen on growing up in a nightclub

john leo gillen reflects on why time is his main design material and why the moments that matter most can’t be captured.

For most of its history, the nightclub was built on a simple premise: you had to be there.

John Leo Gillen was born and raised in a nightclub in the west of Ireland, and came of age just as the nightclub began to disappear. Outside the family business he threw illegal raves, then learned architecture to build temporary club spaces. Temporary Pleasure, the practice he founded, combines the two — the architecture of a club with the emotion of a rave — into a single idea: the ephemeral nightclub.

His projects include Choreomania at Horst Arts & Music, Joyride at the Barbican and The Superclub at WeCanDance, and he is the author of Temporary Pleasure: Nightclub Architecture, Design & Culture 1960–Today (Prestel, 2023). designboom speaks with Gillen about time as a design material, the crowd as the show, and why the moments that matter most can’t be captured.

‘The nightclub once offered something radical: a moment suspended in time that could only be experienced by those who were lucky enough to be in the right place at the right time,’ Gillen tells designboom.

designboom (DB): You grew up inside a nightclub in the west of Ireland. How did that lead you to the idea of a temporary nightclub?

John Leo Gillen (JLG): My family business was a nightclub in the west of Ireland. I was literally sleeping there as a baby while my parents worked, and I worked there all through my teens — collecting glasses, working the bar, eventually managing it. I spent my entire life fantasising about the nightclub I would design. Then I came of age just about exactly when the nightclub as we knew it started to disappear.

I started organising illegal raves, and I had this idea: imagine a nightclub that existed in each place just for a moment. The architecture of a nightclub — with the emotion of a rave. Designed and built, with all the physicality and specificity of a real nightclub, but with the emotional urgency of a rave. So Temporary Pleasure is a nightclub that exists in each place only for a moment, before disappearing and re-appearing somewhere else. A warehouse in Barcelona or Dublin, a car park in London, on a beach in Belgium.

A space known to disappear communicates urgency, heightens behaviour, and produces meaning rooted in impermanence. When architecture carries this message, people act differently: more present, more invested, more alive.

Everything that came after — architecture, show design, performance, even image — was all about presence. Tools for creating, restoring, elevating presence. This is not nostalgia. It is an act of definition: what is club culture when its traditional containers have disappeared, the medium has been forgotten, but its aesthetic and language are still being used?

DB: The clubs you write about from the 1960s and 70s used light, sound and the crowd itself almost as architectural material. What did they understand that’s been lost?

JLG: The nightclub was a distinct spatial invention — a deliberate break from the concert hall, against stages and audiences, performance as something you just watched. Designed to dissolve the central focus, erase stage hierarchy, fracture orientation. No divide between stage and audience. Platforms at different heights, some lit, some dark — every inch was the stage. Everyone was on stage, and no one was. You weren’t watching the show — you were in it.

Nightclub architecture evolved as a total interior world: facades, doors, entrances, thresholds, loops, dancefloors, bars, bathrooms, seating zones. Compression and release. Enclosure and circulation. Darkness, density, intimacy, anonymity, disorientation. Friction and disappearance. Social zones without spectacle.

Spaces to see and be seen, to disappear and re-emerge. Total worlds where the club itself was the headliner. Behaviour emerged from the way space was organised — possibly accidentally. The way bodies moved, gathered, circulated, danced. The nightclub didn’t present culture — it produced it.

The name remains, but the conditions that made a nightclub a nightclub mostly don’t. Stages return. Dancefloors face DJs. Sound becomes frontal. LED screens dominate orientation. The booth becomes the focal point, and the rest of the room becomes infrastructure for servicing it — something to be managed rather than inhabited.

The nightclub has become the very thing it was designed to break: a concert.

DB: You’ve talked about how club culture has become more focused on watching the DJ, while your work tries to put the attention back on the crowd. When do you think that shift happened?

JLG: We’ve forgotten what a nightclub and a dancefloor actually is. It’s not just a space in front of the DJ booth — it is the club. The crowd is the source of the energy, not the recipient of it. Dance is fundamental — physical, risky, collective. Everyone performing for each other, in real time. The moment someone takes the risk, someone else follows. Anything else is a concert. It’s rare to find a dancefloor where people are dancing with each other — it feels like they’re dancing to the DJ.

The DJ was never meant to perform at the crowd, but to service the dancefloor. DJs were mostly residents, obsessing over the energy every night, as much a part of the club as the walls, the speakers and lights. At Paradise Garage, Larry Levan played from a bird’s-eye nest above the crowd — he could see the dancers, but they couldn’t see him. The dancefloor was the instrument, not the decks.

Clubs put the DJ booth on stage and erased the rest of the room. Lineups made DJs the destination. We stopped going to a place and started going to a DJ.

We’ve designed clubs that make people bystanders, then wonder why everyone watches. Perhaps the reason people aren’t dancing is that dancefloors stopped being dancefloors.

DB: When you say ‘the crowd is the show,’ who are people actually performing for? The camera, each other, themselves?

JLG: A real rave isn’t about watching — it’s about being essential to the moment. The space should make people feel like this wouldn’t be happening without them — because it wouldn’t. That they are the energy. That they are the event. The club did not happen to them; it happened because of them.

What happens when everyone is fully protagonised? Exhibitionism, play, competition. Contagious dance energy. Everyone and no one on stage simultaneously. The whole space is the stage, and the crowd is the show.

DB: A lot of your work is about designing spaces that still leave room for spontaneity. How do you choreograph an experience without making people feel their behavior has already been scripted?

Platforms at different heights, balconies, mezzanines. Sound and light move, eyes follow. Nothing is fixed. Nothing lasts. Platforms shift, stairs loop, sightlines fracture. Architecture that leaves gaps — and rewards risk.

A single moving spotlight. It searches the room, looking for something, and lands on a lone dancer. It jumps to another on the opposite platform, then another, and the whole room’s gaze follows it — a body rolling, a foot stomping, arms jacking. No one knows when it will land on them. Surreal, elevated moments that feel almost cinematic, like you’ve just stepped into a music video or like: what the fuck is this? How is this happening? And then back to chaos.

The architecture creates the dare, but someone still has to take the risk. So it’s scripted but unscripted. You should never know where the energy is going to come from — or where it’s going to go next.

DB: Today almost everyone walks into a club with a camera in their pocket. How has that changed the way people behave in these spaces, or even the way clubs are designed?

JLG: The nightclub was something to be entered, not consumed visually. Its value lay in what could not be fully captured, replayed or verified — what lived on only as fragment: in memory, in myth, in distortion.

Modern image culture has changed not only how clubs are seen, but how they are designed and function. Today, image precedes experience. Presence is replaced by extraction. The moment is no longer lived for itself, but for its afterlife as content — designed to be replayed before it has even happened. That fundamentally changes why people are there and how the experience is lived.

If image is the primary output, if the experience itself has no implicit or sacred value — why gather physically at all?

DB: You’re drawn to spaces that disappear, but your book preserves them through photographs and stories. What can an image actually tell us about a nightclub, and what gets lost once the night is over? John Leo

JLG: An image can tell you what a thing looked like — a fragment, a clue, a trace. But it can’t give you the thing itself.

DB: With Superclub, you recessed the DJ, wrapped balconies around the dancefloor, and really pushed the idea of people watching each other. Did you manage to recreate the nightclub experience inside a festival?

JLG: Not entirely — and I think that’s important.

A nightclub is a space with its own rules, codes and belief system, shared by the whole crowd even if never explicit. They permeate the music, the programming, the staff, the door, the crowd, the promotion and the way people behave.

With Superclub, we were trying to challenge the assumptions of the festival format from within it. Festival logic is a stage, a frontal view, a crowd facing one direction, a DJ elevated above everyone. We wanted to fight against that from within — decentralising the DJ, breaking the spectacle and the frontality, putting the audience back at the centre.

But we were still working within a festival. We were leading the conceptual and spatial design of the stage, but not the programme, the staffing, the promotion, the messaging or the audience. We could change the physical conditions. We couldn’t completely change the cultural conditions around them.

The bigger challenge isn’t building the structure. It’s fighting for the nightclub as a format — and for the kind of collective experience that the format makes possible.

You can build a room that looks like a nightclub very easily. Creating the conditions that make it behave like one is much harder.

DB: Temporary Pleasure also works with cultural institutions. What happens when ideas that came out of underground club culture move into institutions? Can that energy survive the change of context?

JLG: The issue is not confined to institutions. Most of what we call club culture today is inverted. The language of the club is everywhere, the conditions are nowhere. Contemporary culture borrows the aesthetics and rhetoric of the club while operating under logics that fundamentally betray it.

It comes down to intent — a commitment to the culture, not just its kudos, clout or credentials. Institutions are often drawn to club culture for its optics, energy and audience. To appear as a club is safe. To actually offer it is risky. The question is whether they’re willing to offer the conditions, not just the aesthetic: darkness, duration, risk, a crowd that’s allowed to take over the room.

Are we actually creating a situation where people are participating, taking risks, behaving differently and producing something together? Or are we simply representing a history of participation?

We’re interested in temporary systems, one-night formats and conditional architectures — prototyping with real bodies, in real time, with real risk. Because you can’t fully design a club from the outside. If you’re genuinely trying to create a collective, emergent experience, you can’t completely determine what happens. You have to be willing to give up control.

#5. Rosana Paulino’s Pantheon of Black Plant Goddesses Arrives in Paris

The growing visibility of Rosana Paulino’s work reaches a new chapter with the opening this week of her first solo exhibition in Paris, at Mendes Wood DM’s outpost in the French capital.

Titled “Bloom in the Sunlight, Dream in the Moonlight,” the exhibition introduces new plant goddesses into the Afro-botanical pantheon Paulino has been building since 2019 as part of her ongoing series “Senhora das Plantas” (Lady of the Plants), which elevates Black women to the status of goddesses in communion with nature, without implying a romanticized view. The 16 paintings—five on paper and 12 on canvas—take on renewed vitality on a larger scale and via a deeper exploration of color and increasingly ingenious bodily poses. Related Articles Art Basel Paris Opens Avant Première with 'Good Energy,' a Smattering of Sales, and One $100 M. Work An Eva Gonzalès Retrospective Puts the Non-Impressionist Artist Back on the Map

The central question guiding Paulino’s work has long been “What is it like to be a Black woman in Brazil?” Active since the 1990s, she had seemingly answered it, until 2018, through an indictment of the enduring consequences of slavery in Brazilian society in works like Parede da Memória (Memory Wall, 1994), which engages with the extensive gaps in the family trees of Black Brazilian families, and Assentamento (Settlement, 2013), three photographs of an enslaved Black woman printed on fabric that she fragmented and stitched back together, adding a heart and a baby. Appropriated from images taken by Auguste Stahl and taken during the 1865–66 Thayer Expedition to Brazil, Paulino’s gesture aimed to restore the woman’s humanity and history from a set of photographs made to substantiate claims of racial degeneration supposedly caused by racial mixing.

At a 2018 retrospective at the Pinacoteca de São Paulo, Paulino debuted a series of drawings from the early 2000s that anticipate the psychological exploration seen later in the goddesses of Senhora das Plantas.” Marked by restless lines, these works depict a woman tentatively emerging from a cocoon in a ritual of transformation and emancipation. “Drawing is a central foundation of Rosana’s practice; it sheds light on her imagination. Forms and ideas that she develops through drawing later acquire spatiality,” Valéria Piccoli, the exhibition’s cocurator, told ARTnews. “It was important to emphasize that she was the first voice in the 1990s to speak about the issue of Black women, but also to highlight that this was part of a much broader context of her interests and desires.”

Less than a year later, she would show the earliest iteration of her botanical goddesses. A different sensibility had emerged: The figures, drawn in earth tones, were nude, but the hypersexualization of the Black female body was nowhere to be found. Instead, the works suggested a new way of conceiving wisdom and communion with nature. The series has its roots in the plants Paulino keeps in her studio. Before she named them goddesses, she initially called the plants in the series’ early works “folhas” (leaves).

“I gradually realized that it couldn’t be that simple: plants have a history, so I began to approach them more specifically,” Paulino explained in a recent interview in her studio, noting that she began the series because she could find no Black goddesses in books devoted to the sacred feminine.

She started first with snake plants (Espada de Iansã in Portuguese). “Then I turned my attention to the jatobá tree,” she added. Works from the series soon appeared in the world’s two oldest recurring exhibitions: the 2022 and 2026 Venice Biennales and the 2023 Bienal de São Paulo. For São Paulo, Paulino moved from watercolor on paper to painting on canvas, scaling her drawings up to nearly 9 feet by 20 feet. Next, she introduced the mangrove. The goddesses in these paintings have a serene air, with roots firmly anchored in the earth, but also a crown of leaves that sway with the wind.

This year, her investigation into Comigo Ninguém Pode (scientifically known as Dieffenbachia), a toxic plant also associated with spiritual protection, lend the Brazilian Pavilion its title. The pavilion’s curator Diane Lima first saw the works at Mendes Wood DM’s New York space, which had “the day and night series, in which Rosana paints and draws against a black background. I had never seen these works in person before. They convey a sense of mystery and magic; there is a certain aurality to them that truly moves us,” she said of her decision to include work form this series in Venice. “And it had that same impact in Italy. It is the exhibition’s great amulet, and it’s no coincidence that it is positioned right at the entrance.”

Approaching them as if she is still drawing at a table, Paulino lays flat her canvases, which she prepares with gesso mixture to seals the weave so they behave more like paper when she adds watercolor and acrylic on their surfaces. Her decision to work horizontally, however, also reflects a conceptual choice. “I’m not going to reproduce the watercolor brushstrokes on canvas. But at the same time, this idea of vertical painting is very Western. […] My thing is to work on a table,” she said.

Her plant goddesses have recently become more ambiguous as she has become interested in species that thrive in shade or offer it, like Comigo Ninguém Pode. And Paulino’s research into plantas de poder (plants of power), used for spiritual protection in Afro-Brazilian religious traditions, has only deepened, the relationship between her plants and the cycles of day and night becoming more expansive.

In Paris, she will show what she is calling “nocturnal” canvases featuring new goddesses—or new versions of existing ones—associated with angel’s trumpet (Brugmansia). A genus known for its exuberant flowers in a range of colors—white, salmon, purple, lilac, pink—they possess a particular luminosity that makes the petals seem, in a sense, translucent. Their alluring quality belies their extreme toxicity; at times used as a hallucinogen, their ingestion can cause severe mental confusion and even death.

Paulino is drawn to this duality: “It’s a plant with a certain weight to it—a size, a scent. But it’s one of the most dangerous plants there is. Many people have lost their lives after ingesting teas containing it.” In Angel’s trumpet (2026), a figure sits on the ground, roots dangling from her knees. Branches emerge from her eyes, bearing the plant’s trumpet-shaped flowers. In her seduction, this goddess exudes strength. An untitled 2026 work, featuring a bromeliad goddess, inhabits a different atmosphere. The seated figure twists her torso in a yoga-like pose, while leaves emerge from her mouth as if she had been chattering animatedly. Her expression is gentle, and her hair cropped short, with a texture resembling tightly coiled hair. Paulino achieved this effect using a tool she made herself: a branch with a sponge attached to its tip.

“You don’t need long, flowing hair to be a goddess,” she said. “My series ‘Senhoras das Plantas’ exists because woman is an archetype that the West cannot fully comprehend,” the artist concludes.

#6. Kohei Yamada: MY SCREEN TESTS @ Gr Gallery, New York (UPDATED with Installation Imagery)

GR gallery is pleased to present My Screen Tests, the first New York City solo exhibition by Kohei Yamada. The exhibition examines the enduring value of the authentic relationship between artist and artwork, engaging in themes of irony, introspection, and visual metaphor, which draw inspiration from contemporary practice and Yamada’s nuanced admiration for American Pop art.

Presenting a new suite of paintings on canvas -each paired with its esquisse on paper- In My Screen Tests, Yamada searches within New York City’s identity as the art capital of the world in order to infuse his work with a distinct vitality, revealing his admiration for Andy Warhol through motifs referencing the Silver Factory era and its entourage, and evoking tension between a sense of historical prestige and vibrant pop expressions. This interplay initiates a critical conversation between perceptions of art and is worthwhile in examining the creative directions of today’s world.

My Screen Tests is defined by motivations that comment on the ambiguous nature of art’s true value beyond its creator, while also alluding to Yamada’s need to remain bound to art for the rest of his life. The work also critiques the world’s normalization of deceit and capitalistic greed, alongside a persistent

longing for freedom that remains just out of reach. New York City lies at the core of Yamada’s practice, serving as both subject and catalyst for exploring the interplay between personal perception and nostalgia. It also functions as a cultural bridge between American and Japanese influences, tracing the artist’s journey from childhood through his engagement with the legacy of Andy Warhol, as well as other Japanese and American artists. Through a combination of brushwork, abstraction, and figuration, Yamada weaves a narrative rich in contemporary art history, while also confronting the true value of an artist’s existence.

Over half of the works exclusively made for My Screen Tests are imbued with references inspired by Warhol’s practice and artistic values, cast against New York City as a hub for experimentation where art meets and even challenges commerce. Repetition and humor are also at the core of the artist’s creative process, adding a wittiness and discipline to his work, while also connecting it on a deeper level to the Pop tradition. Yamada draws upon the city as both muse and stage, invoking a range of artistic influences as main characters, while ultimately revealing each to be a projection of his own identity.

The opening reception will take place on Friday, May 15 from 6:00 pm to 8:00 pm. The artist will participate in the opening reception.

#8. Dear Art World, We Can Tell When You’re Using AI

Institutions, especially well-resourced museums, foundations, and cultural organizations, have no excuse for relying on generative tools instead of paying writers.

Wall labels. Press releases. Artist statements. In today’s fast-paced art world, the written word stands at a crucial crossroads — and the stakes have never been higher. But here’s the thing: It’s not just about convenience. It’s about authenticity. Because the way we express ourselves matters.

The above paragraph was generated by Claude when prompted to write an introduction for an opinion piece against AI use in art writing, and if it made you recoil in your seat, you may be among those of us who have developed a strong aversion to generative text. You’ll know it when you see it: that uncanny cadence that’s overconfident in style yet hollow in substance, like a motivational LinkedIn post that feels relatable at first but leaves you with as much nourishment as a spoonful of Stevia.

People like me, who read, write, and edit words for a living, are perhaps more attuned to the artificial staccato and mawkish pathos of generative text. Still, its growing pervasiveness in the so-called “art world” (the sphere of museums, galleries, fairs, et al.) is undeniable. As an artist friend who recently DM’d me an obviously AI-drafted press release from a well-respected Manhattan institution put it: “Wow, they really have no shame.”

As an editor at Hyperallergic, a publication that has centered the lived experience of artists since its very inception, I am sensitive to the time- and resource-intensive nature of producing written material. The burden of self-promotion placed on artists and cultural workers has become untenable, particularly for those without a gallery or assistant to outsource such tasks to. Artists are spending precious time out of the studio drafting exhibition texts, lengthy grant applications, or social media copy for the online presence that is increasingly expected of them, often with little training and no compensation. It is no surprise that when tools emerge to optimize these duties, creative people will flock to them, not because they do not value the work of writers but because they wish to protect their own artistic labor.

Institutions, on the other hand, especially well-resourced museums, foundations, publications, and other cultural organizations, have no excuse for relying on artificial intelligence for textual materials (and underpaid, overworked museum workers must be given more time and resources to avoid the temptation of delegating original writing to AI). I would also add to that list PR representatives, marketing professionals, or anyone else whose principal responsibility is to communicate adeptly with the public and members of the press. Needless to say, journalists and other writers — who unfortunately face similar conditions of precarity as artists — have a moral responsibility to uphold the integrity of our profession by keeping AI out of the heart of the writing process: crafting original sentences whose form deepens their substance. As Wired elegantly puts it in its own AI guidelines: “We think someone who writes for a living needs to constantly be thinking about the best way to express complex ideas in their own words."

#9. Will the real Arts Council England please stand up? A new book tells an incomplete history of the funding organisation

This is a book that nobody needs, and only a few arts bureaucrats want. It is presented as a celebration of “eighty years of public investment in creativity”. The 80 years belong to Arts Council England (ACE), established in 1946 as the Arts Council of Great Britain. The book also marks the departure of Nicholas Serota as chairman after nine difficult years, and he provides an introduction.

This is not a book about the real Arts Council. You will find nothing about the crises that led to the disappearance of the Regional Arts Boards. There is no discussion of the National Lottery, neither of its beneficial effects nor of the complete disappearance of “additionality” that once separated government grant-in-aid from lottery money. There is nothing addressing the crisis in the arts since 2010, when ACE lost a third of its funding. There is nothing about the loss of local authority funding. You will learn nothing of the activities of Tory arts minister Nadine Dorries. There is nothing about ACE’s decision to abandon a ten-year strategy, “Let’s Create”, in the wake of the 2025 report by Margaret Hodge. There is no simple, clear outline of what ACE thinks it is doing. And no hint that the arts might be about upsetting ideas and people, rather than adding a pleasing texture to public life.

Instead, we are presented with 16 essays by various hands, who for the most part have reason to see ACE as a “Good Thing”. The Arts Council is indeed a “Good Thing”, since it distributes roughly £1bn a year. That does not mean that it is well run.

As Serota admits, “our sector’s health depends on money”, and the actual, dire state of funding for the arts keeps breaking through. The UK is second only to Greece at the bottom of the European league for arts funding. Carlos Acosta, the director of Birmingham Royal Ballet, writes: “If you look at the core audience of the ballet world, it’s shrinking, and there is not a replacement”. According to Bobby Seagull, the ambassador for National Numeracy, our stewardship of libraries has “faltered”. A discussion of “massively undervalued” arts centres points out that the past 20 years has been spent “removing most of the space” they had. Jacqui O’Hanlon, the director of creative learning at the Royal Shakespeare Company, asks: “How is it that in 2026 we have still not found a universal system that ensures every child, regardless of background, can encounter the arts, and can fulfil their potential?”

Two contributors are more direct. In a rare break into history, the arts consultant Amanda Parker examines the late Naseem Khan’s 1976 The Arts That Britain Ignores, a report on “minority arts” that launched the Arts Council into the issue of “diversity” that has plagued it ever since. Parker argues that Khan’s emphasis on community arts, rather than the professional creative potential of ethnic minorities, unintentionally perpetuated a “patrician, paternalistic, quasi-colonial view” that lingers today. Though representation is better than it was, between 2010 and 2020 less than 3% of funding for regularly funded (National Portfolio) organisations went to Black, Asian or minority-led groups: “funding decisions are still largely made by individuals unfamiliar with the communities they are assessing”.

The same can be said of disabled people, though Jo Verrent, the director of the disabled artists commissioning organisation Unlimited, points out that 25% of the British population has a disability of some kind: “the arts sector has systematically excluded disabled artists” and she is “exhausted”.

While Nigel Higgins, the chairman of Barclays, makes a coherent economic case of funding the arts, “leaving the poetry to others”, the essays conclude with ACE’s chief executive Darren Henley, in post since 2015, giving another account of his tours around the country. His title is “Excellence. For Everybody. Everywhere.” ACE’s new mantra. He uses the term regularly, but nowhere does he dare define what excellence is.

Sarah Crown, Martin Prendergast and Nicholas Serota (eds), Made in England: Art and Culture in Changing Times, Comma Publishing/Arts Council England, 222pp, 4 b/w illust., £12.99 (pb), published 7 July

• Robert Hewison is a cultural historian and commentator

#10. red-and-white aluminum safety barriers convert into public seating at dutch design week

the ‘stop!’ collection by studio martins mezulis and 13_0663_tsx reinterprets standard construction barriers into modular benches and stools, transforming restrictive street infrastructure into inviting spaces for public gathering.

M.Mezulis edited by christina vergopoulou October 21, 2026 2 min

A signature element of Dutch urban infrastructure, the red-and-white aluminum traffic barrier (schrikhek), serves as the primary design reference for ‘stop!’, a new collection of outdoor benches and stools by Studio Martins Mezulis and 13_0663_tsx. Typically deployed across the Netherlands to signal construction zones and redirect public traffic, these standardized aluminum structures have been reconfigured to serve a social rather than restrictive function in public spaces.

The ‘stop!’ collection by Studio Martins Mezulis and creative 13_0663_tsx reinterprets the visual language and material composition of traditional safety infrastructure into functional street furniture. Instead of diverting pedestrians and cyclists away, the modified forms invite users to pause, sit, and gather. By recontextualizing the familiar high-visibility aluminum panels into seating, the project explores how utilitarian safety elements can be adapted for community interaction. The collection makes its public debut during Dutch Design Week, with installations positioned at Strijp-S Ketelhuisplein and Design Perron in Eindhoven.

#11. Leica and Formula 1 Shift Into Gear With Limited Edition Q3 43

Leica and Formula 1 Shift Into Gear With Limited Edition Q3 43

Leica and Formula 1 have teamed up for a limited-edition version of the Leica Q3 43.

The two legacy brands from different but overlapping worlds have combined to create a sleek version of the popular Leica Q3.

The Leica Q3 43 Formula 1 edition comes with a wireless charging handgrip with a carbon fiber shell, a soft-release button with a carbon inlay and red rim, and a matching thumb rest.

Fans of Formula 1 will recognize the significance of carbon fiber. It’s a material the sport’s engineers rely upon to create the world’s fastest prototype machines.

There are more racing references on the camera: it also includes a non-slip Microvelour covering modeled on a racing steering wheel, an F1 logo on the top plate and lens cap, and a rope strap included in the set that is in keeping with the carbon fiber components and bears both brands’ logos.

Leica says it approaches a camera in much the same way a well-drilled Formula 1 team approaches a season.

“Formula 1 races take place in an environment exerting the highest technical demands. Performance does not stem from a single element, but from the precise interplay of components and team members,” Leica says.

“A Leica camera is created with a similar approach: the optics, sensor, design and mechanics are fine-tuned until there is nothing that stands between the photographer and their subject.”

Leica says it does not typically use carbon fiber in its cameras, but the material features prominently in this edition.

Carbon is used in Formula 1 because it is low weight while remaining extremely rigid. The carbon fiber parts for the Leica Q3 43 Formula 1 Edition have been manufactured and tested exclusively in Germany.

“This creates a cohesive look from the handgrip to the thumb rest and soft-release button, and the exceptionally even finish makes the craftsmanship palpable,” Leica says.

“Light falling on the surface emphasises the texture, giving it shifting visual depth with every movement. Carbon fibre is positioned at the key points where the camera is held and operated. The connection to motorsport is therefore not just visual, but can be felt with every shot.”

The camera also has red accents, again inspired by the world of F1 where steering wheel buttons are often color-coded to help the driver find them quickly. The soft-release button and one of the two function buttons on the thumb rest feature the same colour scheme.

Underneath the hood is the Leica Q3 43 that has a 43mm APO-Summicron f/2 ASPH lens, providing a field of view that closely resembles the way the human eye perceives the world.

The BSI CMOS full-frame sensor provides the option of 60, 36, or 18 megapixels. A fast hybrid autofocus system and extensive video functions complete the package.

There is also a “Formula 1” Leica look exclusively baked into the camera. It’s designed to create a rendering that complements the world of motorsport. Higher contrast and richer saturation capture the atmosphere of the racetrack and paddock in the final image.

It’s available via the Leica Fotos App and can be applied immediately while taking photos so that the effect is visible in the viewfinder, rather than only emerging during post-processing.

The Leica Q3 43 Formula 1 was officially unveiled at an exclusive event held at the Leica Store and Leica Gallery in Los Angeles. The collaboration was presented to guests by Formula 1 presenter Ariana Bravo and 2009 FIA Formula 1 Drivers’ World Champion Jenson Button.

A series of 26 motorsport photographs by Callo Albanese were also on display at the event. The Italian photographer specializes in Formula 1 and motorsport photography.

The Leica Q3 43 Formula 1 edition is available from October 21 in all Leica stores, online, and from specialist retailers. The recommended retail price is $9,950 / £7,300 / 8,500 euros.

#12. Bathing With the Nymphs

Olivia Zubko combines our favored legends with humankind’s most sacred pillars: beauty and bathrooms.

Perhaps because it appeals to universal truths, we can’t seem to shake classical mythology. Humans, then and now, are freaks, drawn to stories of trickery and violence.

Not a pleasant revelation, but it may explain why Nymphaeum, Chicago-based artist Olivia Zubko’s solo show at Western Exhibitions, is so beguiling. The show combines our favored legends with humankind’s most sacred pillars: beauty and bathrooms. In this marriage, Zubko’s work is striking, pervaded by the unsettled discomfort of intimacy.

Zubko’s wall sculptures are altars to lavatories, their devotional air echoing historical nymphaeums — monuments consecrated to water nymphs. In the Hellenistic and Roman imperial periods, they were built around natural grottoes, but today, you only need to go as far as a medicine cabinet or gym to witness rituals of allurement.

Olivia Zubko, “Echo’s Basin” (2026), glazed stoneware, glazed porcelain, metal hardware (left); Olivia Zubko, “Circe” (2026), glazed stoneware, synthetic hair

#14. An Interview with Surreal Salon 18 Winner, River Reishi

We are so excited to share our interview with Surreal Salon 18 winner, River Reishi, selected by guest juror, Swoon. On the occasion of the win, we spoke with Reishi about the work in the show, the history of Surreal Salon, and her upcoming travels.

Juxtapoz: Congrats on the big win! Talk about the winning work, what the story behind it is, the process, and even the process of submitting it to the Surreal Salon?River Reishi: The piece is called Surface Tension. It shows a figure emerging from dark water, her hands reaching forward as if she is about to break through the surface and step into our world. She is half submerged, suspended in that strange moment between two realms. Around her is an ephemeral field of black sand and amber.

From land, the surface of water looks smooth and transparent, almost empty. But of course it hides an entire world that is not ours. I have always been fascinated by that threshold. The installation tries to hold that exact moment where the two worlds meet.

The sculpture also glows faintly from within, which was a little hard to see in the bright gallery lighting but becomes visible as you approach. I like that quiet surprise. The piece looks still at first, but there is a sense that something is about to happen. Water is often a symbol of life, but it also carries danger and power. Louisiana and the Gulf region know that reality very well. I think some of that tension found its way into the work.

The black sand surrounding the sculpture is loose and hand-drawn into patterns, so the installation only exists in that form for a short time. Even small vibrations change it. I am interested in that fragility, in works that cannot quite stay fixed.

It was already an honor to be included in a show curated by Caledonia Curry (Swoon). When I arrived to install the piece and saw the other works for the first time, I remember thinking how haunting and memorable every single one was. So hearing the piece announced as Best in Show later that night felt surreal in the truest sense.

Had you followed the Surreal Salon in past years? What did you know about it? I had heard about the Surreal Salon through the pop surrealist art community for years, but this was the first time I lived close enough to attend in person. I kept hearing that it felt a little like an unofficial kickoff to Mardi Gras season, that people came in elaborate costumes and that the whole evening had this celebratory, slightly otherworldly atmosphere.

What I did not realize until participating this year was that some people actually design their costumes based on the artwork in the exhibition. That was amazing to see. At one point someone came up to me wearing a costume inspired by my piece, and getting to watch him model it and explain how the sculpture influenced the design completely made my night. It felt like the work had briefly stepped out of the gallery and into the room!

Also, it was a wonderful addition to have SWOON be the juror for this year's contest. I have done it in the past, and it was hard, fulfilling work. What did you know of SWOON's work and did that inform your submission at all? I have admired Swoon’s work for a long time, especially her installations and the way she moves between sculpture, architecture, and public intervention. I first heard about her in 2009 when she brought the Swimming Cities of Serenissima project to the Venice Biennale. A fleet of sculptural rafts floating into one of the most formalized spaces in the art world was such an unforgettable gesture.

The act of arriving that way, without waiting for institutional permission, became part of the artwork itself. That kind of boldness has always stayed with me. It is difficult to break into the art world, especially in spaces where voice is carefully selected and curated. Seeing an artist carve out space for herself so creatively was incredibly inspiring.

I also love the direction her work has been taking recently with the Sibylant Sisters project. My own work is deeply inspired by myth and storytelling, so it has been fascinating to watch her develop that world, creating her own oracle cards and building a living mythology around the work. There is something powerful about artists inventing symbolic languages that people can enter into. So having the chance to meet her and have her encounter one of my installations was a very meaningful moment for me.

You work in a few different mediums, and sculpture and installation seem to be your focus. Talk a little bit about your process and where you feel most comfortable as a maker? I am not sure I feel comfortable in any single medium, and I think that is probably a good thing. I tend to move toward whatever material feels necessary for the idea at hand. In many ways my practice grew out of practical constraints. For a long time I did not have a large studio, so I had to find ways of making work that could expand into a space temporarily and then disappear again. Sand, modular sculptural elements, and ephemeral materials all emerged from that reality.

Over time those limitations became part of the language of the work itself. I am drawn to materials that hold a sense of fragility and transformation. Installation allows me to build an environment around the sculpture where those ideas can unfold more fully, where the viewer is not just looking at an object but stepping into a moment or a story.

What sort of artists influenced you as you began to find your own voice? And, sort of as a nice anecdote, what is the last work that made you stop in your tracks and get back into the studio and create?

Voice is an interesting concept to me as a woman, because women often face particular obstacles when it comes to the emergence of voice. It takes a certain measure of audacity to say something and commit it to art. In a way you are asking the world to listen. Because of that, I am especially inspired by women who make art without asking permission.

I mentioned earlier how powerful it was for me to learn about Swoon bringing her Swimming Cities project to the Venice Biennale. That gesture has always stayed with me, not only because of the work itself but because of the confidence behind it. The willingness to claim space in a world that does not always easily offer it. Moments like that remind me that voice is not only about what you say as an artist, but about allowing yourself to say it at all. That idea continues to shape the way I approach my own work.

As for the last artwork that made me stop in my tracks, I recently visited the Museo Nacional de Antropología in Mexico City. Walking through the galleries of figurative ceramics from different regions of Mexico was completely mesmerizing. The Mayan ceramics in particular took my breath away. There is so much spirit in them, such a sense of presence. I encountered one ceramic face that affected me deeply. I have gone back to see it several times now, and each time I leave feeling more inspired to return to sculpture.

What else do you have lined up this year? Are you someone who likes to work in a gallery situation, or do you prefer alternative means to show your work? This summer I will be working with Raf Gallery in Reykjavik, Iceland during the month of August. A total solar eclipse will pass directly over Reykjavik on August 12, and later that month the city celebrates Menningarnótt, a large citywide festival of arts and culture.

Raf Gallery works with both artwork and Baltic amber jewelry, and I have always been drawn to amber as both a material and a mythological object. For the exhibition I will be installing sculpture and a sand installation that tells the myth of the birth of Baltic amber while also reflecting on eclipse mythology and the relationship between darkness and light.

The sand will come from the local shoreline, and at the end of the exhibition I invite the community to dismantle the installation with me. We carry the sand back to the ocean and return it with a wish, prayer, or intention.

I love Iceland deeply. The black sand I often use in my installations was inspired by the volcanic beach at Reynisfjara, so being able to create work there during such a rare celestial moment feels very meaningful.

As for where I like to show my work, I enjoy many different contexts. My installations have appeared in galleries, museums, empty storefronts, and even city halls. But my favorite place for ephemeral work is the beach.

When I lived near the sea in Washington State, friends and I would sometimes build temporary altars from flowers, driftwood, shells, and plants as offerings to the water. The tide would slowly carry everything away. There is something very special about building something together that only exists for that one night.

What did you like about the whole Surreal Salon experience? What were some of the highlights?The whole evening had an incredible energy. The costumes alone were extraordinary, and everywhere you looked there was another small moment of creativity unfolding. Music, conversation, artists reconnecting, people discovering work for the first time. It felt celebratory in the best way.

There was also an unexpected moment early in the night. Someone accidentally backed into the platform holding my installation, and when the platform shifted the sand vibrated and many of the detailed designs disappeared. Thankfully the person who tripped was completely fine, which was the most important thing. But in a strange way the moment also revealed something essential about the work. Some people had assumed the sand had been glued down or painted in place. When it shifted, it suddenly became clear that the entire surface was loose and hand-drawn. I sat beside the piece and carefully repaired it, re-drawing the patterns into the sand and amber while people watched.

For me that moment captured the spirit of the work. The installation only existed in that exact form on that particular night. It could be recreated, but it would never be exactly the same again. Everyone there was witnessing something temporary, something that belonged only to that moment in time. And in a way that felt very fitting for the Surreal Salon itself.River Reishi is a multidisciplinary artist whose sculptures and ephemeral sand installations explore myth, grief, and the mysterious threshold between worlds. Drawing on feminine water deities and ancient storytelling traditions, she works with materials such as sand, amber, and light to create environments that exist only briefly in time.See more at riverreishi.com and on Instagram @riverreishi.

#15. Visual Identity: Montreal Jazz Festival Concept

A bold visual identity concept for Montreal Jazz Festival pairs generative TouchDesigner trumpet forms with agile jazz typography.

Designing for an institution like the Montreal Jazz Festival means grappling with decades of visual heritage. I've always loved digging through classic festival archives. When you sift through fifty years of festival posters, the visual languages shift wildly from era to era. Yet one instinct stays unbroken: raw, expressive color. That historical continuity sparked this self-initiated project. The goal wasn't to wipe the slate clean, but to channel that historic warmth into a responsive, modular system built for contemporary stages and digital channels.

Typography carries the heartbeat of the identity. A tall, condensed display face tilts at an aggressive angle. Its elongated vertical stems mimic guitar strings pulled taut across a wooden fretboard. For dense lineup schedules and stage times, a calm grotesque keeps functional information legible. But the real spark comes from loose, hand-drawn lettering. These gestural letterforms twist across the layout like an improvised trumpet solo. They scale up, duck behind photography, and break out of the margins. Structured information and loose expressive riffs play off each other continuously.

To translate live acoustics into graphics, the system relies on node-based networks in TouchDesigner. Sound waves expand through concentric rings that echo the brass bell of a trumpet. This procedural pattern ripples across large outdoor building banners, staff credentials, transit posters, and canvas deck chairs. Because the graphic engine generates infinite variations, no two festival touchpoints ever look identical. It captures the very essence of live jazz: disciplined structure giving way to spontaneous joy.

Physical collateral brings this energetic language down to earth. Printed guides use tactile folds that tuck easily into festival pockets. Silk-screened enamel keychains turn the trumpet motif into an enduring keepsake, while woven wristbands separate zones through punchy color contrast. Everything feels unified without turning repetitive. It honors the soul of live music while giving the Montreal Jazz Festival an agile toolkit for the future.

#16. Art Basel Paris Opens Avant Première with ‘Good Energy,’ a Smattering of Sales, and One $100 M. Work

By Maximilíano Durón, Devorah Lauter October 20, 2026 5:04pm

What’s the vibe in Paris, you may be asking? While the detritus of the weekend’s protests marks many of the city’s arrondissements, the art world is proceeding with business as usual, with events and openings going on as planned Monday night and Tuesday, culminating in the opening of Art Basel Paris’s Avant Première preview at 3 p.m.

Around 10 minutes before opening, only a short line had formed to enter the Grand Palais, the architectural marvel that is home to Art Basel’s French fair. It was an indication that this year’s affair seemed a bit less busy than last year’s debut of Avant Première, the ultra-VIP event that now precedes the fair’s regular VIP opening days. That early observation proved all too true throughout the following four hours: aisles were full but navigable, and the blue-chip booths were brimming with buyers. The fair and the galleries had seemingly edited down their lists of VVIPs to only the most serious of collectors. Related Articles An Eva Gonzalès Retrospective Puts the Non-Impressionist Artist Back on the Map Ibrahim Mahama's Most Ambitious Show Yet Is Headed to Paris--But Its Core Is in Ghana

While some dealers and advisers told ARTnews that they knew of collectors who had canceled their trips to Paris amid the ongoing protests—though they declined to give specifics—any concerns that American collectors wouldn’t show up proved unfounded as well. Around the floor, ARTnews spotted Top 200 Collectors like Allison Berg, Glenn Fuhrman, Pamela Joyner, Nancy A. Nasher, Bob Clark, and Jason and Michelle Rubell, as well as Anne-Cecilie Speyer, Jessica Seinfeld, and Adam Lindemann. US museum directors and curators were also spotted, including Michael Govan (Los Angeles County Museum of Art), Massimiliano Gioni (New Museum), Ruba Katrib (MoMA PS1), Giampaolo Bianconi (Art Institute of Chicago), and Max Hollein and David Breslin (Metropolitan Museum of Art), with the Met hosting a large trustee group in Paris. Actresses Katie Holmes and Natalie Portman were also spotted in attendance.

Adviser Ana Sokoloff told ARTnews that she had been impressed by what she had seen so far and that she felt the booths were especially “curated and well thought out” this year, adding that it’s hard not to be seduced by the Grand Palais: “This place is magical.”

When asked how this year’s edition of Avant Première was, dealers resoundingly reported “good energy” all around. “We’re off to a great start—we’re at home,” Mathieu Templon of Paris-based Templon said just over an hour into the event. The gallery confirmed at least one sale: Bilal Hamdad’s L’envers du soir (2026), which sold for €65,000. Hamdad had a solo show at the Petit Palais during last year’s Art Basel Paris, and Templon described heavy demand for the artist’s work, with his upcoming March show being hotly anticipated.

Because of Avant Première’s shortened timeline, most galleries were only able to report a sale or two, far from the lengthy reports that typically accompany the close of business on the opening day of Art Basel’s other fairs and those put on by its competitor Frieze, which just hosted its hometown London fairs last week.

While much has been written about the London-versus-Paris debate, collector Will Paley, who splits his time between New York and São Paulo, described the two fairs as “complementary,” adding, “Frieze is primarily for young galleries, young artists, and young collectors with a more adventurous tone [while] Art Basel Paris has a higher price point.”

Hauser & Wirth president Marc Payot similarly told ARTnews that top-tier attendance is “the strength of this fair”; however, “the problematic side is that you get distracted by the city. People come here to see a thousand things.” The fair is just one, albeit important, part of the mix.

Thaddaeus Ropac agreed, telling ARTnews that he has found that “collectors make decisions fast in Paris” because the fair is competing for attention. While some clients had said they would be back Wednesday morning for the official VIP opening, others said they would skip it to see the bevy of museum and gallery shows on offer, or even do some shopping. Even so, that hasn’t stopped dealers like Ropac from bringing choice and pricey works to Paris, once the sole domain of Art Basel’s Swiss fair, where the “focus is on the fair.”

Among the 15 sales the gallery reported Tuesday were four Picassos (for undisclosed prices) dating from 1906 to 1938, a 1953 mixed-media Lucio Fontana for €1.8 million, and a 2019 Georg Baselitz for €800,000. “We’re doing very well—but it was expected, to be honest,” Ropac said.

Payot echoed that sales tend to happen more quickly at fairs than in the gallery, but he noted that collectors continue to take more time to close deals. “It’s definitely a slower pace than about five years ago, but great things do find great homes.” Indeed, in just the short span of Tuesday afternoon, Hauser & Wirth sold Gerhard Richter’s 1965 work Rokokotisch (Rococo Table) for a price in the region of $10 million. (The rare early work had been an unexpected addition to the booth and was not in previews.) The gallery also sold Georg Baselitz’s Der Hirte (The Shepherd) (1965) for a price in the region of $10 million, George Condo’s Woman with Designer Shirt (2026) for $2.9 million, Lucio Fontana’s 1961 work Concetto spaziale (Spatial Concept) for €1.7 million ($1.9 million), Philip Guston’s Untitled (1969) for $1.5 million, and Alexander Calder’s Four Dots and Brass Tail (ca. 1953) for just under $1 million, to name a few.

Pace Di Donna Schrader unveiled what is believed to be the most expensive artwork at the fair: a rare, striking painting of a reclining nude woman by Amedeo Modigliani, titled Nu étendu (Lolotte), from 1917, valued in excess of $100 million. The gallery said the painting has not been seen in about a century and was part of Modigliani’s 1917 exhibition at Galerie Berthe Weill, which caused a scandal for indecency and would be his only solo show in his lifetime.

Emmanuel Di Donna said the start of the fair was hugely successful, though the Modigliani would take time to place. Otherwise, “it’s been like drinking from a fire hose,” he said of overall sales activity.

Declining to provide specific prices, Gagosian said it had sold a 1987 Willem de Kooning for eight figures, as well as a Peter Doig. White Cube reported 16 sales, including two Julie Mehretu paintings (one from 2001, the other 2018) for $7.85 million each. Its booth featured historical works on paper, including a Picasso that sold for €150,000 and a Léger for €65,000.

Other sales that ARTnews learned of include a Victor Man painting for $1.3 million and two Wangechi Mutu collage works for $325,000 each, sold by Gladstone, and a Haegue Yang sculpture sold by Kurimanzutto for $110,000.

Brussels-based dealer Xavier Hufkens reported 10 sales, the priciest being a Charline von Heyl painting for $475,000. “Despite a rather turbulent weekend, we’ve felt a genuine enthusiasm for art from the very start of the fair,” Hufkens said in an email. “There’s something about Paris: its contradictions, its restless energy, its ability to surprise you at every turn. Fluctuat nec mergitur, as the city’s motto goes. It feels particularly fitting this week.”

Mike Homer, a partner at David Kordansky Gallery, said that several holds had converted into sales, confirming that there is “a desire to see works in person, in the round—it’s a nice return.” One of those sales was a rare Sam Gilliam hard-edge abstraction, Mycenaean Ode (1965), for $300,000.

This year, the fair had 12 shared booths representing 24 galleries, more than any previous edition. One standout example is the one shared between Layr (Vienna) and Kraupa-Tuskany Zeidler (Berlin, Munich) on the fair’s second floor, where both galleries said they had sold several works. “We sold a lot of things that we were very keen on placing in very prominent collections, so we’re very happy,” said Amadeo Kraupa-Tuskany, who specified that the collections were located in Europe. Emanuel Layr added that the gallery had placed works with American collectors as well.

The booth featured historic and contemporary pairings from both their programs. There was Franz West’s Passstück (1983/1984), a sculpture meant to be used like a strange crutch that would modify how a person moves about. Alongside it was Anna Uddenberg’s 2026 sculpture White Noise (Soft Skills), featuring a life-size, faceless mannequin whose body is contorted by a futuristic interpretation of ergonomic office-style furniture contraptions.

“Something that really matters to us is staying excited ourselves, but also exciting other people, and asking new questions,” said Layr. “Now you have to be super open about how you operate—how you present yourself, and how you join forces.”

Art adviser Nicolas Nahab, cofounder of NG Partners, agreed that galleries are increasingly finding creative ways to collaborate in light of a continued “period of adjustment” in the art market, particularly related to skepticism over pricing for ultra-contemporary artworks.

“Collectors today don’t trust prices like they used to, and don’t take them at face value,” said Nahab. “This lack of trust makes them doubt and interrogate information given to them. They need reassurance, research, and a global understanding of an artist’s practice and market before making a decision, which is why the decision-making is so slow.”

“If trust is there,” he added, “then the decision is easy for collectors.”

Blackmagic Design's DaVinci Resolve Studio is a powerful node-based video and image editing app available for Windows, Mac and iPad. The software is made by the Australian company Blackmagic Design, which whose main line of business is making high-end cinema cameras for the film industry. On the Fusion Page, there are around 70 new motion graphic effects and tools via the Krokodove integration. DaVinci Resolve 21.1 added an MCP (Model Context Protocol) server for AI assistant integration.

The software's node-based colour grading and effects workflows present a bit of a learning curve compared to more basic video editing apps, but the beauty of DaVinci is that you can go as deep as you want. Just note that colour grading and effects work in DaVinci Resolve can be demanding in terms of computing power. Blackmagic cites 16GB RAM and 4GB of VRAM as minimum requirements, but you might want significantly more than that if you're editing long videos or using advanced tools.

#18. Glen-Gery clads Princeton University health centre in bricks made with reclaimed materials

Burgundy-coloured bricks incorporating reclaimed manufacturing waste wrap Princeton University’s Frist Health Centre in Princeton, New Jersey, as shown in this video carousel produced by Dezeen.

Called Ponderosa Western, the bricks are part of North American manufacturer Glen-Gery‘s Western Series and incorporate materials recovered from its own manufacturing process.

The extruded bricks, which were laid in a horizontal running bond pattern, feature sharp, precise edges and a surface texture that combines velour, grooved and sanded finishes.

The facade was designed to complement the century-old Gothic brickwork of the university’s historic Eno Hall, which was constructed in 1924.

The new building features metal sunshades to help reduce solar heat gain, alongside mineral wool insulation behind the brickwork to support the centre’s energy performance.

Courtyards, green roofs and diverse plant life surround the building, creating a landscape designed to provide a calming environment for students and faculty.

Exposed mass timber and visual connections to the outdoors continue throughout the interior of the building.

The project has been recognised by AIA New York State for its use of biophilic design and adaptive reuse.

Frist Health Centre at Princeton University is a 76,500-square-foot facility dedicated to holistic health and student wellbeing. It opened on the university’s campus in 2025.

Glen-Gery is a brick manufacturer that specialises in creating custom facades for cultural, residential and educational institutions across North America.

This process means that the artists themselves were unsure of what the pieces would look like until they were completely finished.

“The thickness of the shingle coat varies depending on the complexity of the shingled area,” Wegwerth and Dehn said. “As a result, the final silhouettes and tonal values only emerge gradually during the process.”

#19. An expert’s guide to Frida Kahlo: five must-read books on the Mexican Surrealist

Frida Kahlo, Untitled (Self-portrait with thorn necklace and hummingbird) (1940) Nickolas Muray Collection of Mexican Art

• Click here for more reading lists on the world's greatest artists

Frida Kahlo (1907-54) is arguably the most recognisable artist in the world. The Mexican painter’s reputation grew following her death but over the past few decades her image has exploded in the popular consciousness, from being portrayed on the silver screen and referenced in The Simpsons, to having her image spray-painted on walls around the world and plastered on merchandise. This elevation to global fame is explored in the exhibition Frida: The Making of an Icon at Tate Modern (until 3 January 2027). Here, Beatriz García-Velasco, the exhibition’s assistant curator, picks out five key books for learning all about Kahlo’s life and career.

“A good place to start is with Hayden Herrera’s biography. Translated into more than 25 languages, it introduced Kahlo to vast global audiences and inadvertently catalysed the ‘Fridamania’ phenomenon. The book is a meticulously researched, incisive art-historical study that nevertheless reads like a page-turner. Drawing largely on first-hand interviews with those who knew Kahlo intimately, Herrera examines the artist’s work through her lived experience, with particular focus on Kahlo’s accident, lifelong disability and suffering.”

“Gannit Ankori’s writing brings a much-needed, fresh perspective. Questioning the essentialist readings that often rely on autobiographical myth or pseudo-psychoanalytical assumptions, Ankori argues that Kahlo was a trailblazer, who deliberately constructed her own identity and was ahead of her time in breaking taboos by openly portraying the female body, gender, cross-dressing, hybridity, identity and disability—themes that continue to resonate strongly with audiences today.”

“Functioning essentially as a catalogue raisonné, this monumental publication brings together exquisitely reproduced images, documentation and commentaries on every known painting by Kahlo. It’s a book you can lose hours in, turning its lush pages to inspect the detail and texture of her work.”

“For those wanting to get even closer to Kahlo, this accessible facsimile reproduces the notebook she kept over the final decade of her life, which remained hidden until her private rooms were unlocked in 2005. Turning these pages immerses you in her brilliant, and at times tormented, mind.”

“Written in Spanish, this is a personal and vital intervention by the Mexican curator and philosopher, Helena Chávez Mac Gregor. The title takes its cue from André Breton’s famous 1938 characterisation of Kahlo’s work as ‘a ribbon around a bomb’, a phrase Mac Gregor brilliantly upends by arguing that there was perhaps never any ribbon at all: only bombs, and they continue to detonate across time.”

Tate show provides a decent selection of the artist’s work but somewhat unravels in its attempt to fully assess her star status

The exhibition will explore the late Mexican artist’s impact on women artists across Mexico, the Americas and Europe

A new show will explore the Mexican artist's complex personality and her rise to fame over the past 50 years

The book traces the Mexican artist’s extraordinary life and the commercial afterlife of her persona
