#20. hedley studios shrinks the porsche 550 spyder into a handcrafted electric two-seater

limited to 250 examples, the miniature racer revives a 1950s motorsport icon with vintage curves and a 50 mph top speed.

There’s a tiny silver Porsche parked among a sunlit meadow in the English countryside. With its rounded rear fenders and tiny windshield, it’s quite similar to the 550 Spyder that Porsche raced in the 1950s. The proportions are familiar, but something is slightly off. This is the Porsche 550 J, a miniature, fully electric version of the historic race car, recreated by British manufacturer Hedley Studios at roughly 80 percent of its original size.

Developed in collaboration with Porsche to celebrate 75 years of the company’s motorsport history, the 550 J is an officially licensed, handcrafted vehicle limited to 250 examples. The ‘J’ stands for ‘Junior,’ although the little roadster is large enough to accommodate two people. Measuring just 2.9 meters (9.5 feet) in length and 1.2 meters (3.9 feet) wide, it retains the low profile and flowing aluminum-like contours of its predecessor.

The original Porsche 550 Spyder holds a special place in the company’s history. Developed specifically for motorsport, the lightweight, mid-engined racer made its name competing against considerably more powerful cars. At the grueling 1954 Carrera Panamericana in Mexico, Porsche drivers Hans Herrmann and Jaroslav Juhan finished third and fourth overall after five days of racing. The two Spyders also won their class, which helped to establish the ‘Carrera’ name that Porsche continues to use today.

For the miniature recreation, the team at Hedley Studios was granted access to Porsche’s corporate archives, allowing the team to study the historic vehicle and reproduce its distinctive form. The round headlights and sculpted wheel arches are immediately recognizable, while the rear bodywork retains the original’s characteristic twin ventilation grilles. Inside, a cream-colored steering wheel sits ahead of a compact dashboard with circular gauges. The open cockpit is wonderfully spare, with just enough contemporary technology to accommodate the electric drivetrain.

Beneath its 1950s-inspired bodywork, the Porsche 550 J is powered by a 48-volt electric system, producing approximately 8 kW, or 11 horsepower, in its standard configuration. An optional RS Package doubles that output to 16 kW, or around 21 horsepower. The little racer can reach a top speed of approximately 80 km/h (50 mph), a surprisingly brisk pace for something with such compact proportions. The 550 J is intended as a collector’s vehicle, with public-road driving off limits.

Each example is built by hand at Hedley Studios in Bicester, England, with a selection of finishes drawing from Porsche’s racing history. Alongside the classic silver bodywork, customers can choose bright heritage-inspired colors and racing liveries, including the vivid blue example pictured with white competition numbers. A bespoke program offers further customization.

With just 250 units planned, the 550 J miniaturizes one of Porsche’s most iconic racing silhouettes, while retaining enough power to be driven and enjoyed.

#21. Vivo’s Mid-Range V80 Smartphone Has Impressive Zeiss-Engineered Cameras

Vivo’s Mid-Range V80 Smartphone Has Impressive Zeiss-Engineered Cameras

Vivo has announced the V80, a new mid-range smartphone with a camera system co-engineered by Zeiss.

Compared to Vivo’s recently announced X Fold6 and X500 Series smartphones, the V80 has a decidedly less advanced camera system. This is little surprise, given that the phone costs about 580 euros, or about $650, rather than the 720 euros ($810) of the base X500. The even better X500 Pro Max is about 910 euros ($1,020).

That said, the V80 still has reasonably impressive main and telephoto cameras. The 50-megapixel main camera has a Type 1/1.56 image sensor and a 23mm f/1.9 lens. The 50-megapixel telephoto camera is also solid on paper. It uses a Type 1/1.95 chip and a 73mm-equivalent periscope telephoto lens.

The V80 really fails to measure up with its ultrawide camera. This camera is only 8 megapixels, and although Vivo doesn’t specify the sensor size, it’s likely very small. It has a 115-degree field of view.

Zeiss Center-Stage Portrait mode replicates the bokeh of classic Zeiss lenses, including a 100mm equivalent mode with Planar-style bokeh and a soft, low-saturation tone, and an 85mm mode with Sonnar-style bokeh.

While these cameras match the V70 released earlier this year, the V80 embraces an all-new design. Vivo has unified its mid-range model into a single, one-piece design.

“Vivo V80 features a refined design that prioritizes comfort, durability, and visual simplicity. It uses Flagship One-Piece Cold-Carved Glass, in which the back and camera area are shaped from a unified piece of glass,” Vivo says.

“This creates a seamless transition around the Floating Camera Module, with a smooth surface that feels natural in the hand. Cold carving also makes the glass significantly stronger than traditional hot-bent glass, and its form helps protect the lens assembly during a fall,” the company continues.

The V80 also marks the industry debut of a laser holographic lithography finish with the Starwish Purple colorway. The company spent two years testing over 20 custom materials to etch more than 3,600 4K-resolution images onto the back cover using nano-scale lithography. The result is a “True 3D Stellar Design” with what Vivo describes as real spatial depth. While it’s impossible to show in photos, the finish changes color and texture with every movement, and it looks like a star-filled galaxy.

The Vivo V80 has a 6.59-inch AMOLED display with a 5,000-nit peak brightness (locally). Its full-screen max brightness is 1,800 nits.

As mentioned, the Vivo V80 is about 580 euros, or around $650. It’s avaliable in some global markets now.

#22. Sunset Park, Where You Can Still Get an Artist Studio for Under $600

At the Brooklyn neighborhood's Open Studios festival, artists showed off the works they make in converted factories, warehouses, and three-story walk-ups

Lizzy Plapinger had barely settled into her studio in a sunny corner of Industry City before visitors spilled into the space on Sunday, October 18, to see a handful of her brightly contrasting geometric paintings laid against her walls for Sunset Park Open Studios.

“I just moved in two months ago from Bushwick, and I’m still getting to know the area, but it feels very welcoming,” Plapinger told Hyperallergic. “I like that it’s close to other artists and designers, which makes it feel ripe for collaboration.”

When New York artists needed a place to work after being priced out of their communities over the past decade, Sunset Park became one of their last refuges for affordable studio space. Known as an industrial manufacturing hub and enclave for Mexican and Chinese immigrants, the southwest Brooklyn neighborhood has drawn enough artists and creative workers to its converted factories, warehouses, and three-story walk-ups to sustain a three-day arts festival featuring more than 300 spaces.

#24. William N. Copley "X-Rated (1972–1974)" @ Galerie Max Hetzler, Berlin

Galerie Max Hetzler, Berlin, is pleased to announce X-Rated (1972–1974), a solo exhibition of paintings and works on paper by William N. Copley. This is the fourth presentation of the artist’s work at the gallery, and the show will be on view through April 22, 2026.

Copley came to painting from an unusual position. He had ambitions to become a writer before becoming a painter, and, for a brief period in the late 1940s, he co-founded and operated a gallery in Beverly Hills that focused on the Surrealists. The Copley Galleries – which he ran with his brother-in-law, the artist John Ployardt – brought him into close contact with exiled Surrealists such as Man Ray, Max Ernst and Marcel Duchamp, as well as the dealer Alexander Iolas, who encouraged him to pursue his nascent art practice. Adopting the signature CPLY around the time the gallery closed, he debuted his first exhibition at a bookstore in Los Angeles in 1951, shortly before he moved to France.Even though he was a generation younger than the Surrealists, Copley’s work is deeply informed by the movement on a conceptual and personal level. While his bold black outlines and self-taught figurative style recall comics and Pop art, Copley approached painting with a literary sensibility, using narrative strategies that both embodied Surrealist principles and drove the structural evolution of his compositions. Like many Surrealists, Copley embraced humour, psychology and eroticism as fundamental to his creative process, yet his engagement with overtly sexual subjects went far beyond the playful eroticism of his peers.On view in the exhibition are works from Copley’s prolific ‘X-Rated’ series, created between 1972 and 1975, and first exhibited in 1974 in an eponymous show at the New York Cultural Center. This body of work draws on erotic imagery and ritualised motifs from adult magazines, seeking, in the artist’s own words, to ‘break through the barrier of pornography into the area of joy.’ 1In a decade when the sale of hardcore pornography was still illegal in the United States, Copley would buy ‘adult magazines’ under the counter, using them as a source for inventive figurative and narrative paintings that explored eroticism, sexual politics and the pursuit of pleasure. The artist was able to convey a wide range of tone in the ‘X-Rated’ paintings: some, such as The Seven Year Itch, 1973, are tender; others, including  Viridiana, 1973, are exuberant; and almost all of them are openly humorous. Underscoring the open-endedness of sexual expression, Copley stated: ‘That’s what makes sex so much fun: since nobody really understands it, the possibilities for originality are endless.’ 2Copley typically produced two stages of preparatory drawings before starting a painting: an initial, small-scale study, followed by a larger version in which he refined the composition, introduced changes, and heightened the work’s pictorial dynamism. The resulting paintings maintain a deliberately slapdash style, with figures treated loosely rather than meticulously rendered. The exhibition makes this developmental process visible through multiple pairings of preparatory drawings and completed paintings, including Calcutta, 1973, and its counterpart Untitled, 1973.Scenes of copulations and orgies are set against vivid, brightly coloured backgrounds animated by bold, geometric patterns, making them almost ‘too artful to be libidinous, let alone lascivious’, as critic James R. Mellow has remarked. 3 It is both this treatment of the backgrounds and the contorted, entwined bodies with their attenuated limbs and schematic outlines that has prompted critics to draw a link between Copley and Henri Matisse more than once. Yet, while depictions of the nude and sexual imagery throughout art history have traditionally relied on suggestion and idealisation, Copley presents the sexual act directly, leaving nothing to the imagination.With titles borrowed from Hollywood movies such as Les Quatre Cent Coups, The Exorcist or Tobacco Road, Copley tempered the shock of the pornographic image through comic playfulness and pop cultural sensibility. Manifesting a Surrealist disjunction, the movies rarely align explicitly with the images’ content, but the titles nevertheless set in motion a cascade of associations for the viewer. The title of the series, likewise, draws on terminology from the film industry: until the 1990s, the film-classification term ‘X-rated’ was used in the US for films only suitable for adults. Despite the cautionary notices that some visitors might find the subject matter offensive, the 1974 exhibition at the Cultural Center – curated by the newly appointed and strikingly progressive director Mario Amaya – received a notably positive critical response. Art in America writer Peter Schjeldahl hailed the presentation as a ‘uniformly gorgeous exhibition,’ noting that it marked ‘a highly satisfying development in Copley’s work’. 4The ‘X-Rated’ series represents a singular chapter in Copley’s oeuvre, deliberately set apart from the prevailing currents of the early-1970s art scene. Even in today’s uncensored and image-saturated world, Copley’s suggestive canvases retain a subversive charge. By merging art and eroticism, Copley challenged conservative norms and rejected the notion of artistic neutrality, clearing away moralistic constraints in favour of directness and humour.

#25. Cricut StickerPix Print + Cut review: a playful, professional printer with a hidden cost

The Cricut StickerPix Print + Cut is easy to set up, quick to use and delivers lovely results, from stickers to photo prints to cards. It’s small, light and simple to store, and Design Space makes it easy for beginners to get creative. The locked-in materials and ongoing ink costs keep it from being perfect, but if you’ve got a phone full of photos begging to be printed, it’s a joy.

Why you can trust Creative Bloq Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

Most of us have thousands of photos sitting on our phones that never see the light of day, and if you think that's an exaggeration, my dad never goes anywhere without his cameraphone 'just in case'. The Cricut StickerPix Print + Cut aims to fix that: a handy photo printer that delivers crisp, colour-accurate prints in under a minute (or two), and after putting it through its paces, I’m pleased to say it does so with real style.

It’s a brand-new kind of machine for Cricut, better known for its cutters, like the Maker 5 (for more, read our best Cricut machines guide). Until now, making stickers meant pairing a Cricut cutting machine with a separate inkjet printer, then burnishing laminate sheets by hand. The StickerPix rolls printing, laminating and precision cutting into one compact box, and that’s its biggest selling point.

There are two models, and it’s worth knowing the difference before you spend any money. The StickerPix Print ($169.99 / £159.99 with its Essential Bundle) prints and laminates onto 4 x 6 in pre-cut sticker sheets. This beginner model uses only pre-made templates, so you're limited to what Cricut offers. The Print + Cut ($299.99 / £249.99 with its Essential Bundle) takes 4 x 7 in (about 10 x 18cm) sheets and cuts around your own designs, so you can use any shape you like and create your own stickers and designs.

Bundles also vary, so it's worth shopping around, but as a rule, Cricut's official StickerPix Print + Cut bundles are a good choice, as they include Cut Ink Cartridges, Sticker Sheets, and Photo Paper. The Print cartridge is rated for 54 prints, and the Print + Cut for 36. Both also handle 4 x 6 in photo paper, so you can switch between photos and stickers on the same machine. If circles and squares will do, the Print option saves you £90. If you want custom shapes and to create more personal stickers and photo prints, go with Print + Cut, which I tested.

Unboxing and setup are painless. Inside you’ll find the machine, two plug adaptors, an ink cartridge, 18 sheets of photo paper and 18 sheets of sticker paper, all neatly packed. The StickerPix + Cut measures 8 x 11.3 x 4.1 inches, and the loading tray is roughly the same size (see my photos for a laptop-sized comparison). It’s light, and the tray slots into the top when you’re done, so it tucks away easily on a shelf. The StickerPix + Cut comes in a swish dark blueish grey (the StickerPix machine is a softer two-tone shade of blue and light blue, almost the reverse of the Joy 2).

The instruction manual is genuinely helpful, with a clear diagram of the components and simple steps for fitting the cartridge and tray. Software setup is just as easy: head to Cricut for instructions, choose your machine and follow the prompts. The first time you pick stickers or photos, a short tutorial shows you how to remove the tray and load the paper. When you connect for the first time, the firmware updates automatically, and once it says registration is complete, you’re ready to go.

Everything runs through Cricut’s Design Space software, which connects to the machine over Bluetooth. It’s easy to find your way around, and the home screen gives you three ways in: start a new project, pick a category (stickers, labels, photo prints, or cards and invitations), or begin from a template. That last option is a highlight: thousands of pre-designed templates are available, and you can upload your own images and text or start from a blank canvas.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

The AI tools are the fun part, particularly if, like me, you're not an artist (I'm a sewer and quilter) but want to create fun family gifts. Cricut says Design Space has a library of more than 1.8 million sticker images, and the stylised options are cute. You can choose a look, such as spray paint, oil painting, comic book, or crayon drawing, upload a photo, and tell the AI what to add. I uploaded my niece's photo, asked it to create her as a witch for Halloween, and it did. I asked for an additional cat, and it added the animal and produced a selection of sticker-ready images to choose from. Keep in mind that the full library and Cricut AI require a paid Cricut Access subscription, though the bundle includes a trial voucher.

The StickerPix + Cut uses dye-sublimation, laying down each colour in turn and applying a protective laminate in the same pass. Cricut quotes 300dpi, and the finished prints resist water, scratches and fading. My stickers came out bright and crisp, on paper with a pleasant weight.

Photo prints are the real surprise for me. I printed off some photos from my phone and was surprised how accurate the colours are, how sharp the detail is, and how they look like they came from a proper photo lab. A print takes just one to two minutes, with no fiddling or adjustments; just load the paper shiny side up, click the tray into place, press connect and go.

The same ease carries over to the machine’s other jobs, and I had great fun creating things in an afternoon. Labels print on sticker paper, and plenty of ready-made designs make personalising your Christmas gifts a breeze; for example, I made a set of present tags to stick on the family gifts. Cards and invitations are just as quick and handy if you run a small business and want branded thank-you cards. I now have a nice insert to package with every quilt I make for customers on Cotswolds Creations, with a photo of their quilt and a bespoke message from me

The cutter really shines on stickers. It kiss-cuts custom shapes around your design and leaves the backing intact, so you simply peel each sticker off the sheet. That also means it can’t cut through the backing, and there’s no white ink either, as the printing is dye-sub with a clear protective layer.

If you already own a Cricut, you might wonder whether you need this. The StickerPix + Cut does in one go what normally takes a cutter, an inkjet printer and hand-applied laminate, and it takes up far less desk space. But it isn’t a replacement for a cutting machine. It only cuts its own sticker sheets, so if you want to work with vinyl, cardstock or fabric, you’ll still need a Maker or an Explore. It's worth noting the cost, as StickerPix + Cut is $100 / £100 more than the latest Explore 5, and the Maker 5 is only $50 / £50 more, and both do more.

The difference? The StickerPix + Cut creates professional photo prints and stickers without needing anything extra (so technically you'd need to add the cost of a good inkjet printer to your Maker 5 setup). It's also faster, easier, and less hassle, with results that are as good as, if not better than, the others.

Likewise, if you just want quick prints of your phone photos, a simple dedicated photo printer will do. The StickerPix + Cut earns its price if you also want laminated stickers, labels, and cards, plus Design Space’s templates and editing tools to make them. It suits crafters, journalers, parents, and anyone selling at markets who wants quality, professional, branded labels and cards without a bulk order or going through the hassle of finding and ordering supplies.

The main catch is that the StickerPix + Cut is fussy about what you feed it. It only works with Cricut’s own paper, and the cartridge and sheets are model-specific, so you can’t mix and match between the Print and the Print + Cut, which, in its own quirk, makes the more expensive model a better option, as it'll cost less in the long run if you want to upgrade.

I’d love to see Cricut add foil or metallic sheets, which would give crafters a lot more to play with, and although the stickers are water-resistant, they aren’t dishwasher-safe, so don’t push your luck with your favourite mug.

The locked-in materials are the real catch. The starter bundle gives you only 18 sheets each of sticker and photo paper, which won’t last long. Refill cartridges then cost between £24.99 and £47.99, and how many stickers you get from one depends on how well you pack each sheet. Work out your cost per print before you commit.

But with all that said, it's a common setup for modern printers. Ultimately, I didn't really know what to expect from StickerPix + Cut as it's a little outside my sewing and quilting workflow, but after spending time with it, I've already found uses for its cards and sticker designs to accompany my finished products and help market my brand. I've also made far too many fun stickers for my nieces and had a great time creating, and that's really all you need to know.

Julie Dean is a former doctor and occupational therapist by profession, which inspired her to start sewing and quilting as a therapeutic activity. She is passionate about her craft and has been quilting and using Cricut for over five years. As well as selling her own designs and products on Etsy, Julie has taken commissions for interior design agencies to create bespoke quilts, including Beata Heuman. Julie's work has appeared in Architectural Digest.

#27. How EVERLAND Reimagined Urban Kind Branding

EVERLAND built Urban Kind branding on a single device: the shield. Saturated color, script product names, and raw amber-glass packaging.

Skincare is a crowded shelf, and most of it whispers. EVERLAND went the other way for Urban Kind, the vegan brand founded by Peter TernstrÃ¶m: one loud, unmistakable shape repeated until you can spot it across the store. The shield is the whole idea, a universal icon the studio chose to visualise protection, and every product in the range wears a different one, cut in a different saturated color. Hot pink, acid green, signal red, tangerine. The color is the navigation. You learn the routine, preparing skin for a new day through settling in for the night, by following the shields across the shelf.

Three type voices share the work, each with a fixed job. The wordmark is a blunt blue grotesk, URBAN KIND set straight and loud, carrying headlines and the oversized vertical type that runs down the kraft cartons. Under it, a handwritten script gives every product an emotional name: Urban glow, Balance rest, Urban Defense, Instant Shield, Detox facial. Then the clinical register: mono caps listing ingredients like a formula sheet, NIACINAMIDE BARRIER SERUM, niapur plus prebiotics plus seven antioxidants. Blunt, intimate, clinical. The tension between the three is what makes the system feel designed rather than decorated.

The materials are deliberately honest so the color can shout. Amber glass droppers, aluminium tubes, uncoated kraft cartons with exposed grain, the kind of raw substrates that read as transparency in the hand. The saturated shield palette does the shelf standout and stretches unchanged across social, web, and out-of-home. And through everything runs the ritual line, Recover - Refresh - Resume, stamped on packs, posters, and cartons until it reads as the brand's signature.

See more from EVERLAND on the studio's website.

The same case page carries Urban Kind's sister brand, Raw Perfection, from the same founder: vegan skincare drawn from Nordic nature, an LL Circular logotype, intentionally imperfect illustrations, and circular stamp-of-approval text patterns on glass and aluminium packs in FSC-certified recycled paper. Two brands, one founder, and the same belief that raw materials carry the message.

#28. STG Design unveils upcoming “unconventional, sinuous” Houston skyscraper

Texas architecture studio STG Design has released renderings of O27, an office skyscraper covered with triangular panels that is planned for Houston’s River Oaks area.

The 32-storey building will contain flexible office floors, as well as luxury amenities and a rooftop terrace on top of its nine-storey base.

It will have a parking garage block at its podium and a tower that rises in an undulating form.

The design is the result of an “intensive computational design process” by STG Design that sought to prioritise “highly efficient, repeatable floorplates” within the building’s curved geometry.

Renders show two, curving glass facades folded around either side of the building. They are divided at the middle, where a spine of terraces travel up its length.

“Its unconventional, sinuous form resists the rigid verticality that has come to dominate contemporary office buildings, resulting in a structure that feels fluid, expressive and perpetually in motion,” said the team.

Its facade will be made up of triangular glass panels to create a “shimmering skin” that will appear to shift in the changing light of the day.

Other elements include an entrance drive covered in a sculpted ceiling embedded with lights to “evoke a night sky” and a double-height, glass-clad lobby, both designed by international design practice Design ALT + TAB.

Interior renderings show spaces covered in a metallic bronze, with black-and-white marble surfaces and curved seating.

According to developers Broadview Capital, the project was informed by the admiration its founders, brothers Anish and Ashay Bavishi, have for Houston’s Williams Tower, designed by architects Philip Johnson and John Burgee.

The skyscraper symbolises “ambition, possibility and global sophistication” for Houston, said the team, an element the designers and developers hope to bring to the city’s “prestigious” River Oaks area, known for its historic estates and luxury shopping.

“O27 serves as both a geographic marker and a tribute to a neighbourhood whose century-long legacy has been defined by thoughtful planning, architectural distinction and enduring relevance,” said the team.

The building is expected to be completed in 2028.

STG Design is based in Austin, Texas and was founded in 1976.

Other projects recently announced for Houston include a coffee plant set to be converted into a music school by OMA and a performance space created by Theaster Gates and Studio Zewde.

#29. Giant mirrored globe will rise on Miami Beach during art week

Digital rendering of Christopher Joshua Benton’s A Lore Supreme on Faena Beach Courtesy the artist and Faena Art

A monumental, mirrored orb will land on Miami Beach this December. The 28ft-tall, 44ft-wide sculpture, A Lore Supreme, will serve as a public space for gathering and celebration during the 2026 edition of Art Basel Miami Beach. In the middle of Miami Art Week, the group Major Lazer will headline an exclusive concert at the sculpture, sited at Faena Beach.

This is the first major installation in the US for the Abu Dhabi-based artist Christopher Joshua Benton, whose work unites research into dance and public space. Faena Art organised the presentation and the piece will be installed on the sand behind Miami Beach’s Faena Hotel. It will be free and open to the public, along with another Faena-commissioned work by Marinella Senatore (both 1 December-6 December).

A Lore Supreme will consist of 7,000 mirrored facets evoking a spinning disco ball emblazoned with a reimagined map of the world. Benton’s “globe” privileges the countries—throughout Africa, the Caribbean and Latin America in particular—that have contributed to Miami’s vibrant culture.

Embedded speakers will play fragments of conversations and music that the artist compiled during his extensive research into Miami’s music scene. Benton has focused on these diasporas’ influences on forms that range from disco and dancehall to dembow, descarga, salsa, house and techno.

Throughout his practice, Benton explores how immigrant populations create forms that preserve elements of their homelands. His ongoing projects include the creation of a Black dance archive with scientists from the Immersion Lab at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and the re-imagination of overcrowded, low-income housing in the United Arab Emirates. As part of the 2024 Public Art Abu Dhabi Biennial, the artist created an enormous public park featuring an astroturf ground designed to look like a massive carpet. As a creative director, Benton illuminated the façade of Dubai’s Burj Khalifa, the tallest building in the world.

Public programming under the umbrella of “Island Funk House” will variously transform A Lore Supreme into a space for wellness activities and sound documentary. At sunset, the sculpture will become site for events including live performances. Participating acts will include Jacob Lusk, Richie Hell, DJ Le Spam, DJ Pressure Point and PaperWate.

“Miami... feels like a dance floor, a shared space where different cultures and communities come together, each bringing their own rhythm while moving alongside one another,” Benton said in a statement. His preparatory research led him into a pirate radio station, a Cuban folklore dance class, and a community choir. He even learned to play güiro, a percussion instrument with pre-Columbian origins and the body of a hollowed out gourd, while eating a Cuban sandwich in Little Havana.

Chase Sapphire Reserve is supporting the programme, and on Wednesday 2 December cardmembers will have access to a sunset cocktail, seated dinner and afterparty at A Lore Supreme featuring Major Lazer.

Senatore is similarly promoting togetherness in her own Faena Art commission, An Expanded Baroque Crown, a light installation at the Faena Cathedral. The Italian artist takes inspiration from celebratory traditions in her home country. Her “crown” of light will host readings, poetry, dance, music and other moments for gathering. The local poetry organisation O, Miami will collaborate on the affiliated programming. The project is in line with Senatore’s large-scale, participatory works, which she has realised at the High Line in New York, Palazzo Strozzi in Florence and other major venues around the world.

“Participation is... a way of thinking,” Senatore said in a statement. “I’m interested in creating spaces where people can gather, take agency and feel the work belongs to them.” She hopes that her new piece will create a social plaza that will be activated by a diverse group of visitors.

Both projects are emblematic of Faena’s larger ethos. “At Faena, we believe in the power of art to transform, bring people together and enrich the life of a city with free and open to the public programming,” Alan Faena said in a statement.

The hotelier and real estate developer established Faena Art in 2011. In recent years, timed to ABMB, he and his team have commissioned public projects including a library on a rotating platform by Es Devlin, a major presentation of items from Marina Abramović’s archive and an enormous labyrinth by Sebastian Errazuriz.

“Each year, the Faena District becomes a canvas for artists to dream and create at an extraordinary scale, bringing art out into the open and into the life of our community,” Faena added. “We open our doors to the world, bringing together artists, ideas and people from across the globe in a celebration of culture.”

#30. jean-baptiste fastrez turns an inflatable boat and a wall fixing into mirrors to look and to be looked at

'I like the paradox of an object that has such a strong physical presence, yet whose image is almost entirely made up of whatever surrounds it,' says the french designer, who has spent more than a decade of his practice reworking the mirror through different forms and materials.

sofia lekka angelopoulou October 20, 2026 9 min

‘The mirror is, after all, a utopia, since it is a placeless place,’ said Michel Foucault in a 1967 lecture, explaining that in a mirror you see yourself where you are not, ‘in an unreal, virtual space that opens up behind the surface.’ He then called it a heterotopia as well, since the mirror does exist in reality, where it ‘exerts a sort of counteraction’ on the position you occupy. No other object in a house behaves this way, since everything else in a room is looked at while a mirror hands the room back with its viewer inside it. That duality, between what the object looks like and what it does to whoever stands in front of it, has given the mirror an unusual position in design. Creatives have worked on both halves of it, the form and the surface, which is why the object keeps producing experiments in both how it looks and how we see.

In Jean-Baptiste Fastrez’s case, the mirror is ‘one of the objects that offers the greatest freedom to explore ideas somewhere between design and sculpture.’ The French designer, who has spent more than a decade of his practice reworking this one object through different forms and materials, tells designboom that he likes the paradox ‘of an object that has such a strong physical presence, yet whose image is almost entirely made up of whatever surrounds it.’ Two of his recent designs for Paris-based design company Moustache push that paradox in two very different directions.

Both pieces Fastrez developed for Moustache begin from something that already exists. The Zodiac mirror borrows its form from the inflatable boat it is named after, so that what looks like an inflated tube is in fact high-gloss ceramic. Sphera, on the other hand, takes its cues from the hardware once used to hold mirrored walls together, reworking it into a set of oversized chrome spheres that clamp sheets of flat mirror to a wall.

‘With Zodiac, I was interested in the idea of the ready-made, or rather the fake ready-made,’ he says. ‘I wanted to create objects that looked as though they had been made by repurposing something else.’ The image was precise from the start, an inflatable boat whose inflated tube becomes a sort of floating frame, and the story he wanted was of a boat that had somehow ended up hanging on a wall and turned into a mirror. ‘I really enjoy these collisions between completely different types of objects,’ he says. ‘They can create narratives that are both strong and open-ended, with something almost mysterious about them.’

The idea for Sphera arrived in a particular room. ‘I remember very clearly that the idea came to me while visiting Carlo Mollino’s house in Turin,’ Fastrez says. ‘Some of the walls in his preserved apartment are covered with mirrors made up of several sections, held together by small chrome fittings. I found this fascinating, before realising that the system was actually nothing particularly unusual.’ The fitting was not a Mollino invention and was never rare, and he is precise about where it lived, ‘quite common throughout the twentieth century, in sophisticated architectural interiors as well as much more ordinary settings, like a bathroom or a student bedroom.’

What he saw in it was a frame with no shape of its own. ‘I started to see it as perhaps the most minimal frame imaginable, but also one of the most universal,’ he says. ‘It allows an enormous variety of formats, compositions and uses.’ His decision was then not to redesign the principle but to change its volume. ‘I wanted to take this principle almost exactly as it was, but give these little fixing elements a much stronger presence. I increased their size and transformed their geometry into something spherical, almost sculptural.’

What makes a mirror worth more than a decade of a designer’s attention is how little it asks. ‘A mirror is an object whose function is reduced to its absolute minimum,’ Fastrez says. ‘As long as something has a reflective surface, it can essentially be considered a mirror.’ Hung on a wall it carries nobody’s weight and resists nothing, so it never faces the structural tests a chair or a table has to pass, and what remains is a single geometric demand, which is that it stay more or less flat.

He treats that as a paradox rather than a gift, one severe constraint in a single direction and almost total freedom in every other, and says constraints are what he finds stimulating in the first place. By his own account it is probably the object that leaves him the most room to work somewhere between design and sculpture, and the one most willing to carry a story.

Both of these pieces then do something that reverses what a mirror usually is, which is to use the glass as structure rather than as surface. Zodiac’s ceramic frame is half a ring, built from two moulded sections, and where the ceramic stops the reflection continues, so what the eye reads as two inflated tubes floating one above the other is a single tube and its image. ‘The reflection becomes an essential part of the object’s construction,’ Fastrez says, and in doing that work the mirror very nearly disappears. Sphera relies on the glass just as literally, since without the rigidity of a sheet of mirror the fixing system has nothing to hold and nothing to hold it. ‘With Sphera, the object is visually made of nothing but chrome and reflections,’ he says. ‘Its appearance depends entirely on its surroundings, which are reflected faithfully in the flat mirror and distorted across the chrome spheres.’

‘I’m very interested in the idea of taking something as ordinary as a piece of hardware and reworking it until it becomes the strongest aesthetic feature of a project,’ Fastrez says. Both pieces end as arguments about ornament, and he makes the argument himself rather than leaving it to be inferred. ‘Ornament is something I actively pursue in my work as a designer, but I find it particularly interesting when it isn’t simply added to an object, but becomes part of its construction or the way it functions,’ he explains, and he describes that as possibly the most interesting form design can take, an object acquiring a sculptural character directly out of the logic that produced it. Sphera, by his account, began at the moment he realized that emphasising the small functional elements would generate ornament without costing the original system any of its functionalism.

The second half of the argument is about the word function itself. ‘I also think our definition of an object’s function is often far too restrictive,’ he notes. ‘An object never serves just one purpose. A mirror’s primary function might seem to be reflecting an image, but to me that’s a very incomplete definition. A mirror also serves to decorate an interior, to give it character, to place a space within a particular period, style or narrative.’ He then goes further than most designers would be willing to, and says that this ornamental function can be as important as the reflective one and is sometimes more so.

That produces a reversal of the sentence design students have been handed since Louis Sullivan wrote it in 1896, and of the century of suspicion toward ornament that followed. ‘If we accept ornament as a function in its own right,’ Fastrez says, ‘Zodiac and Sphera are, in their own way, functionalist objects whose form also follows their ornamental function.’ Zodiac arrives there through the relationship between a frame and its reflection, Sphera through the repetition of a fitting that spent fifty years being hidden, and in both cases the decoration is not sitting on the object but holding it up.

#32. V&A Museum Staff Set to Strike Across All Four London Sites

Allegations of “Amazon-style” working conditions and calls for pay raises prompted unionized workers to authorize yet another strike at the UK museum network.

As negotiations continue at the Victoria & Albert Museum (V&A), unionized staff have publicized their intent to strike across all four London sites on October 29 and 30, citing continued disputes regarding pay and working conditions. The escalation comes after two strike actions at specific locations at the beginning and end of September.

Born from accusations of “Amazon-style” working conditions at the newly opened V&A East Storehouse — namely the alleged lack of sufficient breaks for hydration and restroom use — staff organized under Prospect Union’s heritage division and the Public and Commercial Services Union (PCS) voted overwhelmingly in favor of strike action this summer.

“Prospect members are dedicated to their jobs, and it is these dedicated staff who make the museum the world-class attraction it is,” said Prospect Union's general secretary, Mike Clancy, in a press statement. Clancy also accused V&A Director Tristram Hunt of refusing to participate in negotiations with the unions, “show[ing] the level of disdain in which he holds his staff.”

Both unions are also seeking minimum pay increases of 4% across the board, as well as an additional bump to bring the minimum hourly wage for the lowest-paid staff to £14.80 (~$20), which would make the V&A a Real London Living Wage accredited employer.

#33. Pearla Revela Edits RAW Photos and Videos With a Single Set of Tools

Pearla Revela Edits RAW Photos and Videos With a Single Set of Tools

Swiss developer Pearla Mostra, formerly known as House of Mars, has launched Pearla Revela, its new post-production workspace designed for Mac, iPad, and iPhone. The RAW processor includes cataloging, non-destructive node-graph editing, search tools, compositing, export tools, and more.

Pearla Reveal has been in the works for two years and, as the developer says, is an entirely original application, built from the ground up. It is “not an AI clone of an existing editor,” Pearla Mostra is quick to point out. It aims to separate itself from existing editors by emphasizing preservation to the nth degree.

Pearla Mostra founder Guy Cassidy says the app took two years to make, largely because the company built it natively without copying other work.

“Every established editor splits a job across a catalog, a photo editor and a video application. Revela treats the source, the edit and every finished version as one structure. If it already exists, we don’t build it,” Cassidy says.

“The source stays whole, the edit stays readable, and every finished version stays tied to the decisions behind it,” Pearla Mostra explains.

What this ultimately means is that one single source file can be edited and adjusted, with every change fully visible as a node on a canvas, and then delivered in many different formats.

“A print, a social post, a video trim or an alternate grade branches from the same source, each with its own crop, format and color space, so the finish is part of the edit rather than a separate export after it,” Pearla Mostra explains.

“A graph preset saves that whole structure, adjustments, masks, outputs, formats, trims and color spaces, and applies it to one asset or a whole collection. Collection export then produces the primary output or every output across hundreds of files in one operation,” the company continues.

Users can edit photos and videos on the same graph, using the same nodes and tools for both stills and motion pictures. Like DaVinci Resolve 21, which added photo editing with its node-based editor, Pearla Mostra wants creators, especially hybrid ones, to use the same workflow for every format and deliverable.

Tools like healing, frequency separation, curves, color wheels, and masks work the same on videos as they do on photos. Frequency separation runs in video with automatic tracking, by the way. Retouching can happen in the project’s wider color space or a specific, narrower deliverable color space, too.

Pearla Revela also includes the company’s robust film simulation technologies, including precise grain and halation tools. Grain is modeled at negative and print stages and is exposure-aware.

A Revela catalog includes the assets, grades, outputs, metadata, notes, references, selects, tags, and ratings in a single place, and these can be synced across devices using a repository on existing cloud storage platforms, like iCloud Drive. PearlaRAW files shot in the company’s camera app, Verana, are fully supported, of course, and can be synced as well.

Each Pearla app, including Revela, is built on the company’s Pearla Wide Gamut color space engine, which has been engineered around human vision. The post-processor converts RAW stills and RAW video from sensor-level data into this color space and supports log video from 800 cameras across 19 manufacturers. It also supports SDR and HDR processing pipelines. A full list of supported cameras and RAW files is available here.

Pearla Revela is a very different type of photo and video editing app, so it may have a bit of a learning curve. Pearla Mostra is fully aware of this and has started creating detailed tutorials.

Pearla Revela for macOS is available now. It requires an Apple Silicon-powered Mac running macOS 26.1 or later. A perpetual license is $349. There’s also an annual subscription, which includes access to all versions of Revela, for $89.99 per year. Either license runs on two Macs. A seven-day free trial is also available.

Pearla Revela for iPad and iPhone is coming later this year. Revela Lite is already part of Pearla Verana for iPhone. Pearla Cloud, built to support collaborative workflows, is also coming later this year.

#35. Final Fantasy Resonance (Switch 2) review: modern-retro at its finest

A proper, meaty turn-based JRPG that brilliantly welds the charming ethos of early Final Fantasy games to modern (yet retro-referencing) visuals and production values.

Why you can trust Creative Bloq Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

Format: Switch 2 (reviewed), Switch, PS5, Xbox Series X/S, PC

Square Enix has been on a mission for some time now to breathe new life into its much-revered back catalogue of seminal Japanese RPGs (JRPGs), most notably with its epic three-part modern reimagining of Final Fantasy VII, and its development of what it calls HD-2D graphics technology, applied so far to various Dragon Quest games, as well as the Octopath Traveler franchise.

Over the decades (the first instalment was released as far back as 1987), Final Fantasy has become a labyrinthine franchise with fifteen main iterations and a head-spinning number of spin-offs. In that context, Final Fantasy Resonance looks like an anomaly; nominally, it is based on Final Fantasy Brave Exvius, a retro-style 2015 instalment that, unprecedentedly, was released for iOS and Android.

But as soon as I started playing Resonance, it felt like more than another mere cul-de-sac among Final Fantasy’s ever-expanding streets. Much of its significance comes from being the first time Square Enix has applied its HD-2D technology (underpinned by Unreal Engine 5) to Final Fantasy, opening up all manner of possibilities for revisiting a mouth-watering back catalogue.

By now, at least for fans of retro-JRPGs, the visual language HD-2D brings should be pretty familiar: characters in HD-2D games remain 2D and pixelated, but now traverse 3D backgrounds, invariably rendered in bold, lush colour palettes. That basic blueprint applies to Final Fantasy Resonance, but the game also goes noticeably further than existing HD-2D games visually.

For example, it plays much more with perspectives. While there are still plenty of moments when the overall view tends toward the isometric, at other times (such as when wandering around the game’s many towns), the camera moves toward the ground and uses visual effects like depth of field. Plus, there are plenty of cutscenes, some of which use conventional 2D characters on 3D backgrounds, while others (such as special attacks in battle) enter full-blown anime-style visual territory, often mixing 2D and 3D rendering cleverly.

The overall effect always has a retro edge, yet it still feels strikingly modern: I'd say it marks a moment when Square Enix has pushed HD-2D beyond what I’ve seen before, which bodes very well for the future.

Final Fantasy Resonance Producer Keisuke Nakashima explicitly says that one of Resonance’s raisons d'être was to preserve “The charm of the classic Final Fantasy titles from I through VI” while creating “An experience that modern players can enjoy comfortably.” Roughly translated, that means it has a determinedly turn-based battle system, but also plenty of save points (where I could heal my characters in tents), and I could fast-travel around the map and, in the latter stages, even navigate the game world by airship.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

Resonance is positively stuffed with classic Final Fantasy tropes, with airships, Chocobos, Moogles, and crystals featuring heavily. Story-wise, it starts a tad slowly (I found the early dialogue somewhat stilted) but gradually unfurls into something suitably convoluted, with a welter of twists and sideways turns, and even, at one point, a magical excursion into one character's psyche.

The two main protagonists, Rain and Laswell, start as the top Royal knights of the kingdom of Grandshelt; sent to investigate a disturbance at the shrine of the Earth Crystal, which apparently guards Grandshelt, they encounter a mysterious, super-powerful armoured being (one of a group of baddies known as the Sworn Six), who overpowers them with ease and destroys the crystal. Luckily, a young yet powerful girl called Fina magically appears to save them from death, and the trio embark on a quest to save the remaining crystals, dotted around the game world’s other kingdoms, from destruction by the Sworn Six.

A growing cast of characters with varied skills soon joins them, from which four can be selected as a battle party. Resonance may be turn-based, but it’s up against titles like Metaphor: Refantazio and Clair Obscur: Expedition 33, which aim to prove that turn-based battle systems are no less effective than real-time ones.

Resonance’s battle system prioritises staggering enemies: once I reduced them to a dazed state by identifying and exploiting their elemental weaknesses, I could pile on the damage. Staggering all enemies, or the last remaining one, triggers a Sweeping Stagger, which in turn accelerates characters’ ability to launch devastating Limit Bursts and so-called Resonance attacks.

The game's battle system includes a clever device called Visions, which prove handy in combat and make the game’s Final Fantasy nostalgia even more explicit. Visions are ghostly versions of Final Fantasy protagonists, including Cloud Strife, Noctis, the Onion Knight from Dissidia, Cecil from IV, Bartz from V, and Terra from VI. In all, there are 26 of them to find.

Visions are liberated from crystals in caves, and I could equip each of my battle-characters with one, adding the Vision’s abilities and spells to the character’s own. I was rewarded for swapping Visions around, giving my battle-characters improved attributes, perks, and abilities I could equip permanently. Essentially, they let me upgrade characters to my liking. They also let me trigger Resonances, powerful Limit Burst-style attacks with different effects and elemental affinities.

Fina could also summon Espers, elemental creatures (one of which brought defensive perks) that stick around for three turns; they proved particularly handy in boss battles. Towards the end of Resonance, a sequence of consecutive boss-battles tested my intimate knowledge of the battle system, and its impressive tactical versatility, to the limit. The battle system has a lot of moving parts, but it isn’t as complex as it sounds, and it's very satisfying once mastered.

On the surface, Final Fantasy Resonance seems like an exercise in nostalgia, but it's much more than that. Sure, it evokes the feel of those early Final Fantasy games, but its turn-based battle system feels sophisticated, and its production values easily hold their own in the modern gaming landscape.

It feels like a proper, full-blown Final Fantasy game, reinforced by the fact that it takes over 50 hours to complete. Sure, its attempt to create a sort of everyman Final Fantasy story begins slowly, but it redeems itself in the end. It creates a good impression as a harbinger of HD-2D versions of the original Final Fantasy games, but more than that, it stands up very impressively on its own. Let’s hope it's successful enough to spawn a sequel, and thereby a whole new strand of Final Fantasy games.

#36. Inside COLLINS’s Branding for Crane Stationery

Explore the Crane branding by COLLINS, pairing 250 years of American cotton papermaking with engraved crests and cloth-bound keepsake boxes.

Paper has real weight here. Stephen Crane founded his Massachusetts paper mill in 1770, selling sheets to Paul Revere for the American colonies' very first paper currency before becoming the official banknote supplier to the U.S. Treasury in 1801. Two and a half centuries later, even with digital messages dominating daily communication, demand for heavyweight cotton correspondence hasn't vanished. Still, European luxury houses like Smythson and Montblanc were steadily eating into Crane's retail shelf space. Crane brought in COLLINS to sharpen its prestige and rethink how physical paper lives in a modern home, framing the entire effort around etiquette in society, business, politics, and personal correspondence.

The type does the heavy lifting right away. COLLINS drew a high-contrast serif wordmark anchored by a fluid, ribbon-like ligature that loops the arch of the lowercase r directly into the bowl of the a. It feels classic without looking dusty. Set flush along the bottom edge of the boxes in InDesign, the logotype gives the upper two-thirds of every surface room to breathe. Across the inner sleeves and National Stationery Show invitations, billowing botanical scrollwork refined in Illustrator rises in thick, sculptural relief, looping directly through the letterforms in acid chartreuse, pale lilac, and slate blue.

Most stationery boxes end up hidden in a desk drawer. COLLINS wanted these out on the coffee table. They kept the signature Crane blue â dialing up its cobalt saturation across woven bookcloth, and paired it with unexpected combinations of violet and burnt orange, slate and forest green, plus saffron and crimson folders. Inside the trays, ecru cotton note sheets feature playful blue utility stamps with an analog clock face to log the exact date, time, and city of a handwritten note, while blind-debossed envelopes open to reveal metallic silver and lavender linings.

#37. Forbo Flooring spotlights creative possibilities of custom flooring

From digitally printed floral and graphic patterns to photographic images and precision-cut inlays, flooring brand Forbo Flooring Systems offers custom design possibilities to make flooring an “integral part of the identity and story of a space”.

Across Forbo’s Flotex, Vinyl, Entrance Flooring and Marmoleum collections, the brand offers customisation techniques that incorporate graphics, branding and messaging upon a floor.

Each technique creates custom floor designs that introduce graphic messaging in hospitality interiors, direct visitors to a certain space, or help support orientation in education or healthcare settings.

Forbo’s flooring can also be used in a museum setting, distinguishing one exhibition from another, or used to reinforce a brand identity in a retail or workplace environment.

“The result is a floor that does more than provide a surface,” said the brand.

“It can contribute to the character of an interior, communicate identity, support zoning and wayfinding, and connect different spaces through a coherent design language.”

The brand’s Flotex flooring has a densely flocked design, allowing detailed patterns, graphics and imagery to be reproduced at high resolution. In comparison, its vinyl collection is digitally printed, making it possible to translate more detailed bespoke patterns, graphics and imagery onto the material.

Across its Marmoleum collections, Forbo uses a specific Aquajet technology that uses high-pressure water to precisely cut material, which can then be combined to form detailed designs.

This enables Forbo to adapt flooring to specific colours and patterns to create individual graphics, imagery, logos or wayfinding.

“The technique makes it possible to translate a wide variety of ideas into the material, from geometric patterns and decorative elements to lettering, logos and intricate artwork,” said Forbo of its Aquajet technology.

“Designers can develop their own concept and work with colours from the Marmoleum palette to create an individual composition.”

Forbo also offers Coral Entrance Flooring, allowing a building’s entrance to connect visually with its identity while helping prevent dirt and moisture from entering.

“Digital printing creates extensive graphic possibilities for Flotex and vinyl,” said Forbo of its process. “Aquajet technology enables precise compositions in Marmoleum, while custom techniques for Coral bring individual design into the entrance area.”

Rather than presenting its collections as separate products, Forbo explained that projects often involve different flooring collections as part of one portfolio.

For example, a project might begin with a customised entrance, continue with an individual floor design and use colour, graphics or patterns to define different zones and destinations.

According to Forbo Flooring, the diversity of its collections allows designers the opportunity to choose the flooring material and technique that best suit both their creative vision and the functional requirements of the space.

“The flooring can therefore contribute to aesthetics, identity, orientation and the overall experience of a space, while different products continue to respond to the functional requirements of each area,” it added.

Forbo Flooring explained that customisation can start at different levels. For example, designers can build on an existing Forbo design, adapting its colours, or develop something entirely new.

“Depending on the flooring type, an original graphic, photograph, pattern, illustration, logo or other visual concept can be translated into the floor,” said the brand.

As a result, this flexibility allows flooring to respond more closely to the architecture, identity and purpose of a space.

To learn more about Forbo’s custom flooring, visit its website.

#39. Found objects and fall-outs: a new book reveals new sides to Donald Judd and his work

Donald Judd’s To Susan Buckwalter (1964) art: © 2026 Judd Foundation / ARS, New York; Photo: Alex Marks © 2026 Judd Foundation

The US artist Donald Judd (1928-94) remains one of the most celebrated and studied figures of post-war American art—and one of its most difficult to pin down. In a new book, The Sculpture of Donald Judd, the art and architectural historian Neil Levine offers a fresh reading of the Minimalist artist’s work, tracing its development from painting to three-dimensional objects in the first chronological analysis of the artist’s practice. A friend of Judd’s from roughly 1965 to 1975, when the two had a falling out, Levine draws from decades of following the artist’s practice, as well as anecdotes from their friendship.

The Art Newspaper: A lot has been written about Judd—and by Judd. Why did you decide to write this book?

Neil Levine: I’ve had a long-standing belief that theory and art practice are very different. What artists write is writing, and what artists make is art, but the two do not necessarily correlate. A lot of Judd’s writings are about other people’s work. They give clues to what Judd was thinking about his own art, but these writings are not directly about his work. I love the language he used, but writings, like his often-quoted [essay] Specific Objects are totally opaque. If we keep using Judd’s writing to discuss his work, does it illuminate anything about the objects? I feel there are other meanings to discover.

Did you come across any discoveries while writing the book?

I had not been as aware of the importance of the found object on Don’s work. I always knew of the famous black painting with a baking tin inset that is in the Museum of Modern Art [in New York], but I never put it together how significant found objects were to Judd’s early work. I think there’s a clue to some of the meaning: that in its relationship to real objects, Judd’s work stands as a form of concrete art rather than abstract art. In its concreteness, it’s critical of the abstractness of modern life.

Judd's Untitled (1961) is in the collection of the Museum of Modern Art in New York art: © 2026 Judd Foundation / ARS, New York; Photo: MoMA, New York. Gift of Barbara Rose

Did having a personal relationship with Judd affect the way you approached writing about him?

Yes and no. Before even meeting Judd, I had a challenging relationship with writing about him. I wrote for Artnews after college and was assigned to review a group exhibition at Green Gallery that included Judd. This was the spring of 1965, and there was a sculpture called To Susan Buckwalter, of projecting volumes hanging from the wall, that just knocked me over. It scared me, it was strange. I’d never seen anything like it. I was so nervous that I was unable to review the show. That piece is on the cover of my book now.

Being friends with Judd didn’t mean getting to know him in the way you might think. One of the reasons I was keen to take the trip to France in 1975 was to get into his head. In the evenings, we’d sit outside and I’d ask him questions, but the answers were never very forthcoming. My comments struck a nerve, and this trip, as I share in the book, was the last time Judd and I spoke. There’s a reason he’s known as having been taciturn.

• Neil Levine, The Sculpture of Donald Judd, Yale University Press, 180pp, $40/£30 (hb)

#40. pieni III: kenko’s ultra-tiny camera captures lo-fi photos without a screen

with its miniature film-camera styling and unpredictable framing, kenko's latest release makes taking pictures a little more spontaneous.

Japanese photography brand Kenko Tokina has released the Pieni III, a tiny digital camera that weighs just 18 grams and hangs around the neck like a pendant. Measuring 53 millimeters (2 inches) wide, the working camera is small enough to fit between two fingers, with a familiar silver top and circular lens that recall the proportions of an old film camera. It arrives in four colors, including pastel pink Strawberry and pale blue Soda, alongside Milk and Black.

The Pieni III also has a curious omission. There is no screen or viewfinder, and thus leaves photographers to point the lens toward a subject and press the shutter without seeing exactly what they’re capturing. The images remain a mystery until they’re transferred to another device. A subject might drift toward the edge of the frame, or an unexpected detail could make its way into the shot. Part of the fun is eventually discovering what the little camera has actually seen.

Kenko keeps the controls simple, with just two buttons handling power, shutter release, and the switch between photography and video. A small indicator light on the back glows red for still images and blue for video. The camera also captures footage with sound, at a resolution of 720 × 480 pixels and 30 frames per second. Despite its miniature dimensions, the Pieni III functions as a standalone digital camera.

Its photographs have a peculiar character of their own. Inside is a tiny 1/10-inch CMOS sensor with just 0.32 megapixels of effective resolution. Still images are saved as 1440 × 960-pixel JPEGs through digital interpolation, so the files contain far less detail than their dimensions might suggest.

In Kenko’s sample photographs, flowers become fuzzy patches of vivid color while foliage softens into something approaching watercolor. The coarse edges and unpredictable exposure give the images the familiar appearance of early digital photography, with their imperfections coming directly from the camera’s hardware.

The camera’s small body holds another useful detail: a built-in magnet on its back. This allows the Pieni III to attach to compatible metal surfaces, including a refrigerator or a railing, for hands-free recording. A neck strap is included for carrying it around, making the miniature camera easy to keep within reach whenever something catches your eye.

Photographs and videos are stored on a removable microSDHC card, supporting capacities between 4GB and 32GB. The card is sold separately. For this third-generation model, Kenko has introduced USB-C connectivity, allowing files to be transferred directly to compatible smartphones with the included cable. The same connection handles charging, so the entire process remains fairly straightforward once the photographs are ready to be viewed.

#41. Jenny Holzer on Paris Protests: ‘It’s Gruesome That Kids Have to Fight for a Better Education’

Executive Editor, ARTnews & Art in America

In an interview conducted earlier this month, after the first large-scale demonstrations in Paris, Jenny Holzer addressed the protests that have continued to roil the city in the weeks since. “It’s gruesome that kids have to fight for a better education or for teachers to be paid properly, for their schools to be clean,” the artist told T: The New York Times Style Magazine. “I worry about the kids’ safety.”

The occasion for the interview was Holzer’s solo show at Musée d’Orsay, which includes an LED panel work that bears a message penned by the French writer Émile Zola in 1860: “I think of the future and see it so dark, so dark that I shrink back terrified.”

A different part of the show features scrolling text projected on the museum’s exterior, including quotations from 30 cultural figures such as Charles Baudelaire, Vincent van Gogh, and Auguste Rodin, and other parts include paintings and sculptures bearing inscriptions, such as a marble bench with a message from artist Mary Cassatt: “As you say the world is mad just now.”

About the quotations she worked with, which came from the archive of the Musée d’Orsay, Holzer told T: “The shock was how contemporary the issues are. And a warm surprise was how companionable the writing is. Sometimes they’re talking about being devastated; other times they’re making bad jokes, pontificating, being vulnerable. It’s like, ‘Oh, hi there. Thank you for passing the time with me.’”

#42. DxO ViewPoint 6 Fixes Photographers’ Geometry Problems

DxO ViewPoint 6 Fixes Photographers’ Geometry Problems

DxO has announced ViewPoint 6, the latest version of its perspective correction software. The French software company calls ViewPoint 6 its “most precise version yet,” thanks to new AI masking technology.

“DxO Viewpoint 6 puts every element of the scene under precise geometric control, with local corrections guided by AI masks,” DxO explains.

For photographers, this means they can precisely reshape individual aspects of a scene. For example, users can correct the perspective or geometric distortion of one building independently of another.

This builds upon the ReShape Fusion tool introduced in ViewPoint 5 two years ago, although new AI masking promises to make the tool significantly more powerful and useful. Instead of manually creating masks to use ReShape Fusion, the software can now build them automatically through subject analysis. ReShape Fusion can also automatically correct distortion, although users can, of course, take manual control.

“Photographers have long accepted a trade-off when correcting perspective: straighten the geometry and you can lose part of the frame,” says DxO’s VP of Product Strategy, Jean-Marc Alexia. “With AI masks in ReShape Fusion, photographers can define the element they want to work on, refine the mesh where greater precision is needed, and control how the correction transitions into the surrounding image. They are rearranging the components of the scene while preserving the framing they chose.”

DxO offers numerous examples of when geometry problems can rear their ugly head in a photo. A building that leans because of its position relative to the photographer is common, or a building that looks wrong because the photographer had to tilt the camera up to capture it all. DxO also mentions a person in a group shot looking distorted because they are closer to the edge of the frame.

ReShape Fusion promises to fix these issues without affecting the rest of the frame, which means no more needing to crop a shot after performing perspective corrections. With traditional corrective measures, the entire image gets stretched and manipulated, which introduces blank space to maintain the same overall aspect ratio and pixel size.

“That cost has always been the trade-off. Conventional perspective tools work on the whole image: straightening converging verticals tilts the entire picture plane, the rectangle becomes a trapezoid, and recovering a rectangle means cropping. The stronger the correction, the more image area goes with it,” DxO explains.

However, ViewPoint does not create pixels from scratch. It does not generate pixels to fill in the edges. The software provides pixel-level control through a sophisticated mesh on the original image.

DxO says ViewPoint 6 corrects the three common, recurring geometry problems in photography. These issues, more prominent with a wide-angle lens, include converging vertical lines from a tilted camera, subjects near the edge of the frame being deformed by volume distortion, and straight lines bowing due to barrel distortion. There are also other tools, though, including horizon correction and a Miniature Effect.

DxO ViewPoint 6 works directly on RAW files, although it also supports JPEG and TIFF images. RAW files are opened using DxO’s own camera and lens profiles. The app also includes exposure and white balance corrections, but DxO’s other software is needed for robust RAW photo editing, like PhotoLab 10, which includes ViewPoint 6’s geometry tools in the Geometry palette.

ViewPoint 6 is especially useful for users who don’t use DxO’s other photo editing applications. ViewPoint 6 can be used as a standalone application or as a plugin for Adobe Lightroom Classic and Adobe Photoshop.

DxO ViewPoint 6 is available now for $129.99 (€119.99 / £109.99) for new users or $84.99 (€74.99 / £69.99) for ViewPoint 5 owners as a discounted upgrade. A 30-day free trial is also available.

#43. The MIT Professors Bedazzling Security Cameras to Highlight Campus Surveillance

The intervention is responding to the university’s recent $3 million investment in more than 500 new AI-integrated campus surveillance cameras.

Tenured faculty members at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) are decorating the university's surveillance cameras with googly eyes, rhinestones, and glitzy decorations to protest its investment in what they call "Big Brother technology."

Faculty members Catherine D'Ignazio, Marah Gubar, Tanalís Padilla, Dwai Banerjee, and Karrie Karahalios began decorating the cameras in August, four months after the student newspaper, The Tech, reported that MIT would be spending over $3 million on more than 500 surveillance cameras from 2025 to 2026. According to the report, the cameras can be activated to identify faces and objects with AI, and are stationed in exterior locations and academic facilities, among other high-traffic areas around campus.

"We have these little buckets of gems and tinsel, and create these little Gumby-type creatures with googly eyes," D'Ignazio told Hyperallergic in a phone interview. None of the adornments interfere with the camera function, but are intended to remind passersby that they are under surveillance.

In a faculty newsletter announcing the deliberately unwieldy project name, "The Initiative to Beautify the AI-capable Surveillance Benevolently Installed by our Administrator Overseers and the MIT Corporation In Collaboration with Big Brother Tech Companies," the faculty members said that the campus had been transformed into an "AI-capable Panopticon."

"Many of us would not feel safer with cameras on all around us, especially not ones with AI," Gubar told Hyperallergic over the phone. While the university established a faculty advisory committee to determine whether the cameras should utilize AI technology, many eligible members were barred from participating, as first reported by local outlet Cambridge Day.

"They knew where we were coming from and what our viewpoint on the committee would be," D'Ignazio added. "Our viewpoint isn't just a matter of opinion. It's grounded in scholarly expertise. I've worked on how data, surveillance, and technology particularly affects women and marginalized groups."

An MIT spokesperson told Hyperallergic that the new cameras are "intended to close gaps in MIT’s existing security camera coverage."

Faculty took inspiration from artist and MIT alumnus Jill Magid, who rhinestoned CCTV cameras at Amsterdam's police headquarters in 2002.

"I wanted to question the visible and invisible parts of surveillance," Magid told Hyperallergic. After Amsterdam police initially turned down the artist's request to bedazzle the cameras, Magid created her own temporary fictitious company, System Azure Security Ornamentation, and successfully got herself a paid job. She advertised her business on silk screen posters that read "Big Brother in Drag," and when the larger police system shut down her enterprise, she distributed flyers urging, "Bring Back the Glam."

Faculty printed out several of Magid's posters and distributed them to students, faculty, and staff, many of whom have joined in on the seven decoration sessions so far.

While MIT Police usually only intervene by removing the decorations after the sessions, Gubar allegedly had to give her name to a suspicious officer on one occasion.

"I wasn't going to let a student or staff member give their name," said Gubar, who clarified that her tenured status protects her from severe administrative pushback.

The professor has noticed that most other participants, especially students, are hesitant to speak out about the surveillance cameras or disclose their names for fear of retaliation, an anxiety confirmed by other universities' tactics and actions. During the 2023-4 academic year, Columbia University's surveillance cameras helped administrators identify and punish pro-Palestine student protesters. In May 2026, a pro-Palestine student filed a federal lawsuit against the University of Michigan for surveilling and harassing him over his advocacy.

"The goal should be for all of us to be able to protest against surveillance, whether that be students or staff," Gubar added. "It shouldn't just be a privilege for tenured faculty."

#44. Rippling water informs wildlife pavilion by Desai Chia Architecture

Intersecting circles make up the Chatham Pond Pavilion, which was designed by US studio Desai Chia Architecture to be a wildlife-viewing station on a private property in Upstate New York.

Located in the rural town of Chatham, the pavilion sits within an 80-acre (32-hectare) property belonging to a couple with grown children.

New York City-based Desai Chia Architecture has designed other structures for the site, including a main house, guest dwelling, livestock barn and large greenhouse.

A meandering path leads to the pavilion, which is perched on the edge of a spring-fed pond formerly used for agricultural purposes.

“Once used as a livestock watering hole, it has now been remediated and restored as a natural wetland haven for wildlife, birds, fish and pollinators,” said Desai Chia Architecture.

In addition to wetland creatures, the area is populated with bears, foxes, deer, raccoons and possums.

To minimise disruption to the habitat, the architects conceived a viewing structure lifted above the ground.

The 380-square-foot (35-square-metre) pavilion is shaped like the number eight in plan and is composed of two platforms of differing heights.

The higher platform extends over the water, allowing visitors to “observe natural wetland habitats at the pond, as well as activity in the forest beyond”.

The structure is topped with a sculptural canopy made of three intersecting, hollowed-out cylinders.

“The intersecting forms were inspired by overlapping concentric ripples of water created when raindrops fall on the pond’s surface,” the team said.

One of the cylinders has a solid roof with a solar-powered ceiling fan, with a PV array atop the roof.

The pavilion is constructed of galvanised steel columns and curved steel beams, which were fitted together on-site. The canopy is clad in standing-seam panels made of 98 per cent recycled aluminium.

“The exterior of each cylinder is finished in a luminous satin grey, reflecting the surrounding forest and sky, while the interior is coated in a copper finish that casts a warm glow within,” the team said.

The pavilion sits on the southwest corner of the pond, enabling it to be shaded in the afternoon and to capture dramatic views at dusk.

“As the sun sets, the light rakes across the pond from the west and lights up the forest canopy to the east, giving the pavilion an ideal sight line to the glowing row of trees and through the illuminated understorey,” the team said.

Other projects by Desai Chia Architecture include a New York home with crisp silhouettes and cedar cladding, and a Connecticut residence with courtyards for exhibiting artwork.
