#45. Chris “Daze” Ellis "Orchid Rain on the Underground" @ PPOW Gallery, NYC

PPOW are pleased to present Orchid Rain on the Underground, Chris “Daze” Ellis’s third solo exhibition with the gallery. The show is on view through April 25, 2026. Featuring a new series of paintings, multimedia installation, and a site-specific mural, the exhibition harnesses the passion and spontaneity of the graffiti movement of the 1970s and 80s while demonstrating a thoughtful and meticulous practice honed over the past five decades. While the version of New York City that fostered Daze’s beginnings as a fine artist may feel like a bygone era, the works in this exhibition are evidence of its enduring legacy. By revitalizing that foundational energy for the present moment, Daze affirms the continued relevance of those figures and places, and their profound influence on the creative spirit that persists throughout the city today.

Born in Brooklyn in 1962, Daze became inspired by early graffiti writers like Blade, Lee Quiñones, and PHASE 2 while attending High School of Art and Design in the mid 1970s. As he began to establish his own name as an artist, he was also a frequent visitor to what would become historic landmarks of the city’s nightlife, including the Lit Lounge in the East Village, Danceteria on West 21st Street, and the Mudd Club in Tribeca. These nightclubs, which often doubled as art galleries and performance venues, functioned as generative sites of social and artistic experimentation and part of the driving force behind Daze’s early works. By the early 1980s, he had begun transitioning from tagging subway cars to developing a studio practice that encapsulates the ethos of the city.

Inspired by early 20th-century urban realist artists, including John Sloan of the Ashcan School and Reginald Marsh of the WPA era, Daze’s works honor New York City’s streets and subways as important sites of his creative evolution. Simultaneously influenced by the lyrical abstraction of works by Joan Mitchell and Willem De Kooning, Daze combines gestural swaths of acrylic and spray paint with detailed renderings of train car interiors, tunnels, and stations. In Gem Spa In the 80s, 2025, Daze depicts the now iconic newspaper stand and candy store that once operated on the corner of St. Mark’s Place and Second Avenue. Gem Spa was a central destination and meeting place for members of the city’s subcultures and is referenced by literary figures like Jack Kerouac and Allen Ginsberg (who called it a “nerve center” of the city). Important people from Daze’s life can be found throughout the composition, among them critic and curator Carlo McCormick as well as artist Martin Wong, who both emerge amongst the crowd in the painting’s foreground. In other works, technicolor throngs of flowers ascend from heaps of urban rubble, representing optimism amidst inequality and the beauty that can arise out of destruction. Throughout the exhibition, these varied combinations of tropical flora and local flowers from the artist’s home in upstate New York function as poignant memorials to what has been lost and hopeful testaments to the beauty and creativity that can still be found around every corner.

The exhibition will also include a site-specific mural, bringing an aspect of Daze’s practice often relegated to the outdoors into the interior setting of the gallery. Covering the walls of a hallway, the mural gives way to the final room of the gallery, featuring a multimedia installation that transports viewers into a composite scene from the artist’s youth. Combining a light-up dance floor and disco ball, actual subway car seats, and a curated track fusing house, disco, hip-hop, and club music, the installation emphasizes the freedom and creative inspiration that arose from these settings, and their importance to Daze’s personal and artistic development. Combining elements from throughout his career, Orchid Rain on the Underground showcases Daze’s never-ending exploration of daily life in New York City while paying homage to the people and places that comprise its vibrant cultural heartbeat.

After a string of disappointments, 'extraordinary' demand suggests the new iPhone has captured the public imagination in a brand new way.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

For a few years new, tech writers (including this one) have been remarking on how Apple, and the tech world in general, is desperate for another 'iPhone moment'. 2007 still feels like the last time a truly game-changing piece of hardware was introduced. Subsequent attempts to position something as a vision of the future—Vision Pro, various AI gadgets— have fallen flat. Meanwhile, over the last twenty years, the iPhone itself has started to feel increasingly stale. But with the unprecedented hype machine that is the iPhone Duo, maybe, just maybe, things feel different this year.

If you haven't already pre-ordered your iPhone Duo, you have a long wait ahead of you. Delivery dates have slipped into 2027, suggesting demand for the thing is through the roof. Which, considering the starting price tag of $2000, is kind of incredible. If so many people are willing to drop that much money on a device that isn't even in stores yet, it must represent something new.

Which, by the way, foldable aren't. Brands like Samsung and Huawei have been making them for years. But Apple is doing its Apple thing and putting out its own take on a maturing product category. While often successful (the iPhone wasn't the first smartphone, nor the Apple Watch the first smartwatch), it hasn't always worked of late. Vision Pro, Apple's attempt at a VR headset, is one of the company's highest-profile flops of recent years.

Everybody blamed the failure of Vision Pro on the price. $3K turned out to be too hard to stomach for most. But the early success of the iPhone Duo is throwing a spanner into the works for that narrative. $2K is arguably a ridiculous amount of money to spend on a phone. But this time, people are going for it. Even Apple is calling the demand "extraordinary".

It's curious that while dramatically new products like Vision Pro have failed to cut through in recent years, so have more minor redesigns of the iPhone itself. The iPhone Air, which shares some DNA with the iPhone Duo thanks to its lightweight titanium frame, failed to capture the public's imagination last year.

But with the iPhone Duo, Apple seems to have finally discovered the sweet spot. Different enough to get people excited, but same enough to make them take a risk with their cash. It's an iPhone. But it's one that unfolds into an iPad. Same but different. Maybe that's what the people wanted all along?

#48. łukasz twarkowski turns theater into a live cinematic spectacle

the polish director builds immersive stage environments in which live performance, moving images, and shifting scenography challenge how audiences experience theater.

Before Oracle begins at Onassis Stegi in Athens, a camera captures the audience and projects its image onto a screen. Spectators appear as grainy black-and-white figures, their faces transformed into a strange, almost anonymous collective portrait. Those who have come to watch find themselves becoming the spectacle. It is an introduction to the work of Polish director Łukasz Twarkowski, in which live performance and cinema become inseparable. Twarkowski brings theater and cinema into a shared space, making the process of filming part of the performance. The stage divides horizontally into two visual fields: the live theatrical action unfolds below, while a screen above displays footage captured by cameras operating within the set in real time. The audience watches the actors perform while simultaneously observing how their movements are framed and transformed into cinematic images.

For the director, video is not just an addition to the performance. Theater and cinema happen at the same time, with cameras filming the actors live and projecting the footage onto a screen above the stage. The audience can watch the actors perform or follow the action through the camera, constantly switching between the two.

For most of the three-hour-and-40-minute performance, the filming process remains visible to the audience. Camera operators move within the set, framing actors whose actions are simultaneously experienced in the theater and on screen. The projected images offer close-ups and carefully composed perspectives, while the stage reveals the bodies, movements, and technical decisions behind them. The audience is free to move between these viewpoints, but neither provides a complete account of the event. The screen can draw attention away from the physical stage, offering a familiar way of experiencing a narrative through selected frames. Yet looking away from the screen reveals another performance unfolding around the act of filming itself. Twarkowski makes this competition for the audience’s attention part of the experience, exposing how easily the mediated image can take precedence over the reality it represents.

The set is made up of separate modules, each built around a corner with walls and a ceiling. The units can be joined in different combinations, either in pairs or around the center of the stage, creating a range of spatial arrangements. Depending on how they connect and rotate, they can form enclosed rooms, corridors, or a series of open frames that suggest a street or a cluster of buildings.

The lighting further changes how these spaces are perceived, shifting their atmosphere from one scene to the next. The production rearranges the same elements to create different environments and conditions for the action. The transformations remain visible, making the changing structure an active part of the performance.

What makes Twarkowski’s approach relevant beyond the theater is its engagement with a culture increasingly organized around screens, live images, and mediated experiences. In ORACLE, the audience is first transformed into an image and then invited to watch performers undergo the same process. The camera becomes both a tool for revealing detail and an instrument that determines what can be seen.

The subject of the production, which moves between Alan Turing, the history of computing, and the emergence of artificial intelligence, adds another dimension to this inquiry. Its use of thermal and infrared imaging evokes technologies associated with surveillance and military applications, complicating the assumption that images provide neutral access to reality. What appears on screen is always shaped by a system of interpretation.

Twarkowski uses the resources of contemporary theater to examine how images are constructed and how audiences respond to them. His work suggests that spectacle lies in the systems that organize attention, mediate experience, and determine what becomes visible.

#49. Major London museums join forces for new South Asian arts festival

Giants on the Move: A Puppet Street Parade, directed by Dadi Pudumjee, The Ishara Puppet Theatre Trust and presented by Serendipity Arts at the Great Exhibition Road Festival, London 6-7 June 2026

Some of London's leading cultural institutions are joining forces with the Indian organisation Serendipity Arts to stage a major festival celebrating South Asian creativity.

The Victoria and Albert Museum (V&A), Science Museum and Natural History Museum are among the partners for Serendipity Arts Festival London, which will take over Exhibition Road and South Kensington's cultural quarter between 19-27 June 2027.

The festival, which is in partnership with the Great Exhibition Road Festival led by Imperial College, will also be joined by the Royal Albert Hall, Royal Geographical Society, Royal College of Art (RCA) and Royal College of Music, which are all participating.

The festival will feature established and emerging artists from India and its diaspora, with a programme spanning visual art, music, dance, new media and food. Events will take place in galleries, concert halls, cafés and outdoor spaces.

Shefali Munjal, the co-founder and patron of Serendipity Arts, said: “South Asian creativity cannot be understood through a single discipline, tradition or geography. It lives as much in food, sound and movement as it does in a gallery.”

Six women curators have been appointed: Veeranganakumari Solanki and Nancy Adajania (new media), Latika Gupta (visual arts), Preethi Athreya (dance), Sneha Khanwalkar (music) and Elizabeth Yorke (culinary arts).

Kristian Volsing, a senior curator at V&A South Kensington, tells The Art Newspaper the partnership is “an incredibly timely collaboration”, ahead of the museum's exhibition South Asia Now: Fashion. Art. Design. at V&A East in spring 2027 and the reopening of its South Asia Gallery in 2028.

He added that the festival would create an “opportunity to centre South Asian creative talent”, with the programming “reflecting London's diversity and creating a welcoming space for all communities”.

The festival builds on Serendipity Arts’ annual event in Goa, India, which celebrated its tenth anniversary in 2025. Since launching in 2016, it has attracted more than one million visitors and participants and supported over 10,000 artists. The organisation introduced its work to London in June this year through two public projects with the Science Museum and Great Exhibition Road Festival. Other international partnerships this year include collaborations with the National Pavilion of India at the Venice Biennale, Rencontres d'Arles, the RCA and the Centre national des arts plastiques (Cnap) in Paris.

The Royal Geographical Society will develop an exhibition inspired by objects in its collections relating to the Indian subcontinent. Its director, Joe Smith, tells The Art Newspaper: “Applying creative methods and cross-cultural perspectives to these items will uncover different stories and learnings, deepening the connection between past and present and helping us see the world differently.”

He added: “We hope visitors to the exhibition find the experience enriching and leave considering how they can learn from times, places and cultures that may be different from their own.”

The partnership will also extend to India, with London's Natural History Museum presenting its Wildlife Photographer of the Year exhibition at the Goa festival this December. Further programme details will be announced in the coming months.

#50. Kössen Wayfinding: Inside Andrea Gassner's Stitched Sign System

Atelier Andrea Gassner's KÃ¶ssen wayfinding stitches copper cross-stitch lettering into warm plaster at the new Education Center KÃ¶ssen.

Walk the corridors of the new Education Center KÃ¶ssen in Tyrol and the walls read back at you. The signage is built letter by letter from a copper cross-stitch, each character a small woven sculpture held slightly off the plaster. Warm light rakes across the surface and doubles every letterform in shadow, so the walls carry two texts at once: one stitched, one cast by the day itself. The letters are custom-produced in pearl copper, their woven geometry catching light at every angle, and the stencil-like openness of each glyph keeps the hand of the plaster visible between the stitches.

The studio drew its alphabet from the region's own craft language. The cross motif, long used in Tyrolean historical craftsmanship, becomes the construction unit for letters, numerals, and icons: every glyph is a field of X-shaped stitches, dense enough to read from across the hall and open enough that the wall shows through. The same unit scales from a small room code to building-height lettering without changing its logic, so a corridor sign and a facade sign speak the same dialect. Numerals and icons get the same treatment, and the signage oscillates between two and three dimensions: read flat at a glance, it reveals its depth the moment you step closer.

Material does the heavy lifting. Rough, porous plaster in a warm natural tone meets custom-produced characters in pearl copper, the metal's warmth answering the wall's. Because the letters stand off the surface, light and shadow turn the walls into a second display that shifts as the day moves. Outside, the theme continues at a larger scale, with building signage precisely milled into the wooden slats of the facade. Ornament here is never decoration for its own sake; the studio treats it as narrative woven into the architecture. The result is a KÃ¶ssen wayfinding system that reads as craft first and signage second.

Police ordered the Grand Palais to briefly shut down amid the nationwide student protests.

The Grand Palais in Paris went into temporary lockdown during installation for Art Basel Paris on Saturday, October 17, amid nearby protests over France’s education system and public services, a fair representative confirmed to Hyperallergic.

The Paris Police Prefecture ordered the Grand Palais — which has housed Art Basel Paris since 2024, two years after the Swiss art fair network replaced the exhibition hall's longstanding FIAC (Foire Internationale d'Art Contemporain) — to briefly shut down to “ensure the safety of everyone on site and the protection of the artworks,” an Art Basel spokesperson told Hyperallergic. The lockdown occurred at 5 pm, and the building sustained no damage, another fair spokesperson said.

"No one could get out, and no one could get in," an anonymous source from a New York gallery exhibiting at the fair told Hyperallergic. "There were moving trucks loading and offloading works, and at a certain point, they were told to pack up and go."

#53. David Chipperfield Architects builds concrete gallery around singular artwork in Germany

Photography by Studio Menges Tugushi

The Berlin office of David Chipperfield Architects has added a monolithic concrete gallery housing just one Anselm Kiefer painting to the grounds of the Carmen Würth Forum museum in Germany.

Situated on a grassy mound in Künzelsau, the Anselm Kiefer Pavilion was built in the sculpture garden of the Carmen Würth Forum, an art museum and conference hall by David Chipperfield Architects that opened in 2020.

The form of the gallery was determined by German painter Kiefer’s Schwarze Flocken, or Black Flakes, a large-scale artwork that had before been too large to exhibit in the museum.

David Chipperfield Architects worked with Kiefer on the design of the pavilion to create a suitable setting for the 11-by-7.1-metre artwork, which was named after a poem by Holocaust survivor Paul Celan.

Designed to have a calming, sculptural appearance, the Anselm Kiefer Pavilion has a cuboid shape with a canopy that protrudes over the entrance.

It was made from brick and bush-hammered concrete, which references the concrete surfaces of the nearby Carmen Würth Forum building.

“The building’s form directly traces the interior volume specified by the artist and focuses on a few, precisely placed elements,” said David Chipperfield Architects.

“This structure is precisely tailored to the work and enables its first-ever public presentation,” it continued.

“A restrained portico provides shelter from the weather and marks the transition between landscape and exhibition space.”

Inside, clay plaster lines the walls and the timber roof structure overhead was left exposed.

Rooflights were designed to let natural light in and show its changing qualities throughout the day and seasons.

“The aim is not uniform illumination, but a focused, tranquil atmosphere that slows down the act of seeing and directs attention to the artwork,” said David Chipperfield Architects.

“Unlike conventional exhibition spaces, the room is not subject to strict climate control or lighting parameters,” it conitued.

“Its three-layer wall construction, comprising concrete, brickwork and an internal layer of clay plaster, is designed to adapt to varying climatic conditions and maintain frost-free conditions without active climate control.”

David Chipperfield Architects recently published a video celebrating two of the studio’s most important projects – the Hepworth Wakefield gallery in West Yorkshire and the Turner Contemporary museum in Margate.

#54. Donors Are Secretly Trying to Save the Kennedy Center’s Artworks from ‘Destruction’ or Disposal Amid Trump Takeover

It has been widely reported that the Kennedy Center is at the center of a power struggle between the Trump administration and preservationists, as the president wants to rename it in his own honor and insists that the decaying building must close for renovations. He has threatened that it will be razed if he does not get his way.

Now, CNN reports that donors who have given artwork to the institution are trying to reclaim their gifts, fearing for their safety amid a renovation and in the wake of layoffs. They are not convinced that the leadership, largely appointed by Trump, values the artworks as part of the institution’s holdings. Related Articles Whistleblowers Say Kennedy Center Leaders Put Off Fixing the Same Problems They Now Blame for Closing the Building Rep. Joyce Beatty Asks Judge to Make 'Crystal Clear' Trump Cannot Demolish Kennedy Center in Wake of Viral Photo

According to an internal document reviewed by CNN, officials have been working since at least late last year on a plan that proposed the “disposal” of artworks, whether by “return to country of origin, transfer or exchange with another institution, public sale, or destruction.”

“I want to get that sculpture out of there,” one person who donated a piece told CNN.

Donors, as well as artists and their families, have been trying for months to get answers, the report says, to questions about how the artworks will be safeguarded, where they are, and whether they will be returned. Their fears were not assuaged when Trump ordered the disassembly and removal of a monumental Joel Shapiro sculpture from the institution’s grounds. The work had been gifted to the center but was sold to its former chairman, David Rubenstein. The reason for its removal has not been explained.

“We remain in regular contact with the foundations and entities who have donated art to the center,” a Kennedy Center spokesperson told CNN. But an unidentified person described as close to the Kennedy Center said the institution’s response has been “a little bit disjointed” and that donors are “not given detail in any way.”

The Kennedy Center has long been home to hundreds of unique works of art and antiquities, including sculptures and tapestries, donated or loaned by individual benefactors and other countries, CNN notes. Officials say the proposal contemplating the “destruction” of art “was never envisioned as a sweeping purge.” They told CNN that the “cornerstone of the collection—historic international gifts given to the center for its opening—remains intact.”

The Kennedy Center did not immediately respond to a request from ARTnews to clarify how much of the center’s collection falls under that “cornerstone” designation, or what circumstances would lead to the destruction of artworks.

Officials told CNN that all artwork will be “fully safeguarded” during the renovation, with some pieces relocated if necessary to ensure their safety. But sources also told CNN that objects belonging to the archives have been “inadvertently” taken home by staffers.

Following Kennedy’s assassination, world leaders rushed to donate artworks: France gave tapestries by Henri Matisse, and Tunisia gave a reproduction of a third-century mosaic for the rooftop terrace, CNN notes.

Josef Palermo, formerly the curator in charge of visual art programming, was laid off earlier this year. He wrote in an Atlantic essay that he had been instructed to begin removing artworks on view.

CNN also notes that the Kennedy Center recently convened, with no announcement, its first visual arts committee, “to curate and expand public installations of performing and visual arts.”

#55. Nat Meade's "Franklin" @ HESSE FLATOW, NYC

HESSE FLATOW is pleased to announce the opening of Franklin, an exhibition of paintings and works on paper by Nat Meade, marking his third solo presentation with the gallery. The show is on view through April 18, 2026.

The emotional arc of life’s struggles and triumphs take shape within Meade’s figurative works, reflecting the artist’s everyday experiences as he navigates being a father, son, partner, and academic. Far from portraits of actual individuals, his protagonists mirror timeless archetypes. At times, we encounter a lone traveler searching for existential validation; at other times, we see through intergenerational dynamics. This allegorical distance via painting provides a realm for Meade to explore personal challenges through absurd, somber, and humorous tropes, while also furnishing a space rife with human nature that bears unequivocal resonance.

Meade’s reflections on his relationship with his father after his recent passing, and subsequent reevaluations of his own role as a parent percolate throughout the works in the exhibition. Vulnerability, pain, and mortality are themes Meade does not shy away from, yet the introduction of younger males in this body of work casts a sense of hope, acceptance, reconciliation, and renewal.

Faced with a pair of dangling legs from a cloud in Poise, we question whether a figure is ascending or descending from the heavens, a suggestion perhaps on the interchangeability of birth and death, be it physical or spiritual. Ghostly specters hover over certain individuals – a metaphor for inherited trauma and release. In the same way that a soul peels away from an expiring body in classic cartoons, we observe a spirit looking back on itself with what might be  happiness or regret. The exhibition’s title Franklin is a subtle nod to the 1974 horror film Texas Chainsaw Massacre, known for its portrayal of a deranged patriarchal family. Meade embraces this inner turmoil of contending with one’s violent and antagonistic impulses as his characters are visibly sublimated or put in their place. A vulture picking away at a corpse recalls the eternal punishment of Prometheus by Zeus, while a bearded figure on his hands and knees echoes William Blake’s portrayal of Nebuchadnezzar, condemned for his lust for power.

In contrast to the adults, Meade’s younger figures appear more harmonious. A young boy charts his own path as he steers a boat with a radiant torch, unclouded by societal and familial pressures. A sense of childlike wonder and adventure beholds an adolescent ankle-deep in a secluded cove, reaching in to touch the sea floor brilliantly covered in starfish, anemones, and mussels. In a related work, we observe two pairs of legs belonging to father and son in the same shallow pool, one tenderly guiding the other. Having in the past shown his figures wrestling with or victims of forces of nature, physically being overtaken by turbulent wind and crashing waves, Meade’s focus on calmer seas signals a turning point. He recognizes the need to acknowledge one’s rocky histories in order to heal and release future generations from similar burdens. Despite what may seem like an insurmountable heaviness, he reminds us of the stubborn resilience of human nature, making progress attainable.

#57. sandbag castle casts sustainable concrete alternatives into floating installation in eindhoven

floating in the dommel river beside eindhoven’s van abbemuseum, a fortress built from sandbag-shaped modules highlights over ten emerging lower-carbon concrete formulations, translating protective infrastructure into a live material study.

Yvonne Mak edited by christina vergopoulou October 20, 2026 3 min

Visual artist Yvonne Mak’s installation Sandbag Castle addresses the environmental impact of conventional cement by showcasing low-carbon concrete alternatives. Positioned in the Dommel river beside Eindhoven’s Van Abbemuseum Café, the five-meter-wide by three-meter-high structure consists of hundreds of stacked, sandbag-shaped concrete forms resembling a castle.

The installation by artist Yvonne Mak incorporates several key design elements to communicate its structural and environmental themes. Cast in concrete, the sandbag-shaped modules reference temporary flood barriers, highlighting the widespread reliance on concrete for protective infrastructure. Positioned atop the castle, red warning flags reference beach safety warnings. These flags feature a custom coat of arms incorporating symbols for water, bridges, flora, and hands, representing the intersection of nature, infrastructure, and human intervention.

The physical composition of the work directly incorporates over ten distinct low-carbon concrete variants, including calcined clay, alternative binders, geopolymer concrete, recycled aggregates, and self-healing concrete formulations. Developed with main partner TBI alongside specialized material and technology contributors, Sandbag Castle demonstrates existing and emerging structural alternatives designed to reduce the CO₂ emissions of concrete construction.

#58. Legal troubles and family feud keep Klimt portrait off the market

Gustav Klimt, Portrait of Fräulein Lieser, 1917 © Auktionshaus im Kinsky GmbH, Wien

The consignor of Gustav Klimt’s Portrait of Fräulein Lieser (1917), whose €30m sale at the Vienna auction house Im Kinsky in 2024 was later cancelled because of disputes over its tangled provenance, now faces yet another hurdle to selling the painting in the form of a lawsuit filed in the United States that could keep it off the market for years to come. This latest dispute centres around a bitter 1942 divorce and a betrayal whose repercussions have reverberated across generations and continents.

The identity of the young woman portrayed in the portrait has long been a puzzle and the subject of debate. It is also key to determining which members of a Jewish family owned it before it was lost during the Nazi era.

Little is known about the portrait’s provenance. What is known is that it was still in Klimt’s studio at the time of his death in 1918 and is not quite finished. The name of the person who commissioned the portrait from Klimt was documented only as Lieser, a family of important industrialists in the Austro-Hungarian Empire.

The authors of the Klimt catalogue raisonné believe it was commissioned by Adolf Lieser and portrayed his daughter, Margarethe. Im Kinsky, however, said at the time of the 2024 auction that there were indications it was instead commissioned by Henriette Lieser-Landau, the ex-wife of Justus Lieser, Adolf’s brother, and portrays one of her two daughters. Lieser-Landau was deported in 1942 and murdered by the Nazis in 1943.

Heirs of both Adolf Lieser and Henriette Lieser-Landau were included in a potential settlement that would have divided the revenue of the sale between the claimants and the current holder of the painting, Eva Ropper. According to correspondence between lawyers representing claimants recently obtained by The Art Newspaper, 60% of the revenue was to go to the claimants, and 40% to Ropper.

At the April 2024 auction, the advisory Patti Wong & Associates bid €30m on behalf of an anonymous Hong Kong buyer. While this was at the low end of Im Kinsky’s estimate, it was the highest price ever bid at an auction in Austria. But the sale fell through when another claimant emerged: Patricia Leahy, the granddaughter of Hans Lieser, who was Margarethe’s brother. Her lawyer filed a complaint in April in the Supreme Court of the State of New York against Im Kinsky and Ropper.

The lawsuit alleges that the Hong Kong buyer “sought indemnification from all potential claimants”, including Leahy. The claimants all “signed agreements disclaiming further claims in exchange for payment” except for Leahy, who was not included in the original settlement, according to the complaint. When attempts to negotiate an agreement with Leahy failed, the Hong Kong buyer withdrew, it says.

Leahy’s suit requests a declaratory judgment that “the plaintiff is a rightful heir and a rightful owner of Portrait of Fräulein Lieser”. It urges Im Kinsky and Ropper to “immediately deliver Portrait of Fräulein Lieser to plaintiff”.

By mid-October, six months after the complaint was announced and widely distributed to news media, it had not yet been served on Ropper, according to her lawyer in Vienna, Robert Bachner. “It appears that the plaintiff has so far taken no steps to do so,” he said. “From Ms Ropper’s perspective, the complaint is without justification. The background to the complaint appears to be primarily a dispute between the Kraft Estate/Patricia Leahy and Hannes Staal, the sole legal successor to Hans Lieser.”

The Austrian newspaper Der Standard reported in June that Ropper has also commissioned a more detailed provenance report in an attempt to uncover which part of the family owned the painting.

The reason Leahy was not included in the original settlement is that, despite being Hans Lieser’s granddaughter, she is not—according to the lawyer for another claimant, Hannes Viktor Staal—his rightful heir. Hans Lieser’s 1968 will, a copy of which was made available to The Art Newspaper, states that his sole heir is his second wife, Margareta Lieser.

Some dark family history explains why Leahy’s claim is disputed by the other claimants. Hans Lieser married his first wife, Edith Böhm, in 1934. She was not Jewish. Their son, Nikolaus, was born in Vienna in June 1938, three months after Adolf Hitler’s annexation of Austria.

According to a court affidavit written by Hans Lieser and dated 23 January 1947, members of the Lieser family had entrusted Edith with their company and with shares to protect their assets from “Aryanisation” by the Nazis. Hans and Edith Lieser moved to Budapest in September 1938.

Hans Lieser’s affidavit states that his initially harmonious marriage soured when Edith began an “intimate relationship” with a Gestapo and SS officer, Tibor Collas. In the affidavit, Lieser wrote that Edith, who was often in Vienna as the nominal manager of the company business, ended up moving there permanently with their son Nikolaus in 1939 and “from that point onward regarded the company as her own property”.

Not only that, but according to the affidavit and to a Hungarian newspaper article from 1946, Collas used his Nazi connections to pursue Hans Lieser, who was arrested and deported to Slovakia.

The Liesers’ marriage was dissolved in 1942 and Lieser was once again arrested on the basis of a complaint filed by Collas, he wrote. Edith established a new company and transferred to it the assets and rights of the original family-owned company. In November 1945, after the end of the war, Hans Lieser filed a police complaint and, in the affidavit, estimated that Edith had appropriated more than 1m Reichsmarks from the Liesers—the equivalent of several million dollars today.

Edith married a US army colonel, James Kraft, and moved to the US after the war with Nikolaus, who adopted his stepfather’s name—the recent US complaint identifies him as Nickolas Johann Kraft. Nickolas Kraft had little contact with his biological father but sued him in 1967, before his marriage, for payment of a dowry, according to documents made available to The Art Newspaper. Under Austrian law, parents are, under certain circumstances, obliged to give a settlement to their children on marriage. The draft of a letter Hans Lieser wrote to Kraft shows that he responded with outrage.

When Lieser died in 1978, his widow Margareta inherited his estate. Lieser’s will states that Nickolas Kraft should only receive the “compulsory share” of his estate because he “gravely violated his duties towards me as a son, making contact with me only when he expected to gain financially”. Under Austrian law, even disinherited children are entitled to a share of the inheritance, which Kraft duly received.

As she had no children, Margareta left the estate to her sister, who, in turn, bequeathed it to her son, Hannes Staal. According to his lawyer, Louis Rönsberg, Staal says he remembers Hans Lieser and had a good relationship with his uncle. Rönsberg says his client is the only rightful heir to Hans Lieser’s 15% share of the revenue of Portrait of Fräulein Lieser—when and if it is eventually sold.

While disinherited children are entitled to a share of the estate under Austrian law, they do not qualify as heirs and must claim their share from the beneficiary of the will.According to a 2024 letter from Leahy’s Austrian lawyer to Rönsberg that was made available to The Art Newspaper, that share in this case is 37.5%. Rönsberg, however, argued in his response to the lawyer that Leahy’s claim has by now expired due to statutes of limitation.

After the failed 2024 auction at Im Kinsky, the consignor and claimants included in the original settlement agreed that the next attempt to sell would be at a major international auction house. But as long as the threat of a US court case against Im Kinsky and Ropper is pending, “a sale is impossible,” Rönsberg says. “Ms. Leahy and her lawyer are blocking everything. The case is not advancing and they are not helping to find a solution.”

Leahy’s New York-based lawyer, Oren Warshavsky, did not respond to repeated requests for comment. A spokeswoman for Im Kinsky declined to comment on Leahy’s suit, saying only that the auction house is no longer in possession of the picture and no longer has a relationship with the consignor.

Following the auction and the failure to reach an agreement, “Ms Leahy has apparently now decided to use the complaint, together with the accompanying PR campaign, to exert pressure”, says Bachner, Ropper’s lawyer. Her failure to advance the suit, he adds, “reinforces the impression that the plaintiff’s primary objective was to achieve the greatest possible publicity with minimal effort”.

The price paid by a buyer from Hong Kong was at the lower end of the estimate range, but still an auction record for Austria

#59. To Be Alone With Your Thoughts in '70s New York

Fred Camper's contemplative film "Suicide Note" was born out of grief and a city in collapse.

Editor’s Note: The following story contains mentions of self-harm. If you or someone you know is struggling, call or text 988 or visit 988lifeline.org to reach the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline.

There is a specific feeling, easy to recognize emotionally but hard to elucidate in words, about trying to power through the numbness of depression to simply live your everyday life. I’m writing these words amidst such a period. Artist, filmmaker, and critic Fred Camper sought to capture that feeling with Suicide Note, which he describes as “born out of an intense personal despair, and a desire to depict a failure of the self.”

He shot the footage mainly in New York from 1976 to 1984, and since its completion, it’s been exhibited only a handful of times. The Chicago Film Society’s restoration of the film — still on 16mm rather than transferred to digital — showed at this year’s New York Film Festival, pulling it out of its quasi-cryptid past and giving new audiences a chance to experience it. Because the film's few previous showings were on workprints, this year’s NYFF was technically its true premiere, half a century after Camper started work on it.

Suicide Note came from Camper’s grief over his stepfather’s death by suicide, his own struggle with depression, and what he saw as the broader symbolic suicide of the human race.

#61. Box 9 used “brick on every surface” in Soho restaurant Kid

Local studio Box 9 has used bricks made from recycled construction waste for the interior of London restaurant Kid, where the material clads everything from the grill to the wine room.

The 307-square-metre restaurant in central Soho sits on a corner and is made from two formerly separate units, which Box 9 combined to make Kid, a modern take on a Turkish mangal restaurant.

While the Frith Street side of the restaurant has a more traditional Victorian feel, the Bateman Street side was given a contemporary design, with the use of brick joining the two sites.

“The site’s two shopfronts offered an opportunity to connect their contrasting elevations through a shared design approach,” Box 9 co-founder Lou Davies told Dezeen.

“Frith Street retains a beautiful Victorian upper storey with distinctive brick patterns that reflect Soho’s merchant-trading history, while Bateman Street has a new elevation and a central section rising to the residences above,” she continued.

“The building itself suggested uniting the spaces with a single material.”

Brick was chosen not just because of its use in the building the restaurant is located in, but also because of its connection to traditional hospitality spaces and the Turkish heritage of Kid chef Sertaç Dirik.

“Brick became central to the concept because it connected so many elements of the project,” Davies explained.

“It has a centuries-old relationship with restaurants, kitchens and cooking with fire, forming the basis of traditional fireplaces and hearths,” she continued.

“It also reflected the heritage of Turkish cooking and Sertaç’s family background, while connecting to the history of the Soho building and its original brick patterns.”

Guests enter the two-storey Kid restaurant through a discreet door on Bateman Street, where they are met by a large, central grill.

Like most of the interior at Kid, this was made from material company Kenoteq’s K-Briq, which is crafted from at least 90 per cent recycled construction and demolition waste and requires no fossil fuels or firing to produce.

According to Box 9, this means that it releases a tenth of the carbon emissions of traditional fired-clay bricks.

“We loved the idea of using brick on every surface,” Davies said of the material choice.

“There was a raw humbleness to it: wine cellars, kitchens and grills would traditionally have been built with brick,” she continued.

“It wasn’t about fancy materials; it was about using the best material for the purpose.”

Upstairs, visitors will also find the wine room, which seats 14 people and was similarly made entirely of brick.

The studio chose slightly different designs to define the two upstairs rooms, using a traditional bond with a traditional joint for the Victorian side and a soldier bond and a raked joint for the more contemporary section.

Downstairs, Box 9 designed Kid’s open bakery, which features moveable bespoke tables by design firm Jan Hendzel Studio to allow the room to be used as an events space.

Overall, the main aim for Box 9 was to create a space that would complement Dirik’s food, which was formed through his cooking at his family’s restaurant Mangal II.

“We needed to create a completely unique restaurant that represented Serta,” Davies concluded.

“His personality is big, and his background is rooted in generations of cooking in Turkey and his family’s cooking style, as well as how they cooked at Mangal II. All his training was in cooking with fire.”

London has seen a spate of recent restaurant openings, including a French-style restaurant by Cassette and a London pizzeria designed by Isern Serra.

Awe-Inspiring Architecture Celebrated in International Photo Competition

Exterior, interiors, facades, and friezes are all on display after the Architecture Photography MasterPrize (APMP) revealed its 2026 winners.

Photographers from 59 countries entered more than a thousand projects across exterior and interior architectural photography.

An international jury of photographers, editors, curators, and visual professionals selected the winners, and 53 projects received the Best of Best distinction. The jury then named the two top titles, Exterior and Interior Architecture Photography of the Year, from that group.

#64. Molly Bounds "The Light That Loses, The Night That Wins" @ Mrs Gallery, Maspeth, NY

Mrs. is pleased to present The Light That Loses, The Night That Wins, Molly Bounds’ New York debut solo exhibition, on view at the gallery’s 6040 56th Drive location. This exhibition marks the Los Angeles-based artist’s second presentation with the gallery following The Armory Show in September 2025. The show will be on view through May 2, 2026.

Opening on the vernal equinox, a rare moment when the hours of daylight and night are equal, Molly Bounds offers light as the protagonist in her new series of paintings. It is versatile and ever-changing; it both conceals and reveals, and reminds us of the unrelenting forward movement of time. Depicting her subjects both in contemplation and in the midst of candid movement, Bounds continues her investigation into liminal moments where stillness and urgency shape the mood. Much like the transition from winter to spring, these figures appear on the threshold of a transformative shift.

Bounds captures her subjects in solitude. Her interior scenes feature slumped and draping bodies signaling rest and repose that slowly gives way to unease. These are psychological portraits, capturing something that persists behind dormant states and tired eyes. In The Armchair, the warm glow of a fireplace highlights a textured and lush interior, contrasted against the cold, early evening blue sky seen out the window. Contemplation gradually reveals tension - a mind dwelling, scheming, planning; upholstery seams unravel. The woman maintains a vacant stare that lingers in an eternal way, in bliss or something else.In Privacy Glass, another figure secludes herself from the outside world, rendered dramatically in both warm and cool hues. The glass offers a clear diffusion to illuminate the subject from behind, while letting a distinct  beam permeate the inside from the outside. The result obscures her face and accents her draped clothing, recalling a Georges De La Tour: like the vanitas, Bounds conveys the fleetingness of time and inevitability of darkness.

There are also moments of escapism. In both It Sings in Me and Among of Green, Again a figure moves freely amongst rolling green hills, illuminated under the sun. The landscape appears bucolic and perhaps overly so - is this real or imagined? For Bounds this is less important; the ability to build optimism and a belief in renewal and rebirth is paramount. Contrasting with the scenes of pensive interiority, these landscapes communicate urgency, celebration, possibility, and fantasy. After the darkness of winter, spring wins.

This piece depicts the workshop district of Nording Town, part of my world-building project. In this world, divine blessings descend from the stars, passing through the veil above and condensing into star sand, the region’s primary source of energy.

This magical resource shapes not only the local industry but also the culture and daily lives of its people. I wanted the architecture to reflect the relationship between technology and faith, while using the starry sky as the visual core of the scene.

Small props and workshop tools were added to enrich the world and make it feel lived in. Every element reflects the logic of the world (if you need to build your own art setup, see our guides to the best drawing tablets or the best laptops for drawing).

I began by establishing the story, architectural language and composition of Nording Town’s workshop district. Key motifs, such as glowing chimneys and starlight-infused smoke, were used to connect the workshops to the night sky.

I created a 3D base using Daz Studio for posing the main figure. I imported this into Blender to further build out the scene using assets from the Blender Kit library, setting up the lighting and adjusting the models using basic sculpting.

It’s a very useful process if you don’t want to repaint every adjustment from scratch.

For the final touches, I added atmospheric effects, star particles, textures and small props such as containers, tools and decorative lights to reinforce the setting and make the world feel alive.

#66. Five Essential Books About Pop Art

Pop Art arrived in the middle of the 20th century, as artists experimented with pictures and processes borrowed from mass media. Their high-low mashups, nostalgic references, and high-octane colors remain alluring, relevant, and surprisingly misunderstood. In time for the Whitney Museum of American Art’s retrospective on Roy Lichtenstein, read these five books to revisit the significant cultural movement and track its continual reinvention.

Art movements tend to be situated as hard breaks with their immediate past, but great art historians address how a movement is drawn out of the world it inherits. In The Long March of Pop, Thomas Crow argues that Pop artists were forged in post-World War II classrooms that welcomed a surge of veterans and explored the “image worlds” of American folk art as source material. He organizes the text with chapters on key artists (Robert Indiana, James Rosenquist, and Robert Rauschenberg among them), but his analysis radiates out to include Americana treasures from surfboards to Woody Guthrie songs.

Appraisals of Pop art’s visual characteristics rapidly and narrowly consolidated around men, forcing women artists to the margins of the movement’s propulsive trajectory. Seductive Subversion provides exacting observations of how the art world excluded such artists as Pauline Boty, Faith Ringgold, and Marjorie Strider, who fit the formal cues of Pop art so precisely that one is reminded of rampant sexism and racism as well. But where this catalog for a traveling exhibition in 2010 really shines is when it cracks open the canon to argue for the Pop sensibilities of artists like Chryssa, Lee Lozano, and Alina Szapocznikow, who have largely been claimed by historians of other movements and styles.

Pop art is replete with images of consumer goods that, as this catalog for a 2015 Walker Art Center exhibition reminds us, circulate in a global marketplace. The rigorously researched compendium of essays, with a stellar timeline, dives deep into nation-specific histories of Pop from countries spanning the Americas, Asia, and Europe while also seriously considering the implications of the movement’s rise alongside American economic domination. This book is careening, festive, and incisive, bringing together a number of artists still overdue for solo museum shows. (Plus, Walker Art Center publications are always worth picking up for the design alone.)

Pop artists turned to images and processes borrowed from print advertising as interest in gestural and expressionistic mark-making waned. This shift reflects a set of concerns that remain relevant today, from the role of the artist in society to technological innovations’ impact on how we picture the world. Michael Lobel’s 2002 book sets itself apart in illuminating how such narratives surface in Roy Lichtenstein’s art, including an in-depth account of what is one of Pop art’s more fascinating origin stories. See: Lichtenstein’s training at Ohio State University’s “flash lab,” where students drew images that were screened in a blackout room for one-tenth of a second, effectively turning the body into a mechanical recording device.

Retail culture made its way into Pop art imagery and also influenced how artists and curators installed work, pulling inspiration from department store windows and marketing displays. This publication accompanied a 2020 exhibition in Vienna that focused on Andy Warhol’s approach, from maximalist wallpapers to towers of Brillo boxes. Come for the fascinating archival photographs but stay for the book’s last essay, by Jennifer Sichel: a groundbreaking reconsideration of Warhol’s conception of homosexuality based on recently discovered tapes of an early interview he did with the chronically underknown critic Gene Swenson. In Warhol’s intriguing appraisal, Pop art transcends a mere exploration of the consumer landscape into a radical field of queer desire. (Sichel also wrote Criticism Without Authority, a book focusing on Swenson and fellow queer critic Jill Johnston, published just last year.)

#67. Applications Open for the MFA in Studio Art at Maine College of Art & Design

Apply by January 17, 2027 to be considered for a full-tuition scholarship.

The Master of Fine Arts in Studio Art (MFA) program at Maine College of Art & Design (MECA&D) in Portland, Maine, offers an interdisciplinary approach that encourages students to think across traditional academic boundaries, expand their art practice, and challenge their intellectual curiosity.

Our six-term curriculum emphasizes the intersection of studio practice, individual research, and critical analysis. Built on a commitment to one-on-one student mentoring by distinguished faculty, visiting artists, critics, and curators, MECA&D’s MFA program offers a dynamic and supportive learning environment for artists who want to define and pursue a sustainable and transformative vision for their art practice.

Embedded within our MFA is a level of flexibility, allowing students to choose between Full and Low Residency. MECA&D’s Full Residency option provides 24/7 access to private studios and fabrication facilities where students work alongside peers and faculty. Among the first programs of its kind in the country, MECA&D’s Low Residency option combines intensive periods of on-campus instruction with the freedom and independence of working from home, anywhere in the world. Intensive group sessions, woven throughout our two-year curriculum, bring all MFA students together for research, travel, and dialogue.

All MFA students are in residence in Portland, Maine, for eight weeks each summer. As the first and fourth terms in a six-trimester course of study, these Summer Intensives function as catalysts for community and exchange. Renowned faculty, visiting artists, and critics deliver public lectures, conduct studio visits, and participate in group activities and discussions with graduate candidates during their respective visits to the MECA&D MFA Program.

To learn more and apply, visit meca.edu/mfa.

#68. What does an Old Master smell like? Meet the perfumer commissioned by Sotheby's

Lyn Harris qualified as Britain’s first classically trained female perfumer in the 1990s Courtesy Perfumer H

Art of Luxury magazine, published twice per year by The Art Newspaper, explores how grande marque fashion, jewellery, travel and lifestyle interact with artists, the art market and the museums and heritage sector.

“It’s about the earth, because everything comes from the earth,” says Lyn Harris, describing Clay, the latest scent from her fragrance house Perfumer H. The perfume was launched late last month, but the idea emerged over a year earlier during a visit to a wood kiln in a bamboo forest on the outskirts of Jingdezhen, the city that has been home to China’s porcelain industry for 1,700 years. For Harris, the smells—and the memories they triggered—evoked a heady mix: juniper, birch tar, musk, burnt ash, minerals, malt; the sweetness and warmth of charred cedar and sandalwood; and the effervescence of orange flower and mandarin. The resulting scent captures the universality of the ground beneath our feet, as well as its relationship with everything around it—the nature embedded in it and the light that bounces off it. “It’s an interesting fusion—quite young, it has a gentle sweetness and depth, as well as a twist,” Harris says.

Most of us would struggle to describe a scent in even two words, let alone the dozens that make up Harris’s baked clay accord. But as a classically trained “nose” (and the first British woman to achieve this), Harris is among the rare few who can break down a smell into its multiple constituent parts, describe it and reconstruct it—not just materially but also emotionally. It has led to a 30-year career, in which she has built a brand that creates perfumes, incense, candles and cosmetics, as well as teas, jams and oils, that sell in stores all over the world.

Perfumer H’s flagship store in London’s Marylebone Photo: Tom Fallon Photography

Of all the luxuries, scent is the most evanescent. Ephemeral and invisible, its success depends heavily on how it is delivered, something Coco Chanel knew only too well when she developed the disarmingly modern Chanel No.5 in its minimalist bottle. Harris communicates to those with less gifted noses by working with a range of collaborators to craft a sensory experience through other media.

The glass bottles that contain the 100ml of eau de parfum are hand-blown in Michael Ruh’s London glass-blowing studio (and cost £650). She is accompanied on all her travels by João de Sousa, a Portuguese film-maker who provides unique visual stories. Studio Frith, the chosen graphic designer of everyone from Artangel to Valentino, creates the clean packaging, while the Retrouvius studio, which specialises in clever reclamation, has designed the interior of her flagship store in London’s Marylebone. Together, these tell a story that words alone cannot.

In 2022, Harris was invited by Sotheby’s to develop three scented candles around an important auction of 17th-century still-lifes and landscapes by Dutch Old Masters—like perfume, priceless in their emotional impact. “What I found particularly clever was Lyn’s ability to draw out subtle aspects of a painting through scent,” says Alex Bell, chairman of Sotheby’s UK and Old Masters worldwide, who commissioned the project. “It was the first time we had explored scent as a way of interpreting and enhancing the experience of an exhibition in our galleries. We introduced Lyn to the paintings in the collection and invited her to respond to them in her own way. It was fascinating to see how she translated visual elements, atmosphere and mood into scent.”

Harris created the bespoke Smoke in Woods fragrance to perfume Sotheby’s in London during the preview and sale of Abraham Govaerts’s early 17th-century painting A wooded river landscape with travellers and peasants on a path, men in a boat and a village beyond Courtesy Sotheby’s

Rather than responding literally to each artwork, Harris teased out alternative readings. In a painting by Abraham Govaerts of peasants in a clearing by a river (A wooded river landscape with travellers and peasants on a path, men in a boat and a village beyond (early 17th century)), she homed in on the flickering light coming from a distant fire for a scent called Smoke in Woods. For Osias Beert the Elder’s floral still life of a fading floral bouquet (Still life of roses in an oriental lacquer and canework bowl, on a ledge with a butterfly and dragonfly (around 1615)), she picked up on the butterfly and dragonfly and created a fragrance called Rose and Insects—it’s one she often wears herself and contains no trace of rose, but honey, immortelle, papyrus and vetiver. “It’s about beauty, with imperfections,” she says.

She traces her love of fragrance back to her childhood in the Yorkshire countryside. “Nature has always been my thing,” she says. “From the minute I was born, I loved being outside.” Holidays were spent with her grandparents on their smallholding in the Scottish Highlands. “There was the smell of cooking, of jam, of the fire, of my grandmother’s garden with sweet peas and geraniums,” she recalls. “There isn’t a day goes by that I don’t think about that place.”

Her career has partly been shaped by the rhythm and simplicity of that carefully crafted life. “My grandfather was a carpenter. He had a place where he made furniture, and he always wore the same jacket, dungarees and boots,” she says. “My grandmother made our clothes. They didn’t buy a lot of things, but the way they curated their life with authenticity and dignity intrigued me.”

Clay, Harris’s latest perfume, captures the earth, the natural world embedded in it and even the light that bounces off it Photo: João Sousa

Recently she was inspired by her late grandmother to create a new fragrance called Soap for her friend Nick Wakeman’s fashion brand Studio Nicholson. In an episode of the label’s in-house podcast, Wakeman says the starting point of the project was sniffing fabrics and asking, “What does flax smell like? What does wool smell like? What does cotton smell like?” Then the conversation turns to how fabrics feel against the skin. “We wanted the perfume to feel like it was like a fabric that would veil you,” Wakeman says, while Harris tells me Soap is designed to be “a layer between your skin and your clothing. It’s clean, utilitarian and easy, with a whiteness—a starched smell that I’ve used sparingly.”

As a teenager in the 1980s, Harris was a rebel. She bleached her hair and dyed it red, and was eventually asked to leave her strict school. Her parents encouraged her to work in a perfume shop in their home town, and it was there she saw how scent could transform a person. “Women would come into the store and I could see how fragrance defined them—like lipstick, but more so,” she recalls. Today her work is still about how people feel when they wear her scents. She often tests then on any available “subjects”, including her son—her fragrances are intended to be unisex.

In 1992, she started training with Monique Schlienger, a renowned perfumer who had set up her own school in Paris in 1976. Perfume-making was traditionally a male-dominated field, but Harris was determined to be taught by a woman. “Monique taught me not to be scared of my emotions when being creative,” Harris recalls. She did further training at Robertet, in Grasse, near Cannes, before co-founding the luxury fragrance line Miller Harris in 2000. In 2015, she set up her own house, Perfumer H.

Harris describes her career as a continuous education. “In your first ten years you’re completely an innocent, finding who you are,” she says. “When your fragrances start to work in the marketplace, you become much more confident. In 20 years, you know your materials and your palette—you streamline, you cut back.” It has been a gentle progression. “Everything’s so rushed in today’s world,” she continues, “so a lot of new perfumers don’t have the luxury of time that I had. I would spend weeks floating around, dreaming.”

This summer, the first visitors to the fancy new St Clement Hotel in London have engaged inadvertently with Harris’s work. The hotel’s elegant foyer, hung with artworks by Richard Prince and Mark Grotjahn, is infused with a bespoke fragrance by Perfumer H. While the establishment takes its name from the nearby church of St Clement Danes in Aldwych, Harris has derived the scent’s bergamot and bitter orange notes from the opening lines of the nursery rhyme “Oranges and lemons, say the bells of St Clement’s.”

For the newly opened St Clement Hotel in London, Harris devised a bespoke citrus-based perfume, which infuses the building from foyer to penthouse Courtesy St Clement Hotel

The hotel’s founder Nick Jones, who also opened private members’ club Soho House in 1995, wanted something fresh, and told Harris that he especially likes the smell of freshly baked bread in the morning. She has blended that with toasted sesame, cardamom and tonka to develop what she calls a “moreish” smell.

“Lyn’s far cleverer at this than I am,” Jones says. “I’d have stopped at oranges and lemons; she’s put all this warmth underneath. When you walk in and smell it, you relax. You don’t know why, but you do.” Beyond the foyer, the same fragrance is used in all the soaps, hand creams, body lotions and haircare products throughout the hotel—in refillable glass bottles, at Harris’s insistence.

“It feels real and useful,” Jones adds. “It’s not scent as decoration, for its own sake. It does something.” And indeed for Harris, scent is anything but a decorative layer; it is an integral part of everyday living. It is not just in her grandmother’s garden, the soil of Jingdezhen or the stylish lobbies of St Clement, but “in my blood, my breath, my heartbeat”.

#69. vincent darré brings new life to historic paris theater with le magnifique hotel

the french designer brings his eccentric imagination to a historic building in montparnasse, filling its interiors with hand-painted frescoes, mythological references, bespoke furniture, and a swimming pool.

French designer Vincent Darré has brought his theatrical imagination to Hôtel Le Magnifique, a hotel on Rue de la Gaîté in Paris’ 14th arrondissement. Located in a neighborhood historically associated with theaters, cabarets, and the artistic life of Montparnasse, the project transforms hospitality into an immersive experience shaped by fantasy, mythology, and the performing arts. The building itself carries an unusual history, having originally housed Les Mille Colonnes, a renowned theater dating back to the early 19th century. Its historic façade now introduces a series of interiors where decorative elements, unexpected colors, and references to Parisian cultural heritage unfold throughout the hotel.

The project was initiated in 2024 by hotelier Jacques Blanc, who envisioned a property that would depart from conventional hospitality design. Already the owner of Bellechasse, a Parisian hotel designed by Christian Lacroix, Blanc approached Darré after an introduction through mutual friends. Their collaboration developed around a shared ambition to create something deliberately unconventional, with the designer’s initial proposals eventually expanding the scope of the project to include a swimming pool. For Darré, who was born in the 14th arrondissement and has spent his life on the Left Bank, the hotel also became an opportunity to revisit the artistic landmarks and personal memories of his childhood.

The theatrical narrative begins in the entrance hall, where Darré reinterprets architectural references from the surrounding neighborhood. The columns of the former theater have been redesigned in homage to those of La Coupole, the celebrated Montparnasse restaurant, and the former Saint-Germain-des-Prés drugstore, whose columns were once crowned with oversized sculptural hands. A large hand-painted fresco created by artisans extends across the walls, introducing colorful figures and swirling motifs inspired by art and the circus. White plaster birds emerge from the composition, adding a sculptural dimension to the illustrated surfaces.

Other details continue this dialogue between architecture and storytelling. The reception desk is decorated with antique keys collected over time, recalling the traditional front desks of historic hotels while introducing a playful reference to paradise and Saint Peter. Nearby, the staircase railings evoke musical scores, connecting the movement through the building to the district’s performing arts heritage. These interventions establish a visual language in which functional architectural elements become part of a larger decorative composition, drawing visitors into an imagined version of Paris shaped by Darré’s personal references.

At the heart of the hotel, Le Picabia, a bar named after the French painter Francis Picabia, draws inspiration from the atmosphere of historic Parisian theaters. Clad in wood and illuminated by rows of glowing bulbs, the space combines a curved counter with richly colored surfaces and decorative details that recall theatrical interiors. The bar is designed to operate in rhythm with the neighboring performance venues, displaying showtimes and ringing a bell at the beginning of performances and the end of intermissions. A grand piano introduces the possibility of spontaneous musical encounters, while the setting welcomes theatergoers, neighborhood residents, artists, and hotel guests.

Another unexpected feature is the hotel’s swimming pool, conceived as a mythological retreat within the building. Visible from the reception area, the pool is surrounded by columns and decorated with mosaics depicting classical figures, creating an atmosphere reminiscent of a Greek palace. The blue-tiled basin opens onto a patio, establishing a visual connection between water, architecture, and garden. Its decorative treatment continues Darré’s interest in transporting visitors into imaginary settings, with references to antiquity extending the hotel’s narrative beyond the history of Montparnasse.

The experience continues through five floors, each conceived around a different imaginary universe. A glass elevator decorated with mermaids, seahorses, and starfish connects spaces inspired by the Garden of Eden, classical mythology, the deep sea, Art Nouveau, the Milky Way, and legendary artists from Paris’ past. Rather than following a uniform decorative scheme, the hotel moves between different periods and visual references, allowing each level to introduce a new chapter. This sequence of environments reflects Darré’s approach to interior design as a form of storytelling, where architecture, ornament, and imagination are closely connected.

The guest rooms follow the same principle, with each conceived as an individual composition featuring original pieces imagined by the designer. Bespoke furniture, lighting, ceramics, carpets, and stretched wall textiles contribute to interiors that combine French decorative traditions with Darré’s distinctive visual vocabulary. The hotel’s name itself pays tribute to the artists of Montparnasse, whose initial, the letter M, inspired Le Magnifique, while also referencing the spirit of the French Nouvelle Vague. Through its layered interiors, the project reconnects the building with the creative history of the Left Bank, transforming a stay in Paris into a journey through the designer’s theatrical imagination.

#70. TDC 43rd Annual — Editorial Design by Tereza Bettinardi

Tereza Bettinardi crafts the editorial design for The 43rd Annual of the Type Directors Club, turning expanded counterforms into a bold book.

Designing an awards annual for the Type Directors Club of New York carries real weight. Since 1955, the competition has invited names like Paula Scher, Chip Kidd, Collins, and Triboro to shape its annual monograph. When the club tapped Tereza Bettinardi Studio in 2021 to build the identity and book for the 68th competition, published in 2022 by Verlag Hermann Schmidt as The World's Best Typography, she looked right inside the letters themselves. Working alongside Gabriela Gennari and Lucas DâAscenÃ§Ã£o, Bettinardi built the entire system around expanded counterforms â the trapped negative spaces inside letterforms. Those inner shapes do all the talking.

Pick up the hardcover and you feel that tension right away. Across the fluorescent pink front board, metallic silver foil and matte black geometric blocks trace the interior voids of the letters t d c and the numerals 43, while a black cloth spine stamped in crisp white condensed caps anchors the binding. Open the cover and the paper stock hits you first. A matte black endpaper faces an electric pink sheet where the lowercase tdc counterforms glow in acid-green and yellow gradients. On the title spread for the 68th Communication Design and 25th Typeface Design competitions, custom display headlines flip positive and negative space so solid black counterforms carve out every glyph.

Nothing in the grid feels static. Set in InDesign and printed in Cracow, Poland, the colophon and table of contents pit a pink left page against a pitch-black right page, pairing Dinamo's sharp serif Laica A with Commercial Type's condensed Proxy Cond. That pacing shines in the opening tribute to TDC Medalist Akira Kobayashi. A monochrome portrait over an acid-yellow gradient faces a full-page MEDALIST geometric lockup, leading into Emma Tucker's three-column essay alongside red, yellow, and blue specimen cards for Akko Rounded, DIN Next, and Neue Frutiger, an ornamental FF Clifford Pro broadside, and a bilingual Tazugane Gothic map of JR Harajuku Station. It's a typographic index that reads like an exhibition.

#71. Fujifilm Invests Another $19 Million To Expand Instax Production

Fujifilm Invests Another $19 Million To Expand Instax Production

Fujifilm has announced a 3 billion yen investment in its Instax production facilities, equivalent to nearly $19 million at current exchange rates. It follows an even greater Instax investment the company announced nearly a year ago.

Fujifilm Corporation says its 3 billion yen investment is going to the Ashigara Site at its Kanagawa Factory and will “reinforce production facilities for Instax film.”

“In order to cater to the growing global demand for the instax series, Fujifilm has been continuously expanding the production capacity of instax film,” Fujifilm says in a press release. “The newly enhanced production facilities will begin operations in stages from spring 2027 and are expected to be fully operational from spring 2028. When the new production lines become fully operational, instax film production capacity will increase by approximately 20% compared to FY2026.”

Since Fujifilm launched Instax film in 1998, nearly 30 years ago, the company has found significant success. Arguably, Instax film really took off once digital had fully taken over the photography industry. Last year, Fujifilm announced that it had sold its 100 millionth Instax camera and printer. Just a couple of months ago, PetaPixel reported that, once again, Fujifilm’s Instax business made up much of Fujifilm’s overall profits.

This is actually the company’s second sizable investment into Instax production in less than a year. Last December, the company announced it was investing approximately 5 billion yen to expand its Instax production capabilities at the same Ashigara site in Kanagawa. The expansion was slated to begin in spring 2026, but Fujifilm clearly believes even more is necessary.

Fujifilm noted today that it has been continuously expanding Instax production capabilities since 2022. Once the latest investment is realized, product capacity will have increased by about 70% since FY2022.

Fujifilm’s first recent investment in 2022 was about 2 billion yen, and the company invested another 4.5 billion yen in Instax production the following year.

“Fujifilm will continue to explore the limitless possibilities of photography, expand the world of instax instant photo system that allows people to enjoy on-the-spot photo printing,” Fujifilm promises. The company’s Instax success surely shows no signs of slowing down.

#73. Sophia Huitema "Prussian Blue" @ Harper’s Apartment

Harper’s is pleased to announce Prussian Blue, New York–based artist Sophia Huitema’s first solo exhibition with the gallery. The presentation features new works by Huitema and will be on view through April 25, 2026.

Across the seven oil paintings on view, the visual and chemical properties of the pigment Prussian Blue function as a metaphorical anchor, tying together a cast of watchful female figures within Huitema’s hazy, dreamlike worlds. Working within a restrained range of blue and green tones, the paintings evoke a moody atmosphere through cool harmonies and dimly lit interiors. Prussian Blue, derived from chemical processes historically linked to cyanide while also used as an antidote to certain forms of poisoning, embodies a rare duality in which toxicity and protection converge, mirroring the emotionally guarded, ambiguous presence of Huitema’s figures.

The tension between beauty and menace permeates Huitema’s subjects. Elongated figures with exaggerated limbs and slender necks slink through each scene, often directly confronting the viewer’s gaze. Set within opulent surroundings that recall Gatsby–era decadence, Huitema’s women bear the markers of high society themselves, dressed in elegant gowns and adorned with pearl necklaces or jewel-studded headdresses. Moving through film-noir settings with poise and a quietly calculating air, these femme fatales seem either to lure their audience into a seductive ruse or to deploy their own cunning to evade danger. In Sleeper Car, for example, a woman fitted in a backless evening gown tilts her head slyly over her right shoulder in a relaxed pose while her right hand appears braced and ready to strike. As rain streaks across the coach’s windows and the narrow aisle stretches into an uncertain depth, a moment of cinematic suspense emerges, evoking the apex of a psychological thriller. In this way, Huitema constructs a world of heightened atmosphere and theatrical tension that opens onto the broader visual traditions and painterly languages informing her work.

Huitema’s paintings draw on a range of art-historical and visual references while maintaining a distinct internal coherence. The attenuated proportions and stylized poses of her figures recall traditions of early twentieth-century fashion illustration and Art Deco design, where gesture and embellishment echo the streamlined finesse of illustrators such as Erté and the theatrical poise found in interwar couture and stage design. Her compressed spaces also suggest affinities with aspects of Symbolist and Surrealist painting, in which shallow interiors and phantasmagoric backdrops function less as coherent environments than as psychological realms shaped by subconscious experience. Rather than aligning with a single historical framework, Huitema synthesizes these influences into a contemporary visual language that moves fluidly between illustration, painting, and cinematic staging. Working outside formal academic training, she has developed this vocabulary through sustained studio practice and close observation, resulting in a body of work that situates itself in dialogue with art history while remaining grounded in a self-directed approach to image making. In this context, Prussian Blue operates not only as a chromatic throughline but also as a conceptual one, binding together Huitema’s historical references and recurring motifs of protection and threat in constant tension.
