#74. Golf clubhouse by Graham Baba nods to farm structures in rural Washington

US studio Graham Baba Architects used timber and board-formed concrete to create “warmth and depth” at the Westwood Golf clubhouse and driving range in an agricultural region.

The project is part of a nine-hole golf course in the central Washington town of Yakima.

The semi-arid region is known for its orchards and hop fields, which the architects drew upon while conceiving the clubhouse and driving range.

“The new facilities are designed as a minimalist nod to agrarian structures,” said Graham Baba Architects, a Seattle studio.

The star element is the newly constructed, 12,000-square-foot (1,115-square-metre) clubhouse, which rises two levels and is L-shaped in plan. It contains hospitality space and 28 driving-range stations, including high-tech ones that can simulate golf courses found across the world.

The roof and upper floor are made of mass-timber panels, supported by steel and glued-laminated columns and beams. There is a 20-foot (six-metre) clear span between columns, allowing for unencumbered golf swings.

The facility departs from the standard driving-range facility in terms of its materiality.

“In contrast to more typical pan-deck and painted concrete driving ranges, the exposed timber structure introduces warmth and depth, creating a space that is as much about experience as it is about performance,” the team said.

Shade screens made of Corten steel wrap select areas of the building. Wooden boards were used to form the concrete walls, helping soften the building’s expression.

“The texture breaks down the scale of the concrete and introduces a horizontal rhythm that reinforces the building’s low profile across the flat site,” the team said.

“As light rakes across the surface, the lines draw the eye toward framed views of the green beyond.”

The ground level holds a restaurant, bar and pro shop, along with 14 driving range bays. The upper floor houses 14 additional bays, a second bar and an enclosed event space. A broad terrace overlooks the golf course.

“The lower range is more protected and shaded, shielded from wind and direct sun,” the team said.

“The upper level opens more fully to the air, capturing cross breezes and long views in both directions.”

Below the building is a golf cart garage and a supplemental kitchen to support the restaurant.

The site also includes a green roof and an on-site stormwater management system, which channels rainwater to a pond. The water is used to irrigate the site during the summer months.

Other golf facilities include an indoor club in Montreal by Ivy Studio that features rich shades of green and burgundy, and a golf performance centre in Los Angeles by HA+MA that is made of Alaskan cedar and handmade Danish bricks.

#75. Paris Students Shut Down the Louvre

Artist Rosana Paulino makes a self-portrait of Brazil, protests in France and Colombia, and this month’s edition of Beer With a Painter.

“Brazil is a country that has never really looked at itself,” artist Rosana Paulino — one of the nation’s representatives at this year’s Venice Biennale — tells curator and researcher Daniela Mayer in an interview today. So Paulino sets herself to the task, coopting the European form of the illustrated naturalist album — “images made by foreigners for foreigners” — to represent the experience of Black Brazilian women.

All the world over, art is a flashpoint for political struggle. In Paris, art students block the entrance of the Louvre to protest France’s overcrowded and underresourced schools, Staff Repoter Anna Lee writes. In Colombia, artists are out on the streets, fighting back against the right-wing president's removal of artworks by women and LGBTQ+ artists from the national museum, Senior Editor Valentina Di Liscia reports. And a new film reviewed by Greta Rainbow laments Iranian authorities’ search and seizure of an archive lovingly assembled by painter and conceptual artist Nasser Bakhshi in Tabriz.

Confiscating, censoring, destroying — it’s the very antithesis of art, which safeguards memory, gives voice to the marginalized, builds something new. As Paulino puts it, “Fascism is against art, isn’t it?

For Smiles Meyer, art is an act of divine transformation — both creatively and bodily. In 2024, the Los Angeles-based trans photographer and musician staged “The First Gathering,” in which they recreated Leonardo da Vinci’s “The Last Supper” (1495–98) with trans models. Meyer is part of a growing tradition of queer and trans artists visualizing queer identities with longstanding religious imagery, with artists like Elizabeth Ohlson Wallin recreating scenes including the Last Supper. The series builds on their previous projects like the Mary + I cover and nightclub exorcism shots taken for performance artist Maris, allowing them to unpack religious trauma through art that explores and celebrates their gender identity. | Emma Cieslik

#76. What’s Up with Elizabeth Holmes’s Weird Norman Rockwell–Inspired Background on X?

This article includes spoilers for You Can See Everything, a new documentary about Elizabeth Holmes now playing theatrically in the US.

Did it seem strange to you that Elizabeth Holmes’s X account remained so active after she reported to prison in 2023? You are not alone, and You Can See Everything, a new documentary about the businesswoman that was directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, may offer some reasons for the weirdness of her social media in the past few years.

As stated in the film, Holmes’s fiancé, Billy Evans, has been helping man her X account, which has opined on issues ranging from the assassination of Charlie Kirk to whether or not she is a fan of Taylor Swift. Evans claims in the documentary that he is merely posting messages sent to him by Holmes from prison, where she still has email access. Related Articles White House Historical Association's $7.2 M. Rockwells Are Finally on View A New Immersive Art Exhibition on the Sistine Chapel Is Coming to New Jersey Mall

But might he be putting words in her mouth and writing her posts for her? The film repeatedly raises that possibility, suggesting that Holmes may have lost control of her image while she remains incarcerated. (Her X posts are accompanied by her initials when she has actually written them, one post from September noted. “Posts without that signature are from the team managing this account,” that post continued.)

These questions have led many to revisit her X account, which includes a bizarre art connection in the form of her background: an image of Norman Rockwell‘s 1943 painting Freedom of Speech, in which a man stands up and prepares to speak before a crowd. Rockwell made the painting in response to Franklin D. Roosevelt’s 1941 State of the Union address, wherein he called the right to freedom of speech an essential one. The painting is these days best known as a meme image used alongside an unpopular opinion.

Except that in Holmes’s version, Holmes herself stands in place of the man, wearing her signature black turtleneck. Roosevelt’s painting looks like it has been edited digitally, perhaps using an AI generator. In light of You Can See Everything, it’s an unsettling image: Holmes is unable to entirely speak for herself, even though her X account suggests otherwise.

“There is never a perfect moment worth waiting for,” reads one X from the account that featured the full version of the Rockwell-inspired image. “You have to take every step, every action you can – especially in the worst of circumstances – to fight for every fraction of an inch forward.”

It’s not the only art-related post her account has made. There’s also one featuring Michelangelo‘s Pietà, along with a note that a book about the artist by Otto Mower.

“Last night I read an overview of Michaelangelo’s life by Otto Mower, a teacher who has very special meaning in our lives,” that post from September 2025 notes, misspelling the artist’s name. “He writes ‘for Michaelangelo, God was perfection. He felt that whoever strives for perfection is striving for the divine.’ Strive for the divine.”

That post notably does not have Holmes’s initials appended to it.

Neither does a post from April of this year that featured an image of Rembrandt’s 1633 painting The Storm on the Sea of Galilee, which was stolen from the Isabella Stewart Gardner museum in 1990 and has yet to be recovered. “Today is a storm on all the fronts, and so I rise through every wave,” the post says.

Will beauty become the new peak of professionalism?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It's 9:58; I have a cold, and in exactly two minutes I have a work meeting. Despite feeling like the physical embodiment of a big toe, luckily I've never felt the need to be particularly preened for these colleague gatherings, until I digitally slump myself onto Google Meet and see a message: "Touch up your appearance?"

As a Gen Z growing up in the digital age of Instagram and influencers, I'm no stranger to photo editing software, but for some reason, this innocent enquiry from Google stopped me in my tracks. Yes, we live in a filtered online world, but when did it leak into my workday? And more importantly, should I have to touch up my appearance for a meeting?

While I'm partial to a bit of social media brainrot, I've been wise to steer clear of overly filtered influencers for my self-preservation. I learned very quickly that the online world can blur reality and fiction, leading to a good ol' bit of body dysmorphia if I'm not careful.

With this in mind, I no longer edit my Instagram posts – not as some grand middle finger to FaceTune, but simply because I don't feel the need to anymore. This is what I look like... take it or leave it. But in this moment of morning flu-riddled weakness, I thought to myself, wouldn't it be nicer to look a bit more fresh?

Soon I was plunged down the rabbit hole of Google Meet's various appearance filters, from 'dewy fresh' to 'dramatic eye'. Each looks ridiculous on my sallow-skinned, sickness-ridden face – the beauty filter equivalent of a white-painted landlord special.

Each filter is designed in the style of a makeup aesthetic, likely an attempt to make female-presenting folks feel the need to be 'presentable', even when WFH. I note there are no masculine-leaning beauty filters – no 'rugged stubble' or 'handsome glow' to enhance their looks.

And yes, I realise I'm being dramatic (illness tends to do that to me), but Google Meet's silly filters point to a looming issue that worries me. At what point do we start to lose a sense of what we look like? Will future board meetings be full of flawlessly filtered execs? Will beauty become the new predominant form of professionalism?

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

I do not want to lose the privilege of joining a work call looking slightly haggard. Turning up in my natural form is not just a matter of convenience, but the assurance that I can be taken seriously in my career without the performance of beauty. While the suggestion to "Touch up your appearance?" is an option now, I fear one day it could be a mandatory professional demand.

#78. thai fishing boats inspire rirkrit tiravanija’s dining installation for we are ona in paris

created with we are ona and chef dalad kambhu for art basel paris 2026, the installation brings thai cooking and communal dining into two boat-shaped structures inspired by traditional fishing boats, transforming the act of sharing a meal into a collective artistic experience.

Thai artist Rirkrit Tiravanija has designed two monumental stainless steel tables inspired by traditional Thai fishing boats for Dalad’s, a temporary restaurant presented by We Are Ona during Art Basel Paris 2026. Installed inside a secret location near Place de l’Étoile, the elongated structures function simultaneously as dining tables and working kitchens, with integrated seating and steam pots that allow food to be prepared and served directly in front of guests. Conceived in collaboration with chef Dalad Kambhu and We Are Ona founder Luca Pronzato, the installation places cooking and social interaction at the center of the architectural experience.

Running from October 18 to 25, 2026, the Paris pop-up marks the debut of Dalad’s, a new hospitality project developed by Kambhu and Pronzato around contemporary Thai cuisine and the act of sharing food. Accommodating up to 100 guests, the temporary restaurant replaces conventional dining arrangements with two long communal structures where chefs and visitors occupy the same space. The project also marks Kambhu’s third collaboration with We Are Ona, following previous culinary experiences developed alongside designers Harry Nuriev and Marc Leschelier.

For Tiravanija, the boat-shaped design draws on Thailand’s longstanding relationship with its waterways and the informal food culture surrounding them. Speaking exclusively to designboom, the artist recalls running to the pier in Bangkok to buy boat noodle soup from vendors who prepared and sold their dishes directly from the water. These memories informed his decision to bring the kitchen and dining area together within a single structure, referencing an everyday tradition in which boats operate as places of exchange as much as means of transportation. ‘I think the form itself is both a vehicle and a platform,’ he explains.

The two modular structures reinterpret this relationship through stainless steel, transforming the recognizable silhouette of a fishing boat into a contemporary setting for collective dining. Their integrated cooking stations eliminate the usual separation between the kitchen and restaurant, allowing guests to watch the chefs at work from their seats. For Luca Pronzato, from We Are Ona, the design was also inspired by the practice of giving old fishing boats a second life as floating restaurants. ‘Rather than creating a traditional dining room with individual tables and a hidden kitchen, the boats become the structural backbone of the installation,’ he tells designboom. ‘The integrated steam pods bring the cooking directly into the long communal tables, dissolving the boundary between the kitchen and the dining room.’

At the center of the culinary experience is Thai-American chef Dalad Kambhu, whose approach combines traditional Thai flavors and cooking techniques with seasonal, locally available ingredients. Raised in Bangkok, Kambhu developed her culinary identity across different cities before opening Kin Dee in Berlin in 2017, where her interpretation of Thai cuisine earned a Michelin star in 2019. For Dalad’s, she continues exploring the relationship between food, cultural memory, and place through a menu served directly from the installation. The pop-up offers a four-course lunch and an eight-course dinner, bringing guests together around the preparation and sharing of each dish.

The collaboration also reflects a longstanding friendship between Kambhu and Tiravanija, whose shared interest in cooking extends beyond the restaurant itself. The artist explains that their conversations have often explored what it means to prepare Thai food in places where its traditional ingredients are unavailable, raising questions about cultural identity and authenticity. ‘So it’s like finding authenticity, which is your own, which is yourself, in a foreign place,’ Tiravanija tells designboom. This perspective carries through the Paris experience, where references to Thai culture and the collaborators’ personal histories extend from the recipes to the tableware and spatial arrangement.

Founded by Pronzato in 2019, We Are Ona has developed a series of temporary culinary experiences connecting gastronomy with art, architecture, and design, collaborating with figures including Carsten Höller, Cristina Celestino, and Sabine Marcelis. The installation for Dalad’s continues this approach while engaging directly with Tiravanija’s artistic practice, which has long challenged conventional exhibition formats through everyday activities such as cooking and eating. ‘For me, artworks are not simply objects to be observed; they are experiences to be lived,’ Pronzato explains to designboom. Within the Paris installation, the tables provide the physical framework, but the interactions between chefs and guests complete the work.

This relationship between participation and artistic experience is central to Tiravanija’s work, in which the boundaries between artist, audience, and artwork are deliberately blurred. At Dalad’s, the installation is activated through the preparation of food, the presence of diners, and the conversations that emerge around the communal tables. Rather than presenting the boats as sculptures to be admired from a distance, the project invites visitors to inhabit and use them, allowing the experience to change with every gathering. As Tiravanija puts it in his conversation with designboom, ‘a beautiful meal with friends and even strangers is a beautiful work of art.’

#79. Flashback’s New Analog-Inspired Half-Frame Digicam Is All Grown Up

Flashback’s New Analog-Inspired Half-Frame Digicam Is All Grown Up

Flashback has announced the One75, a new reusable digital camera that promises to bring the spirit and vibes of a classic half-frame film camera.

Unlike the Flashback One35 V2, which is effectively a “non-disposable disposable camera,” the One75 employs a more premium design and build quality.

While the $119 One35 V2 is predominantly plastic, the One75 features an aluminum and brass body, including stylish brass buttons on the top deck. The One75 also has a top OLED screen, something the One35 lacks, and a tripod mount, another feature the One35 omits.

Given that the One75 is inspired by classic half-frame cameras, it’s little surprise that its built-in viewfinder uses a portrait orientation rather than a more traditional landscape one.

As for the camera’s specs, it has a 13-megapixel digital image sensor, although Flashback doesn’t specify much else about the sensor, including its size. The company also doesn’t say anything about the built-in lens, other than that it has a thread to accept filters and other accessories. PetaPixel has reached out to Flashback for more information and will update this story accordingly if any arrives.

Flashback has shared other interesting details about the One75, including a built-in, old-school xenon flash. This means that photographers can recreate that classic flash look, something the relatively more common LED “flashes” on many new compact cameras cannot do.

The One75 also includes a self-timer, double-exposure mode, a replaceable glass lens protector, a rechargeable battery, internal storage, and RAW photo export (DNG files to PC or Mac only, not a smartphone). The camera recharges via USB-C, and Flashback says it should shoot through “around 15 rolls per charge.”

For those unfamiliar with how the One35 works, the One75 likewise has digital “film rolls.” The camera works alongside a phone (or computer), and that’s the only way that users can actually view their images. Photographers capture up to 27 shots per “roll,” and then transfer them to the app. In Digicam mode, users can view these images instantly in the app. While a “Classic Mode” recreates the waiting game associated with real-world analog photography, making users sit on their hands for 24 hours before they can see their shots. The app is free, by the way.

The Flashback One75 also includes built-in film types, another way it emulates the experience of film photography. It offers eight built-in styles, and users can also customize their own.

The Flashback One75 is available to preorder now for $179 in brushed aluminum and “noir” colorways, with shipping expected before Christmas. For a limited time, users can also get a free vegan leather case with the camera, which is $23 separately. While the camera is compatible with add-on accessories, none are available yet, and there are no details on what they will be.

#80. All six of Edward Hopper’s early oils, long thought to be original works, revealed to be copies

Edward Hopper's Old Ice Pond at Nyack (around 1898-1900, top) is in fact a copy of Winter Sunset by Bruce Crane (bottom), which was published in the December 1890 issue of Art Interchange magazine Hopper: Copyright 2026, Heirs of Josephine N. Hopper/Licensed by DACS, London; Image courtesy of Heather James Fine Arts. Crane: Photo by Louis Shadwick

Around the age of 13, Edward Hopper converted the attic of the Nyack family home into a makeshift painting studio and private haven. Here he put into action his dream of becoming a painter. Though he had attempted some watercolours in the early 1890s, Hopper now began painting in oils, demonstrating a newfound artistic seriousness.

The first oil that Hopper painted was probably Rowboat in Rocky Cove, a quaint image of a placid stretch of water replete with distant ships, signed and dated 1895. He produced at least five more finished oils before enrolling in art school, all left in the attic, remaining unseen for decades. When they were eventually discovered and exhibited after the artist’s death, they were heralded as his first original compositions in oil. But the truth of their origins revises the accepted story of Hopper’s artistic development.

The most intriguing of these early oils is Old Ice Pond at Nyack, made between 1898 and 1900. The painting has been regarded as one of Hopper’s only confirmed depictions of Nyack in oil, seemingly offering a window into his formative environments. Depicting a snowy landscape presided over by an evocative sunset, the work has been cited as evidence of the young artist’s talent, his romantic connection with the American scene from an early age, and his prophetic interest in sunlight as an agent of mood.

The title of the painting refers to the old ice pond in Nyack, which until the 1950s existed at the top of Main Street, a short walk from the Hopper family home. Postcards and photographs of the pond reveal its placid beauty in warmer weather and frenetic activity in the winter season, when it froze over and was thronged with skaters and ice cutters. Hopper’s illustration A Pair of Slippers, of 1899, alongside several other early drawings depicting ice skaters, suggests his participation in this annual tradition, since it portrays two boys—one a likely self-portrait—slipping about on a frozen pond.

Old Ice Pond at Nyack certainly does function as a window into the little-discussed cultural environment of Hopper’s youth, albeit not in the manner previously thought. The work’s title, placing the landscape in Nyack, did not come from Hopper at all. Rather, it was bestowed by the painting’s first owner, Reverend Arthayer R. Sanborn, shortly after the artist’s death. Sanborn had discovered Old Ice Pond at Nyack and Hopper’s other early oils in the attic of Hopper’s childhood home in the late 1960s, alongside a trove of unseen early drawings, oils and watercolours. Rowboat in Rocky Cove was stowed here, too, and was titled Rowboat on Hudson by Sanborn—once more linking the painting to the Nyack scenery of Hopper’s childhood. The title was later altered, but the original affiliations to Nyack stuck, with writers continuing to relate both paintings to Hopper’s childhood environments.

Neither Old Ice Pond at Nyack nor Rowboat in Rocky Cove bear any relation to Nyack. They are actually faithful copies after paintings by other artists. Old Ice Pond at Nyack is a copy of A Winter Sunset by the then-popular tonalist artist Bruce Crane, while Rowboat in Rocky Cove is a copy after the watercolour Lake View by an unknown painter. Crane’s Winter Sunset depicts a landscape in Long Island or Connecticut, while Lake View is inscribed “Athelstane” and so possibly depicts a lake near Athelstane, Wisconsin, though this may also suggest the signature of the unknown painter.

Both paintings appeared as collectable colour plates in the Art Interchange, a widely read periodical for amateur artists that encouraged its readers to copy from its pages. Crane’s Winter Sunset appeared in the December 1890 issue and Lake View in February 1891. In both cases, the colour plates were accompanied by comprehensive sets of copying instructions, which explains the existence of numerous other extant copies of A Winter Sunset by amateur artists. The instructions for Lake View stated that the painting was “a very simple subject and well adapted to beginners”. There is little mystery, then, as to why Hopper copied the plate for likely his first serious attempt at oil painting; indeed, his beginnings as a painter seem to have been much more tentative than previously imagined.

Lake View by an unknown painter, which appeared in the February 1891 edition of Art Interchange, is the basis for Edward Hopper's painting Rowboat in Rocky Cove (1895) Photo by Louis Shadwick

These were not the only copies Hopper made. All of his early oils before he enrolled in art school, long deemed original compositions, are in fact copies. His painting Country Road (around 1896) is a copy after a painting titled A Landscape Study in Color by the American tonalist artist John Francis Murphy. This work again appeared as a colour reproduction in the Art Interchange on 27 March 1886. Hopper’s Ships, meanwhile, produced around 1898, was a copy after Marine View by Edward Moran, which appeared in the Art Interchange’s issue of mid-August 1886. Another early Hopper oil, originally titled Winter Scene by Sanborn and later renamed Church and Landscape, was again a copy, not a portrayal of a “snowy Nyack Baptist church”, as one writer has claimed. Though its precise source remains unknown, its status as a copy is confirmed via the existence of two paintings of the same scene by the painter Edgar Barnes Gilson that date to 1893, as well as a Victorian porcelain plaque on which this same scene is depicted.

Across these works, Hopper made no acknowledgment that any were copies, signing them either with the initials “E.H.” of “E. Hopper”. Only Church and Landscape remained unsigned. Rather than any attempt to mislead, the signatures suggest the artist’s youthful pride in his earliest achievements in oil that were never intended to be seen publicly. In any case, it is possible that Hopper did not produce an original oil painting until he enrolled at the New York School of Art in the autumn of 1900. What’s more, contrary to prior belief, no boyhood oils of Nyack by the artist exist.

Of course, all aspiring artists copy. It has long been established that Hopper made sketches from printed material and that eventually, when he reached art school, he was encouraged to copy after other artists. But knowing that all of Hopper’s first oil paintings are copies challenges prevailing myths surrounding the artist—namely, that his gift for painting emerged during adolescence with essentially no instruction and that he was little exposed to American art groups or movements until art school.

Hopper’s copies reveal the artist’s close study of contemporaneous painting from an early age, most specifically his interest in a now overlooked style known as American tonalism that achieved widespread dominance around the turn of the 20th century. These discoveries open a window into the much broader cultural fabric of Hopper’s youth, not least the centrality of illustrated periodicals to both the values that the young Hopper absorbed and to his formative conceptions of American art and culture.

Most alcohol-free bottles try way too hard to mimic traditional wine chÃ¢teaux. They lean on heavy crest engravings or apologetic zero-proof badges. Colour-coded paper neck strips in yellow, coral-red, and mint-green fold right over the silver metal crown caps. Photographed by Anne Valeur on the wet brewery floor beside stainless-steel pressure gauges and coiled hoses, these bottles don't feel like a compromise at the table.

#82. OMA dresses faceted French courthouse in coloured glass

Photography by François-Xavier Gbré

Dutch studio OMA has completed the Palais de Justice de Lille, a six-sided law court in northern France with a faceted facade lined with coloured glass.

Located in Lille, the project was commissioned by the Ministry of Justice to host the city’s high and district courts.

Palais de Justice de Lille occupies a verdant landscape adjacent to a star-shaped fortification, built in 1667 by the French military engineer Sébastien Le Prestre de Vauban.

OMA’s design has a pointy, hexagonal form, with each elevation finished in coloured glass, intended to mimic this fortress.

The Palais de Justice de Lille is arranged in three volumes, accessed via a publicly accessible base.

Its first volume is a plinth that holds the major courtrooms, from which a triangular central tower containing minor courtrooms extends. Above, a faceted ring of offices surrounds the tower, which helps draw light into the building.

According to OMA, each volume has “its own material expression and spatial character, reinforcing clarity and orientation throughout the complex”.

However, they are unified by light finishes and furnishings, and an ambition to feel welcoming and “free of the intimidation”, it added.

Completing the Palais de Justice de Lille is a series of outdoor spaces, distributed across its three volumes.

This includes a public plaza at ground level and a roof garden overlooking the city.

OMA, officially known as Office for Metropolitan Architecture, was founded in 1975 in Rotterdam. It won a competition to design the courthouse in 2018 and was originally due to complete the project in 2023.

The studio’s other recent projects include an affordable housing development in San Francisco and a pyramidal building in Hangzhou designed as a “three-dimensional village”.

Other law courts featured on Dezeen include one in Toronto by Renzo Piano Building Workshop that aims to display “the identity and values of a modern justice institution” and a 10-storey federal courthouse by SOM currently under development in Florida.

Photography by François-Xavier Gbré

#83. Cinga Samson "Ukuphuthelwa" @ White Cube Gallery, NYC

South African artist Cinga Samson’s exhibition of new paintings is titled ‘Ukuphuthelwa’, an isiXhosa word in the artist’s native language that translates as ‘unable to sleep’. Unlike the English word ‘insomnia’, the isiXhosa term carries no negative connotation and accordingly, for Samson, sleeplessness is not a condition to be cured but a state of spiritual alertness, a sensitivity that deepens in the dark. Rendered in the artist’s signature occluded palette of near-blacks, carbon and deep Prussian blues, Samson’s scenes depict men-like figures, dogs in overgrown fields and portraits of plant life native to South Africa. Encouraging slow, contemplative looking, a sense of existential gravity pervades Samson’s new series of oil paintings, attempting to depict a vast reality that is continuously in motion. As the artist has it, his quandary pertains to the existential question of how to create a ‘true and honest painting'. The exhibition will be on view through April 18, 2026.

With ‘Ukuphuthelwa’, Samson considers his role as an artist in relation to his inability to represent the whole truth of reality, and the fact that he can merely make symbols. Between the static, painted sign and the fluid experience it gestures towards, he contends that there exists a gulf that no image can close. Though the technical mastery and convincing realism of these paintings appear to invite interpretation, the artist asserts that his work confronts the very dilemma of representation: that the image can only ever be a relative symbol of what it reflects, never its equivalent. Acknowledging the open-ended nature of symbols and their subjective interpretation, Samson takes the figure of the dog as an example. The viewer may, for instance, look at Intsingiselo II (2026) and perceive the loyalty conventionally associated with dogs, while an amaXhosa understanding might highlight the dog as signifying the guiding, protective principles of ancestors. Comprising painstaking detail and deft brushwork, Samson’s paintings do not disguise the limits of representation but, rather, aspire to harness his skills towards that which exceeds the representable. Above all, the artist’s work seeks out the authority of the unnameable and the territory of the sublime, one in which the divine is not found elsewhere but present in the vernacular of all things.

Samson’s larger compositions carry a palpable sense of reverence and ceremony. In Umlindo (Watcher) (2026), figures are gathered in a forest clearing with wildflower bouquets and lengths of fabric, a scene that carries the visual grammar of ritual without specifying its addressee or terms. For Samson however, ‘the ritual itself is not the important thing – it’s an opening to what exists beyond’, and the paintings use the aesthetics of ritual to speak to a collective need for orientation, as well as the capacity of ritual to mediate an encounter with a vast unknown. That the works are titled with enigmatic words and phrases in isiXhosa, such as Imfihlo (Secret) and Intsingiselo (Meaning) (both 2026), infer the same problem the paintings contend with – the instability of interpretation as it pertains to the knowable and unknowable. Each word carries a weight in isiXhosa that its English translation approaches but can never fully reach; here, just as between the painted sign and living referent, meaning slips between the interstice of two languages.

The objects, people and settings that recur in these paintings and across Samson’s oeuvre are identifiable and quotidian, yet Samson corrals in each an unexplained mystery. In Tshee (2026), a vast field stretches out, the silhouetted trees meeting a murky sky, though the void of the night is interrupted by a moonwashed cloud, its brilliant white destabilising the eerie, cold atmosphere suffused with majesty. ‘The sky can be so friendly, but sometimes so heavy, dark, so scary. It’s the same energy, but it exists in different forms’, Samson notes, conjuring an oscillation between the approachable and the overwhelming that recalls the affective register of the sublime. Sithini ngelilitye (2026), distils the same sensation: a rocky crag emerges from arid undergrowth, its surface rendered in forensic detail against a sky of barely-there wash, charging the scene with the same quality of mute enormity.

Marshalling light ‘like a magic trick’, Samson imparts a unique kind of rhythm to his paintings – a flickering that emerges and disperses across the picture plane, granting varying degrees of visibility to the dark, nighttime scenes. Producing an unsteadiness that is at once optical and psychical, the artist leaves large sections of the painting’s under-drawing visible to lend moments of transparency to the work. In Isiganeko (2026), for example, thin layers of glaze are applied and wiped back in his typical style, a means of building colour that lends the figures a brooding chromatic density, whilst elsewhere, in the undergrowth and the bird caught mid-flight, the under-drawing is left entirely exposed. In all Samson’s figures, the pupils of the eyes are left unpainted and allow ‘light’ to further circulate, a decision that renders them porous, so they are ‘completely one with the whole painting’. Without pupils, these figures are not personified identities, but ‘human’ forms enmeshed with the painting’s landscape and atmosphere, no element ever possessing full mastery over the other. In places where the ‘trick’ of painting reveals itself, it is as if Samson’s works were stepping back from the pretence or promise of representation. What ‘Ukuphuthelwa’ reaches towards is not individual transcendence in subordination, but rather the mystery that can be unearthed in ordinary forms, whose immanent magic is available to those who are sensitive to it. This is the condition that ‘Ukuphuthelwa’ ultimately describes: not an absence or deficit, but a hypersensitivity that affords everything in existence the same potential for eliciting wonder or fear. Samson’s pupilless figures do not ‘look’ outward because the figures’ knowing comes from within the world they inhabit, a shared knowledge that exists between the bowing foliage, the vigilant dog, the bird in flight and the foreboding of the night sky enshrouding them all. In Samson’s hands, each optical device and representational motif prises apart what it cannot contain, in service of painting ‘a thing that links us to God – by God, I mean everything’.

#84. Art Books on Needles and Threads

We recommend titles on fiber art, weaving, and textiles, plus Megan O’Grady on a new John Berger biography.

So much has been said about John Berger over the past five decades that it almost feels trite to pile on. You know the familiar takeaways: that the critic and novelist taught us how to look and pay attention, believed art belongs to the people, exposed how the male gaze shapes our perception. So, it’s especially astounding that a new biography by Tom Overton has managed to both capture the scope of Berger’s influence and reframe him, first and foremost, as human.

Author Megan O’Grady, who reflects on many of the same questions as Berger in her recent book How It Feels to Be Alive: Encounters with Art and Our Selves, penned a sensitive review of the biography and its approach to addressing the complex personal life of this near-mythologized figure. It’s a poignant, refreshing read, and reminds me of the conversation around the sanctification of artists and writers like James Baldwin, whose work gets flattened in the process.

In fact, how we tell the story of an artist’s life (and afterlife) just might be our primary preoccupation this month. Lauren Moya Ford reads one scholar’s novel approach to the canonized Vermeer, searching for the influence of his signature narrative ambiguity across mediums and forms. Meanwhile, Lavinia Liang grapples with a biography of Dorothea Tanning and its treatment of her relationship with her artist husband, Max Ernst, a perennial dilemma facing any author who seeks to move an overlooked woman’s legacy out of the shadow of her male partner.

More from our critics below, plus a round-up of some of our favorite recent art books on textiles, fabric, and fiber art. One of my personal go-tos is Stories in the Seams: A People’s History of Black Quilts and Their Makers by the wonderful Sharbreon Plummer, and we also recommend books on Palestinian embroidery, Diné weaving, and the Bayeux Tapestry. Read up, and let us know what’s on your list this month!

—Lakshmi Rivera Amin, associate editor, books

There’s a reason the lexicon of textiles and fiber lends itself so well to storytelling — we thread the needle, weave the tale, spin the yarn. Writers have reached for these metaphors for centuries because they feel true to life, but artists know they’re also true to craft and its tangled histories. We’ve gathered a few recent books on embroidery, fiber art, weaving, and more that deserve a closer look, from Black Southern quilting and Korean bojagi to Palestinian tatreez and contemporary Diné weaving. Refreshingly, so many of these titles complicate or refuse reductive, familiar frameworks and open up new ways to understand the meditative and political dimensions of textile traditions, moving past the false dichotomy of “craft versus art” and sexist and tired notions of “women’s work.” You might even say these books piece together a new history of textile art, stitch by stitch.

Discover R. Buckminster Fuller’s Intuition

New from David Zwirner Books: R. Buckminster Fuller’s lyrical case for intuition as the force uniting the sciences and the arts. Originally written in 1968 by the creator of the geodesic dome, this concise work returns with a new introduction by Anahid Nersessian as part of the ekphrasis series.

The late novelist and art critic asked Tom Overton to wait to write his biography until after his death. The result is deeply informative, deferential, and perceptive, sometimes lyrically so. | Megan O’Grady

Artists, filmmakers, poets, and the art market itself still bear traces of the Dutch painter’s influence, writes historian Ruth Bernard Yeazell. | Lauren Moya Ford

A team of researchers excavates the story of Earl Stendahl, a mid-century gallerist who shamelessly stole ancient Mesoamerican objects and marketed them to the institutional art world. | Armando Pulido

A new biography attempts to make the case for Tanning’s independence and artistic strength in her own right, but remains frustratingly tethered to her husband. | Lavinia Liang

Bold New Books in Art and Visual Culture from the MIT Press

From activist art and trans aesthetics to lowriders, global skateboarding culture, and Vilém Flusser’s prescient vision of the screen age.

Lakshmi Rivera Amin, associate editor, booksI’m digging into Story Telling: A Writing Life (2026), Isabel Allende’s new memoir of nearly five decades spent on her craft (thank you to the unusually short hold queue at the Brooklyn Public Library). At 84, she speaks plainly about approaching death; not fearfully or morosely but with reverence for the life she has led and the writing that animates it. I do find it telling that the original Spanish title is La Palabra Mágica: Una Vida Escrita. “The Magic Word” certainly feels more true to Allende’s literary worlds. Maybe I should put a library hold on a Spanish copy, too …

#87. designboom listens: what does space sound like to kengo kuma?

the music of ryuichi sakamoto, brian eno, and mulatu astatke offers a glimpse into the memories, rhythms, and ideas that accompany the architect’s creative practice.

For Japanese architect Kengo Kuma, music is closely tied to the way he thinks about space. A longtime admirer and personal friend of Ryuichi Sakamoto, he sees parallels between the composer’s approach to music and his own work in architecture. ‘He created a new image of what an Asian artist could be, crossing boundaries between East and West, tradition and modernity,’ Kengo Kuma tells us. His selections for this edition of designboom listens move between jazz, ambient music, classical compositions, and experimental sounds, with each track offering a different point of entry into his creative practice.

In our weekly series, we explore the music behind creative practice, asking people from different fields what they listen to when they need inspiration, get stuck on a project, or find themselves drawn back to a particular memory. For the architect, these questions lead back to the relationship between sound and space. Reflecting on Brian Eno’s 1/1, from Ambient 1: Music for Airports, he shares: ‘Brian Eno taught me that music can create an environment, rather than simply exist within it,’ an idea he hopes to bring into his own work. Cecil Taylor’s unconventional structures remind him that ‘sometimes we need to destroy existing rules in order to discover something new,’ while Beethoven’s Seventh Symphony echoes his interest in how simple elements come together to form a larger whole. Find out what Kengo Kuma listens to while working, reflecting, and finding inspiration, and tune in to the full playlist below.

What song best captures your creative practice? Kengo Kuma (KK): Ryuichi Sakamoto – andata (from async). Ryuichi Sakamoto was also a personal friend of mine. He created a new image of what an Asian artist could be, crossing boundaries between East and West, tradition and modernity. His approach to music has always been a great inspiration to my architecture.

What is the very first track you play to clear the air and get inspired when starting a new project? KK: Mulatu Astatke – Yèkèrmo Sèw (Homeless Wanderer). I love the unique rhythm and the way different musical traditions come together. It encourages me to think beyond established forms and conventions.

Is there a song that instantly takes you back to a specific memory or place from your past? KK: Yumi Arai – Hikōki-gumo. This song evokes the landscapes and atmosphere of Japan in my younger days. Music has the power to bring back memories of places that no longer exist.

What song is stuck in your head right now? KK: Ryuichi Sakamoto – Bibo no Aozora. There is something both delicate and powerful about this melody. It stays with me, like a landscape that continues to exist in one’s memory.

What is your ultimate 2 AM studio track? KK: Herbie Hancock – Chameleon. The repetitive rhythm creates an incredible energy. I like how a simple pattern can develop into something complex and unpredictable.

What song do you put on when you are stuck and need a breakthrough? KK: Cecil Taylor – Steps (from Unit Structures). Cecil Taylor completely breaks away from conventional musical structures. His music reminds me that sometimes we need to destroy existing rules in order to discover something new.

What track is dominating your speakers this week, and is it influencing what you are making right now? KK: Abdullah Ibrahim – Bra Joe from Kilimanjaro (from African Piano). This music brings back memories of my travels in Africa. I was deeply impressed by the landscapes, the people, and the strong connection between everyday life and nature. His music reminds me of the unique rhythms and atmosphere I experienced there.

What song helps you slow down and focus on the tiny, quiet details? KK: Brian Eno – 1/1 (from Ambient 1: Music for Airports). Brian Eno taught me that music can create an environment, rather than simply exist within it. This idea has deeply influenced the way I think about space. I want to achieve something similar through architecture, creating an atmosphere rather than just a physical object.

If people were to wear headphones while experiencing your latest work, what one song should be playing? KK: Ryuichi Sakamoto – 20220302 – sarabande (from 12). The simplicity and fragility of this piece are deeply moving. I hope my architecture can create a similar experience, where even the smallest elements become meaningful.

What is your favorite album cover art? KK: Ryuichi Sakamoto – Merry Christmas, Mr. Lawrence (Original Soundtrack). The visual identity of this album is inseparable from the atmosphere of the film and its music. It shows how an image can carry an entire world of emotions and memories.

What track best describes your favorite project you have worked on so far? KK: Beethoven – Symphony No. 7, II. Allegretto (NHK Symphony Orchestra). I am fascinated by the way simple, repetitive elements gradually form a powerful structure. This is very close to my approach to architecture, where small pieces come together to create a larger whole.

#88. Hilma af Klint painting could break artist's record next month in Stockholm

An abstract painting by the pioneering Swedish artist Hilma af Klint will be sold at the Stockholm auction house Bukowskis on 19 November, with an estimate of SEK6m to SEK8m (around $600,000 to $800,000).

Ser III No. 5, which measures 38.5cm by 29cm, was bought by a private collector in 1995, when it was deaccessioned by the Hilma af Klint Foundation, and has remained in the same hands ever since.

The oil and graphite on canvas is dated January 1920, a time when af Klint’s was at her most productive, making 85 works in just a few months, a flurry of subtly different arrangements of triangles, circles, and rectangles punctuated with symbols and signs, including variations of the Theosophical Society’s seal. However, this spurt of hard-edged geometric abstraction came to an abrupt stop in March 1920 when af Klint took a break from painting to study Goethe’s colour theory before restarting in 1922 with looser, wet-in-wet watercolours inspired by anthroposophical artistic principles.

It is highly unusual for af Klint’s work to come to auction, as her foundation (established in 1972 by her nephew and heir, Erik af Klint) tightly controls the supply of her abstract paintings. Those that do come onto the open market tend to be earlier, more traditional landscape paintings, such as Vid ankdammen, a watercolour on paper of a mother and child watching ducks from 1910, which sold for £40,640 at Christie’s in March, far above the £6,000 to £8,000 estimate. Such a dearth of supply also means the record for af Klint’s work is relatively low, at $165,825 for The Power of the Spleen, a watercolour on paper from 1931, which sold at Stockholms Auktionsverk in 2019.

“The artist’s non-figurative legacy is preserved and administered by the Hilma af Klint Foundation, and her abstract paintings have consequently remained almost entirely beyond the reach of the public art market,” says Louise Wrede, the head of Bukowski’s art department, adding that only two abstract paintings (as opposed to works on paper) by af Klint have previously sold at auction, “both more than three decades ago.”

Inspired by natural sciences, spirituality and philosophy, af Klint (1862–1944) was an artist well before her time and her visionary abstracts were little appreciated in her lifetime. It was only in 1986, when some of her work (including this very painting, Ser III No. 5), was featured in the Los Angeles County Museum of Art’s show The Spiritual in Art: Abstract Painting 1890-1985, which brought af Klint’s work to an international audience.

Since then her star has risen, and particularly sharply since 2018, when the Guggenheim Museum in New York held Hilma af Klint: Paintings for the Future, a much-lauded show which became the most visited exhibition in the museum’s history with over 600,000 visitors. The public and institutional appetite for af Klint’s work show no sign of abating—the first major retrospective of her work in France took place at the Grand Palais in Paris over the summer, Hilma af Klint: Paintings for the Temple (1906–1915), and just last week, the National Gallery of Ireland opened Hilma af Klint: Artist and Visionary, which runs until 7 February 2027.

The Narnia: The Magician's Nephew trailer has sparked a lot of debate about Greta Gerwig's upcoming interpretation of CS Lewis's novel. The first story in the Narnia saga chronologically but the sixth to be published, the novel has been passed over for screen adaptations until now, perhaps partly because it's the most fantastical of the seven.

If you want to read it before Netflix's movie reaches cinemas in February, publisher HarperCollins has a treat for you. It's re-publishing the entire Narnia series with cover art inspired by the film: and the special editions are more interesting to look at that the usual movie tie ins.

A post shared by The Chronicles of Narnia (@official_narnia)

The seven books in The Chronicles of Narnia have sold more than 120 million copies worldwide and have been adapted into more than 60 different languages to date. There's long been a debate about the best order to read them: the Magician's Nephew first, or before The Last Battle to reflect the order of publication?

Either way, there's a new Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew Movie Tie-in Paperback going on sale November 10, 2026. But more interesting visually is the Deluxe Collector’s Edition with a shimmery foil jacket, foil-stamped case, digital printed edges and endpapers and vibrant cover illustration.

Unlike many movie tie-in, this edition eschews photography from the film and shows its connection in a different way: the artwork is by Vance Kovacs, who was the concept artist for the film.

Vance's previous work has ranged from Dungeons & Dragons to movies like The Lion King and Jungle Book and Black Panther to games like God of War. His Magician's Nephew cover depicts Aslan singing Narnia into existence, with vibrant streams of light, stars, and colors bursting upward from the lion's mouth.

Five emblems suspended within the rays of light feature key elements from the story: Fledge, the winged horse, Aslan's Profile, the apple of life, the lamppost and a bell-hammer representing the world of Charn.

#90. Hundreds Protest in Colombia After Far-Right President Removes Works From National Museum

In a Trumpian move, the government of Abelardo de la Espriella took down works referencing LGBTQ+ and women’s rights and political violence.

Hundreds protested at Colombia’s national museum in Bogotá this weekend, days after the country’s far-right government ordered the removal of objects addressing political violence, women’s rights, and LGBTQ+ history — including a rainbow Pride Flag — in a move straight out of the Trumpian playbook.

Inside the museum, images taken by locals showed stripped-down gallery walls bearing the haunting silhouettes of dismantled pamphlets and photographs; at the entrance, rows of police in riot gear stood at the ready to suppress demonstrators with water cannons and stun grenades.

Under the order of President Abelardo De la Espriella, approximately 30 artworks referencing LGBTQ+ and feminist movements, victims of state violence, and the “Acuerdo de Paz,” the 2016 peace negotiations between the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) and the government, were removed from display at the Museo Nacional de Colombia last week.

De la Espriella said he had instructed Minister of Culture Paola Holguín to ensure that “all those odes to terrorism featuring Pizarro and the other terrorists are removed from public places,” invoking the name of Carlos Pizarro Leongómez, a former guerrilla commander and one of three presidential candidates assassinated in 1990.

Among the withdrawn works were a Humberto Rincón Perfetti photograph from an LGBTQ+ rights march, a Pride Flag that belonged to activist Elizabeth Castillo, and a pamphlet on women's reproductive rights. Also removed were ephemera addressing the assassinations of Pizarro Leongómez and leftist leader Bernardo Jaramillo Ossa of the Patriotic Union Party, as well as a pen made out of a bullet that was used to sign the 2016 agreement with the FARC. Crafted by the Ministry of Education under then-President Juan Manuel Santos, the pen was inscribed with the phrase, “Bullets wrote our past, education will write our future.”

De la Espriella’s directive drew widespread and immediate condemnation from members of Colombia’s arts community. Over the weekend, leaders at six modern art museums across the country penned a joint declaration expressing "deep concern" over the works’ withdrawal and calling on the culture minister to reverse the decision.

“Museums have the responsibility of allowing us to know the complexity of our history, including that which makes us uncomfortable, confronts us, or is difficult for us to acknowledge,” read the statement, signed by the directors of modern art museums in Medellín, Bogotá, Cartagena, Barranquilla, and El Tolima, as well as the Museo El Rayo.

Beatriz López, co-founder and artistic director of Instituto de Visión gallery in Bogotá and New York, denounced the silencing of voices that “long occupied the margins of the official narrative” in a statement shared with Hyperallergic.

“May the objects return to a place where they can recover their voice, and may the museum once again be a space where history is not dictated but researched, shared, and kept open to questioning,” López wrote.

Reached for comment, a representative for the Museo Nacional directed all press inquiries to the Ministry of Culture. The latter referred Hyperallergic to Culture Minister Holguín’s posts on X, in which she states that the museum may not serve as “an instrument of political indoctrination” or “a hub for spreading biased versions of our history.”

Echoing President Donald Trump’s crackdown on the Smithsonian Institution and exhibits that grapple with slavery, civil rights movements, and diversity, most of the objects targeted by De la Espriella’s officials were in a gallery dedicated to Colombian social and political history. Inaugurated in 2019, the “Making Society” gallery examines “processes of coexistence, resistance, and revindication,” according to a museum description.

Other items were displayed in a section devoted to socially engaged printmaking and photography of the 1950s and ’60s. Among the targeted pieces were works by late artists Antonio Caro, known for his subversive interventions into mass-media symbols like the Coca-Cola logo, and Luis Caballero, celebrated for his paintings of the male nude.

De la Espriella, a former criminal defense lawyer with no previous political experience, was sworn in this August after defeating leftist senator Iván Cepeda by the narrowest margin in the country’s recent history. He campaigned on a conservative “antiwoke” agenda redolent of the right-wing rhetoric taking hold across Latin America, with El Salvador’s Nayib Bukele and Argentina’s Javier Milei.

Bogotá-based independent curator Jaime Cerón, who curated the city's 2025 biennial, told Hyperallergic that removing works from the national museum aligns with the administration’s broader attacks on the arts. In September, the Culture Ministry suspended a long-running federal stimulus program for artists and creative workers, drawing backlash.

“The changes the Colombian government has made overall represent a setback for the cultural rights of communities that, throughout history, have been rendered invisible, marginalized, or censored,” Cerón said.

But Cerón also said he believes De la Espriella’s directive will backfire spectacularly.

“Acts of censorship have become the most effective way to make what one wants to erase omnipresent and ultra-visible,” Cerón said.

He cited the case of the Medellín mural “Las cuchas tienen razón” (“The mothers were right”), which honored the women searching for their disappeared children after a period of violent paramilitary conflict. When the city’s mayor had the mural whitewashed, artists quickly repainted it, and the titular phrase subsequently spread to walls and fences across the country with unprecedented fervor.

Medellín-based artist Pablo A. Medina shared a similar sentiment.

“This goes beyond a shameless act of censorship,” Medina told Hyperallergic. “It's also an attempt to erase a history and culture that are an undeniable part of this country. But what they don't realize is that what you try to erase only becomes stronger.”

#91. Leica Competitor Pixii Is Facing Financial Collapse

Leica Competitor Pixii Is Facing Financial Collapse

French camera maker Pixii has reportedly entered judicial liquidation, France’s formal insolvency procedure.

As Leica Rumors reports, Pixii has faced significant financial challenges for nearly a year. The company entered court-supervised restructuring last December, an attempt to get the company’s financial situation in order.

On May 20, 2026, the Commercial Court of Besançon, which initiated the restructuring, extended Pixii’s period under observation until December 10, 2026. However, on July 22, the court converted the restructuring process into a liquidation one. The court officially entered the liquidation judgment in France’s business notices in early August, and the company was authorized to continue business operations until July 31, 2026.

While Pixii’s website still exists, the company is pushing its latest camera update, and its cameras are still available for purchase, the company is effectively done with new business, at least for now. As Leica Rumors notes, Pixii has been seeking investors, partners, collaborators, and any other company that can help it survive and release its next product.

That’s right, “next product.” Nearly a year ago, in October, Pixii began teasing its first redesigned digital rangefinder camera. While its first three cameras, including the Pixii and Pixii Max that are available for purchase now, looked essentially the same, the next camera promised a very different form.

Unfortunately, it seems unlikely this camera will ever see the light of day.

As for Pixii’s current cameras, the Pixii Max is $500 off right now, and has been for a while, bringing it down to $4,499. It’s a 24.5-megapixel full-frame digital rangefinder with a Leica M mount. The 26-megapixel APS-C Pixii (A2572+) is $800 off, bringing it down to $2,799.

Pixii MaxBuy new on B&HPixii MaxBuy used on KEH.comPixiiBuy new on B&HPixiiBuy used on KEH.com

“Judicial liquidation” is an interesting term, and one worth looking at more closely. This formal insolvency procedure means Pixii has been legally ordered to stop all business activities and work to pay its creditors, including by selling its assets. It is effectively a last resort and a way to try to make creditors whole.

Technically, one path out of this situation is for a company to swoop in, acquire Pixii in part or in whole, and resolve the debt issue. If Pixii can resolve its debt issues one way or another, it could resume operations. Any potential resolution requires approval from the French commercial court before it can proceed.

It certainly doesn’t look good for Pixii right now, which is a real shame. While PetaPixel did not especially like the Pixii Max, it is undeniably a good thing for a small, niche company to try and make compelling digital rangefinder cameras and offer real competition to the monolithic Leica. If Pixii ultimately withers on the vine and never releases its new camera, that is just sad.

Hopefully a miracle arrives, and Pixii can continue to exist. The photography industry deserves more players.

PetaPixel has reached out to Pixii for comment.

#92. Historic town hall in Limoges set on fire during French protests

Photography by Sergey Dzyuba via Shutterstock

Significant parts of the 143-year-old Limoges Town Hall in France have been destroyed in an arson attack, as protests broke out across the country over the weekend.

On 17th October, Limoges Town Hall was set on fire. Videos taken by people on the ground show its slate roofs ablaze and its central bell tower collapsing.

Officials have not yet confirmed the state of the town hall and whether the rest of the building is at risk of collapse, according to the BBC.

Designed by French architect Charles-Alfred Leclerc, the neo-Renaissance Limoges Town Hall was built in 1883 and was listed as a historical monument in 1975.

An estimated 550,000 people in France took to the streets over the weekend to protest the rising cost of living and poor school conditions.

Some demonstrations turned to violence and disorder, with hundreds of shops being looted and destroyed. Around 2,400 people have been arrested.

In addition to Limoges Town Hall, other buildings in France were set on fire in arson attacks, including a tourist office in Lyon.

The mayor of Limoges has demanded a “Notre-Dame plan” to restore the town hall. A huge fire broke out at the iconic Notre-Dame Cathedral in Paris in 2019, which saw the Gothic landmark’s 90-metre-high spire and parts of the roof collapse.

After five years of reconstruction work, the cathedral reopened in 2024 with restored interiors and the spire rebuilt as a replica of the 1859 version lost to the fire.

#93. Nuart Aberdeen 2026: Poetry In The Streets

Welcome to the latest edition of Nuart Aberdeen. As far as we can ascertain, this will be the first street art festival in the world with a focus primarily on poetry and text-based works. Over the years, for better or worse, the large scale colourful figurative mural has come to dominate the culture we work with, and although it’s an aspect of the culture we support, due to the resources required to produce murals, they’re perhaps also the least democratic form of art on the streets. As curators, researchers and producers working in “festival” culture, we have a responsibility to not only showcase and celebrate the most interesting and technically competent works of our time, but to also ensure the culture’s development and survival. The only way to do this, is to inspire and encourage those without the privilege of a fine art degree or access to the arts, to have a go themselves. This has always been Nuart’s primary goal, not just to produce art, but to also inspire and produce the next generation of artists. A lofty goal, particularly as it’s often in conflict with the stated needs of sponsors and partners, on paper at least, and no one stands in front of a Tower block mural and thinks, I’ll pop home and have a go myself on the gable end of Gran’s house.

What we do have evidence for, is that the smaller, more human scale works – the stencils and paste ups and interventions – do have this effect. You could say that the ease of copying a Banksy stencil, which requires no more than a craft knife, a piece of cardboard and an idea, is the very foundation of this culture. We’ve seen this happen time and time again. Indeed, several of the producers and artists joining us this year, started their artistic journey as assistants and volunteers at Nuart.

At Nuart, we’ve always prided ourselves on not only showcasing the BIG names in muralism, but on also using the festival as a place to explore and experiment with new forms and ideas that engage with the idea of the whole city as a canvas, and not just the wall. In this respect, Nuart Aberdeen have been fortunate enough to have the support of some of the most thoughtful and progressive partners that an event such as Nuart could possibly have, and this year is no different.

Whilst pondering this issue, how to balance the needs of partners, tourist boards, with the need to impress the public, and create works of curiosity and interest for scholars which inspire the next generation, I imagined a city without art on the streets, with no forms of public expression, where all art is concealed behind the walls of city institutions and under guard 24/7. And then I recalled a piece of graffiti sprayed on the walls of Paris during the 1968 student uprising, an event which saw waves of creative energy explode onto the streets. It read, “La poésie est dans la rue”, or “Poetry is in the Streets” – could we harness some of this energy at Nuart to revitalise and energise the culture?

A short while later, I remembered a quote from pioneering UK graffiti writer Mode2. He was discussing how graffiti culture had taken hold and blossomed in the UK in the 1980s, and in a throwaway quip had said, the reason it took hold was because regardless of how interested you were in making art at school, if you couldn’t draw or paint realistically, you were bottom of the class. Then graffiti came along, and it struck everyone that all you had to know to create and engage with it, was your ABC’s.

And that was it. It was these two quite innocuous events that formed the genesis of this year’s poetry and text based Nuart. These are forms of creative expression that we all have access to and I hope the festival sparks the public’s imagination in the same way that those early bubble letters and Banksy stencils did.

Thank you as ever to all of our sponsors, partners and to the city council, for allowing us once again to make a contribution to what we believe is a magical and inspiring city.

— Martyn Reed, Nuart Founder and CuratorArtists include: Alisa Oleva (UK) Ciarán Glöbel (SCT) dr.d AKA Subvertiser (UK) HICKS (UK) James Klinge (SCT) KMG (SCT) Molly Hankinson (UK) Remi Rough (UK) Robert Montgomery (SCT) The Rebel Bear (SCT) The Writing Is On The Wall (UK) Trackie McLeod (SCT)  V2k | (LT - SCT)

#94. Inside the Craft of Peko-Peko branding by Manifiesto

Manifiesto's Peko-Peko branding builds a 3D universe where kawaii meets Mexican cariÃ±o, anchored by a balloon-letter logo.

Mexico City studio Manifiesto calls the project "Mexicute is a mood," and the phrase carries the whole concept: Peko-Peko starts from a pair of charming mascots and grows into what the studio describes as a boundless universe, blending the timeless charm of Japanese culture with the vibrancy of Mexican expression. The anchor is the axolotl, Mexico's unmistakable salamander, reimagined as a pink 3D character with a flower crown and a tiny cross-body bag. Around it the studio builds a cast, a cat and a frog, each ready to melt into caps, packaging, and print. The palette does as much work as the characters: bubblegum pink, grape purple, mint, peach, and lime, applied in soft 3D scenes with the kind of squishy lighting that makes every render feel touchable. Nothing here is decorated for decoration's sake; the joy is the system.

The wordmark sets the tone in one gesture: "peko-peko" in fat, lowercase balloon letters, built twice as a 3D object. One version is white and puffy, floating on a purple gradient. The other wears pink glitter with a purple outline and a white cloud halo on peach. The letters read like something you could squeeze. Supporting type stays quiet, a clean grotesque for names and phone numbers on the stationery, so the balloon letters keep all the volume.

Every artifact plays along. The characters become bottle caps: a cat lid on an amber bottle, a frog on a yellow one, the axolotl on purple. A strawberry-scented body wash arrives as a pink bear-shaped bottle wearing the wordmark on its belly. The business card is die-cut with a scalloped edge that quotes the balloon letters. The letterhead keeps the pink wordmark small and centered on white, framed by a single star. It is a world, not a logo sheet.

#95. “Architecture Must Return to Its Essence”: Wang Shu and Lu Wenyu on the 2027 Venice Architecture Biennale

"Architecture must return to its essence." With this statement, Wang Shu and Lu Wenyu establish the central premise of their curatorial vision for the 20th International Architecture Exhibition of La Biennale di Venezia, taking place from May 8 to November 21, 2027, across the Giardini, the Arsenale, and throughout Venice. Titled "Do Architecture – For the Possibility of Coexistence Facing a Real Reality", the exhibition calls for a return to the physical act of making architecture, at a time when, according to the curators, the discipline has become increasingly disconnected from lived reality through excessive abstraction, commercialization, and digitalization.

"Architecture must return to its essence." With this statement, Wang Shu and Lu Wenyu establish the central premise of their curatorial vision for the 20th International Architecture Exhibition of La Biennale di Venezia, taking place from May 8 to November 21, 2027, across the Giardini, the Arsenale, and throughout Venice. Titled "Do Architecture – For the Possibility of Coexistence Facing a Real Reality", the exhibition calls for a return to the physical act of making architecture, at a time when, according to the curators, the discipline has become increasingly disconnected from lived reality through excessive abstraction, commercialization, and digitalization.

Rather than focusing on what architecture might become, the curators propose a renewed engagement with the present, questioning what it means to practice architecture today through materials, construction, local knowledge, and direct experience. This approach builds on ideas that have long informed the work of Amateur Architecture Studio, founded by Wang Shu and Lu Wenyu in 1997, particularly their exploration of traditional building techniques, material reuse, and the relationship between architecture and place.The exhibition also places the question of coexistence at its center, exploring how architecture can bring together seemingly opposing conditions, from technology and craftsmanship to urban and rural ways of building, while remaining grounded in the specific realities of each place.

#96. Experts Call for Indigenous Artifacts in Canadian Tycoon’s Collection to Be Repatriated

A Canadian seafood tycoon’s financial troubles have turned into a debate over who gets to decide what happens to his art collection, which includes dozens of Indigenous artifacts that some experts say should be returned to their communities of origin.

John Risley, the billionaire businessman who cofounded Clearwater Seafoods, is caught up in a dispute over hundreds of artworks and antiques following the collapse of his investment company, CFFI Ventures, which entered creditor protection in March with nearly $1 billion in debt. Related Articles Kavi Gupta Gallery Hit With Restraining Order Amid $2 M. Art Dispute Art Lender Accuses Maddox Gallery of Inflating Value of Art Used as Collateral--'Bizarre and Irrational' Claim, Says Gallery

Among the objects ensnared in the proceedings are roughly 30 Indigenous artifacts, including baskets, moccasins, textiles, and bone carvings. According to the Canadian Press outlet CBC, which first reported the concerns, some are attributed to Inuit, Mi’kmaq, or Cree makers, while others have the vague identifier “Indigenous” and no listed artist or date.

That lack of information has prompted calls from repatriation experts for Indigenous communities to be consulted before the objects change hands.

Cody Groat, a history and Indigenous studies professor at Western University, told the Canadian Press that the dispute raises broader questions about when Indigenous nations should have a say in the sale of objects associated with their cultural heritage. He believes the best outcome would be for culturally significant objects to be returned to their communities.

Risley, however, disputes the idea that his collection contains objects that should to be repatriated.

He told the Canadian Press that he supports repatriation in principle but believes his acquisitions were made through reputable dealers and auction houses, where culturally sensitive material would already have attracted scrutiny.

“Our collection would not include any such pieces,” he said, adding that dealers and auction houses have little interest in handling objects that might raise repatriation concerns.

The Canadian Museums Association‘s Indigenous Council disagrees with his reasoning. In a statement to the Canadian Press, the council argued that Indigenous communities themselves are best equipped to determine the cultural importance of such objects, rather than collectors, dealers, or museums.

The spat comes as Risley’s creditors attempt to recover money from the collapse of CFFI Ventures.

In September, a Nova Scotia court approved the transfer of most of the company’s assets to New Tide Capital, an affiliate of New York–based HPS Investment Partners, which held most of CFFI’s debt.

The assets included a collection of more than 1,200 artworks and antiques valued at approximately $8.1 million. Among them were more than 95 paintings by Canadian folk artist Maud Lewis, works by members of the Group of Seven, and pieces by Inuit artists Jessie Oonark and Irene Avaalaaqiaq Tiktaalaaq.

But the ownership of 669 objects became a separate point of contention. Risley maintains that those works belong to him personally rather than to his company. A lawyer for New Tide told the court that the firm would seek to resolve the dispute privately.

The Indigenous artifacts appear on that disputed list.

Canada has no comprehensive legal framework governing the repatriation of Indigenous cultural objects, and private collections present particular challenges. Unlike museums, which often face pressure to disclose their holdings and investigate provenance, private collectors generally aren’t under a similar obligation.

Lauren Wheeler, executive director of the Canadian Museums Association, told the CBC that the limited information available about Risley’s holdings illustrates how hard it can be to identify culturally significant objects in private hands.

The association has developed guidance encouraging museums to work with Indigenous communities to identify and return objects acquired through coercion, forced displacement, or other questionable circumstances. Wheeler thinks private collectors should follow similar practices.

Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami, a national organization representing the Inuit in Canada, has also offered to help examine any potentially significant Inuit objects in the collection and facilitate their return where appropriate.

For now, there’s no proof that the Indigenous artifacts in Risley’s collection were improperly acquired, nor has a specific community established a claim to any of the objects identified in the court proceedings.

Maurizio Cattelan Photo: LaPresse / Alamy Stock Photo

The art world’s most mischievous japester, Maurizio Cattelan, showed his more human side in a recent interview in The Guardian newspaper on the eve of a major new show at the Neue Nationalgalerie in Berlin.

The Italian artist—known for taping a banana to the wall (Comedian, 2019)—stressed that he is not just a provocateur, explaining: “My work has always been serious. The problem is people often stop at the joke.” Cattelan also addressed what happens next, pointing out in an arch philosophical way: “I don’t have a foundation. I don’t have a studio, never had. I also don’t have a family. A legacy would be like being so conscious about yourself that you have these constructions.”

And what about his links to Berlin? The Guardian revealed that during his early years in the city, Maurizio was a postman, a mortuary attendant and a sperm donor—death and life all rolled into one.

#98. Gowanus Open Studios Turns 30

This year’s iteration of the artistic assembly was a love letter to the neighborhood and its craftsmanship amid an era of remediation, development, and gentrification.

Though I spent six hours sauntering through the neighborhood for the 30th iteration of Gowanus Open Studios (GOS) on Saturday afternoon, I barely covered a tenth of the over 100 participating sites. Scattered throughout GOS' post-industrial labyrinth of stairwells, hallways, and nondescript entrances was a love letter to the notorious canal and the creative community formed along its banks, capturing the neighborhood's past and present as it hurtles toward its future as a shiny waterfront development.

In the literal sense, I encountered a fair bit of plein air work spotlighting water remediation efforts on the canal and documenting familiar street corners before they change in the blink of an eye, as the entire neighborhood has done in the last five years alone.

“It makes me a bit sad,” Elizabeth O'Reilly, a landscape artist with a large studio at 543 Union Street, told me when I asked her about her experience witnessing Gowanus's full 180-degree turn from a site of profound industrial abuse and infrastructural neglect to a place housing glimmering, luxury high-rises in various states of completion near the canal, which admittedly still smells quite a bit and floods with raw sewage when it rains.

O'Reilly has maintained a studio on the same block as the Union Street Bridge since 1992, and displayed myriad paintings and collages of the canal and neighborhood. The works channeled the area's architectural angularities and the canal's reclamation of them through scattered reflections on its oily surface. Most of the work she had out was from the late 2000s and early 2010s — right as the polluted canal was designated a Superfund site by the Environmental Protection Agency and entered its second phase of development
