#99. Sirui’s New Tripod Head Doesn’t Make You Choose Between a Ball or Fluid Head

Sirui’s New Tripod Head Doesn’t Make You Choose Between a Ball or Fluid Head

Sirui has announced the BH-60, an integrated Ball and Fluid Head designed for photographers, content creators, and hybrid users. It promises to combine a ball head’s photography-friendly versatility with a fluid head’s smooth, video-friendly control in a single system.

The Sirui BH-60 includes a dual-mode design that the company says makes it ideal for both photography and video. Per Sirui, users can easily switch between ball head mode and fluid video mode, compose with the ball head, then switch to the fluid head for smooth camera motion during video recording. Many photographers prefer a ball head design because it’s fast and easy to set up a composition, but it lacks smooth, controlled movement.

That’s where a fluid head excels. The Pan-Tilt Mode uses an integrated fluid damping system to deliver smoother camera movements than the ball head. This means that users can have more controlled pans during video recording and capture stabler, smoother video. The head has a +/- 40° tilt range, Sirui adds.

The BH-60 also includes a detachable control handle, which is particularly useful for controlling movements during video. The handle is 230 millimeters (nine inches) long. It can be attached to either side of the tripod head. The company notes that the handle may not add much for photographers, so detaching it makes for a lighter, smaller tripod kit.

The BH-60 includes a dual-locking mechanism, a safety lock-equipped quick release plate, and an Arca-Swiss compatible design.

For panoramic photographers in particular, the BH-60 includes an independent panoramic locking system and a 360-degree rotating base.

The BH-60 attaches to a wide range of tripod legs, including Sirui’s own offerings, and is built from aluminum alloy. The BH-60 supports a maximum payload of five kilograms (just over 11 pounds), which should work well for a wide range of kits. For example, a Sony a7R VI with a Sony FE 70-200mm f/2.8 GM OSS II lens weighs about 1,750 grams (3.9 pounds), showing the kind of kit users can reasonably mount on the Sirui BH-60.

The Sirui BH-60 Ball and Fluid Head is available now through Sirui and its authorized retailers, including B&H. It is $219 in the United States and €239 in Europe.

#101. Traditional Thai lanterns inform blue-and-gold Bangkok cafe interior

Photography by Pichan Sujaritsatit

Japanese studio I IN drew on traditional Thai festivals, where thousands of paper lanterns are released into the sky, when creating the interior for the first Blue Bottle Coffee cafe in Bangkok.

The interior of the cafe is dominated by the large Blue Lantern installation above the coffee counter.

“The main idea came from Thailand’s traditional lantern festival,” I IN co-founder Yohei Terui told Dezeen. “We wanted to capture the feeling of a lantern floating in the sky and bring that into the space in a contemporary way.”

“This became what we call the Blue Lantern, a large sculptural element extending from the ceiling above the drip station,” he continued.

As it is the brand’s first cafe in Bangkok, the studio wanted to design a “bold and dramatic” space that would also nod to local culture.

“The lantern idea came from the local culture, and from the beginning, we wanted to make it as large and impactful as possible,” Terui said.

“We placed it at the location where customers first enter the cafe, so it would immediately catch their attention and become a symbol of the store.”

The furniture and fixtures in the 178-square-metre cafe were made from teak wood, a material that is often avoided in the West due to concerns about illegal logging, but which is local to Thailand.

“Every country has their own approach to natural materials, depending on what is locally available and traditionally used,” Terui said.

“In Thailand, especially in the north, teak is a very familiar material and commonly used in the interiors and architecture.”

Blue Bottle Coffee cafe Bangkok is drenched in blue hues, with the brand’s signature colour used for the lantern and coffee counter.

For the rest of the space, I IN chose a pale blue colour to “give guests a sense of brand identity and the feeling of a sky,” Terui explained.

After visiting the city, the designer also decided to add gold details to the cafe interior.

“The idea of bringing gold into the interior actually came from my personal experience of walking around Bangkok,” Terui said.

“As you walk through the city, you suddenly come across these beautiful, strong gold colours, and I found this contrast very unique,” he continued.

“It was something that stayed in my memory of Bangkok, and I wanted to bring a little of that feeling into the cafe.”

I IN also recently designed the concrete Andersson Bell store in Tokyo and clad the Human Made store in Seoul in handcrafted tiles.

#102. Jewellers Buccellati create collection inspired by Venetian lace-making

A Serenissima collection necklace in white and yellow gold, set with brilliant-cut diamonds; the centrepiece of the pendant is a tanzanite gemstone Courtesy of Buccellati

Art of Luxury magazine, published twice per year by The Art Newspaper, explores how grande marque fashion, jewellery, travel and lifestyle interact with artists, the art market and the museums and heritage sector.

The Buccellati family is Milanese through and through, but earlier this year the jewellery house launched a new collection inspired by Venice. It’s called Serenissima, naturally, and re-creates in finely wrought metals the art of the lace makers found on the island of Burano. The craft is said to originate from fishermen’s wives translating their skill with mending nets into something more refined.

“I really didn’t like Venice when I was younger,” says Maria Cristina Buccellati, the company’s global communications director, speaking on the phone to Art of Luxury. It is after the launch and she is relaxing in Puglia. “We always went in winter and I couldn’t see what was so special. Now, of course, I find it absolutely magical.”

Also part of the Serenissima collection, inspired by Burano’s lace-making tradition, are a bracelet and earrings Courtesy of Buccellati

Buccellati still uses the traditional Renaissance methods for jewellery making, training young graduates scouted from Italian design schools. “They have to be extremely gifted and then it takes maybe eight years to become a qualified artisan,” Buccellati says. Because of this, fully fledged masters are few, which means it takes at least two years to deliver each new high-jewellery collection. “The work is incredibly challenging, and we are the last jewellers to fully engrave all our pieces,” Buccellati says. “The only shiny part is on the back of the jewel.”

The house was established in Milan in 1919 by Mario Buccellati, who opened his first store near La Scala. Though now owned by the luxury conglomerate Richemont, there are still a notable number of family members working in the company; Andrea Buccellati is the creative director and his daughter, Lucrezia, is part of the creative team. Its company headquarters remains in Milan, moving to a new building behind Corso Magenta in 2020. It is perhaps this that has allowed the house to hold on to its very specific identity.

Mario Buccellati was always fascinated by Burano lace, seeing in its lightness and transparency something he wanted to capture in his designs. For Serenissima, artisans have quite literally turned gold and diamonds into what appears to be lace, and should lay as delicately on the skin, while panels of open-worked metal demonstrate the unique piercing that is an exclusive technique of Buccellati. It is all a balancing act: the calibration of gold to empty space, and between gold and diamonds. The results? Airily light, timeless—and expensive.

#103. Typography: Server Mono by Blaze Type for INTDEV

Blaze Type and INTDEV team up on Server Mono, an open-source monospaced font built for terminal legibility and crisp web typography.

Developers stare at terminal windows all day. If a zero looks too much like an uppercase O, you're going to waste twenty minutes hunting down a broken variable. When Jimmy Lee at Seattle's Internet Development Studio Company (INTDEV) reached out to French foundry Blaze Type, the goal was straightforward: build the foundry's first commissioned open-source font under the SIL license, free for anyone to download, modify, or ship in production code. Type designers Matthieu Salvaggio and Tim Vanhille looked back at Apple's San Francisco Mono and classic ASCII art, drawing a two-style family in Regular and Slanted that holds its edge across low-res command lines and wide web layouts.

Every glyph sits inside the exact same horizontal box. That fixed width is what keeps code indentation honest. Look closely at the vermilion-orange character sheet and you'll spot how Salvaggio and Vanhille solved the classic disambiguation traps in monospaced typography: the numeral 0 carries a crisp diagonal slash, the figure 1 plants a flat base serif against a hooked top flag, and the character set packs both double-story and single-story lowercase a alternates alongside tall curly braces and brackets. Nothing in the spacing feels cramped. Even in the three-column Python specimen running generate_random_string and recursive factorial functions across vermilion, slate-grey, and off-white cards, the vertical rhythm stays locked to the pixel.

The specimen art direction refuses to play it safe. Instead of showing dark IDE screenshots, the layouts drop rounded vermilion, grey, and off-white pill badges â reading Script, Foundation, Blockchain, Quantum, and Robotics, against pitch-black canvases and classical oil paintings, including a gold-leaf panel of St. Michael slaying a dragon behind red Excalibur and grey BL4D display type. Another frame parks white Terminal lettering and red [DENIED] Access warnings right over a giant charcoal X. It's a sharp reminder that technical typography doesn't have to look clinical when the letterforms have real bones.

#104. Beer With a Painter: Melissa Brown

“I want to visualize the fact that, despite our perception, reality is changeable,” the Brooklyn-based artist said of her paintings.

Melissa Brown has worn cat-eye makeup every day since she was a teenager. I can’t help but associate it with her paintings, where the sacred and profane converge amid mirrored surfaces, shop windows, psychics’ tables, and bedroom altars. The cat-eye flick is dramatic and powerful, dating back to ancient Egypt, where women wore mineral liner for its health properties and as protection against the evil eye.

To connote the layering of our daily experience, Brown collages a spectrum of techniques: photography, plein-air painting, CMYK printing, airbrush, and stencil. Sometimes her paintings come with QR codes that send the viewer to an animation. Her painting “Commute” (2020) shows a hand with long fingers and press-on nails spinning shiny meditation balls in an otherwise empty pandemic-era subway car passing in front of the Brooklyn Bridge, a glowing orb of sunlight visible through the window. A painted strobe effect animates the fingers and the reflective balls — a nod to British Vorticist painter Sybil Andrews.

Brown’s studio is on the second floor of a building in Flatbush, Brooklyn, with a busy deli in the storefront and a braiding salon upstairs. The experience of visiting is a bit like walking into one of her paintings, where the mundane and the performative elements of beauty rituals collide through glass shop windows. Last month, we met there to talk about her favorite Renaissance painting, the magic of encountering motifs while walking around the city, finding answers in flotsam, and how paintings can manifest experience.

Melissa Brown was born in 1974 in Morristown, New Jersey, and received her BFA in Printmaking from the Rhode Island School of Design (RISD) and her MFA in Painting and Printmaking from Yale University. Brown also attended the Skowhegan School of Painting and Sculpture in 2000. She is currently a professor at Lehman College of the City University of New York and co-curated a two-venue group exhibition, Does This Taste Funny? Humor in Contemporary Art, on view at Lehman College Art Gallery and the Gallery at Heimbold Visual Arts Center at Sarah Lawrence College. Brown’s recent solo exhibition, Window Shopping, was presented in New York at Derek Eller Gallery, where she has exhibited since 2017.

Hyperallergic: How did you connect with art as a young person, and what brought you to RISD?

Melissa Brown: I was born in New Jersey, where all of my family is from, but I grew up near Philadelphia. When my parents first moved from New Jersey to Philadelphia, we had an apartment in Center City, near the Ben Franklin Museum. It had recently been updated for the Bicentennial. There was an infinity mirror room with a lot of neon, and an interactive room with phones that you could pick up and listen to someone from history. There was also a glass harmonica. As a child, I was constantly asking to go there and my mom would take me. I even went through a phase where I wanted to be called “Ben Franklin.” We visited his print shop a million times. It must have had an influence.

When it came time to visit colleges, one of them was RISD. I was seduced by it, and that was the determining factor. I went into their Woods-Gerry Gallery and felt it was where I wanted to be.

#105. Inherited Ground: Designing Houses on Contaminated Land

Industrial activity can end long before its effects disappear from the land. Factories close, buildings are demolished, and former industrial districts gradually become part of new residential developments. Yet the soil beneath them may still contain traces of their previous use, sometimes requiring extensive intervention before construction can begin.

Industrial activity can end long before its effects disappear from the land. Factories close, buildings are demolished, and former industrial districts gradually become part of new residential developments. Yet the soil beneath them may still contain traces of their previous use, sometimes requiring extensive intervention before construction can begin.

Redeveloping these sites raises a question about how much of the existing ground can remain and what it takes to build housing above it. The extent of contamination affects what must happen before construction begins, while the cost of preparing the land can influence the development itself. Much of this work eventually disappears beneath the completed buildings, leaving little indication of the site's previous condition.

#106. 10 Winners From the Epson International Pano Awards

10 Winners From the Epson International Pano Awards

The 17th Epson International Pano Awards have announced its 2026 winners, with Spanish photographer Daniel Viñé Garcia named Open Photographer of the Year.

Garcia took the top honor in the Open category on the strength of a portfolio that spans the high Andes and the Argentine Puna. His winning image, The Sleeping Giant, was made at Parinacota Volcano in Chile, rising more than 6,300 meters (20,670 feet) and paired with the neighboring Pomerape at over 6,200 meters (20,340 feet).

“The original capture was a 360-degree aerial panorama made from 33 individual exposures,” Garcia says. “After one last burst of light, the landscape gradually took on magenta tones, wrapping the volcanoes and the high-altitude lakes in a particularly special atmosphere. I later refined the framing from the full panorama to concentrate the final composition on the volcanoes, the light and the shapes of the landscape.”

His work also earned places in the Open Nature and Landscape category with Cathedral of Starlight, a night panorama made at around 3,100 meters in the Argentine Puna and My Perfect Night, photographed on a salt flat in Catamarca at more than 3,300 meters.

This year’s competition drew 4,084 entries from photographers in 93 countries, an increase of 19 percent on 2025. Entries were divided into 2,122 in the Open competition and 1,962 in the Amateur competition, with the field including 680 entries in the new Aerial categories.

The Epson Digital Art Prize, which is decided by the executive team at Epson Australia from the top 50 entries in each category of the Open competition, was won by Preeti and Prashant Chacko. In addition to their creativity, these entries must show excellence in digital post-processing as well as exceptional photographic technique.

“Southern white rhinos are, in their normal state, surprisingly unthreatening – calm grazers who move around at a leisurely pace,” say Preeti and Prashant, who entered as a couple.

“One morning at Solio Game Reserve in Kenya we were photographing a group of eight rhinos with a few cattle egrets walking among them, a rare sighting in most other national parks.

“Something suddenly shifted and five of the rhinos broke into a run. We understood in that instant why a group of rhinos is called a crash. Neither of us has ever played rugby, but from the point of view of the egrets this is how we imagine a forward pack must look, heads down and all that weight already committed.”

Mikel Iraeta of Spain won the Open Nature and Landscape category with Double arch on Milford Sound, an image he describes as close to impossible to make.

“Milford Sound is a place where it rains on average 300 days a year,” Iraeta says. “The day before I visited, the access road was closed due to snow avalanche danger. It is very difficult to have an entire clear night with no rain, no clouds, no moon and for all of this to coincide at the end of September when it is possible to capture the double arc of the Milky Way. The final image is the result of combining 107 different photographs.”

Xuecheng Liu of the United States won the Open Built Environment category with ‘Center of the Cosmos’, a stitched panorama of Times Square from above. Winner of the Open Built Environment category. ‘Center of the Cosmos’ by Xuecheng Liu.

“Times Square is one of the most photographed places in the world, so my challenge was to find a perspective that could make such a familiar place feel unfamiliar again,” Liu says. “I stitched together 25 frames to create an ultra-wide aerial panorama, with countless points of light resembling stars surrounding the center of a galaxy.”

Tomás Sánchez Ruiz of Spain claimed the Amateur Photographer of the Year title, winning the Amateur Nature and Landscape category with Double Arch Over Stokksnes in Iceland.

“On the night I took this photograph, the aurora forecast was not particularly promising,” Ruiz says. “When I pulled back the curtain of our hotel room and saw a green glow in the sky, I knew this could be the night we had been waiting for. The black sand was completely covered in freshly fallen, untouched snow. And there I was, finally taking the photograph I had been waiting for, with a smile on my face.”

To see all of the winners and finalists, and for details on next year’s competition, head to the Pano Awards website.

Personality and storytelling make an impression.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

When Stefan Sagmeister founded his solo design studio in New York in 1993, he sent out a promotional postcard featuring a photo of himself wearing nothing but dress socks. These days, there's a plethora of digital platforms available, but getting the attention of potential clients can be more difficult than ever. There's competition not just from other designers, but AI. And Instagram doesn't allow full-frontal nudity.

Still, a designer has managed to get massive attention on social media this week for a single striking calling card: a highly polished film shot in 8K with a full crew and Barbieland sound stage. The scale of the production has some other designers wondering if making a movie trailer is what it takes to find work these days, but the video's real takeaway is in the content more than the format.

A post shared by Darshita Patankar (@darshitapatankar)

Darshita Patankar is a visual designer and illustrator based in Bengaluru. After what she describes as "a year full of anxiety" amid frustration around the impact of AI, she decided to pitch herself to potential clients in a different way. Instead of persevering with a traditional portfolio site and social posts of previous work, she enlisted her brother Vikrant to produce a sleek four-minute film showcasing her skills and personality, and they really pulled out the stops

"Everyone says design is dead and AI killed it. But the real parasite was hiding in plain sight," is Darshita's hook at the start of Design is Dead. She goes on to discuss her early introduction to design via MS Paint, how that curiosity still influences her work today, the importance of storytelling and specific projects, including how she created a typeface and her visual design work on the Codebusters game.

She also presents an argument for the importance of design itself, not as a mere output but as something that should be at the core of the decision-making process for any brand.

Within less than a day, the video had received nearly 3 million views on X and thousands of likes and comments on Instagram and LinkedIn. It's also generating a debate about the lengths graphic designers need to go to promote themselves in 2026.

this is who you're competing with in the job market btwOctober 19, 2026

Will clients expect every designer to make a 'Hollywood-level' video pitch? No, but Darshita has demonstrated how any designer can make an impression; not necessarily through the same format but through the authenticity of the presentation. The production values on Design is Dead are impressive, but what stands out most is the designer's personality, creativity, and the memorability of the pitch, which is what will really attract clients.

The film shows how, at a time when everyone's worried about AI's impact on the industry, designers can stand out by showcasing storytelling and craft in surprising ways, and most of all by being themselves. You might not have a film crew, but you might find another way of showing the world who you are, whether it's with physical flyers on lampposts, engaging social media content or sending out nudes.

#109. Thin concrete plane defines minimalist villa in Ibiza by Fran Silvestre Arquitectos

A thin white-concrete plane folds and steps down a hillside to enclose Bellavista 11, a minimalist home overlooking the sea in Ibiza, designed by Spanish studio Fran Silvestre Arquitectos.

Bellavista 11 is the first villa to be completed in The Roca Views development, a cluster of six homes designed by the Valencia-based studio in the town of Roca Lisa on Ibiza’s eastern coast.

The villas will be united by pared-back, rectilinear forms with thin white walls, designed by Fran Silvestre Arquitectos as a contemporary take on the island’s traditional white-walled buildings.

“The project begins with a very simple question, ‘Can we build on this hillside by placing a single element on it?’,” studio founder Fran Silvestre told Dezeen.

“The aim is to create a continuous element that follows the topography and, through its different folds, gradually finds the best conditions offered by the site,” he explained.

“It is an apparently very simple operation that allows many things to be resolved at once – adapting to the slope, organising the programme, orienting each room towards a different condition of the landscape and extending the architecture to generate shade.”

Bellavista 11 is divided across three low-slung volumes, beginning at the top with a garage and access stair, moving through to a central social volume and ending in a block of five bedrooms.

The thin white concrete plane that defines the home is just 15 centimetres thick. As it steps down the site, it creates expansive roof terraces atop the lowest two volumes, folding around to create the interior floor plates and a series of lower terraces.

“We like to think in terms of an evolved tradition, learning from what works in Mediterranean architecture – shade, protection from the sun, clarity of materials – and resolving it through contemporary construction techniques,” said Silvestre.

Alongside the open-plan living, dining and kitchen space is a swimming pool, while the bedroom block overlooks a seating terrace. Both are accessed via walls of full-height sliding glass doors with slender frames and hidden tracks.

The villa’s interiors continue the deliberate simplicity of the exterior, with white walls, pale stone floors and timber carpentry chosen to emphasise the movement of light and shadow across surfaces throughout the day.

“White appears naturally because of its relationship with traditional Mediterranean architecture and because of its performance under intense solar radiation,” Silvestre explained.

“At the same time, it allows light to transform the spaces throughout the day. This is something that particularly interests us, we understand light almost as another material within the project.”

Silvestre founded his eponymous practice in 2005. The studio previously used a similarly singular geometric gesture for a home in Madrid, which is housed in a cluster of white cylindrical volumes.

Its other recent projects include the stepped Villa 95 in Andalusia and the winding Sabater House in Alicante.

#111. Exhibition highlights overlooked William Morris collection and his collaborations with women makers

Penelope (around 1865) by Kate Faulkner, who worked for Morris & Co. as a designer © Fitzwilliam Museum, Cambridge

In myriad exhibitions, books and documentaries in recent years devoted to the English designer William Morris (1834-96) and the contemporaneous Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood, one major collection and resource has been almost overlooked—the thousands of drawings, paintings, designs, letters, books and other objects in the Fitzwilliam Museum in Cambridge, acquired by Sydney Cockerell, who became the friend and private secretary of William Morris. Cockerell brought his collection with him when he became the most famous director of the Fitzwilliam, and expanded it as he reigned there from 1908 to 1937.

A Call to Art: William Morris and the Pre-Raphaelites, which opens this month at the museum, will explore Morris and the Pre-Raphaelite milieu’s “collective vision, collaborative action and shared belief in the power of art and beauty to bring about positive social change”, according to the organisers. The show will include loans from other UK public and private owners, but its core will highlight the Fitzwilliam’s own collection for the first time, with most of the objects never previously displayed.

“There have been so many exhibitions [on the topic] but this valuable collection has barely been studied, and it really deserves its day out,” says Jan Marsh, the exhibition’s co-curator and a noted scholar of the Pre-Raphaelites. “Much of the collection is on paper and cannot be shown all of the time. But there is also a feeling that previous generations at the museum really couldn’t be bothered much with it.”

William Morris’s La Belle Iseult (1858) © Tate

Luke Syson, the director of the Fitzwilliam, is adamant this is no longer the case. In his catalogue introduction he calls Morris “unquestionably one of the great revolutionaries, changing attitudes to design and making forever” and insists “at the Fitzwilliam, we are still inspired by Morris”.

Unlike Oxford, Cambridge itself is rarely associated with Morris. Although Morris and the Pre-Raphaelite Edward Burne-Jones went on to carry out major work for many of the colleges, when they first visited in 1855, Morris described the city as “rather a hole of a place”.

Marsh says: “The exhibition is intended to show off the collection, to appeal to everyone who loves Morris, but also to appeal to people who are either bored by or really don’t know anything about him. And my aim is also to give visual pleasure, to delight—you know when your eye just likes to look at things.”

Marsh and her co-curator Karen Livingstone also say their exhibition has used the Cambridge collection to draw out of the shadows some of the previously anonymous women who worked with Morris on creating embroideries, textiles, furniture and wallpaper designs. (The twining patterns became the hallmark of progressive good taste for the affluent middle classes, and many are still being reproduced in every conceivable medium.)

The women included Morris’s wife, Jane, and daughter, May, who became head of the influential embroidery section of Morris & Co. The exhibition will also highlight for the first time in any exhibition Kate Faulkner, one of only three designers apart from Morris himself who made designs for Morris & Co. (her Carnation fabric design is still in production). Faulkner was renowned for her skill in moulded and gilded gesso plaster, and the exhibition will include her massive altarpiece on loan from the chapel at the University of Roehampton in southwest London for which it was commissioned.

“Morris was in many ways a man of his time,” Marsh says. “But he was entirely gender neutral in his workshops if someone was useful and skilled.”

Although the exhibition will focus on the women as creators and workers rather than their famously tangled love affairs, one small poignant object will be exhibited for the first time: a lock of Elizabeth Siddal’s hair. Siddal, spotted working in a hat shop, modelled for many of the artists—including for John Everett Millais’s painting of Ophelia floating to her death, one of Tate’s best-loved works—and became muse and eventually wife to Dante Gabriel Rossetti. She was also an artist in her own right, although recognition of her stature came more than a century after her death.

The exhibition will include several of Siddal’s works, such as her 1857 watercolour illustrating the poem Clerk Saunders. Marsh notes that when in 1910 the museum acquired it as a gift from the artist Charles Fairfax Murray, he insisted that it had been directed and heavily worked by Rossetti.

When Siddal died in 1862 aged just 32, of a deliberate or accidental overdose of laudanum, Rossetti laid a hand-written volume of his poems in the coffin beside her. When he infamously had Siddal’s body exhumed to reclaim the book seven years later, her distinctive flowing red hair—described as “copper gold” and immortalised in many paintings—reputedly filled the coffin when it was opened. The lock of faded red hair will bear witness to her tragically short life and enduring legend.

#112. World Press Photo Adds Nature and Sports Awards for 2027 Contest

World Press Photo Adds Nature and Sports Awards for 2027 Contest

World Press Photo has added three awards to its 2027 contest that will recognize nature and sports photography from around the world.

World Press Photo says that the introduction of nature and sports is in response to feedback from World Press Photo’s exhibition audiences and industry partners, who “missed seeing nature and sports photography represented among the Contest’s winning work.”

Nature and sports photography is part of news and documentary photography. The back pages of newspapers are traditionally taken up by sports coverage and animal photos frequently appear as standalone pictures among news articles.

“Nature and sports are part of how people understand the world. We hope these awards encourage photographers from all over the globe to enter stories that are visually exceptional and reveal something new, whether from a local, regional or global perspective,” says Joumana El Zein Khoury, executive director of World Press Photo.

For the 2027 Contest, the jury will select three Nature Awards and three Sports Awards from eligible Singles and Stories entries submitted across all regions. Neither award will function as a standalone submission category, and photographers do not need to enter separately.

The World Press Photo Nature Award will recognize visual stories exploring the relationships between people, animals, and the ecosystems they share.

It focuses on themes including ecological healing, adaptation, friction, coexistence and animal agency, and aims to highlight stewardship and resilience, including solutions-oriented reporting that documents restoration and meaningful ecological healing. While the award encourages hopeful narratives, the jury retains full discretion to consider nuanced and complex entries where human and environmental interconnections meet.

“As with all World Press Photo awards, work must demonstrate exceptional visual quality and meaningful storytelling. The award seeks stories that capture human-animal interconnections and deepen public understanding of issues affecting people, animals and shared ecosystems,” World Press Photo says.

The Nature Award is distinct from environmental crisis reporting. Work primarily focused on the climate crisis, severe pollution, and other aspects of the global environmental crisis will continue to be eligible across all regions in the Singles, Stories and Long-Term Projects categories.

The World Press Photo Sports Award recognizes work that captures the energy, action, and human emotion of individual and team sports.

It encompasses the full spectrum of sports photography, from decisive single moments to broader narratives and thematic issues within the sporting world. Eligible work includes major sporting events and high-profile news moments, as well as socio-political dynamics, cultural connections and protests within sport, alongside everyday sporting life, community traditions and local sporting cultures.

The 2027 World Press Photo Contest opens for entries on December 1. Further information about eligibility and the entry process will be announced on November 3 via World Press Photo’s website and social media channels.

#113. Art + Water: A Fluid Brand Identity by MacFadden & Thorpe

MacFadden & Thorpe and Anisha Sachar craft a fluid brand identity for Art + Water, an alternative art hub at San Francisco's Pier 29.

Art school tuition has reached absurd heights. Watching emerging talent get priced out of creative careers pushed Co-Directors Rebecca Teague and Nicole Avril, alongside artists Dave Eggers and JD Beltran, to build a working antidote. Eggers, the celebrated author and McSweeney's founder whose community-driven educational experiments like 826 Valencia redefined grassroots literacy, brings a lifelong commitment to accessible public storytelling. Beltran, an acclaimed conceptual artist, filmmaker, and former longtime President of the San Francisco Arts Commission, contributes deep civic leadership and institutional vision. Together, they partnered with the Port of San Francisco to lease an expansive historic pier, resurrecting the apprentice model: ten established artists receive paid studios, mentoring twenty emerging artists on a completely tuition-free basis. San Francisco studio MacFadden & Thorpe teamed up with London-based designer Anisha Sachar to shape the visual ecosystem, favoring an expressive language built around movement, warmth, and collective craft.

At the center of this brand identity is the concept of flow. It acknowledges the bay waters lapping against Pier 29, but it primarily honors the transfer of knowledge between artists working under one roof. The custom-drawn wordmark introduces undulating, elastic letterforms that bend with liquid ease. Typography frequently breaks free from standard horizontal baselines, meandering along curving paths and wrapping around imagery. Fluid photo containers swell, contract, and reshape across print spreads and digital surfaces. Nothing here feels locked down or static. The letterforms expand to monumental scale across transit shelters, or compress into dense margins around exhibition documentation.

The color direction draws directly from the waterfront climate, pairing hot fuchsia and electric aqua against salty coastal tones. That chromatic tension carries straight into physical production. Pier banners, heavy canvas totes, and printed collateral rely on bold color floods rather than sterile gallery white. For the exterior of Pier 29, massive architectural supergraphics establish an unmistakable beacon along the Embarcadero. Ahead of the December inaugural show, Forced Perspective: The World of Boots Riley, the visual system proves that cultural institutions can feel genuinely accessible, open, and alive.

There's no way of avoiding the fact: this is an expensive screen. Thankfully, the Apple Studio Display XDR is also an excellent one, with remarkable brightness, broad colour coverage and a 120Hz refresh rate. It also has the Apple logo on it, and is really only compatible with the company’s latest Macs. So while it makes the ideal companion for a new Studio or MacBook Pro, the combination of its price and its niche appeal mean you might not see too many of these on your colleagues’ desks.

Why you can trust Creative Bloq Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

The Studio Display XDR was unveiled earlier this year and sits at the top of Apple’s screen range, which consists of just two models. It’s every inch the professional’s screen, and requires a Mac to pair with it too. Creatives will appreciate the 5K resolution, wide-colour display, enormous brightness from the mini-LED backlight and smooth 120Hz panel, as well as how easy it is to set up. It comes with three microphones, six speakers, a Center Stage camera and the guts of an iPhone hidden inside to control it all. It’s a big investment, though, with the kind of price tag that will make many studios look elsewhere. Like the best monitors for graphic artists, this isn’t a monitor to get because it looks good, though it does, but because it helps you to do your job more effectively.

-5° to +25° tilt, 105mm height adjustment

• Only Thunderbolt input• Excellent build quality

The Studio Display XDR is a major step up from Apple's standard 27-inch monitor, also called the Studio Display but missing those three key letters at the end. Retaining the same sleek, silvery aluminum build and slim black bezels it looks identical. Round the back, it features two USB-C ports and two powered Thunderbolt 5 ports, one of which is the video input. It also comes as standard with Apple's height- and tilt-adjustable stand, which was an optional upgrade to the non-XDR display, though a VESA-mount option is also available for (surprisingly) less money. Inside, it’s powered by the A19 Pro chip from the iPhone 17 Pro to handle built-in processing, and there's a cooling fan that seems to run all the time the screen is switched on. It’s not particularly loud, and will dissolve into the usual office background noise, but it’s noticeable in moments of silence.

The key upgrades lie within the panel itself. Moving from standard LEDs to a mini-LED backlight, with 2,304 local dimming zones, this version of the Studio Display offers more precise lighting, deeper blacks and brighter highlights. The XDR also adopts Apple’s ProMotion, delivering adaptive refresh rates up to 120Hz for fluid scrolling and cursor movement as well as for high-framerate video and even games. The panel dynamically adjusts its framerate to match media playback, or it can be locked to a specific frequency if that’s what you need.

Connectivity is straightforward: you won’t find HDMI or DisplayPort, but it works with most M-series Macs through Thunderbolt, though driving the display at 5K and the full 120Hz requires an M4 chip or newer (M5 if you’re using an iPad Pro), and the MacBook Neo can drive it at 4K resolution rather than 5K. The Thunderbolt 5 ports support daisy-chaining multiple monitors if you really feel like splashing out on a matching pair. Limited functionality is available on PCs, though you can find adjusting the brightness challenging and it’s not really what the screen was made for, and unlike most monitors with an HDMI at the back, games consoles need not apply.

• Center Stage camera• Incredible brightness in HDR

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

The Apple Studio Display XDR is a really exceptional screen, boasting remarkable brightness levels of up to 1,000 nits for standard content and a peak of 2,000 nits when displaying HDR material. Full-screen brightness displaying SDR content was around 500 nits, but the XDR is capable of much more than this if you feed it HDR.

It’s factory calibrated for high colour precision across both the P3 and Adobe RGB gamuts, though our tests show only 83% of Adobe RGB and 91% of P3 using the XDR-P3 preset. You can get this up to 94% of Adobe RGB and 97% of P3 using the XDR-P3 + Adobe preset, but you may need to do a little manual tuning to get any higher. The display adjusts itself for ambient lighting conditions, and it’s noticeable how upon changing the display preset it starts off cool and dim before warming and brightening (Apple’s True Tone technology, which dynamically adjusts colour temperature to minimise eye strain, at work). In our testing lab it always seemed to be just a little too dim, requiring the automatic brightness setting to be switched off, but this may be a matter of personal taste.

Thanks to the pre-calibration, the screen offers an impressive setup for photo and video editing right out of the box. For more specialised workflows – such as video production, colour grading or even medical imaging – Apple enables custom calibrations and provides a comprehensive suite of preset colour reference modes to match industry standards.

Both True Tone and the automatic brightness controls can be quickly toggled off whenever critical colour accuracy is required. An adaptive refresh rate reaching up to 120Hz ensures ultra-smooth scrolling, precise cursor tracking and fluid animation that’s actually rather reminiscent of modern smartphones. The display tailors its frequency to match video playback, or it can be manually locked to a specific framerate if fixed timing is essential.

With its tilt- and height-adjustable stand, as reviewed here, the Apple Studio Display XDR starts at £2,999 or $3,299, with a nano-texture glass upgrade the only option. You can save some money by choosing the VESA mount adapter instead of the stand, but there's no getting away from the fact this is an expensive screen, with BenQ’s PD2732U 4K 27-incher about a third of the cost. The brightness and Mac-centric features, as well as the 5K resolution, are what makes this screen desirable.

There's little point in picking up the XDR if you don’t have a recent Mac that can make use of its features. And even then, you’ll have to weigh that fearsome brightness and Centre Stage camera against the savings you’d make from getting just about any other screen.

Exceptional build quality, but only Thunderbolt inputs.

An excellent 27in 5K panel, but all the really good stuff has been saved for the XDR.

A pro 4K monitor for graphic designers and anyone else who cares about accurate colour, the Benq PD2732U has a lot going for it.

ASUS has crammed 32 million pixels into the 32-inch mini-LED screen of the ProArt Display PA32KCX. It produces excellent detail, brightness and colour as a result.

#117. Karimoku New Standard and ASICS create furniture made from crushed trainers

Photography by Karimoku New Standard

Furniture brand Karimoku New Standard has announced the global release of its KNS x ASICS Collaboration, which repurposes upcycled foam from unused ASICS trainers as cushioning for two seating designs.

The KNS x ASICS Collaboration uses deadstock and sample footwear from ASICS that would have otherwise been discarded.

Karimoku New Standard, a sub-brand of Japanese manufacturer Karimoku, used the same technique that ASICS has utilised for its upcycled Neocurve trainers to create the material for the collaboration.

The ASICS footwear is dismantled, sorted and crushed to extract Ethylene Vinyl Acetate (EVA) foam, a flexible, light material commonly used as cushioning for midsoles, outsoles and footbeds.

After the foam has been extracted, it is blended with cotton and paired with a three-millimetre condensed foam sheet to create a hybrid structure, according to Karimoku New Standard.

The material is then used as cushioning in the brand’s Castor Lobby Sofa and Polar Lounge Chair, which also feature an embroidered tag as a symbol of the collaboration.

The KNS x ASICS Collaboration, which was introduced in Japan earlier this year before the recent global launch, came about after Karimoku New Standard was working on seating for the meeting spaces in ASICS’ Tokyo office.

“Through rigorous sessions with ASICS – leveraging their expertise in sports science – and a meticulous adjustment process for real-world office use, Karimoku repeatedly prototyped to transform an unfamiliar material like shoe waste into true furniture comfort,” Karimoku New Standard said.

“This uncompromising, hands-on exploration led to the creation of the innovative hybrid structure,” the brand continued.

“Beyond merely reusing materials from a sustainability standpoint, it turns them into a functional added value.”

Karimoku has previously collaborated with brands including Zaha Hadid Design.

ASICS recently released the “minimalist” Hyper Taping trainers with fashion brand Issey Miyake and has also designed pastel-coloured trainers with Danish brand Hay.

#119. One of the Last Masters of the Platinum Photo Printing Process

One of the Last Masters of the Platinum Photo Printing Process

While Cleveland and Ohio were having their moment in the baseball playoffs, a documentary began circulating about hometown photographer Herb Ascherman, whose voluminous archive includes images of nighttime fireworks after a Guardians’ victory.

A “fiercely proud Clevelander,” Ascherman is one of the last masters of large-format photography and the platinum printing process. He stars in the short film The Eye of Cleveland, which screened October 17 at the PhotoMuse Festival of Photography in Thrissur, India.

A post shared by PHOTOMUSE INDIA (@bafphotomuseindia)

Released in 2025, The Eye of Cleveland was named Best Documentary Short at the Columbus (Ohio) International Film and Animation Festival. It has more than 100,000 YouTube views and has screened at the Barcelona Indie Filmmakers Festival and the 2025 Chagrin Documentary Film Festival near Cleveland.

For over four decades, Ascherman has chronicled greater Cleveland and its people, making more than 9,000 portraits, mostly black-and-white. Thirty-two of his photos are part of the collection of the Cleveland Museum of Art.

Both a student and teacher of photography, Ascherman owns more than 2,300 books on photography. His philosophy, he says, is the “pursuit of quality.”

Curious crowds form when he sets up outdoor shoots with his 15-pound Deardorff 8×10 view camera and 15-pound tripod.

In 1977, Ascherman founded the Cleveland Photographic Workshop, which showcased more than 1,000 photographers. In 2006, he founded the Cleveland Society of Alternative Photographers to promote the 19th-century photographic processes still being used today.

Ascherman’s 1985 project, 50 Faces: The Holocaust Remembered, has been shown nationwide.

Born in 1947, Ascherman continues to use platinum photo processing, the 19th-century method that replaces traditional silver halides with platinum/palladium metals. Platinum particles are absorbed directly into the fibers of high-quality cotton or rag paper, resulting in a matte finish with exceptional tonal range.

Prints are long-lasting, without fading. The platinum process requires a negative the same size as the print. Each print takes two hours, says Ascherman.

“Only a dozen (photographers) do platinum processing commercially,” he says.

Ascherman learned platinum processing more than a quarter-century ago from renowned photographer/printer Salvatore Lopes of Boston.

“Smart phones, social media, and artificial intelligence have made it very difficult, if not impossible, for a photographer to make a living dedicating oneself to their craft like Herb did,” says filmmaker Jim Koenigsaecker.

Trained as a photojournalist, Koenigsaecker was the 2023-2024 Knight Fellow in Visual Communication at Ohio University, learning filmmaking. For his master’s project, he made a 12-minute documentary on Ascherman (The Eye of Cleveland).

The film documents Ascherman making an in-studio portrait and features interviews with a curator at the Cleveland Museum of Art, a local gallerist, and a volunteer at the Cleveland Orchestra (Ascherman made portraits of orchestra musicians).

Ascherman appreciates the film as a tribute to his craft and his city. Plus, he says, the Cleveland-based documentary highlights photography talent outside major markets like New York.

The documentary ends with Ascherman photographing Cleveland’s evening skyline with his bulky camera on a tripod.

Fireworks illuminated the skyline after a Cleveland Guardians victory, as viewers hear celebratory booms near the downtown stadium.

Cleveland, a small-to-midsize market for pro baseball, is battling in the 2026 playoffs. Down two games against the Chicago White Sox, the Guardians won that series 3-2. The Guardians ultimately fell to the Tampa Bay Rays in six games in the American League Championship series, though.

“Cleveland is a comeback city,” says Ascherman. “This area used to have 26 steel mills, now there is one. But now we have two of the top hospitals in the country. We have a fine orchestra. A fine art museum.”

… and a playoff-caliber baseball team. The Guardians may very well return to play more October baseball next year. Plus, the 4-2 Cleveland Browns won on Sunday, October 18, defeating their division rival Baltimore Ravens.

#120. Embracing Playful Imperfection With The CSS `random()` Function

Brecht De Ruyte is a self-taught front-end developer located in Belgium with a passion for UX and Design. After more than a decade of working in tech, he … More about Brecht ↬

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

In design, we love spending hours obsessing over consistency, grids, and alignment. But when I heard that the native CSS random() function landed in Safari and is rolling out in Chrome 156, I started wondering: where does randomness actually make sense on the web? Is it something we want in our design system? To find out, I did what I always do in doubt: I built a bunch of playful CodePen demos exploring organic typography, bouncing letters, splayed cards, and a punk fanzine.

As someone who loves building design systems and tinkering with CSS architecture, a big part of my day job revolves around control. We set up spacing scales, lock down typography, set up color tokens, and make sure everything aligns on a grid. Consistency is usually our bread and butter as design engineers and a proud badge of skill when creating design systems. If a card suddenly jumps 20 pixels to the left on a refresh, it’s not creative expression; it’s a bug that the project manager will log.

So when I first heard that the native random() function from the CSS Values and Units Level 5 spec was shipped in Safari, and is currently rolling out in Chrome 156 (with positive signals from Mozilla on Firefox as well), my first reaction was: that’s pretty cool!

And my second reaction was: wait… where would I actually use this without making a mess? How can I convince designers that random might be a good idea for a design system?

Because let’s be honest: why on earth would we want randomness in our stylesheets when we’ve spent the last decade trying to make the web more predictable? Even when using flexbox or fluid typography, we’re still trying to make things as aligned and uniform as possible.

If you step away from the browser for a second and look at physical things around you, nothing is ever truly uniform.

Take an old letterpress print: the ink bleeds slightly into the paper grain, some letters have a microscopic tilt, and the baseline isn’t always that straight. Or think about a deck of Polaroid photos dropped on a coffee table; those photos aren’t perfect, probably not straight either. Or what about lights flickering in a street at night? That little bit of analog messiness is what makes things feel alive, organic, and human.

On the web, we’ve gotten so good at pixel perfection that sometimes our interfaces end up feeling a bit sterile. We notice this even more now with rapidly created designs by an unguided LLM; we usually end up with the same sort of design we had 10 years ago. Everything is squared off, aligned, neat. It works, but frankly, it does get a bit boring.

Randomness in CSS doesn’t have to mean throwing your design system out the window. It’s about little imperfections and playfulness. Maybe let’s even call it fun.

To see what this actually looks like in practice, I spent a few hours tinkering in CodePen. The demos might feel a bit isolated, but I’m sure that many designers could make the best of this controlled chaos. But before we look at those demos, let’s take a look at the syntax.

Meet Smashing Workshops on front-end, design & UX, with practical takeaways, live sessions, video recordings and a friendly Q&A. With Brad Frost, Stéph Walter and so many others.

The random() function is specified in CSS Values and Units Module Level 5. It generates a pseudo-random value inside your CSS without needing JavaScript or a build-time Sass loop.

The formal specification looks like this:

In practice, and across current browser implementations, you can just write comma-separated arguments:

It won’t be a shocker for most people, but I thought I should at least mention that your minimum and maximum bounds must share the exact same unit type.

The CSS parser needs to know what dimension it’s dealing with. You can use lengths, angles, time, percentages, or plain unitless numbers:

If you ever need to combine units, you’ll have to reach for calc() inside the arguments so each side resolves properly.

The optional third argument is the step size. If you don’t add it, the browser picks from a continuous range. But if you provide a step, it rounds the random value to discrete increments:

This can be helpful in cases where you want things to jump around a bit, but you still want them to land on your pre-defined grid.

Normally, every time random() is evaluated on a property, it creates an independent random value. But there could be an example where you create a box that sets inline-size and block-size at random, but at the same time you need them to match so the element stays a perfect square.

Because both declarations reference --square-size on that element, the browser engine shares the same computed value between them.

To see this in action, I created a little example. In the top row, the tiles have uncached dimensions, which distorts each tile into an unpredictable, mismatched rectangle. In the bottom row, both inline-size and block-size share --square-size, guaranteeing that each tile remains a pristine 1:1 square. Refresh the CodePen a couple of times and notice the bottom cards keeping the same randomness:

See the Pen [Uncached vs cached random() [forked]](https://codepen.io/editor/smashingmag/pen/01a15422-91ea-716e-96b2-abf22b928537) by @utilitybend.

Because we’re still in the rollout phase, you’ll want to wrap your experiments in @supports:

There’s also another function in the spec called random-item(). While random() handles numerical ranges, random-item() lets you pick from a list of predefined tokens or keywords:

This can be handy to randomise from a set of design tokens. This one does not have any browser support at the moment, but it certainly is something to look forward to.

When I started playing with the feature, I was also doing some typography tricks with animations. So that’s where my first thought went: Typography! What if we just add a tiny bit of imperfection to a word?

Think of vintage book covers. The letters aren’t misaligned by miles, but they have small imperfections.

See the Pen [Imperfection random() [forked]](https://codepen.io/editor/smashingmag/pen/01a1542e-7015-76ac-8e84-f406fd33f3ce) by @utilitybend.

I also added a little hover effect. While you’re reading, the word feels playful. But the second you hover over it, every character snaps back.

One quick accessibility warning here: If you break a word into separate elements so you can style each letter, screen readers will often read it out as individual characters: “i - m - p - e - r - f - e - c - t - i - o - n”, or pause awkwardly between each one. That’s a terrible user experience.

Always hide the visual spans from assistive tech and provide the full word:

Screen reader users get the clean text, and sighted users get the fun visual quirks.

Once I had those letters sitting there with their little tilts, I couldn’t resist: what if we animated it?

I started tinkering with a bounce keyframe. I was just goofing around, but the end result gave me a little smile. If you animate every letter with the exact same timing, you get that clean sine wave we’ve all seen before. But if every letter gets its own jump height, its own duration, and its own landing squash, suddenly the word looks like a bunch of little characters jumping around on a trampoline.

See the Pen [Bouncy imperfection with CSS random() [forked]](https://codepen.io/editor/smashingmag/pen/01a15431-ec8e-77eb-abb5-a458f3a18855) by @utilitybend.

Here is how the bounce parameters are wired up:

Notice the negative animation delay (--delay: random(-3s, 0s)).

If you set a positive delay, the letters sit frozen on page load, waiting for their timers to expire before jumping. By using a negative delay, the browser pretends the animation has already been running for a few seconds. The moment the page loads, every letter is already bouncing at its own rhythm.

We’ve built cards. Lots of cards. So many cards… Portfolio grids, blog summaries, feature lists. And most of the time, they sit in three or four neat, boring columns.

For dashboards, that’s exactly what you want. But if you’re building a lifestyle portfolio, a children’s website, or a collection of vacation photos, we can be a bit more playful. In the following example, I did just that:

See the Pen [Random card tilt [forked]](https://codepen.io/editor/smashingmag/pen/01a15455-297d-72da-8a41-b32706e53877) by @utilitybend.

In the example, playing around with the shadow was a fun experiment. I will probably try more effects with that in the future.

Here is where modern CSS features start getting really interesting. In the previous demo with tilting cards, we used pure randomness. But what if you have a stack of cards that needs to fan out across the screen as you scroll?

In this example, I decided to use math for the structure and randomness for the human imperfection.

See the Pen [Scroll drivin animations with random() tilted cards [forked]](https://codepen.io/editor/smashingmag/pen/01a15456-940a-73fd-ae4e-d3286daed556) by @utilitybend.

If you’ve ever looked at brutalist or high-end fashion websites, you’ve probably seen horizontal marquee text drifting across the screen as you scroll down the page.

Usually, you see developers creating classes like .drift-slow, .drift-fast, .drift-reverse, or using a hefty JavaScript scroll listener to compute transforms.

With random() and a tiny bit of math, we can get procedural drift speeds in just a few lines:

See the Pen [Random() velocity scroll animation [forked]](https://codepen.io/editor/smashingmag/pen/01a15458-05e5-7656-9b7c-7da964a76e86) by @utilitybend.

calc(pow(-1, sibling-index())) gives us alternating directions (1, -1, 1, -1), and random(15%, 44%) decides how fast each row travels. As you scroll, each typographic line moves at its own tempo.

I love photography, and one of my favorite things about prime lenses is shallow depth of field. When you shoot at a wide aperture like f/1.7, only whatever is right on your focal plane stays sharp. Everything else melts away into soft bokeh. Yep, photography is all about that bokeh!

By combining random() with filter: blur(), opacity, and scale, we can recreate that lens feel:

See the Pen [All about that random() bokeh [forked]](https://codepen.io/editor/smashingmag/pen/01a15459-a77a-772a-8b29-f0de968afe03) by @utilitybend.

Some words land at blur(0px) with full opacity right in front of your eyes. Others blur out to 6px or 8px and fade into the background. And when you hover over any blurry item in the back, it rack-focuses right into sharpness. It’s a great little effect for decorative hero sections or tag clouds.

Now that we’ve played with the wild side, let’s talk about where this actually belongs in our daily work.

But! I am happy to be proven wrong here. I encourage you to challenge the status quo and experiment with this.

Any time you use animations, you have to respect user preferences for reduced motion:

If someone prefers reduced motion, it could also be a good idea to flatten the angles, not just the animations. I can imagine that a lot of random angles can also upset people while scrolling. Design should be fun, but never at the cost of accessibility.

Tinkering with random() over the last couple of days was a lot of fun. I’m still not sure if I’ll be able to convince my designer friends, but what I do know is that it brings a bit of joy.

Whenever we wanted a bit of organic randomness on the web, we had to make compromises: either pull in a JavaScript animation library, or write huge preprocessor loops that spit out hundreds of lines of static CSS. Having this built into the browser engine with zero JavaScript overhead is such a welcome addition.

We spent the last decade mastering consistency, tokens, and design systems. Now that we have that foundation in place, maybe it’s time to let a little bit of playful messiness back onto the web.

I really believe that the web is supposed to be fun.

Never mind the defaults; here is CSS random().

See the Pen [Never mind the defaults, here is css random() [forked]](https://codepen.io/editor/smashingmag/pen/01a1545a-ab6a-707b-935e-9cf6dd51a3a9) by @utilitybend.

#121. As France is rocked by explosive protests, art school students have their say

A destroyed car near the Marianne statue at the Place de la République, with a yellow vest put on it, the day after clashes during a national day of demonstrations against the cost of living and rising fuel prices in Paris

Photo: REUTERS/Abdul Saboor TPX IMAGES OF THE DAY

When the French sculptor Léopold Morice designed his 9.5m-tall allegory of French republicanism for the Place de la République in Paris, in the late 1870s, he gave the figure a Phrygian cap. With the bloody Paris Commune of 1871 still fresh in everyone’s minds, this was a contested choice, the so-called “liberty cap” being a symbol of the republic at its most revolutionary.

With similar vestimentary symbolism, protesters attending the nation-wide demonstrations in the French capital this Saturday (17 October) scaled Morice’s Marianne with banners and flags and dressed her in a yellow vest—in reference to the gilets jaunes (yellow vests) protests of 2018-20. Emblasoned with the slogan “2026, the police mutilates high-schoolers”, Marianne’s new yellow vest underscored the widening rift between France’s establishment and its embattled youth. In the weeks leading up to what organisers called the “day of action”, pundits and activists alike have begun using the moniker “gilets jeunes” (young vests) to describe this new movement. Protests began last month with students but have expanded to include parents, public sector workers, unions and “yellow vest” activists. On Saturday, what were mainly peaceful demonstrations escalated in particular places into some of the worst instances of public disorder France has seen in years.

The demands of the pupils and students are both immediate and practical—and all-encompassing. Media outlets have mostly pointed to initial protests at the Lycée Antoine-de-Saint-Exupéry in the Parisian banlieue of Créteil, in mid-September, as the trigger for the movement. However, some pundits are noting that pupils at schools in French overseas territories of Guyana and Mayotte began protesting in late August. All are united in their demands for more teachers and repairs to school buildings. They also want an end to Parcoursup, the online platform the government introduced in 2018 to determine where pupils go after finishing secondary school, and which pupils say is leading to unfair selection.

More broadly, protestors are taking a stand against the rise of the far right, rising living costs and climate change, citing the record brutal heatwaves of 2026 as the moment so many people in France finally experienced, directly, the ecological crisis.

On Saturday, between 550,000 (according to the minister of the interior Laurent Nuñez) and 800,000 (according to the organisers) protesters attended largely peaceful marches across France.

Fringe groups of agitators and looters caused widespread damage, forcing entry into city halls, ransacking shops, and setting cars and buildings on fire. Heritage sites have been affected: city officials in Limoges have said the historic town hall, inaugurated in 1883, was “almost 100% destroyed” after a fire caused the roof and belfry to collapse. The local prefect Maurice Barate called the damage, in an interview with the AFP news agency, a “catastrophe for heritage”. And Le Monde reports that, in an alarming breach of security, protestors got very close to the Elysée Palace.

Meanwhile in Lyon, a tourism office was burned down and 162 local businesses reportedly destroyed.

The police, which authorities have acknowledged were overwhelmed, have responded with force and tear gas. Over 2,400 arrests have reportedly been made and nearly 1,000 police and first responders wounded. One 17-year-old protestor in Saint-Etienne reportedly lost a hand to a grenade.

Art world participants have been both involved in and impacted by the unrest. The Musée du Louvre closed its doors today (19 October) after protestors blocked access to the site. “Dear visitors, due to a student social movement, the museum is closed for the time being. We apologise for the inconvenience caused,” read a post from the museum on X. According to the art historian and curator Mark Godfrey, on Instagram, the opening of Jeu de Paume’s exhibition of work by the Canadian artist Stan Douglas had to be delayed. The Art Newspaper contacted the arts centre for comment. The Art Basel Paris fair, meanwhile, which is due to hold VIP preview days on Wednesday and Thursday before opening to the public, on track to open “as planned”, a spokesperson told The Art Newspaper in a statement. The statement adds that the fair “has extensive protocols in place“ and will “work closely with a private security company and, where necessary, the Paris Police Prefecture to always ensure a safe environment.”

“As part of these measures, anti-ram barriers are installed around the Grand Palais to prevent unauthorised vehicles from entering the site and adjacent pedestrian areas,” the statement continues. “Additional security personnel have been deployed to patrol the perimeter of the fair 24 hours a day. Visitors to the fair will undergo thorough security screening protocols including metal detectors and bag inspections upon entry and exit.”

Meanwhile students at a number of art schools across the country, from the Haute École des arts du Rhin in Strasbourg to the École nationale supérieure des arts appliqués et des métiers d’art in Paris, have joined in the strikes. Ahead of the 17 October demonstrations, several students told The Art Newspaper their goal has been to lend their support to the high-school protestors but also to express their concerns about how the government’s austerity measures—enacted in response to France’s exploding national debt—and political instability ahead of the 2027 general elections are affecting the cultural sphere too. As Paco, a second-year student at the École Boulle, said on 16 October, “we’re fighting for our future”. According to a report in Le Monde, unions have said the protests that have led to the closure of the Louvre were led by students from the École du Louvre, a higher education institution located inside the Louvre Palace.

Jean-Baptiste Carobolante, who teaches at the École Supérieure d'Art in Dunkerque and Tourcoing, said not only are many art schools bearing the brunt of cuts to local authority cultural spend, “because culture is often the first sector to be sacrificed”, reactionary politicians are also castigating cultural actors as the political opposition. “And why fund political opponents?” Carobolante said the thinking goes. The Art Newspaper contacted Carobolante and others to see if they wished to provide additional comment following the 17 October demonstrations.

In a televised address on Sunday 18 October, the French president Emmanuel Macron affirmed the government’s dual responsibility to heed the protestors’ legitimate anger and act on its causes, while ensuring republican order is maintained. He said he understood the country’s young people, insisting they have been at the core of his political mission for over a decade.

That will come as news to the pupils and students who started protesting last month, their primary contention being that they want to feel heard and listened to—but have not been. Since 17 October, Macron’s government has been roundly criticised for not taking the youthful protest seriously early enough, as well as for not taking adequate security measures to ensure the demonstrations did not get out of hand. As curfews and limits are imposed on public meetings in several cities and organisers call for a fresh day of action on Saturday (24 October), the mood in the country is one of great uncertainty.

Institutions remember the turbulent period and consider its legacy

Five demonstrators will go to court on charges of theft

#124. Snøhetta completes landmark opera house in Shanghai

Photography by Yumeng Zhu, Tian Fangfang, Chen Hao and StudioSZ

A giant spiral staircase guides visitors to the roof of the Shanghai Grand Opera House, which international studio Snøhetta designed to be “as much a civic destination as a performance venue”.

Located on the Huangpu River waterfront in Shanghai, China, the 146,786-square-metre opera house was conceived as a major cultural landmark that can accommodate a variety of musical performances.

While Snøhetta‘s design responds to a highly ambitious brief, the studio said it began the project as it always does, by taking time to examine and understand the specific site and its context, no matter the scale.

According to the studio, this helped it to create the desired landmark while ensuring it felt like an extension of the existing public realm, open and accessible to both ticket holders and passersby.

“We always begin the same way, regardless of scale: by understanding the context,” Snøhetta co-founder Kjetil Thorsen told Dezeen.

“A cultural building, any building for that matter, must respond to its surroundings, the people who use it, the performers it serves, and the city it becomes part of,” Thorsen reflected.

“When I last visited the site, I was asked by a Chinese architecture student how we managed to create a building that felt so Chinese despite not being from China. The answer lies in observation and understanding context.”

Shanghai Grand Opera House’s defining feature is its spiral staircase, which dramatically cantilevers at its peak and was intended to emulate everything from an unfolding fan to a dancer or a set of piano keys.

It leads directly to the publicly accessible rooftop, which doubles as a stage, an observation deck or simply a meeting point. According to Thorsen, it was integral to making the building feel part of the urban fabric.

He compared the design to the Oslo Opera House, which the studio completed in 2000, with both designs actively seeking to “reduce thresholds wherever possible”.

“Buildings like opera houses inevitably create thresholds through walls, doors, and ticketed programs. We see it as our responsibility to challenge those thresholds and make the building as much a civic destination as a performance venue,” Thorsen explained.

“People should be able to enjoy the building without attending a performance. It should become part of everyday life, a place to spend time, meet others, and experience the city,” he added.

“A successful landmark is not only recognised by visitors, it is also embraced by the people who live around it and make it part of their everyday lives.”

Shanghai Grand Opera House has a radial plan and contains a trio of auditoriums alongside exhibition and education spaces, restaurants and rehearsal and production areas.

The facade flits between transparent and opaque finishes, depending on where the studio wanted to provide privacy and openness. For example, expansive glass elements maximise natural light and views in the lobby.

Together, the three auditoriums can accommodate 4,200 people and host a range of performances. The main auditorium, called the Harmony Hall, contains 2,000 seats across its five levels, while the second hall, named the Soar Theatre, is more intimate, with space for 1,200 people.

The final auditorium contains 1,000 seats and was constructed as a highly flexible space with adaptive seating and staging, catering to more experimental performances. It is fronted with a large glass facade overlooking the river.

“For younger generations especially, that flexibility can help make cultural experiences feel more relevant, accessible, and connected to contemporary life,” said Thorsen.

Shanghai Grand Opera House’s material palette is a play of contrasts, with the light-coloured white stone, glass, and timber exterior having a more open feel than the darker, more intimate interiors.

Inside, the auditoriums each have a unique aesthetic. The main hall is filled with deep red tones and surfaces, intended to feel as though they are carved from a single block, while lighter wooden materials characterise the other two.

At night, the stage towers that project from the building are illuminated, shifting in colour to “animate the roof and the skyline”.

Minimising the building’s carbon footprint was a significant challenge due to the building’s “scale and complexity”, Thorsen said, but this was achieved through measures including passive design strategies.

The bright roof reflects sunlight and heat rather than absorbing it, and the public lobby opens towards both the river and the park, allowing for cross-ventilation.

A palette of durable materials and an adaptable interior will ensure a long lifespan for the building, while a close connection to public transport minimises dependence on private vehicles.

Shanghai Grand Opera House is complete with a landscape design that connects to existing parkland, wetlands and public spaces to support local biodiversity and provide ample public space.

Snøhetta was founded by Thorsen and Craig Dykers in 1989. It won an international competition to design the opera house in 2016 and developed it with the state-owned firm East China Architectural Design & Research Institute (ECADI) and consultants Theatre Projects and Nagata Acoustics.

Other major cultural projects by the studio include the Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library in North Dakota and the rippled Glasshouse Theatre in Queensland.

Photography by Yumeng Zhu, Tian Fangfang, Chen Hao and StudioSZ

#125. PS1 Is Your Place: A Masterclass in Brand Design by Porto Rocha

Porto Rochaâs PS1 Is Your Place turns MoMA PS1âs 50th anniversary into a living declaration: your place to explore, gather, dance, and discover.

The idea works because it treats identity as invitation. Rather than a logo refresh, Porto Rocha built an adaptable messaging framework around the declaration PS1 IS YOUR PLACE: your place to explore, to gather, to dance, to create, to discover something unexpected. Born out of the Alternative Space movement in 1976 and housed in a repurposed Queens public school, PS1 has spent fifty years as one of New Yorkâs last true third places, and the studio answered with type loud enough to say it from a rooftop.

The systemâs confidence lives in PS1 Slab, the institutionâs distinctive slab serif, which carries every campaign message at poster scale. Porto Rocha keeps the existing MoMA PS1 logo but blows it up and rotates it across applications, letting institutional weight collide with street-level energy. One lockup sets the museumâs Queens address vertically against oversized anniversary numerals; a stencil version stamps the wordmark in white straight onto raw concrete. Every slogan reads like a poster made to be pasted, not scrolled.

That paste-up quality is the whole point. On a construction hoarding, SEE NYC FROM A NEW POV runs in olive slab on acid lime beside a duotone bridge photograph, the paper creasing under the sun, footers announcing Greater New York, April 16 to August 17, and free admission for all. The building-side mural carries MoMA PS1 / YOUR PLACE SINCE 1976 in deep forest green on mint, readable blocks away. Hot pink banners, acid lime wild postings, white stencils on concrete: the platform behaves the way PS1 itself does, public first and completely unpretentious.
