#126. Elgato Convertible Wave Go Is a Clip-On and Handheld Mic in One

Elgato Convertible Wave Go Is a Clip-On and Handheld Mic in One

Elgato, a big name in content creation and streaming, has announced the Wave Go, which it describes as a “convertible wireless mic.”

In one configuration, the Elgato Wave Go looks a lot like many small wireless mics on the market, including something like a DJI Mic. It is a small, rectangular wireless mic that easily attaches to clothing.

However, what sets the Wave Go apart from something like the DJI Mic is that the Wave Go mic capsule fits inside a more traditional microphone-shaped holder, what Elgato calls a “smart handle.” This handle has on-device controls for power, recording, and muting.

“Works both ways,” Elgato says of the Wave Go. “How you record changes. Your mic should too. Wave Go gives you two modes in one, so you never have to make do or carry extra gear.”

The smart handle also has a built-in battery to charge the transmitter while it’s in use. Elgato says it delivers 48 hours of total runtime, though only eight hours when the transmitter is used in its clip-on configuration. 10 minutes of quick charging adds another hour of use.

Whether used as a clip-on or handheld mic, the Wave Go makes the same promise of convenient, high-quality sound. The system automatically adapts to the selected configuration and adjusts its recording to deliver “rich” audio quality.

Unlike some competing wireless mics, though, Elgato isn’t targeting the entire market. The company notes that the Wave Go is designed specifically for use with USB-C devices, like a phone or computer, and not made for direct use with a professional digital camera. The mic works only with its USB-C receiver, and Bluetooth connects only to the companion app. Elgato says the wireless range is up to 100 feet (30 meters).

It has no onboard recording, no additional external mic support (the USB-C receiver supports up to two mics), and records up to 24-bit audio.

Of course, for those who want to use a wireless mic with their digital camera, the Elgato Wave Go is not the right choice. But for users who instead work through their phone or computer, it is an interesting new product. It would be nice to see other manufacturers embrace a convertible, two-in-one design like this, even if most users are happy with a clip-on mic.

The Elgato Wave Go is available now for $99.99 with the USB-C receiver, smart handle, and one mic. A second mic is $14.99 at the time of writing, although the regular price is $29.99. The Elgato Wave Go comes in black and sky blue.

#128. British Museum’s Red Ball sparks Energy Embargo for Palestine protests

Protestors in front of the British Museum during its Red Ball fundraiser

The British Museum’s Red Ball fundraising gala took place at the weekend (17 October) against a backdrop of protests by Energy Embargo for Palestine, calling for the London-based institution to end its “unethical partnerships with oil giants and tech billionaires”, according to the group’s Instagram.

The Art Newspaper observed around 60 protestors at the demonstration outside the main entrance, as high-profile guests arrived including the TV presenter Maya Jama, actor Benedict Cumberbatch and London Mayor Sadiq Khan.

A spokesperson for Energy Embargo for Palestine addressed the heavily-policed crowd saying that “the British Museum has a track record of partnering with the Israeli Embassy” and called on the institution to “end its partnership with Zionist billionaires”. Light projections showing messages such as “Drop BP” and “Blood Ball” were also displayed across the museum façade by the demonstrators.

An Israeli Independence Day event organised by the Israeli Embassy was held at the British Museum in May last year. In 2023 the museum accepted a £50m sponsorship deal with BP. The museum director Nicholas Cullinan told The Art Newspaper’s The Week in Art podcast in 2024: “Ultimately when you have to raise hundreds of millions of pounds, you need to have a very good reason for turning down £50m.”

Meanwhile, the hedge fund billionaire Igor Tulchinsky, who has reportedly given £5m in sponsorship for the Bayeux Tapestry exhibition, served as the event's honorary chair in recognition of his support, the museum says. His links to the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) have been scrutinised.

Energy Embargo for Palestine’s Instagram feed adds: “The museum’s management… have consistently shown that they prefer to align with the interests of US billionaires such as Igor Tulchinsky and Peter Thiel, and oil companies destroying the planet, than their own staff and public good.” The Guardian reported in August that the British Museum provided a private viewing opportunity to Peter Thiel, the co-founder of Palantir and PayPal.

There was further activism within the event itself; attendee Georgie Robertson posted images on Instagram of her wearing a red dress with the message "return the marbles" in front of the museum’s Parthenon Marbles display.

Meanwhile, the museum announced an anonymous £30m donation at the ball, which took place during Frieze week in the UK capital. This gift is separate from the yet-to-be-announced total of funds raised at the event.

Both the £30m gift and the funds raised at the event will go towards the museum’s masterplan, which is estimated to cost at least £1bn; the ambitious overhaul includes a complete reworking of the Western range of the museum, new welcome pavilions and an energy centre designed to reduce the museum’s carbon footprint.

A museum spokesperson tells The Art Newspaper: “The British Museum is investing in one of the largest redevelopment projects ever undertaken by a cultural institution so that we can address the need for modernisation and keep the Museum open to all for generations to come. This project has a significant financial cost and will require a mix of private, corporate and public funding.”

According to a museum statement, “this year's Ball celebrates three extraordinary global milestones: the once-in-a-millennium loan of the Bayeux Tapestry from France (until 11 July 2027), a special display marking the 250th anniversary of the United States (Declaring independence: USA 250, until 29 November) and a landmark exhibition exploring 2,000 years of Korean creativity (Korea, until 31 January 2027).”

The museum has been under pressure for more than a decade to break off its affiliation with the oil and gas corporation

#129. 6 Tile Trends Shaping Design From Cersaie 2026

“Warm, moody colors dominated the aisles of Cersaie 2026 and the windows of almost every storefront in Bologna,” notes Danielle McWilliams, principal at Novità, the communications agency for Ceramics of Italy. “Just like in fashion, Italian tile manufacturers debuted collections in deep burgundy, luxurious browns, earthy terracottas and vibrant reds and yellows.”

Era by Faetano mimics the look of terracotta and comes in six natural and neutral colors. Photography courtesy of Del Conca.

Besides color, large-format tiles, texture and dimension, intricate digital printing, and natural material effects were top trends at the 43rd edition of Cersaie, held for five days at the end of September in Bologna, Italy. The annual trade show brings together manufacturers, architects, and designers to explore the latest innovations in ceramic tile, architectural surfaces, and bathroom furnishings. This year’s show drew more than 90,000 visitors to see ceramic and porcelain surfacing materials from 600 exhibitors across 24 countries.

There was an energy to this year’s fair, and not just from the bustling crowds. That palpable buzz was reflected in the temporary showrooms displaying bold, exciting products.

Photography courtesy of Antiche Fornaci D’Agostino

While stark white and neutral tiles will always be in fashion, ceramic makers did not shy away from richer, more saturated hues this year. “We are certainly seeing a renewed confidence in color,” says Benedetta Borghi, of external affairs at Atlas Concorde. “There is a much greater willingness to use stronger colors as part of the architectural palette.”

Combining bright hues with neutral and warm white tiles offers a refreshed aesthetic. Atlas Concorde’s Boost Hux pairs warm natural tones with accents of green, red, blue, and ember, while Vivia features vivid glazed colors inspired by Italian ceramics. “For us, color is increasingly becoming a design tool rather than simply a decorative accent,” Borghi says.

Cristina Faedi, tile trend expert, consultant to Confindustria Ceramica, and founder and art director of Infinite Possibilità, agrees: “There are Italian companies that have even doubled the colors in their range, and others have made three densities of the same color.”

Photography courtesy of Ceramica Fioranese

Could the popularity of rich-colored tiles be the pendulum swinging back after muted tones and neutrals have been in favor? Maybe. But Faedi also sees the chaotic state of the world influencing tile palettes, citing the seven chakras, which correspond to the colors of the rainbow. Green, for example, represents empathy and emotional healing.

The Eterea collection by Gardenia&Ariana includes onyx-inspired tiles for floors and walls, plus a complementary 3D fluted wall tile called Righe. Photography courtesy of Gardenia&Ariana.

So it makes sense that green is having a moment. “It’s a color that clearly gives a lot of calm and is inspired by nature,” Faedi says. “It’s a narrative of landscapes, of places, of wild herbs, but also of thermal waters and even of oceans.” Along with shades ranging from deep forest to pale sage, earthy palettes of terracotta and other natural tones also stood out.

Plinth by Terratinta Group’s Sartoria, shown here in Moss, Stone Green, and Off Stone. Photography courtesy of Terratinta Group.

Glossy finishes amplify the colors and make them pop. Plinth from Sartoria, part of the Terratinta Group, comes in two shades of green, Moss and Stone Green, and features a 3D surface that adds texture and dimension to walls.

“Ceramic is no longer simply reproducing a material: the surface itself is becoming an architectural element,” Borghi says. “That’s an interesting evolution.”

Marca Corona’s Multiforme Mira wall tiles complement its concrete-effect porcelain floor tiles. The Tassello decorative variant features small, three-dimensional tesserae arranged to create the appearance of a continuous mosaic, with glossy and luster-glazed details set against a matte background.

As part of The Nesting Room collection, Moooi Ceramic Surfaces, in collaboration with ABK, designed Hypnotic Owl, a floor and wall tile with a tactile 3D-relief surface created using ABK’s 3DTECH technology. This proprietary process digitally applies glazes and textures to porcelain stoneware.

Photography courtesy of Moooi Ceramic Surfaces

Gruppo Bardelli brand Appiani introduced Lamiere, part of its Pastelli Strutture collection. Inspired by sheet metal, the through-body ceramic tiles use the chiaroscuro effect to create the illusion of a 3D surface. I found the interplay of light and reflectivity particularly impressive, even mind-bending: the tiles look dimensional but feel flat to the touch.

When real stone or marble isn’t durable enough for a project, or is simply too expensive, ceramic offers the aesthetics of natural materials and the performance of porcelain. While this has been a trend for years, advances in technology have made the effects increasingly realistic.

Magma by Flaviker features the look of slate and lava stone in its color-body porcelain stoneware; it comes in indoor and outdoor versions up to 48 inches. Photography courtesy of Flaviker.

“We are talking about controlled chaos,” Faedi says of tiles that mimic natural stone. “Technology can create this apparently chaotic mix of colors, hues, and shapes, but with a great visual impact, thanks precisely to modern techniques.”

Gruppo Romani brand Verde introduced Essenziale, a glazed porcelain stoneware that mimics the materiality of limestone. Its Contour Tech 3D printing process colors the ceramic body at different depths to reflect the irregularities of sedimentary stone.

It’s hard to believe the Marble Boutique collection from Del Conca isn’t actual marble or onyx. The line includes three finishes—Shine, Natural, and Structured—and six new material options with enhanced colors and veining. Its large-format slabs, measuring 48 by 110 inches, are also on trend.

Large-format tile stood out at the show, even though it has been trending larger for years. “We see large slabs as a way to create greater continuity across different elements of a space, from floors and walls to kitchen countertops, islands, and furniture,” Borghi says.

European manufacturers, particularly in Italy and Spain, pioneered oversized formats in 2001 by using advanced pressing techniques that moved beyond the traditional 12-by-12-inch tile.

In the U.S., the American National Standards Institute officially defined large-format tile in January 2025 as tile with a facial dimension of 23 inches or larger. Many exhibitors at Cersaie showcased extra-large formats, including several collections featured here. Solaris by Cotto D’Este is one of them; it comes in formats up to 24 by 128 inches.

Other products that resonated with me at Cersaie were colorful, intricate decorative tiles made using both high-tech processes and traditional hand-painting. I appreciated the juxtaposition of new technologies and traditional techniques.

Photography courtesy of Ceramica Bardelli

Ceramica Bardelli’s Tulipani, designed by Ronald van der Hilst, features floral decoration in three patterns created using different technologies, from cold digital printing to laser engraving. The brand also introduced the eye-catching Searcus, designed by Riccardo Capuzzo, with two patterns inspired by the sea and the circus, made using cold digital printing.

Photography courtesy of Ceramica Bardelli

In direct contrast, Ceramica Francesco De Maio’s Three Elements, One Matter collection was designed and hand-painted by architect Kengo Kuma. “I sought to let nature emerge through the hand, where each tile carries a continuous human gesture, sometimes as light as rain, sometimes as soft as mist, sometimes as grounded as earth,” Kuma says. “Material, movement, and landscape quietly become one.”

Photography courtesy of Ceramica Francesco De Maio

A 25-plus-year veteran of the interior design industry, Danine Alati began her career at commercial design publication Contract, where she spent 11 years before moving into luxury lifestyle media and working on titles including Hamptons and Art Basel. Based in Brooklyn with her family, she has contributed to AD PRO, DuJour, Galerie, and aspire, among other design and lifestyle publications.

#130. How Much Information Does a BIM Model Really Need?

Building Information Modeling has made it possible to attach an enormous amount of information to each element of a design. A wall can carry its fire resistance class and its cost group, and later even the maintenance information a facility manager will need. That possibility creates a temptation: if the model can hold more data, it should. In the process, an important question of efficiency can get lost: does the project actually need this information, and does it need it now?

Building Information Modeling has made it possible to attach an enormous amount of information to each element of a design. A wall can carry its fire resistance class and its cost group, and later even the maintenance information a facility manager will need. That possibility creates a temptation: if the model can hold more data, it should. In the process, an important question of efficiency can get lost: does the project actually need this information, and does it need it now?

For architects, BIM is often described as a "single source of truth." Every additional property, however, adds work, coordination, and maintenance, and information entered too early or without a clear purpose can quickly become outdated. What matters is having the right information for the decisions being made at each stage of the project. The Stuttgart-based firm KUBUS360 made that question central to its work on an administrative complex in Baden-Württemberg (Germany).

What matters is having the right information for the decisions being made at each stage of the project. The Stuttgart-based firm KUBUS360 made that question central to its work on an administrative complex in Baden-Württemberg (Germany).

The project consists of three wood-concrete hybrid buildings, with public-facing ground floors and offices for roughly 630 workstations above. Known for a "360-degree" approach spanning planning, project management, and sustainability consulting, the firm developed what architect Bianca Hirner and BIM coordinator Freddy Hartmann call leanBIM. Working in Vectorworks Architect, they set out to keep the model detailed without letting it grow heavier than the project required.

Working in Vectorworks Architect, they set out to keep the model detailed without letting it grow heavier than the project required.

Designing the Information Before Designing the Model

For KUBUS360, the BIM process begins before the first line is drawn. The client had limited experience with BIM, so instead of waiting for a long list of requirements, the team helped write the Employer's Information Requirements (EIR) and then built the BIM Execution Plan (BEP) from them. Hartmann explains:

The client had limited experience with BIM, so instead of waiting for a long list of requirements, the team helped write the Employer's Information Requirements (EIR) and then built the BIM Execution Plan (BEP) from them. Hartmann explains:

We primarily aimed to incorporate only the information that would be evaluated later into the model.

We primarily aimed to incorporate only the information that would be evaluated later into the model.

This planning established the Level of Information Need (LOIN) matrix for the project, identifying every building component as an Industry Foundation Classes (IFC) entity while specifying the properties each element would need and the project phase when those properties would be added. Information entered the model as the design developed, rather than being attached all at once. The result was a lighter model with clearer responsibilities and fewer unnecessary data fields to manage.

Information entered the model as the design developed, rather than being attached all at once. The result was a lighter model with clearer responsibilities and fewer unnecessary data fields to manage.

Keeping a model lean is partly a question of where information lives. KUBUS360 organized nearly the entire project around four centralized databases inside Vectorworks Architect: a general IFC database, a component database, a dedicated database for windows and doors, and a placeholder database for facility management information.

Through the Vectorworks Data Manager, elements inherit their fire resistance class and other shared properties from these datasets, and the same values feed visualizations, schedules, and IFC exports. As Hartmann says:

Thanks to the small number of databases, we know relatively quickly where the data is being entered.

Modeling Freely Without Losing BIM Intelligence

Most of the project, from stairs and railings to structural elements and doors, relies on native Vectorworks tools, which KUBUS360 says cover roughly 95 percent of the project's modeling work. Custom elements follow a different logic. KUBUS360 uses class-based assignment, where an object's IFC identity and properties come from its class rather than from the tool used to draw it.

Custom elements follow a different logic. KUBUS360 uses class-based assignment, where an object's IFC identity and properties come from its class rather than from the tool used to draw it.

A parapet can be modeled with a roof surface and still export with the correct cost group. A curved facade pilaster can begin as solid geometry, become an Auto Hybrid object, and carry the same data as any standard component. "The class-based approach is a key advantage for us in Vectorworks Architect, as it allows us to design shapes completely freely," says Hartmann.

Making Information Visible Instead of Hidden

Data becomes useful when architects can verify it visually. One of KUBUS360's workflows uses Data Visualization in Vectorworks Architect to color-code elements based on information stored in the model. Fire protection classes and other properties can be displayed instantly across the building, making inconsistencies visible without searching through schedules.

The team also developed an internal quality-control tool called the Angle Checker. Because polygonal geometries create many irregular angles, the tool shows at a glance which walls have been drawn correctly. Each element receives a simple true-or-false value through the Data Manager, allowing incorrect geometry to be identified immediately.

Information That Extends Beyond the Building

The question of "how much information is enough?" becomes even more relevant when BIM connects to data beyond the building itself. A second Vectorworks example shows how integration with ArcGIS can make geospatial information the foundation of a BIM workflow before architectural modeling begins. Parcels, roads, and existing site features can be streamed directly into a project through ArcGIS Feature Services, creating a geolocated site model from live GIS information instead of static imports.

Existing trees imported from GIS datasets, for example, can carry information about species or health condition and be color-coded through Data Visualization to distinguish which trees should be preserved, removed, or replaced across a site.

At an urban scale, BIM models can also contribute information back into GIS environments. Geolocated building models containing architectural, landscape, and infrastructure data can become part of broader ArcGIS web scenes used by planners, engineers, and facility managers. Not every project requires this level of integration. BIM information becomes valuable when it supports decisions across disciplines, not simply because it exists.

As BIM models become richer in information, deciding what to include becomes a design and management question in its own right. KUBUS360 addressed it early, treating BIM as a tool for reaching project goals and keeping the effort it demands as small as possible. The firm agreed with the client on which information would be evaluated later, defined in the LOIN when each property should enter the model, and kept the data in a small number of databases where the team always knew to find it. The same logic applies to projects of any size: define information priorities before modeling begins, centralize data structures, and use visual checks to keep the model coordinated as the design develops.

#133. Eight converted power stations that show the power of reuse

In this roundup, we take a look at decommissioned power stations that have been given a second life, from the Tate Modern museum in London to the Dyson headquarters in Singapore.

Originally built to generate electricity, these industrial buildings typically have expansive interiors with tall ceilings, giving architects plenty of flexibility for conversion.

Battersea Power Station, UK, by WilkinsonEyre

The Grade II*-listed Battersea Power Station in London stood decommissioned for 39 years before architecture studio WilkinsonEyre‘s transformation reopened it as a shopping, office and residential building in 2022.

Originally built in the 1930s, a bustling shopping centre is now located in the building’s restored turbine halls and glazed apartments were built atop the roof.

Find out more about Battersea Power Station ›

Ballers, USA, by Good City Studio and Hexagon Studio Architects

Local firms Good City Studio and Hexagon Studio Architects revamped the main turbine hall of Delaware Power Station in Fishtown, Philadelphia, into a sports club with indoor pickleball, soccer and squash courts.

Named Ballers, the sports club formed part of the wider plan to transform the 1920s power station into The Battery, a mixed-use complex containing apartments, offices and a hotel.

Dyson headquarters, Singapore, by M Moser Associates, W Architects and Studio Lapis

Technology company Dyson established its global company headquarters inside Singapore‘s St James Power Station, which was transformed by local studios W Architects and Studio Lapis, with interior fit-out by architecture studio M Moser Associates.

The turbine hall of the 1926 building was reimagined as a four-storey atrium framed by exposed black steelwork and a sculptural spiral staircase, while an area of amphitheatre-style seating provides gathering space next to a cafe.

Find out more about the Dyson headquarters ›

Iconic London landmark the Tate Modern was once the Bankside Power Station, originally designed by Giles Gilbert Scott, who also designed Battersea Power Station.

Swiss studio Herzog & de Meuron‘s pioneering transformation of the building opened in 2000, complete with a cathedral-like gallery space in the turbine hall, and ignited a global trend of converting disused power stations into hubs of art and culture.

Powerhouse Arts, USA, by Herzog & de Meuron

In more recent years, Herzog & de Meuron converted the remains of a 115-year-old power plant in Brooklyn into an art manufacturing hub called Powerhouse Arts.

The studio refurbished the brick-clad turbine hall, the only part of the original building left standing, and converted it into an art production centre, while the demolished Boiler House was rebuilt in red concrete.

Shajing Village Hall, China, by ARCity Office

As part of wider plans to transform an industrial site into a public wetland, architecture studio ARCity Office restored and extended a 1980s power plant in Shenzhen, China, converting it into a community hub.

The studio left the building’s concrete remnants as-found, using its structural shell to support a series of new steel and glass volumes that draw upon the spaces found in traditional ancestral halls.

Find out more about Shajing Village Hall ›

Global Leadership Centre, UK, by John McAslan + Partners

British studio John McAslan + Partners added learning space and accommodation to Oxford’s first electrical power plant to form the Global Leadership Centre, designed for the University of Oxford‘s Saïd Business School.

John McAslan + Partners created a triple-height entrance and shared space in the turbine hall, restored the 1890s brick facades and rebuilt and extended the metal-clad upper levels.

Find out more about Global Leadership Centre ›

Innovation Powerhouse, the Netherlands, by Atelier van Berlo, Eugelink Architectuur and De Bever Architecten

The former Philips power plant in Eindhoven was converted into an innovation hub housing a dozen businesses, with offices arranged along a communal street-like passage.

Rotterdam-based Atelier van Berlo worked with Eindhoven-based studios Eugelink Architectuur and De Bever Architecten on the project, aiming to celebrate the building’s original features by preserving its structure and coal chutes.

Find out more about Innovation Powerhouse ›

#134. This Absurd, Adorable $38 1MP Digital Camera Can Be Worn Like Jewelry

This Absurd, Adorable $38 1MP Digital Camera Can Be Worn Like Jewelry

While Kenko Tokina continues work on a lens “like no other,” the company’s first new lens in years, it also continues churning out compact cameras in Japan, like the adorable new $38 Pieni III.

As reported by CAPA Camera Web, the Pieni III is a 1.38-megapixel, teeny-tiny digital camera — like really tiny. The camera weighs a meager 18 grams (0.63 ounces, or 9/1000th of a Noct) and is so small that it can actually be worn like a necklace. It is just 53 x 35 x 18 millimeters (2.1 x 1.38 x 0.71 inches). It’s at least big enough for its microSD card slot.

Unfortunately, it has a built-in battery and charges via USB-C. This is a notable change from the Pieni II, which used an old-school micro-USB port for charging.

A neat feature of the Pieni III is its magnetic back. This means that users can attach it to metal objects, like railings, to take self-portraits.

Arguably, the cute, small form factor is as much of the Pieni III’s appeal as its imaging capabilities. The sensor is laughably small, measuring just Type 1/10, which makes even the smallest smartphone sensors today look monstrously huge. And of course, the 1.38-megapixel billing is not even quite right. That’s upscaled in-camera from 0.32 megapixels. For some reason, the camera even records 720p video at up to 30 frames per second.

With such a small image sensor, it’s little surprise that the built-in lens has an extremely short focal length. It’s a 1.8mm f/2.8 lens, which is equivalent in 35mm terms to a 42mm prime. The lens can focus from 0.3 meters (11.8 inches) to infinity, but given the small sensor, everything is likely to be in focus anyway.

Per CAPA Camera Web, the camera has a fixed ISO of 100 and only offers automatic shutter speed. But again, the photos are really something of an afterthought to the camera’s style and size. There’s not even an electronic viewfinder or screen to view photos, so images can only be seen on another device, like a connected smartphone or computer.

Speaking of style, the Pieni III comes in some standard colors, like baby blue, pastel pink, white, and black. However, it also comes in Hello Kitty-flavored varieties, including ones featuring Hello Kitty herself, plus other Sanrio characters like Cinnamaroll, Kuromi, and the half-fish, half-human weirdo that is Hangyodon.

The Kenko Tokina Pieni III is now available in Japan for a suggested retail price of 6,600 yen, about $38 at current exchange rates. The Sanrio-themed ones are a bit pricier, though, coming in at 8,470 yen, or over $53.

#135. Brand Identity: Globe-Trotter by Ragged Edge

Ragged Edge crafts a character-led brand identity for British luggage maker Globe-Trotter, reviving its 1897 North Star crest and typography.

Luxury branding has a sameness problem. Over the last decade, heritage houses kept stripping away their quirks in favor of flat geometric sans-serifs and polite minimalism. Founded in 1897, British luggage maker Globe-Trotter needed a different route when partnering with new owners Oakley Capital and London studio Ragged Edge. Instead of competing on slick tech gimmicks or surface-level status, the team doubled down on eccentric British character. These handmade vulcanised fibreboard cases aren't precious museum pieces. They're built to get scuffed, sticker-covered, and hauled across continents for a lifetime or two.

The logo goes straight to the archives. Ragged Edge recrafted the idiosyncrasies of the original nineteenth-century lettering and locked the wide, flared uppercase wordmark around a faceted four-pointed North Star compass in place of a standard hyphen. In Illustrator, those beveled star planes also anchor an arched window crest where GLOBEâ¢TROTTER curves above ENG and 1897, as well as a deep blind-debossed impression pressed into fibrous off-white cotton paper stock. Alongside the mark, the verbal direction channels the dry wit of vintage British travel advertising through a sharp serif pairing that flips between upright roman and lively italic cuts.

Every touchpoint feels lived-in. On the Summer 26 issue of the Globe-Trotter Journal laid out in InDesign, a sage-green cover with yellow loop-stitched spine binding frames the masthead and the headline "Go your own way" above pastel leather-cornered trunks from the Tyler, the Creator collaboration open to a custom leopard-print lining. Other layouts pair the roman-and-italic line "Accessory to adventure" against a cobalt-blue case with black leather corners and silver rivets, or set "Accompanying the well-travelled for 128 years and counting." above an ivory trunk covered in hotel labels from Tangier and Villars Palace â right down to the Paris flagship storefront with its brushed-brass signage, emerald-green interior, and papier-mÃ¢chÃ© elephant.

#137. Comment | Art does not function like other commodities, so why is it being priced like one?

Over a barrel? There are parallels between the way the oil market worked in the 1980s with how the art market works now Photo: chitsanupong

The global art market grew 4% last year, to $59.6bn. It is the figure everyone repeats, but it is close to useless, because it combines two markets moving in opposite directions. Works above $10m fell 44% in the first half of 2025 and are down 72% from the 2022 peak; not one lot sold above $50m, against 13 in the first half of 2022. Dealers selling below $250,000, meanwhile, reported sales up 17%. The top is in retreat, the bottom expanding, and the aggregate describes neither. Anyone trained in commodities knows the mistake: you never publish one price for a market that trades in grades. That the flagship research leads with it is a clue about who the research is for.

Strictly defined, Art is not a commodity: a painting is unique and unsubstitutable, and its price may never settle at any “correct” level—the economist William Baumol argued in 1986 that art behaves like a floating crap game, because nothing forces its price toward a fundamental. He was right, and the concession is smaller than it sounds. Art behaves like a commodity everywhere that matters—in how it is supplied, hedged, financed and traded—and the market has built an entire apparatus that treats it as one.

Crude oil in the early 1970s looked exactly as unanalysable as art is said to be now: hundreds of non-comparable grades, sold at prices posted by a few powerful sellers through relationships rather than exchanges. With no benchmark and no public record of what anything traded for, its supply was managed by a cartel, Opec (Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries). Then the infrastructure arrived: futures markets in the 1980s, and a reporting agency, Platts, that gathered the day’s real bids and trades and published an assessed price, turning a private trade into a public one by method alone. Oil did not become legible because its nature changed; rather, someone built the layer that made it legible—a feat that art has not achieved.

The parallels are clear. A gallery that sets a price, keeps it private and offers it selectively is running a posted-price market, as the oil majors did before 1980. An estate metering an artist’s work, or a gallery choosing who may buy and cutting off quick resellers, is doing what Opec does with a quota. A third-party guarantee is a written option; when a guaranteed lot sells to its guarantor, the reported hammer is not a clearing price but the exercise of a hedge. And the most honest number in any commodity market—how much offered supply failed to sell—is the one art buries. The buy-in rate is the clearest demand signal available, and it never leads the report; the record lot does.

None of this makes art a commodity. It fails the definition at its root—fungibility—and no pile of structural matches repairs that. What the parallels capture is structure, not definition, and structure is what finance operates on: a market plumbed like a commodity can be financed like one even though it is not one. The parallels do not prove art is a commodity—they explain how it came to be treated as one.

The market could not make a painting fungible, so it wrapped the painting in instruments that are. Lending against art turns a unique object into collateral. Funds pool works so a share is interchangeable, though no two holdings are. Fractional platforms slice a canvas into tradable shares. None of it makes a painting a commodity; all of it makes claims on paintings behave like one — as finance has always done with unique assets. But every instrument needs a valuation to function, and the wrapper inherits no anchor the object never had. A credentialed appraisal profession exists, but an appraisal is a point-in-time opinion, not a continuous market price, and it says nothing about who owns a work, in what fractions, against what liens. That record does not exist at all.

Hot property: Lisa Brice’s After Embah (2018) sold for £5.4m last year at Sotheby’s © the artist; courtesy of Sotheby’s

Which is how you get Inigo Philbrick. Between 2016 and 2019 he built a business on these very instruments and defrauded collectors and lenders of more than $86m in what the FBI said was the largest art fraud in US history. Philbrick’s was not a valuation fraud—the works involved had plausible values—but an ownership one: he sold more than 100% of individual works to multiple buyers and pledged the same pieces to lenders who knew nothing of each other, because nothing existed to tell them. The prosecutor’s diagnosis was exact: he exploited “the lack of transparency in the art market”. Philbrick is the prosecuted extreme of a quieter, legal exposure sitting in the market every day—the loan against a stale appraisal, the claim written against an ownership no one confirmed.

The cost is highest where data is thinnest. Bonhams’s live Modern and contemporary Middle Eastern art sale last November made £3.2m and set multiple records; its online sale in February took $287,000, with two in five works unsold. Same house, same department, months apart. Read the first and the market booms; read the second and it fails; read the buy-in rate across both and you learn the truth: demand concentrated among committed buyers, not the broad market the record implies.

The capital behind this fast-growing regional market is, at one remove, hydrocarbon revenue on a lag; an analyst who can model that holds a forward indicator on a market most researchers cannot see at all. African art tells a subtler version: Sotheby’s has folded these artists into its premier sales rather than a separate category, and in the main room they reach prices the niche never produced—the South African painter Lisa Brice set a record at £5.4m in March 2025. That is a re-rating, not a rally.

None of this is a market waiting to be discovered. The capital has already arrived, without the price infrastructure that would let a lender, insurer or fund verify what it is underwriting. The missing layer does not gate the money, it gates the safety of money already in motion. If anything, the opacity selects, deterring the disciplined and leaving the field to those willing to write claims against unconfirmed marks. Financialisation is not being prevented by the absence of infrastructure, it is racing ahead of it.

There is a reason the market’s own research does not say this. The institutions producing the flagship studies also lend against art, manage collections, and insure and audit it. Nobody whose revenue depends on volume leads with a buy-in rate, and the most-cited index, Mei Moses, is owned by Sotheby’s. Independent research exists, but none yet combines independence with private-market coverage, transparency and segment detail.

So the claim is not that art is a commodity. It is that art is being financialised faster than it is being made legible—the apparatus treating it as a commodity has outrun the infrastructure that would verify its marks. The notion that art lies beyond economics has always served those who prefer it not examined too closely. It is superb public relations. But it has never been an argument.

• Faustine Jean-Louis is an art market economist and the founder of Apotheosis Advisory

#140. 10 Artful Rug Collections That Bring Pattern, Texture, and Craft to the Floor

In contemporary interior design, the rug has quietly transcended its conventional role as a soft buffer between furnishings and hard floors. Today, recognizable names across architecture, design, and fine art are embracing the medium, reframing the floor as the room’s proverbial fifth wall: an expansive, horizontal canvas ripe for visual expression.

For both designers and homeowners, rugs offer a relatively low-risk way to experiment with bold colors, complex geometries, and rich textures. While painted feature walls or custom cabinetry can feel daunting, a removable floor covering can introduce depth and personality without requiring a permanent commitment. A rug can anchor an entire room or introduce an unexpected visual element, transforming the floor into a space for cultural and personal storytelling.

What makes this movement so compelling is the diversity of designs and production methods available, from bespoke, research-driven one-offs and small-batch heirloom weaves to scalable, high-performance collections. Across these 10 recent releases, historic ornamental details, personal memories, and traditional craft techniques meet computational design and innovative fiber technologies. Whether translated from works on paper, inspired by microscopic structures in nature, or knotted using techniques once reserved for royalty, these collections demonstrate that rugs can hold as much artistic and aesthetic weight as any framed piece on a gallery wall. Given the centuries-old tradition of hanging tapestries, perhaps they always have.

Morocco-based BENI’s ongoing collaboration with artistic director and self-described “placer of things” Colin King has produced The Chelsea Collection, an interpretation of heirloom construction once reserved for palace interiors. The eight designs are the first to feature Royale, Beni’s adaptation of an ancient hand-knotting technique historically practiced for Moroccan nobility. Requiring months of work by skilled artisans, the exceptionally dense weave allows for intricate patterns and a refined, tapestry-like surface.

Drawing inspiration from the hidden gardens of European cities, the collection translates architectural motifs such as wrought-iron gates, garden layouts, and ornamental details into contemporary compositions. The palette of deep blacks, browns, and greens further emphasizes the designs’ intricate geometries, demonstrating how centuries-old craftsmanship can produce something distinctly contemporary.

The Chelsea Collection from Beni x Colin King is available at benirugs.com.

Stockholm-based Nordic Knots introduces Dancing Flower and Matches, two expressive rug designs that draw inspiration from Swedish Grace, a design movement that emerged in the 1920s and combined classical proportions with modern simplicity. Crafted primarily from wool, the designs translate botanical silhouettes and geometric motifs into rich, tactile surfaces.

Dancing Flower features a playful, organic pattern, while Matches takes a more structured approach with rhythmic geometry and touches of bamboo silk. Balancing soft backgrounds with bold linework, the designs bring warmth, artistic character, and visual rhythm to contemporary interiors while celebrating Sweden’s decorative arts heritage.

Dancing Flower and Matches from Nordic Knots are available at nordicknots.com/us.

Marking a material milestone, Australian rug maker Armadillo introduces Venezia, its first collection crafted entirely from pure silk. Inspired by the shifting light of Venice and the way it plays across surfaces, each piece is hand-knotted in India to create a single, uninterrupted field of luminous color.

Defined by a low pile and refined profile, the collection shifts subtly in response to ambient light and perspective. Offered in five stocked colorways—Biscuit, Rosewood, Vermilion, Caper, and Serpentine—alongside 15 made-to-order hues, Venezia demonstrates how monochromatic silk surfaces can anchor living spaces with subtle warmth and visual depth.

The Venezia Collection is available at us.armadillorugs.com.

Part of The Rug Company’s Colour in Residence series, Silk Textures explores the expressive qualities of silk and nuanced tertiary color palettes. Comprising 20 handmade rugs across two distinct finishes—Vara (a handloomed wool-and-silk blend celebrating gentle irregularity) and Caliche (a luminous 100% silk weave)—the collection was fittingly photographed at Malta’s Baroque Villa Bologna.

The rugs feature individually developed colors inspired by mineral tones, from earthy clay to tranquil sage. Through subtle variations in texture, sheen, and color, Silk Textures offers an exploration of how a seemingly simple surface can influence the atmosphere of a room.

Vara and Caliche from the Silk Textures collection are available at therugcompany.com.

Expanding the possibilities of natural fibers in rug design, Patterson Flynn introduces Abstraction, a series crafted from durable abaca. Reframing the material through a contemporary lens, the collection reinterprets traditional decorative arts and artisanal techniques—such as Italian marbled paper and straw marquetry—through bold, graphic designs.

Conceived as individual works of art rather than conventional repeating patterns, each piece makes use of abaca’s natural sheen, dimensional texture, and interaction with light. The result is a collection that transforms a material often associated with more traditional interiors into something distinctly contemporary.

The Abstraction collection is available at pattersonflynn.com.

Interior designer Sara Story’s collaboration with rug maker Christopher Farr draws deeply from personal memory. Titled Hill Country, the three-piece collection—Spider, Landscape, and Grid—translates the sun-washed terrain of Story’s Texas upbringing alongside references to Louise Bourgeois’ monumental spider sculptures.

Hand-knotted in wool and silk, the collection balances architectural geometry with painterly abstraction. Spider, for example, uses raised lines to suggest the form of an arachnid, referencing Bourgeois’ work without reproducing it literally. Rooted in both personal history and artistic influence, Hill Country demonstrates how rugs can introduce a narrative element into contemporary interiors.

The Hill Country collection is available at christopherfarr.com.

Spanish brand Nanimarquina partnered with Eames Office and Form Portfolios to adapt seven original artworks by Lucia Eames, daughter of Charles Eames and stepdaughter of Ray Eames, into expressive rugs.

Rather than simply reproducing the original graphics, designs such as Echo, Rooted, and Sunbirds translate Eames’ organic compositions into tactile surfaces using techniques including hand-tufting, hand-knotting, sculptural relief, and hand-braided jute. Defined by earthy tones and fluid silhouettes, the collection brings a lesser-known chapter of the Eames family’s creative legacy into contemporary interiors.

The Lucia Eames collection is available at us.nanimarquina.com.

Demonstrating how expressive design can coexist with everyday practicality, Jaipur Living’s combines performance materials with traditional craftsmanship. Spanning 75 designs, the series incorporates solution-dyed fibers to create durable, easy-care rugs with the softness and visual appeal of natural textiles.

Produced through a combination of hand-knotting, hand-tufting, and handweaving, the collection offers rich patterns, subtle gradients, and dimensional textures without sacrificing practicality. With options suited to high-traffic areas, CallaLuxe demonstrates that visually compelling floor coverings need not be reserved for spaces where durability is less of a concern.

The CallaLuxe collection is available at jaipurliving.com.

Created for the outdoor Verdant Phenomena, an outdoor group exhibition in Sonoma, California, the Plot rug by Nomadory responds to the relationship between natural growth and the geometry of the built environment. Developed in collaboration with The Bureau and artist Gigi Allen, the design takes inspiration from rectangular planter boxes and the organic forms that emerge within them.

Subtle variations in pile height and contrasting stitch patterns emphasize this juxtaposition, translating the relationship between cultivation and structure into a woven surface. Made from recycled polyester for outdoor use, Plot suggests how the visual language of a garden can be carried into other spaces through textile design.

Inquiries about the Plot rug can be made at verdantphenomena.com.

Melding computational design with traditional craftsmanship, Toronto-based Creative Matters teamed up with Paris architecture practice RDAI to create Zoometry. Inspired by microscopic biological structures—including butterfly wings, spider webs, and coral—the six designs translate digitally generated compositions into intricately hand-knotted rugs.

Crafted in Nepal using Himalayan wool and Chinese silk, the collection uses material contrast and subtle shifts in color to evoke the iridescence and complexity of natural forms. Each digital composition serves as a detailed guide for the artisans, with approximately 1.8 million individual knots required for a 2-by-3-meter rug. Positioned as an experimental, research-driven collection, Zoometry demonstrates how computational precision and artisanal expertise can work together to transform natural geometry into tactile works of art.

The Zoometry collection is available at creativemattersinc.com.

Adrian Madlener is a Brussels-born, New York-based writer specializing in collectible and sustainable design. With a focus on craft-led experimentation, he covers designers and makers who are pushing the boundaries of their disciplines.

#141. Stupid Never Dies review: the Spider-Verse visual blast can't hide the grind

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A riotously colourful punk-rock action RPG with clever combat systems and bags of personality, Stupid Never Dies is fun once it clicks, though repetition and awkward targeting frustrate.

Why you can trust Creative Bloq Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

Format PS5 (reviewed), Xbox Series X|S, PC (Steam)

The heart of Stupid Never Dies is as old as dirt, with a twist: Davy, a zombie, wants to bring a dead girl back to life because he's fallen in love with her. There's a slight snag in this plan, beyond the whole being-dead business: Julia, the girl in question, has never actually met him, so she's not really his girlfriend. Davy doesn't see it that way, naturally, and off he goes into a demon-infested underworld to defeat ‘KOM’ and collect the tech he’s been convinced he needs to defrost her, presumably without much thought for what happens when she wakes up and discovers her devoted ‘boyfriend’ is a complete stranger, and undead.

It's a peculiar setup, and the more you think about it, the more uncomfortable it gets. Back in the human world, Davy picks his nose while his adopted mentor ‘Dr Frank’ explains the plot, rolls around on a Zumba and generally behaves like a man/boy who's never had a sensible thought in his entire undead life. He's a shambling, slow-witted mess, barely interested in anything beyond his own romantic fantasy; then you send him down into the dungeons, and he turns into this zippy, aggressively cartoonish brawler designed around ridiculous transformations – a Mereman that can surf on enemies – and the idea that there’s zero defence and all offence, because ‘stupid never dies’.

The art direction, made in Unreal Engine 5, is fizzy, chaotic fun, a surgical mash-up of anime, punk, graphic design, pop art, manga and even some stop motion animation and scrapbooking for good measure, that feels like somebody's put Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse and Persona 5 in a blender with a bunch of '90s zines and then decided the result needed more colour and a bit of punk’s irreverent attitude. Every menu, character animation, and little flourish seems to have something going on, and I kept finding myself smiling at the sheer cheek of it all. No doubt, Stupid Never Dies will be challenging Romeo Is a Dead Man for the year's most inventive visual design.

The human world, Davy’s mall, has a stark, almost photographic realism, with graphic design and physical details that make it feel solid and lived in, while the demon realm is painterly and splashy, full of loose details and exaggerated shapes. As Davy descends, he runs and brawls through scattered memories of human history, a bit of Norse ice and wind here, a spot of Roman volcanic tragedy there, though these are less sprawling worlds to get lost in than a series of very gamey narrow locations, backdrops as gauntlets to fight your way through.

And then the visual effects kick in. Defeat an enemy and ribbons of rainbow ink explode around Davy and splash across the scenery, while Davy Burst, his temporary powered-up state, arrives with electric-guitar flourishes and multicoloured lighting, as if somebody's cranked the volume up on the entire screen to 11. My favourite touch is the doodled googly eyes and daft little smiles stickered onto enemies, a lovely bit of Spider-Verse-style design that made me smile the first time I noticed it.

There's a lot to look at, and the game knows it. Sometimes it's almost needy in the way it demands your attention, but I was happy to give it, because even when the underlying action starts to feel familiar, the art direction keeps finding little ways to make the next few minutes entertaining.

It needs to, too, because beneath all that multimedia animation and graphic-design flair is a very Japanese action RPG that wants you to grind, grind, grind.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

The basic loop is simple: head into a dungeon, batter monsters, collect their cores to steal their abilities, gather materials, and return to the Shopping Mall hub to improve Davy before going back in. A trip might take five to ten minutes, and each one gets you a little closer to becoming powerful enough to take on the next boss and, eventually, get Julia out of the freezer. It's a lightly Persona-ish rhythm, with a much quicker turnaround since dungeon reruns and levelling up can be immediate, except your day job here is punching monsters in the face and goofing off on a robot vacuum cleaner.

The clever stuff starts with the Bite system. Davy can consume enemy cores to recover health or access different monster forms, known as Styles, each changing how you fight. You can't bring everything to every run, so choosing what to bring takes some thought. The Cyclops helps when a horde closes in, the Werewolf is handy when you need to move quickly and get into enemies, and the flying Harpy is a good choice against bosses that turn the floor into a dangerous mess, such as a dragon I encountered early on. You can experiment with 11 Styles, and they aren't just cosmetic changes to Davy's appearance; each has its own ranking (Common, Rare, etc.) and different special abilities that develop, like the Cyclops, who can swing a baseball bat and eventually throw spinning clubs.

Some Styles seem underwhelming at first, like the Vampire, which I thought would be a hoot but has specials that layer; he zips in all directions, bites enemies, and then releases a zombie bat for each bite, until you realise what they can do over time, such as making use of dark energy pools to explore hidden areas. It's worth experimenting rather than settling on the biggest monster with the biggest fists, although the game doesn't always make those choices obvious.

Then there's Body Hack, which lets you replace Davy's body parts with Overtech equipment to improve his stats and bolt on new abilities. Missile pods, spinning blades, spiked balls, directional dashes – all kinds of sharp weaponry can be attached to your undead frame, and some of the most useful upgrades aren't even about dealing more damage. Better healing, more item drops and a faster Davy Burst charge can make a much bigger difference to a run than another flashy attack or rocket salvo.

The way these systems overlap is what makes the game interesting, because the core combat is fairly simple and limited to light and heavy attacks and special abilities. There’s no typical dodge, block, or parry as such. Stupid Parry lets Davy charge into incoming attacks and reduce the damage he takes, then refill it by eating enemies’ Cores, which only expose themselves when attacking. So it’s all front-footed, and everything feeds into everything. But don’t expect Devil May Cry-style combos, even though some of the game’s team, Eiichiro Sasaki and Hiroyuki Kobayashi, worked on DMC.

Instead, the hook comes from working out which Styles suit the dungeon ahead, which body parts make sense for your preferred approach, and which abilities are worth keeping around, all while hitting fast attacks and connecting kills (there’s a DMC-like ‘style metre’ that rates your performance and increases things like item drops). It can take a while to get your head around, and you'll grind before the best body parts and deeper buffs start opening up, but there's more going on than the daft art style initially suggests.

The idea is that Davy is a zombie, and zombies don't know when they're beaten and technically can’t die, so why should he care about defending himself? Instead of backing away from trouble, you're encouraged to keep attacking, take an odd hit, bite an enemy to recover some damage, and get right back into the fight. Some powerful Heat Attacks, when an enemy glows gold, can be countered with Stupid Impact if you time your Stupid Parry correctly to stun the enemy, while building up enough momentum lets you trigger Davy Burst and turn the whole screen into a colourful, electric-guitar-fuelled mess.

It's a fun idea, and when it works – when you’re Stupid Parrying for damage, breaking down a core, and linking kills – the combat has a tight rhythm, with one action feeding into another and the different systems starting to make sense together. But it can feel a little light where you'd expect more dexterity and combo depth, and the lack of a lock-on makes it frustratingly easy to swing at empty air – particularly on narrow paths above lava or icy drops, and especially when you're trying to punch flying creatures because judging 3D space can be tricky.

The trouble is that Stupid Never Dies can hit the same plateau as plenty of JRPGs: you reach a boss who's just a bit too powerful, head back into the dungeons to gather materials and improve Davy, then try again and discover you probably need to do it all over. The body-part upgrades can get stuck offering the same selection, so you've to grind enough runs to unlock something better, and although each trip is fairly short, the locations start to blur together when you keep visiting them to get stronger.

There's a reason for all this, of course. You're building Davy up over time, collecting resources and improving your chances with every run, and the game wants you to feel the difference between the pathetic zombie you started with and the increasingly Frankensteined monster you've turned him into. But it also feels like a way to stretch a relatively small game, one with a lot of visual personality and a handful of clever systems that don't always have enough new places or encounters to show them off.

The grind can be alleviated by the cast of weirdos you chat to between runs – Acelino's a chihuahua-were-dog who develops the body augmentations, Bessie's a zombie who creates new abilities from fast food, and Goyle is, well… a gargoyle who’s in charge of performance data but can’t remember anything are memorable – and the game has that JRPG quality of just offering enough new conversations, snippets of lore and funny asides to make post-dungeon downtime just a bit worthwhile.

I didn't stop enjoying myself, though, partly because I wanted to see what other daft combination of body parts and monster powers I could put together, and partly because I wanted to see what happened to Davy and his impossible romance. After dungeon runs, you can watch unlocked messages and videos on Julie’s tablet (creepy?) and vicariously get to know her through her life. A strange little tragedy lurks beneath all the silliness, and the game gets more mileage out of its deluded protagonist than you might expect from a story about a zombie trying to thaw out a girl who doesn't know he's alive, dead, or anything else.

Stupid Never Dies is an odd action RPG with enough personality to overcome any of its limitations. The art direction never ceases to impress, turning even the most routine dungeon encounters into little bursts of punk-rock graphic design, and I love how Davy's nice-come-creepy romantic obsession sits alongside all that colour and chaos. The combat isn’t light; it’s just not Devil May Cry, and once you understand how the systems dovetail and feed into one another, and if you’re happy to grind (and grind and grind) for your life, you’ll find a quirky little rockstar in here.

#142. Frank Lloyd Wright’s Taliesin West Closes After Fatal Accident

Taliesin West, Frank Lloyd Wright's former winter residence and architectural studio in Scottsdale, Arizona, is closed to the public until further notice after a visitor died from roofing debris on October 16, 2026. According to the Scottsdale Fire Department, strong winds dislodged material from the roof during a walking tour, striking Rogério Renato Mateucci, 55, rector of the Pontifical Catholic University of Paraná in Brazil. Wind warnings were also issued across parts of the Southwest that day, and authorities are investigating the incident as weather-related. The Frank Lloyd Wright Foundation, which manages the property, confirmed the closure and said it would share no further details while officials complete their investigation.

Taliesin West, Frank Lloyd Wright's former winter residence and architectural studio in Scottsdale, Arizona, is closed to the public until further notice after a visitor died from roofing debris on October 16, 2026. According to the Scottsdale Fire Department, strong winds dislodged material from the roof during a walking tour, striking Rogério Renato Mateucci, 55, rector of the Pontifical Catholic University of Paraná in Brazil. Wind warnings were also issued across parts of the Southwest that day, and authorities are investigating the incident as weather-related. The Frank Lloyd Wright Foundation, which manages the property, confirmed the closure and said it would share no further details while officials complete their investigation.

Taliesin West was established in 1937 in the foothills of the McDowell Mountains as Wright's winter home and a setting for architectural study. The complex was designed to respond to the Sonoran Desert through its use of local stone, desert masonry, and lightweight canvas roofing supported by wooden beams. The original roof panels could be opened and closed to regulate sunlight and airflow, reflecting the seasonal character of the site, where Wright and his apprentices spent the winter months before returning to Taliesin in Wisconsin.

Taliesin West was established in 1937 in the foothills of the McDowell Mountains as Wright's winter home and a setting for architectural study. The complex was designed to respond to the Sonoran Desert through its use of local stone, desert masonry, and lightweight canvas roofing supported by wooden beams. The original roof panels could be opened and closed to regulate sunlight and airflow, reflecting the seasonal character of the site, where Wright and his apprentices spent the winter months before returning to Taliesin in Wisconsin.

The property has undergone several alterations as its use shifted toward year-round occupation. Following a fire in the mid-1960s that destroyed the Music Pavilion, the structure was rebuilt with steel beams and translucent fiberglass roofing. In the 1990s, the roofing system was modified again, introducing fixed acrylic exterior panels and canvas interior panels. For more than a decade, the Frank Lloyd Wright Foundation has been researching ways to return to the original operable fabric roof system using contemporary materials. In March 2026, the Foundation outlined long-term preservation work, including environmental monitoring, energy modeling, and prototype testing, aimed at bringing back Wright's original approach to natural ventilation and light while improving thermal performance in the desert environment.

Taliesin West is part of the UNESCO World Heritage listing The 20th-Century Architecture of Frank Lloyd Wright, which includes eight of the architect's works across the United States. It is also designated a National Historic Landmark and has continued to welcome visitors for tours and educational programs focused on Wright's architecture and its relationship with the desert environment. The property now remains closed to the public, with no reopening date announced by the Frank Lloyd Wright Foundation yet.

#143. This week we revealed the Stirling Prize winner

This week on Dezeen, we reported on the Lion Green Road housing scheme in Croydon winning the Stirling Prize.

Designed by local studio Mary Duggan Architects with Ruff Architects, the project was named the UK’s best new building at a ceremony in London.

Commissioned by Croydon Council, the development contains 157 homes spread across five blocks that are connected by a series of shared green spaces.

Following the win, we discussed the project and its place within the wider Stirling Prize winners on our podcast, Dezeen Weekly.

This week also saw car brand Tesla unveil its flying Roadster at an event in Texas, where the vehicle flipped off a ramp and briefly flew.

The demonstration used compressed-air thrusters that Tesla claimed will enable it to make the world’s quickest production car.

In design news, technology brand Apple unveiled HomeView, a device that consolidates the functions of its app products and home-management software into one device.

The seven-inch screen, which can also stand on a base with an integrated speaker, was designed to function as a centralised location for home controls.

Popular projects on Dezeen this week include a rammed-earth visitor centre for the Twelve Apostles in Australia, a monolithic concrete home in India and a cricket pavilion in Dulwich.

#144. That Satellite Photo of ‘Amelia Earhart’s Plane’ Turned Out to Be a Tree

That Satellite Photo of ‘Amelia Earhart’s Plane’ Turned Out to Be a Tree

Pictures can be deceiving. A group of researchers discovered this firsthand after making a long journey to a remote Pacific island in search of Amelia Earhart’s lost airplane.

The “Taraia Object,” submerged in a lagoon off the island of Nikumaroro, looked vaguely like an airplane in a satellite photo. But a team from Purdue University and the Archaeological Legacy Institute that ventured all the way there found that it was just a tree.

“Unfortunately, we weren’t able to find that smoking gun,” says Steve Schultz of Purdue University, per The Guardian.

Amelia Earhart, along with her navigator Fred Noonan, disappeared in 1937 as she was attempting to become the first female pilot to circumnavigate the globe.

Despite a massive search and rescue operation, Earhart was never found, nor was the Lockheed Electra 10-E she was piloting.

90 years later and people are still looking for her. This latest expedition included a six-day boat journey from Kiribati to the uninhabited atoll.

Not only was the voyage delayed by inclement weather, but the crew was forced to sleep offshore because of giant coconut crabs that have been known to feed on human flesh.

The mission was sparked by the satellite photo. Purdue University confirms in a statement that the image was a “visual anomaly” that’s “likely a collection of large trees deposited along the peninsula’s sandspit.”

Richard Pettigrew from the Archaeological Legacy Institute had suspected there was a metallic glint in the water around Nikumaroro.

“The fragment’s reflective surface, long associated with the idea that the object was a metallic substance, was due to its carbonate veneer. Other items found by the team were similarly coated with a shiny concretized amalgam of coral sand,” Purdue University says.

“While we know this is disappointing to many, including us, this mission adds a new chapter in the quest to find the ultimate answer to the mystery of what happened to Earhart during her attempt to circumnavigate the globe nearly nine decades ago.”

#145. Hungarian art community takes stock of populist Orbán era’s enormous toll

Sweeping away the past: the intervention Deep Cleaning in Progress at Budapest’s Kunsthalle by a group of artists and curators in June Photo: Laura Wilhelm

On 12 April 2026, Hungarians overwhelmingly voted Prime Minister Viktor Orbán and his populist Fidesz party out of power after 16 years. On 2 June, a small group of artists and curators organised a public cleaning of the steps of the Műcsarnok, Budapest’s neo-classical exhibition hall.

The Kunsthalle, as it is also known, had become the Hungarian capital’s signature contemporary art venue in the years after the fall of communism. Known for mounting shows of international figures, the space also featured innovative Hungarian artists such as Little Warsaw, the Budapest duo who made a splash at the 2003 Venice Biennale with The Body of Nefertiti in the Hungarian pavilion. Under Fidesz, the Kunsthalle had become the exact opposite: an outpost of arch-traditional, even frankly nationalist Hungarian art.

June’s symbolic action, Deep Cleaning in Progress, managed to be both hopeful and wistful, an attempt to break with the past and perhaps pick up where Budapest’s art scene had left off before the Orbán era began. There are signs that the government of Hungary’s new prime minister, Péter Magyar, is ready to address the various crises facing the art community. But the long Fidesz era, marked by an ever-tightening control of cultural institutions and a creeping indifference to culture generally, has taken its toll and a morning-after feeling prevails.

Within a few years of returning to power in 2010, Orbán, a previous prime minister then regarded as a centre-right politician, had created a template for what he later called “illiberal democracy”. Using Fidesz’s initial two-thirds majority in the Hungarian parliament, Orbán revamped the electoral and constitutional order by removing a range of democratic checks and balances and remaking the judiciary. The party also used a similar approach to reorder the country’s cultural establishment, says Katalin Székely, a curator affiliated with Budapest’s Central European University.

Fidesz was “very clever”, Székely says, and was able to “use the existing framework to occupy and co-opt institutions”, including the Kunsthalle and the Ludwig Museum, another important contemporary art venue where she had been working since 2008. By 2014, both spaces had new leaders and new exhibition programmes; many staff hired before 2010, including Székely, left or were sidelined by the changes. Meanwhile, the direction of new art was influenced through grants and fellowships administered by the newly conservative Magyar Művészeti Akadémia (Hungarian Academy of Arts).

Selective sponsorship eventually translated into a kind of voluntary censorship, says the Budapest-based collector Zsolt Somloi. Hungarian artists who wanted to get a grant or secure a prime exhibition spot in one of the larger national spaces came to realise that “a lot of topics that are very hot on the international level couldn’t be touched in Hungary”, Somloi says. As a result, he adds, “You didn’t talk about gender, you didn’t talk about immigration and you didn’t talk about climate change.”

Following Orbán’s 2014 re-election on a more aggressive populist platform, his larger plans became clear. Two gargantuan projects were devised to relocate several cultural institutions away from the city’s visually dominant castle district, built around the hilltop Buda Castle to, among other areas, a cluster of new buildings in a large city park, Városliget, on the other side of the Danube. The goal, it seemed, was to connect Orbán and his Fidesz officials to Hungary’s Habsburg monarchs by reverting what had become a cultural enclave into a largely political one.

Ballooning budgets, evidence of cronyism and corruption, and civic objections to the tearing up of the park mired both mega-projects in controversy. Meanwhile, other important cultural institutions—notably Budapest’s Museum of Applied Arts, housed in a landmark Art Nouveau building—were left in limbo.

Being largely kept out of prime venues like the Kunsthalle meant that more adventurous artists resorted to alternative spaces, says Zsolt Miklósvölgyi, a curator at Budapest’s acb Galéria. He cites the OFF-Biennále Budapest, held five times since 2014, and several artist-run spaces as recent torchbearers of the country’s avant-garde. “In an art field that had previously been shaped to a large extent by the state or state-funded institutions,” he says, “cultural foundations and organisations, private galleries and independent actors have gradually had to assume greater responsibility.” He stresses that his own gallery was open to showing “politically sensitive subjects that received little or only limited space” in more established venues.

The 2015 migrant crisis in Europe gave Orbán and his party, who were rapidly adopting a Christian nationalist stance, an international profile that inspired populist movements elsewhere in Europe and, crucially, among the acolytes and promoters of Donald Trump. But by the early 2020s, Fidesz had been in power for a decade and was running out of scapegoats.

As the 2022 election approached, Orbán “couldn’t really rail against the state of the country, because he was responsible for the state of the country”, says the Hungarian political scientist Lorinc Redei, a professor at the University of Texas at Austin. It no longer made sense to invoke the threat of illegal immigration, he adds, in a country with a minimal immigrant population. Like many earlier populist movements, Redei says, Fidesz started to create a new “scary enemy” out of the LGBTQ+ community, a development that had a strong impact on the art scene.

In 2021, Hungary passed a controversial child protection law that sought to prohibit the promotion of LGBTQ+-related content to minors. In 2023, the law was used as a pretext to fire László Simon, the director of Budapest’s National Museum, for refusing to restrict the admission of visitors under 18 to a photography exhibition that contained images of LGBTQ+ people. Simon had been a Fidesz member of parliament and had only been in his post two years.

“The passage of that law was a big deal,” says the Budapest-based artist Gideon Horváth. He says his work, which addresses issues related to queer subcultures, has faced various kinds of censorship, including a museum exhibition whose organisers “rewrote my texts that accompanied my installation”.

Budapest-based artist Gideon Horváth’s Memory that could have been (2023) Photo: Dávid Biró; courtesy the artist and Longtermhandstand

The government’s hardened anti-LGBTQ+ stance became a lightning rod. In 2025, after a revised law threatened to prohibit that summer’s Budapest Pride march, tens of thousands of people showed up in defiance—an event that many now see as heralding Fidesz’s election defeat the following spring.

Looking back on the Orbán era, many in Hungary’s art scene have mixed feelings. It was, for instance, a very productive period for Horváth and he is currently showing in the Biennale de Lyon and has work in the collection of Somloi and his wife Katalin Spengler.

Miklósvölgyi is quick to point out that Budapest’s Museum of Fine Arts managed a successful relaunch in 2018, after a three-year renovation. The museum’s curator of prints and drawings, Kinga Bódi, says she never felt any restrictions when acquiring new works by artists who might otherwise have been looked down on by Fidesz. This summer, after a few years of planning, the museum acquired a nude self-portrait by the LGBTQ+ Roma artist Robert Gabris, who has a show at the acb Galéria this autumn.

Horváth is sceptical about “systematic change”. The directors of the Kunsthalle and the Ludwig Museum are still in place, and Magyar’s party has views on immigration that can seem close to Fidesz’s. But he admits to a change in himself. After years of being embarrassed about the situation in Hungary, he says: “We can be proud of the way Orbán was voted out of power.”

Miklósvölgyi is not convinced “that what existed 16 years ago should simply be reinstated”. A way forward, he believes, would be the appointment of foreign professionals as directors of the Ludwig Museum and the Kunsthalle.

For now, the legacy of the Orbán years is most apparent in two museum construction sites on the Pest side of the city. The Museum of Applied Arts, closed since 2017, is still being renovated behind a ghostly scrim. In Városliget, there is a vast open pit that was meant to be the site of the New National Gallery. The project, to be housed in an eye-catching building by the Japanese firm Sanaa, was cancelled this summer, and the area is surrounded by (graffiti-covered) fencing.

For Zsolt Petrányi, director of the Kunsthalle from 2005 to 2011, these are symbols of the peripheral role the arts played in the Orbán years, when sports “was much more important”. While many museums languished, Orbán and his allies built a host of new sports venues including, most notoriously, a 3,800-seat stadium in his home village of Felcsút—population 2,000.

József Mélyi, an associate professor at the Hungarian University of Fine Arts, is hopeful about the new government, which, he points out, was quick to re-establish an independent culture minister, a position the Orbán regime had demoted. “Five years,” he says, may be just “enough to get us back to where we were 15 years ago”.
