#147. Packaging: The Beemore Rebrand by Boundless

London studio Boundless gives wellness drink Beemore a full rebrand: totemic sun-and-eye can art, ancient symbols, bold colorways.

Three slim cans against a blue sky. The Cloudy Lemon, Peach Passionfruit and Cherry Lime colorways each carry a totemic character: a stick-figure guardian holding a sunburst head aloft, a watchful eye at its center. Chunky black BEE MORE letters stack above the figure, a looping bee doodle threading through them. The big idea comes straight off the can: manuka honey and maca root as the fuel, reframed as "Ancient Energy for Modern Civilisation," instead of another synthetic energy hit. The pastel grounds keep the shelf shout in check, so the black totems hit harder.

Boundless sets the wordmark in a heavy, hand-cut grotesque with irregular edges, stacked tight over two lines, the little bee doodle looping off the capitals. Flavor names read in monospaced caps: GOOD MOOD ENERGY, then the variant. Small-cap callouts arc around the figure, "POWERED BY MANUKA HONEY" and "POWERED BY MACA ROOT," doubling as the ingredient proof. On the OOH panels the same grotesque arches overhead with "ANCIENT ENERGY FOR MODERN CIVILISATION," so can, box and poster speak one typographic voice. The hierarchy holds across every colorway: wordmark top, totem center, flavor base.

The 4-pack boxes push the system sideways. One face carries the can front; the other prints a black-on-color ziggurat of ritual symbols, mountains, leaves and sun rays, stamped with the line "ANCIENT NECTAR THAT ROOTS FOR YOU." Spec blocks add "375MG MACA ROOT EXTRACT" and "4x 250mL," with honey-pot and bee icons dotted around the panels. Stacked box walls turn that symbol pattern into a full retail mural, and the poster series lifts the totem figures off the cans entirely, "WELCOME TO GOOD MOOD ENERGY" included. Pack, shelf and street read as one continuous world.

#148. Davis Furniture Debuts Faba by Mario Ferrarini

A modular system of platforms and cushions, Faba Modular Lounge begins as a foundation for flexible configurations shaped by the needs of each space. Mario Ferrarini designed the collection for Davis Furniture from a curated set of essential elements, a restrained architectural framework that cedes its expression to the surrounding space, materials, and application. Two-, three-, and four-seat platforms carry Faba from a simple backless bench to an expansive sectional configuration in workplace, lobby, hospitality, and public environments.

Faba can be arranged into expansive sectional sofas, with configurations tailored to the needs of each interior. Image courtesy of Davis Furniture.

“Faba is about creating a foundation rather than a focal point,” Ferrarini says. “I was interested in designing something that supports the life around it, allowing people, materials, and architecture to emerge.” Ferrarini works from Milan, where his practice pairs technical precision with an undercurrent of emotional sensitivity. Reticence runs through the portfolio, and his pieces settle into a given setting while holding a strong identity of their own. Faba extends the approach into a system with considerable range, one whose character arrives through the application at hand and the palette specified around it.

Faba supports back-to-back configurations within a single footprint, making it well suited for open-plan offices, lobbies, and shared environments. Image courtesy of Davis Furniture.

Modularity gives the collection its reach, with platforms taking a variety of seats, backs, arms, and corner tables in arrangements a designer can tune to the plan at hand. The interplay between upholstered and hard-surface components widens the range further. Exposed portions of the platform can sit between cushions to function as integrated table surfaces within a single run. When specified without upholstery, a platform can also serve as an occasional table or media unit in the same material vocabulary, extending Faba beyond traditional lounge seating.

Exposed platform sections integrated between cushions create built-in table surfaces within a configuration. Image courtesy of Davis Furniture.

Underpinning each configuration is a precisely engineered platform, an MDF core reinforced with an internal steel support system that holds everything above it dimensionally consistent. Upholstered seating is constructed over engineered plywood frames and layered with multi-density polyurethane foam to balance support and comfort, while heavy-gauge steel plates strengthen the structural connections for exact alignment and long-term durability. Tailored double-needle stitching supplies the finishing detail.

Designers can combine seats, backs, and arms to suit applications from workplace lounges to hospitality and public spaces. Image courtesy of Davis Furniture.

Supporting each platform is a sculptural die-cast aluminum leg, offered polished or in more than 35 powder coat finishes from Davis Furniture. Its shape introduces a subtle counterpoint to the system’s rectilinear geometry, lending movement to an otherwise linear composition. Platform surfaces are available in ash, oak, and walnut veneer, FENIX® Innovative Materials, and standard laminates, giving Faba ample aesthetic latitude from one specification to the next. “The system is intentionally simple, but within that simplicity, there is a great deal of freedom, both in how it is configured and how it is expressed through material,” Ferrarini adds.

Faba’s modular platforms can be combined with one-seat or two-seat upholstered components to create a range of seating configurations. Image courtesy of Davis Furniture.

Faba answers to spatial planning as much as to the eye, supporting back-to-back and multi-directional configurations within one footprint that suit open-plan offices, lobbies, and shared environments where division and flow must coexist. Power modules integrate into the face of the platform, and an optional “J” tray conceals horizontal wire management, allowing the collection to meet the functional demands of contemporary interiors while keeping its visual language cohesive. “Faba reflects a disciplined approach to modular design,” says Rob Easton, Vice President of Design + Development at Davis Furniture. “It gives designers a system that is both highly flexible and highly resolved. The simplicity is what makes it powerful, allowing materiality, configuration, and environment to shape the final outcome.”

A sculptural die-cast aluminum leg introduces a subtle counterpoint to the system’s rectilinear geometry. Image courtesy of Davis Furniture.

Hype for the $1,999 foldable is now through the roof – but you might still be able to get one before January 2027.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The iPhone Duo is Apple's most expensive phone yet, and also it's quickest selling. Preorders for Apple's first foldable opened on Friday 16 October ahead of a 23 October release date, and initial stock flew, with availability getting pushed back to January 2027 on Apple's own site.

Some carriers are claiming earlier arrivals Verizon was stating a 5 November delivery at the time of writing, but its website seems to be struggling. Xfinity states 13 November and AT&T early December . Those aren't guarantees, but they could be the best chance right now of getting a Duo before the end of the year.

The Apple website continues to state a 25 January delivery expectation for the iPhone Duo at the time of writing. That compares to a three to four-week wait for the iPhone X in 2017.

Three months is a long time for a phone. Part of the hype around the annual product cycles is the newness of each release. According to Apple's estimate, customers who order now will be getting their devices just eight months before we might see the iPhone Duo 2 announced if the company sticks to the same schedule. Gougers are already taking advantage, with iPhone Duos appearing on Ebay over $4,000.

There's been a lot of debate about whether the quick depletion of availability is a sign of massive success or poor preparation. Apple blames "extraordinary" demand, promoting the idea that initial stock flew much more quickly than it had anticipated.

But the company's not disclosed production numbers or allocation figures, so it's hard to say whether there was genuinely unprecedented demand or merely scarcity, planned or otherwise.

Bloomberg's Apple expert Mark Gurman said it was a "major mistake" for the company to launch the $1,999 foldable when it did. In his Power On newsletter, yesterday, he suggests the launch was rushed so sales would be included in first quarter financial results despite the manufacturing pipeline not being able to produce enough handsets to meet demand. Apple also pressed ahead with a global launch across more than 70 countries after previously considering restricting initial sales to the United States and China.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

But the decision might not be such a big mistake. It's true that there are some angry complaints on social media from people disappointed at having to wait, but Apple's also benefiting from the massive hype that the scarcity creates, generating more headlines about the Duo and potentially encouraging more people to place orders before the delivery date gets pushed back even further.

A staggered roll out also makes a lot of sense for a product for which it was hard to estimate demand in the first place. Apple is relatively late to a foldable phone space where Samsung and Google have an established presence, and the Duo comes at a time when the global chip shortage has pushed costs upwards. Apple also released the iPhone 18 Pro just a month ago, another expensive phone that. While not revolutionary in its form factor, it has a much better camera than the Duo.

The wait may not be as long what Apple is currently citing. It says it's working to fulfill orders as quickly as possible, and, it has sometimes moved orders forward in the past when production improves or other customers cancel purchases. With the iPhone X, cited waiting times of five to six weeks were generally reduced to fewer than three.

As noted above, carriers and authorised retailers may get the device sooner too, with some citing delivery dates in November and December.

Those hoping to beat the queue by going to an Apple Store in person on Friday might be in for disappointment. According to MacRumors, some employees have been urged to discourage customers from visiting if they don't have preorder reservations because inventory is likely to be limited. Apple’s online store suggests checking again on 24 October for pickup availability.

With the HomeView releasing next month, you might think Apple already has enough on its plate, but it's just announced what will be its third launch event in two months. 'Pro and tell' will take place on 28 October, and the biggest rumour is that the highlight will be an OLED touchscreen MacBook. Will 2026 be the year that Apple caught up on everything?

#154. Okay, the Sony FX5 Really Is Going to Launch This Time

Okay, the Sony FX5 Really Is Going to Launch This Time

This is not a drill. The Sony FX5 really is coming this time. Adorama says the highly anticipated cinema camera is truly launching in November.

As Sony Alpha Rumors reports, Adorama emailed customers, saying the Sony FX5 will release in November.

“We’re pleased to share an update on the Sony FX5,” Adorama writes. “Sony has completed its final quality assurance process. Based on the latest information, customer delivers are currently anticipated in early to mid-November. Thank you for your patience and continued support. We look forward to getting your FX5 to you as soon as possible.”

As of right now, Adorama lists the Sony FX5 release date as November 15, 2026, which aligns with what some official Sony websites began listing earlier this month. Sony Germany and France both listed the FX5’s updated shipping date as November 16, which was one month later than previous estimates. As of yet, neither B&H nor Sony USA has updated its store listings to show a release date.

The Sony FX5 has had a tough start. After being announced in July with an expected August launch, the camera was officially delayed to September, then October, and now, finally, November.

Interestingly, Adorama’s messaging seems to confirm part of why the FX5 was delayed in the first place. As PetaPixel reported early this month, some early customers who received the FX5 experienced issues with the rear LCD, including it separating from the plastic. In Adorama’s email to customers, it specifically references Sony’s “final quality assurance process,” which aligns with well-founded speculation that the company is isolating and resolving a manufacturing issue.

Understandably, some prospective Sony FX5 buyers might not feel comfortable believing anything about release dates and shipping times until they actually have the FX5 in hand. Plenty of hopes have been dashed before.

PetaPixel is keen to get hands-on time with final production units to complete its comprehensive review, but early impressions have delivered plenty of cause for excitement. The FX5 and its new 16-megapixel sensor deliver top-notch video quality and features. It looks like Sony has a winner on its hands.

#156. Is the energy of the 1990s returning to London’s art market?

A series of self-portraits by the YBA Sarah Lucas spanning the 1990s are on show at the stand of Sadie Coles HQ at Frieze London Photo: David Owens

Can there be Frieze without Cool Britannia? The optimism of the late 1990s period, defined by Tony Blair’s New Labour government and an expanding London gallery scene, instilled enough confidence in Matthew Slotover and Amanda Sharp to open the fair in 2003. With the arrival of Frieze, London reaffirmed itself as a global art centre.

This era, and how we remember it, is a prime topic of discussion this Frieze week thanks to Tate Britain’s show The 90s: Fashion and Art, which features star Young British Artists (YBAs) like Damien Hirst, as well as those names the era overlooked, such as the BLK Art Group founder Keith Piper. Meanwhile, as the major patrons of the period enter their golden years, their collections are coming to the block. Earlier this week, Christie’s sold £178m of art from the collection of the Monsoon founder Peter Simon, which included early works by artists from that era, including Mat Collishaw, Wolfgang Tillmans and Hurvin Anderson.

Many artists associated with Cool Britannia have long been central to the identity of Frieze London—it is difficult to imagine stepping into the tent without seeing works by Sarah Lucas or Tracey Emin. Three editions of a neon by Emin, whose popular Tate Modern exhibition has now travelled to the Louisiana Museum of Modern Art in Denmark, sold at Xavier Hufkens for £95,000 each. Meanwhile, Sadie Coles HQ is offering some of Lucas’s most famous self-portraits from the 1990s on its stand.

Hollybush Gardens sold an installation of ceramic works by Lubaina Himid Photo: David Owens

Perhaps jarringly for those who lived through the era, some of these artists are now also found at Frieze Masters. Hazlitt Holland-Hibbert has sold early works by Rachel Whiteread from the 1990s, “priced up to £60,000”, including sculptures from her Torso series. Two paintings by fellow YBA Gary Hume have not yet been placed, but James Holland-Hibbert has recently staged solo shows of Hume’s 90s work accompanied by catalogues and new curatorial essays to offer “greater context for understanding these works and their significance with the benefit of hindsight”. Whiteread’s 90s works are valuable, Holland-Hibbert says, precisely because they “represent an important moment in understanding her wider practice”.

The past decade has also seen the rise of artists whose work was sidelined during Cool Britannia, such as Lubaina Himid, now considered one of the most important voices of her generation, particularly after her 2017 Turner Prize win and her British Pavilion at this year’s Venice Biennale. Hollybush Gardens, the London gallery that began working with Himid in 2013 and which has been pivotal in making her visible on the art market, has sold most of the works by the artist from its Frieze London stand, including an installation of ceramic works and a diptych, with prices ranging from £45,000 to £120,000.

Growing institutional and market interest in this era comes as cultural figures posit a sense of renewed optimism in post-Brexit London as a return to the energy of the 1990s. In a Financial Times op-ed in August, Yana Peel, the Chanel Culture Fund’s chief executive, wrote “the last time the city felt this charged was in 1997—Cool Britannia”. She notes record levels of private philanthropy, notably the £150m donated to the National Gallery by the Julia Rausing Trust, as promising steps, while hoping for the “technology titans of today to invest in the artists of tomorrow”. On a more modest scale, directors of emerging galleries and avant-garde institutions also note a return “to a grassroots energy” of the 1990s to describe the recent proliferation of galleries and non-profit art spaces in the city.

But Hollybush Gardens’s co-founder Lisa Panting is one of several dealers who voice doubt as to whether a Cool Britannia revival is anything beyond “superficial”. She reflects on how this period was in fact a “fabricated market moment orchestrated by a few key players. There is a parochialism in how a handful of artists were thrust into becoming a movement. It simply couldn’t happen today, the scene is so much more diverse, there are so many more components to it now”. Moreover, Panting adds, “the social and economic conditions of today are vastly different”.

Certainly, focusing on the importance of private actors fails to acknowledge that many of the key artists and art dealers during Cool Britannia were the product of socialist education policies and a welfare state that were unravelled by Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher in the 1980s, and then further by Blair. As one London dealer who began their gallery in the 1990s reflects: “My era was the last time you could live in London with no money.”

#157. Boldizar Senteski Explores the Beauty of Decay in the Erosion Collection

A compelling new body of work from Hungarian artist Boldizar Senteski has arrived at StudioTwentySeven in New York City. The Erosion Collection, a triptych of handmade mirrors shaped by oxidation, corrosion, and the passage of time, is designed not only as a reflective surface but also as a means of revealing the intricacies of transformation.

“I’ve always been drawn to the urban environment; the way it carries the marks of time and holds a record of its own transformation,” Senteski says. “I wanted to capture the beauty of change with this new collection, using oxidation and corrosion as a way of allowing time to become part of the work itself.”

The mirrors reflect Senteski’s enduring interest in the ambiguous space between art and design, where functional objects transcend utility to become sculptural, expressive forms. Framed in highly polished stainless steel, the collection draws inspiration from fragments of the urban environment, including Brutalist forms, architecture, raw concrete, and weathered materials. Through oxidation, silvering, and repeated layering, the surfaces gradually transform. Senteski establishes the conditions for this process, then allows the materials to play an active role in shaping the final work.

Photography courtesy of Boldizar Senteski

Handcrafted in Hungary, each of the three mirrors is a unique, signed work accompanied by a certificate of authenticity. The collection is available exclusively through StudioTwentySeven; pricing is available upon request.

At StudioTwentySeven, Senteski’s work explores the shifting boundary between object and reflection, inviting viewers to encounter each mirror as an artifact shaped by time, process, and chance.

For Senteski, creating the mirrors requires a delicate balance between intention and unpredictability. “I establish the conditions for the process to unfold but ultimately allow the material to shape itself. There’s something special about the way each piece finds its own form,” Senteski says. “Every mirror in the collection is unique, carrying traces that can never be replicated.”

#160. Baird Architects releases first furniture collection as "natural extension" of studio

US architecture studio Baird Architects has released its inaugural furniture collection, with seating, tables, and shelving, designed by in-house architects and collaborators and made in Portugal.

The twelve-piece BA Objeto collection was led by Baird Architects founder Matthew Baird, who designed several pieces and also commissioned studio employees and collaborators.

Each piece is credited to its designer, and the designers will receive a portion of the profits, according to Baird.

The works include a solid walnut “surf” table by Baird, a swooping aluminium coffee table by Ines Gulbenkian and a dark brown cork bench by Gina Jiang.

The pieces are primarily produced in Lisbon, Portugal, where Baird Architects has established a new studio to support its furniture making.

Baird said a “considered approach to materiality, a crisp aesthetic, and a desire to push the boundaries of furniture design” draws the collection together.

The move points to an expansion of the studio’s work beyond one-off furniture creation and illustrates a different business model for architecture studios.

“Furniture feels like a natural extension of our architectural practice because it allows us to explore our interests in materiality, form, and craftsmanship at a more intimate scale,” Baird told Dezeen.

“We also wanted to create something that celebrates the individual designers within our studio, giving them the freedom to develop pieces of their own while contributing to a collective endeavour.”

Other pieces in the collection include a mirror by Portuguese designer Teresa Mascarenhas and a plywood and leather chair by designer Katy Cheng.

Baird said the collection is an extension of the furniture the studio has created for private clients over the years, and that the team is already “looking ahead” to a second collection.

From design fairs to heritage brands, designers and architects are currently attempting to restructure business models in the design world, primarily to receive more profit and credit for their work.

Recently, Dezeen spoke with design companies OMHU and Rarify about their unique business models and outlooks that aspire to change the industry.

Baird Architects previously designed a shingled house in Maine.

The Googlebook is Google’s attempt at turning Android into a desktop OS, and on this showing it’s almost there. The hardware is excellent, the whole thing is stable and can do some clever things, not all of them to do with AI, but the software offering is still not quite there. First-gen products are often like this, however, and when new apps are launched and software updates come in, the Googlebook could become a major player in the laptop arena alongside Apple and Microsoft’s efforts.

Why you can trust Creative Bloq Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

It’s easy to look at the new Googlebooks and see them as Chromebooks running on fancy new processors, and there's certainly some Chrome in their DNA. Then you look at the price and decide that, though they look nice, they’re not for you.

Google’s latest attempt at making laptops (though it’s not actually building them, and the example we have here is from Acer) extends to a new OS that’s part Chrome and part Android, even running Android apps, but they’re super high-end with OLEDs and the latest Intel chips.

What this means for creative users is that the mobile versions of things like Photoshop and Lightroom run in resizable windows with mouse support. While they’re not completely like the desktop apps, and video editing is a notable weakness, the Googlebook has become the best way to run them. Whether that makes one a worthwhile purchase is up to you – they will certainly be contenders for our best laptops for students guide.

1x Thunderbolt 4, 2x USB-C, 1x 3.5mm audio

The Googlebook looks like every other laptop, just as Chromebooks did. Acer’s model has the word ‘Googlebook’ below the keyboard, so you don’t go in expecting Windows, an Acer logo on the back of the lid, all very understated, with the Glowbar at the top right of the lid. This is one of the Googlebook’s new features, a close cousin of the Hilight LED on the back of the Google Pixel 11 Pro smartphones. It’s a visual way to get quick feedback about what your Googlebook is doing, a bar of rainbow LEDs that tells you about battery charge and pulses blue and purple when you’re talking to Gemini.

The Googlebook is very much built with Google’s chatbot in mind. There's no key on the keyboard to invoke it directly, like Windows’ Copilot key (though there is a Google key, it brings up the equivalent of the Start menu) so you use a key combo or, even better, say ‘OK Google’. There are other AI functions too, such as Magic Pointer, which opens the AI’s visual search capabilities when you wiggle the mouse pointer, allowing you to click on something to ask about it.

The dark blue finish of the Acer Googlebook is very professional-looking, and it has one more trick up its sleeve: this is a 2-in-1 design, the screen folding back to produce a pseudo-tablet that you can daub at with either your fingertip or a stylus. The OS adapts to the positioning automatically, and being Android-based it’s a touch-friendly environment from the start, with the OLED touchscreen and the way you only have to click on icons once to open them.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

• Decent battery life• Limited software offering

Setting up a Googlebook is easy, and if you’re an Android phone user you’ll be able to log in with the same account, unlock it with the same PIN (there’s a fingerprint reader too) and even transfer over your apps. The OS acts a lot like ChromeOS, though Android apps are more prominent, and there's a new menu on the taskbar that allows you to access the apps on a paired Android smartphone, the app executing on the phone’s processor but streaming over a network connection and appearing in a window on the laptop screen, with mouse support, and this works fairly well though some apps with ads can look a little strange when they’re stretched out of their preferred aspect ratio, and others, such as Amazon Music, display a ‘rotate screen’ message. Some apps in the Play Store, such as CapCut Pad, are starting to have a ‘compatible with desktop’ flash on their listing page, indicating they’ll work well on the laptop.

With a third-gen Intel Core Ultra processor inside, and Snapdragon models available too, we should expect decent performance from the Googlebooks. Using the mobile version of Geekbench 7 gives a score we can compare across platforms, with the Google Tensor G5 of a Pixel 10 Pro phone scoring 2011 for single-core tasks and 5858 for multicore, the M5 in an iPad Pro scoring 3598 and 16614, and the Googlebook scoring 2498 and 11061.

In the Jetstream 2 Javascript and Web Assembly benchmark from Browserbench, which tests a machine’s ability with web apps, the Googlebook manages 404.246. This compares to the Pixel 10 Pro’s 231.237 and the iPad Pro’s 431.947. The Apple device is clearly ahead in raw processing grunt, but costs more even before you add a keyboard case to your order. It's also not all that far ahead when it comes to web apps, which are likely to be a common use case for the Googlebook.

Creative software on Android can be hit and miss, with the mobile versions of Photoshop and Lightroom usable but much simpler than their full Windows or MacOS cousins. Video editing apps tend to be aimed at social media use, particularly with portrait video in mind, and while there's an iPad version of Affinity coming later this year, that app doesn’t support Android.

Battery life, as we’ve come to expect from the third-gen Core Ultras, is excellent, with the laptop able to keep going for a day and a half - 12 hours - before it needs a recharge.

If you’ve become used to the idea of Chromebooks being budget computers, then the price of the Googlebook - starting at £999 or $899 - might come as a shock. And they’ve launched into a very competitive market, with Windows 11 spreading out to cover Snapdragon chips as well as the upcoming Nvidia RTX Spark releases, and Apple striding ahead with its M5 and M6 lines, as well as the iPhone chip that powers the excellent MacBook Neo, which is cheaper than the Googlebook in its lowest-cost incarnation.

Without extreme cheapness to recommend it, you’ll have to like web apps or Android to buy a first-gen Googlebook. With the power of Google and the hardware manufacturers (HP, Lenovo and ASUS are also making them) behind it the platform is bound to take off, it just needs a better app selection.

The blue finish looks great, and it's thin and light.

Lots of AI, and useful Android phone pairing.

Though it’s still not the machine for grinding through video encoding or rendering tasks, the Neo excels at being small, nippy, and lasting just about long enough to get everything done. It’s stripped back compared to some of the laptops we’ve tested, but it has enough power to be useful, and comes in a lovely range of colours.

When it comes to creative apps, there's plenty of processing power here, but it brings with it quality-of-life enhancements such as a long battery life and a well-put-together chassis as well as the inevitable AI apps that every software company is currently desperate for you to use.

A useful all-rounder that lends itself to digital art and painting, as well as all the other work that goes into running a studio. Its bright and colourful OLED touchscreen makes it a useful drawing and media consumption tool.

Ian Evenden has been a journalist for over 20 years, starting in the days of QuarkXpress 4 and Photoshop 5. He now mainly works in Creative Cloud and Google Docs, but can always find a use for a powerful laptop or two. When not sweating over page layout or photo editing, you can find him peering at the stars or growing vegetables.

#163. 60-Year-Old Found Footage Proves Famous Bigfoot Footage Is a Hoax

60-Year-Old Found Footage Proves Famous Bigfoot Footage Is a Hoax

On October 20, 1967, Roger Patterson and Robert “Bob” Gimlin captured just under a minute of shaky, grainy 16mm film footage of Bigfoot. Allegedly. Nearly 60 years later, the new documentary Capturing Bigfoot finally puts the issue to rest: it was a hoax.

Now, I know what you’re thinking: “Of course it was a hoax.” To many of us, the clip was an obvious ruse. That seven-foot-tall hirsute fella is a person in a suit. Bigfoot, like Nessie, the Abominable Snowman, the Jersey Devil, and El Chupacabra, does not exist.

However, for many others, the myth has persisted. Those 59 seconds of distant, shaky footage showing a supposed Sasquatch walking through Northern California’s forests have captivated people for nearly six decades, analyzed and overanalyzed by enthusiasts and respected experts alike. Somehow, the footage has remained oddly magnetic to believers and skeptics alike.

Capturing Bigfoot is as much about why those 59 seconds of 16mm film were so fascinating to people in 1967 and have remained so well into the 21st century. In an era where skepticism toward authority, science, and visual media is at an all-time high, the Patterson-Gimlin film feels emblematic of something much bigger than a brief stroll by someone in a fur suit.

The new documentary is also, as Variety writes in its review, about finally uncovering the truth once and for all. Director Marq Evans unearthed another 16mm reel—a 40-second clip from 1966 showing a rehearsal for the famous hoax. Locked away in a safe for over 50 years and never before seen by the public, this newly surfaced footage offers undeniable proof that the original film was an elaborate fraud.

Capturing Bigfoot lands on Amazon Prime Video tomorrow, October 20, marking the 59th anniversary of the original Patterson-Gimlin film.

Ultimately, though, this new evidence, as definitive as it might be, will do little to persuade true believers of the original 1967 footage. Just as evidence and science do little to convince die-hards today that their favorite cryptids, UFOs, or conspiracy theories aren’t true, what will another roll of 16mm film truly do to change anyone’s mind?

One roll of film is the truth. The other is a lie. Which is which depends on who you ask.

#164. The Korean Pavilion to Explore Urban Shrinkage Through "Catabolism" at the 2027 Venice Architecture Biennale

The Korean contribution at the 2027 International Architecture Exhibition – La Biennale di Venezia will focus on the country's condition of hyper-shrinkage, the accelerated stage of population contraction and societal aging, within the context of global demographic change. Commissioned by the Arts Council Korea (ARKO) and led by curator Janghwan Lee, the exhibition will feature contributions by architects Bae Yoonkyung, Kyo Suk Lee and Jaehyub Ko. The curatorial project is named "Catabolism," after the metabolic process through which complex molecules break down into simpler units and release energy. Moving away from an expansion-focused view of cities and architecture, the team uses the concept as a lens to understand urban shrinkage as a reconfiguration of existing relationships and the emergence of new uses and ways of living.

The Korean contribution at the 2027 International Architecture Exhibition – La Biennale di Venezia will focus on the country's condition of hyper-shrinkage, the accelerated stage of population contraction and societal aging, within the context of global demographic change. Commissioned by the Arts Council Korea (ARKO) and led by curator Janghwan Lee, the exhibition will feature contributions by architects Bae Yoonkyung, Kyo Suk Lee and Jaehyub Ko. The curatorial project is named "Catabolism," after the metabolic process through which complex molecules break down into simpler units and release energy. Moving away from an expansion-focused view of cities and architecture, the team uses the concept as a lens to understand urban shrinkage as a reconfiguration of existing relationships and the emergence of new uses and ways of living.

The exhibition takes Korea's experience of hyper-shrinkage as a starting point to ask what architecture can do in cities beyond growth. Outside Korea's major metropolitan regions, the intensity of urban use is gradually declining, and the demolition of vacant houses leaves scattered open plots. The team behind Catabolism builds on the collective research of the Mid-Size City Forum, which describes this trend as "urban perforation." Vacant plots become parking lots or vegetable gardens, or remain unused, reconfiguring the existing urban fabric and city life. In response, existing buildings are adapted by subdividing, connecting, demolishing, repairing, subtracting, and adding to fit new and different uses.

Outside Korea's major metropolitan regions, the intensity of urban use is gradually declining, and the demolition of vacant houses leaves scattered open plots. The team behind Catabolism builds on the collective research of the Mid-Size City Forum, which describes this trend as "urban perforation." Vacant plots become parking lots or vegetable gardens, or remain unused, reconfiguring the existing urban fabric and city life. In response, existing buildings are adapted by subdividing, connecting, demolishing, repairing, subtracting, and adding to fit new and different uses.

Catabolism examines the transformation and reorganization of existing architectural elements in this context of hyper-shrinkage. It looks at how disappearance results in urban and architectural mutations and by-products, creating new possible scenarios. Drawing on the Mid-Size City Forum's field observation, data analysis, and spatial documentation of transformations in Korea's small and medium-sized cities, the exhibition starts from the reality of already-shrinking cities to ask what should remain and how it can be used under conditions of gradual, constant change. Within this framework, Catabolism presents the architect's role in dismantling, removing, and reusing.

Related Article Shrinking Cities: The Rise and Fall of Urban Environments

Within this interpretation, the curatorial team extends the definition of architecture beyond building new, large-scale, finished volumes to include adjusting the relationships between existing structures, materials and spaces. They point to small, incremental interventions as a response to living conditions, seeking a perspective that does not reduce shrinking cities to places of decline or deficiency. Avoiding romanticization, they address disappearance as movement and possibility rather than an ending, and the declining use of space as an uneven process. Some functions disappear while others take root and welcome new users: aging residents, newly settled migrants and temporary visitors bring different needs and rhythms of life. Recognizing this complexity, the South Korean proposal highlights the possibilities offered by degrowth.

#165. Hommeboys Interiors Brings Warmth to a Los Altos Hills Home

An exclusive semi-rural enclave in California, Los Altos Hills is known for its dense woodlands, rolling hills, and stunning panoramic views. A short commute to Silicon Valley, it’s also a private haven for the tech industry. It’s within this community that Sonoma-based firm Hommeboys Interiors has completed an overhaul of a home for a young couple in tech and their children.

Founded by partners Alex Mutter-Rottmayer and Austin Carrier, Hommeboys Interiors has an inherent talent for dissolving the barrier between indoors and outdoors and crafting layered, textural interiors that emphasize organic materials with a modern sensibility. For the homeowners, who were looking to create a family home that was “grand without feeling cold,” Mutter-Rottmayer and Carrier were a natural choice.

A complete gut remodel, the 6,000-square-foot home was reimagined both inside and out, with the exterior shell reworked to better suit its surroundings. Now clad in stone and timber, the structure was modified to accommodate an expansive gable window wall at the back of the home, allowing ample natural light to penetrate deep into the interior.

Once inside, the connection to the natural world is immediately evident through the carefully curated material palette. Wood and stone once again play major roles, cladding most surfaces and lending warmth and texture. With a pronounced grain, the oak paneling on walls and ceilings throughout is rich with character and diffuses light to create an inviting atmosphere.

Natural stone walls impart a subdued ruggedness that is countered by more refined materials like the various dramatically veined marbles, hand-applied plaster, and patinated steel.

Special attention was paid to the three fireplaces that anchor as many rooms. In the living room, an angular, plaster-clad fireplace was intended to be the “showpiece of the space and to be a functional sculpture,” the designers say. “It sets the tone for the entire room, and the curvature inspired a lot of the furniture.”

Said furniture includes a number of tactile pieces from the designers’ own Haus of Hommeboys line—such as hide- and velvet-covered poufs and castellated planters—along with classics sourced through their atelier, like a vintage Julep sofa from Tacchini and a Raymonde Leduc coffee table.

In the family room, hand-patinated Corten panels cover the entire fireplace wall and lend the space a “warm, moody, and intimate” ambiance. “We love playing with materiality, and the way the steel fireplace meets the plaster walls has both a beautiful symmetry and tension,” the designers say. The third fireplace, in the primary bedroom, is also finished in hand-applied plaster with a linear texture that creates a bold contrast to the otherwise serene interior.

The true heart of the home, the kitchen exemplifies Hommeboys’ unique ability to use natural materials and texture in unexpected ways. Featuring oak paneling, striking Calacatta Monet marble, and natural stone, the kitchen is open and inviting and the perfect place for the family to spend time together and entertain guests, something the couple loves to do. A spectacular 15-foot-long, custom-designed lighting fixture from Ovature Studio defines the room, providing a graphic counterpoint to the organic materials.

“The house is definitely modern, but we leaned into natural materials to add an organic, timeless quality that felt warm and inviting, not fixed and sterile,” the designers say. Approachable, sophisticated, and replete with natural light, the home is now the perfect foil for the family life that unfolds within.

#166. Staff strike at Goldsmiths is now the longest in UK university history

Staff at Goldsmiths in London began their strike over restructuring and proposed redundancies in April Courtesy of Joe Newman

More than 50 postgraduate fine art students studying at Goldsmiths in London say that “[they] are once again paying the price for a dispute the university has failed to resolve” after a strike at the college became the longest in UK higher education history.

Members of Goldsmiths University and College Union (GUCU) started taking action short of a strike from 27 April this year and began indefinite full strike action on 8 June, over the university’s restructuring programme and proposed academic redundancies. The strike has now lasted 130 days, breaking a record held by the University of Brighton. A Goldsmiths spokesperson says it has engaged with GUCU throughout this dispute and has made three offers to reach a resolution, the latest of which was rejected.

Students from the Goldsmiths MFA cohort highlighted the disruption to their courses in an open letter, saying that 10 out of 12 staff are on strike. “Before enrolling, incoming students were not told the extent of the strike, or how severely it would affect teaching. Students have had no academic or workshop inductions, and second years are relied upon to explain how the course functions, whilst being unclear of the structure of their final year and examinations,” say the students.

Second-year students have still not received marks or feedback from their interim assessments, the letter adds, claiming that if they do not pay this term’s fees by 31 October the university will “withdraw us almost immediately, and under its guidelines we will still owe them 25% of the term’s fees”.

Goldsmiths has carried out extensive restructuring over the past five years, launching the Recovery programme in 2021 and the Transformation programme in 2024. GUCU says that the Recovery programme led to £7.6m in recurrent savings while the Transformation programme generated a further £16.1m worth of savings.

The Goldsmiths spokesperson adds: “We have taken extensive steps to minimise the impact on students and maintain teaching and academic support across affected programmes. Fewer than 2% of programme modules across the university are currently impacted by industrial action. Any disruption is regrettable, and our priority remains supporting students to progress and complete their studies successfully.”

Goldsmiths, part of the University of London, has produced a number of famous art alumni such as Damien Hirst, Steve McQueen and Sarah Lucas. Nine Goldsmiths graduates have won the Turner Prize, including Gillian Wearing in 1997 and Laure Prouvost in 2013.

#167. Tesla launches flying Roadster concept car

Electric car company Tesla has unveiled its flying Roadster vehicle with a demonstration in which the car drove upside down, flipped off a ramp and briefly flew, using compressed-air thrusters that Tesla claims will make it the world’s quickest production car.

During a live event in Texas, the two-seat Roadster model drove up a half-pipe ramp and launched off the top, remaining in the air for a few seconds before landing

It also became airborne after building up speed on flat ground, launching over a row of parked vehicles. It then lifted off from a stationary position.

A series of thrusters in the bottom and back propelled the car into the air and cushioned the landings.

It was designed by Tesla and SpaceX, both companies led by businessman Elon Musk, who called the second-generation Roadster “a collaboration with the world’s best car company and the world’s best rocket company”.

The thrusters can also fire rearward to boost acceleration. Tesla demonstrated the car reaching 60 miles per hour in a claimed 0.81 seconds, and said it would be the “quickest” production vehicle to 60 miles per hour.

On the half-pipe ramp, the vehicle was able to remain upside down due to a fan suction system. The air tanks in the vehicle are rechargeable and can be recompressed without fuel, according to Tesla.

Long term, Musk said the car will be the “only manual” vehicle in its lineup, referencing plans for driverless vehicles. Though the demonstration used a pre-programmed sequence with no driver.

Tesla chief designer Franz von Holzhausen said the car was designed with an “aerospace aesthetic”.

It has an angular supercar exterior with scissor doors and a deployable spoiler, and is a coupe with a hard top.

The seats are moulded directly to the chassis, and it features wire steering, which replaces the mechanical link between the steering wheel and wheels with electronic controls.

Musk referenced the uncertainty of street legality for the flying capabilities and said that “success is not guaranteed” before the test.

Production on the vehicle is set for 2028, according to Tesla. The company first unveiled a second-generation Roadster in 2017, with deliveries planned for 2020.

Tesla’s last major launch was the Cybertruck, unveiled in 2019.

Other recent concept cars include Alef’s concept vehicle.

#169. Inside Charline GROEN’s Branding for Galopain

Charline GROEN crafts the medieval-inspired branding for Galopain, a warm-bread tavern built around ancient flours and illuminated initials.

Forget the classic French boulangerie. At Galopain, there's no baguette or butter croissant sitting on the rack. Styled as a "Taverne du pain chaud" (warm-bread tavern), the bakery treats slow-fermented country loaves made from unrefined ancient flours as the main event. To match that stripped-back baking philosophy, designer Charline GROEN looked past polite cafÃ© minimalism and built the identity around medieval manuscripts, battlefield pennants, and royal ink seals from an era when bread anchored daily life.

Every mark carries weight. The custom italic serif wordmark for Galopain leans forward with sharp calligraphic tension â kicking off with a deep looping tail on the initial G, curling the inner counter of the O directly into the crossbar of the P, and finishing with a long descending swash on the N. Alongside the full logotype, GROEN drew two distinct medieval emblems that anchor the branding across print and packaging. The first is an ornate illuminated initial G divided into interlocking black, crimson, and cobalt-blue ribbon segments with thorn-like gothic serifs, while the second shows a gloved hand gripping a spear with a forked swallowtail battle flag stamped with an angular blackletter G.

The color palette stays tight. On the white gusseted paper bread bag, the tricolor illuminated G sits squarely between the two-line serif header "PAINS RUSTIQUES AUX FARINES ANCIENNES" and the wide italic wordmark across the bottom fold. Instead of hiding the graphics on outer boxes, GROEN presses die-cut oval and battle-flag stickers straight onto the blistered, flour-dusted crust of a round country boule balanced atop a dense square loaf. That same stacked-bread still life shares a split-panel postcard with an ultramarine blue block where "TAVERNE DU PAIN CHAUD" stacks in tall black serifs with a looping calligraphic E, backed by white wrapping paper stamped in grainy black, red, and blue ink seals.

#170. Stop Treating CSS Container Queries Like Traditional Media Queries

I Code. I Write. Meme Rules. Ok, but seriously, I’m a web and mobile developer who writes a lot. In my spare time, I like to build products that would … More about Victor ↬

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

To be completely honest with you, I missed the news when CSS Container Queries first shipped. And when I finally heard about it, my very first thought was, “Why exactly do I need this when media queries already exist?”

I’m not proud of that reaction, knowing what I know now, but it was comforting to know that I wasn’t alone. In fact, there are legions of us out there.

What baffles me is that container queries aren’t a new feature, as it currently sits at around 94% browser support. And yet, very few people are actually using it. According to the State of CSS survey, 86% of developers are aware of container queries, but only 41.4% actually use them. Surveys can be biased and not completely representative of our entire field, but this one is certainly the best indicator we’ve got.

Kevin Powell also talked about this at SmashingConf Amsterdam 2026: Container Queries adoption has been terrible. And that is so strange to me, knowing that the ability for components to adapt to the size of their outer container has been at the top of so many CSS wishlists over the years.

I’m not particularly interested in how many people are using container queries as much as in how they are using them. I can’t account for everyone, but from what I’ve seen — including in my own early attempts — many of us are using them wrong.

The bottom line is that incorrect use comes down to the same impression I had when learning about them: they absolutely look just like media queries at first glance. And since they look similar, it’s easy to assume they serve similar purposes and work the same way.

Note: I should state up front that what I’m focusing on in this article is using container size queries, i.e., a responsive design technique for responding to the size of a particular container. There are also container style queries that respond to a container’s computed styles (and are experimental at the time of this writing). You can catch up on those in Juan Diego’s piece here on Smashing Magazine where he examines their possible use cases.

Meet Touch Design for Mobile Interfaces, Steven Hoober’s brand-new guide on designing for mobile with proven, universal, human-centric guidelines. 400 pages, jam-packed with in-depth user research and best practices.

The viewport is a proxy. It always has been. Media queries are what gave us the illusion that screen width alone is responsible for how responsive apps adapt to their environment.

Ask yourself this: When you write @media, what are you asking the browser?

I, like most developers, am asking the browser: How wide is the screen right now? That’s it.

Media queries answer that beautifully, but what happens when this .card component is placed in a grid cell that’s 300px wide on a 1920px desktop screen?

The media query doesn’t care; it does its job. The viewport is still 1920px, so min-width: 1024px fires and the matched query styles are applied, even though the card only has 300px of space to work with. Eventually, everything in the card deforms, overflows, or cramps up.

It’s common to think of responsive design purely as a system for updating complete page layouts, like going from two columns on a large screen to a single column on a small screen.

Container queries are smarter than that. They make responsive layouts more reliant on what’s happening inside a component rather than on the outer context that has no insight into a component’s contents. It is more like: “How much space is available for me in this specific spot, right now?”

Here is the same card code example we looked at in the last section, but with a container query:

This changes everything. The card isn’t influenced by the viewport; its only concern is whether the .card component’s parent wrapper has at least 450px of inline (i.e., horizontal in a left-to-right writing mode) space. If that condition is true, the component goes horizontal; if not, it goes to its default block display.

See the Pen [Viewport vs Container [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/01a0a73d-6f39-709f-8dae-037f6b588852) by Vayo.

A very interesting way to distinguish @media and @container queries is the layout type.

Media queries are for the “macro” layout; they look outward. Stuff like page structure, the header that spans the window, footers, main grid layout, system preferences (prefers-color-scheme), device capabilities (touch screens). You know, anything that is majorly true to the entire page structure.

Container queries, I’d say, are for “micro” layouts, i.e., most things that live inside the “macro” layout. We use them when any content needs to responsively fit whatever space it is allocated. Components that come to mind are things like cards, widgets, forms, navigation, and so on.

In other words, think “page layout” vs. “component layout”.

An element shouldn’t magically become “tablet-sized” just because the width exceeds an abstract width threshold like 768px. Instead, it should switch layout when it has enough space to do so, whether that happens on a mobile viewport or inside a desktop sidebar.

In case you’re still not convinced, did you know there are over 2,300 unique viewport sizes on the modern web? Do you think it is possible to account for all of them?

I’m not hating on media queries. It’s that in this era of responsiveness and component re-use, layout logic is closer to the container than the viewport. When we think in terms of containers and components, we’re effectively relying on the content to determine layout, not the viewport.

Responsive typography is a good example of something many of us have relied on media queries for. The fact that media queries come with their own CSS units — e.g., vw, vh, and so on — that are relative to the viewport size makes media queries look really good for adjusting font size based on the user’s screen size.

This works until that same component is moved into a different context, like a sidebar, where the viewport is completely irrelevant. Now, because we tied the responsiveness to the wrong reference point, the scaled typography can get too big or too small.

Container queries come with their very own units — cqi, cqw, cqb, among others — and we can take responsive components further by coupling those units with the CSS clamp() function, using it for fluid typography that scales with the component rather than the viewport:

See the Pen [Fluid Typography [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/01a0a73f-1a44-750c-8b40-9b0ab774d981) by Vayo.

With this in place, the entire code is self-contained to that element’s specific container.

Interestingly, container queries can, in a way, detect the state of a component’s internal layout. It’s not bulletproof, but it is also something media queries simply cannot do because they only observe the external browser window and are structurally blind to internal layout events like when, for example, flex items wrap onto a new line. Let’s poke at that.

Flexbox is superb at wrapping content (flex-wrap: wrap), allowing flex items to automatically wrap to new lines when the flex container runs out of space to fit them in a single row. But CSS by itself can’t tell when that wrap happens. There isn’t something like a :wrapped pseudo-class or a media query like @media (flex-wrapped: true) that would get us there.

Media queries only observe the browser window, as they can’t see internal changes. That is pretty much what flex wrapping is: a width state change on the item itself.

For example, if you have a horizontal menu that is lined up with flexbox and you want the items to restyle themselves only when wrapped, you’d be in JavaScript territory, using ResizeObserver to get that information. However, when we nest container queries inside flex items, we can come up with a workaround to get what we need without JavaScript, thanks to this technique I learned from Kevin Powell. The core idea is to allow a flex item to flex-grow: 1 when we query the container’s inline size.

See the Pen [Fluid Typography [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/01a0a73f-1a44-750c-8b40-9b0ab774d981) by Vayo.

This works. As the parent size shrinks and the cards wrap to two lines, the card item expands, the container query fires, and applies the necessary styles.

See the Pen [Flex Wrap Detection Using Container Queries [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/01a0a752-150a-754e-a77a-07fe1b046658) by Vayo.

Container queries, like all things, come with some side effects or caveats you will want to watch for before reaching for them.

Container queries need something similar to a parent-child relationship to function as expected. Let’s say we have this markup:

We can’t actually query the .card component to adjust the .card-content, like this:

This doesn’t work because a container cannot query itself. In that last example, we’re querying a card container and then attempting to adjust that container’s display based on its size. It’s an infinite loop.

Instead, we need an additional wrapper that makes the .card a descendant of the container:

From there, we can query the .cards container and adjust the .card layout accordingly:

In media queries, this doesn’t matter as @media does not care which element you style inside the block; its only concern is the viewport, which is always available. So you can just slap a condition on any element and call it a day.

This happens when querying the container’s size (i.e., its block, or vertical, size) instead of its inline-size:

Why? Because the browser calculates the container’s dimensions without looking at its children. If we don’t give the .hero-banner an explicit height (or min-height or aspect-ratio), the browser sets a height of 0px.

For that reason, it’s often better to query a container by its inline-size instead. That is, unless you genuinely need to query the container’s block size.

Media queries aren’t affected by this, as they treat height the same way they treat @media (min-height: ...) does, i.e., ask the viewport and move on.

Another container query limitation: we can’t query against a custom property value:

This is because custom properties depend on values that cascade down the DOM tree. There’s the possibility that a container query that relies on a custom property can change that same custom property. And it can quickly get complicated:

I don’t think any project should wholesale use @container instead of @media. Media queries still play an important role in responsive layouts. It’s about understanding the separation of concerns.

I tend to reach for container queries when a component is used in more than one layout context. For example, a .card element could live in a full-width grid or a narrower sidebar. If that’s the case, then we’ll want the component’s content to determine when it adjusts rather than a media query that looks at the outer viewport.

Similarly, I reach for media queries when a component solely exists at the page level. This would be something like a main navigation that always sits at the top of the page. It is directly influenced by the viewport’s size, meaning that the viewport is a reliable reference for when the navigation needs to adjust. Again, it’s all about “macro” layout versus “micro” layouts.

Here’s a diagram for how I reason about which type of query to use:

At the end of the day, the core reason why container queries look incredibly similar to media queries is simply familiarity. They’re not exactly “new”, but they are way less understood and adopted than media queries. But media queries have plenty of their own limitations; otherwise, we wouldn’t need container queries to fill those gaps.

What we have is a more effective feature for detecting when a specific component’s context changes and a means for adjusting styles based on its content, as it should be when that component can exist in multiple contexts.

#171. I Tried a Starlapse (and Learned a Lot)

Ever since capturing my solar eclipse timelapse, I’ve wanted to explore and refine the technique. There were quite a few takeaways from that previous project in terms of settings and best practices, so I’m carrying those lessons into this next one.

We were out in New Mexico on another project, and with an open sky, a new moon, and minimal light pollution, it seemed like the perfect chance to get some star timelapses under our belt. I also brought along the iOptron SkyTracker Pro, a gadget that tracks the rotation of the Earth, to see whether it earns a place in the workflow.

A daytime timelapse is fairly forgiving. You’ve got a foreground, a tripod, a camera with a built-in intervalometer, and you can see the image you’re capturing, predict the movement of the Sun and clouds, and plan around it. Pointing the camera at the sky in the middle of the night is where it starts to get complicated.

The solar eclipse taught me that the movement of celestial bodies is very noticeable, and you either account for it or find a way to track it. That’s why I brought a star tracker—in this case, the iOptron SkyTracker Pro. (This isn’t a sponsored piece on iOptron; I have heard many good reviews on this particular unit, and it was the only one I could fit alongside all my other gear.) It aligns your camera so it moves with the rotation of the Earth, which matters for exposure because during a long exposure the stars begin to smear across the frame. A little shutter smear can read as pleasing motion, but there’s also value in keeping things crisp and clean.

I set everything up while it was still light out, because once the new moon took over we wouldn’t see anything without a headlamp. The baseline is simple: camera, head, and tripod. If you want to try sky tracking, you add a unit that installs between the tripod and the camera and follows the Earth’s rotation to reduce smear.

I’d always pictured this being better for stills, since a 30-second or minute-long exposure is where star motion blur really shows up, so it helps you get a clean photograph. I wanted to test it for an actual timelapse too. With video, there’s always some blur; it’s unnatural for our eyes to see none at all. So I planned to run it both with and without the tracker and compare.

The way it works: there’s a scope you use to line up Polaris, and the companion app tells you exactly where in the scope’s circle to place the star so Polaris sits perfectly static. On the back there are a few modes. 1x spins at the exact speed of the Earth, giving you zero blur on the stars but blur on the foreground. Half-X splits the difference so both the sky and the foreground stay relatively clean. There are also dedicated Moon and Sun tracking modes, which I haven’t tried; the Sun mode probably would have helped on my eclipse video, but you live and learn. A switch sets N or S for your hemisphere, a slew button moves the motor quickly for big adjustments, and fine knobs handle pan and tilt once you’re close.

Once it’s lined up, you level the bubble, set Polaris in the scope per the app, and the camera goes on top via a ball head. You can frame any part of the sky you want, but you have to account for the camera twisting in the direction the motor points, so with these small units it’s best to aim the camera roughly the same way as the motor and scope. You can set it out in a field and walk away. Because of the long exposures, though, the camera drains fast, so I ran a SmallRig battery to keep it going.

One last addition: with rain clouds moving through the area, I wrapped the camera in a rain cover, cinching it around the front so the lens, the battery, and the battery connections all stayed protected. Then it was time to climb up to our vantage point.

To pinpoint exactly where to aim the tracker, I used a couple of apps. The first comes from iOptron, the company that makes the tracker. It reads your location and time and gives you crosshairs showing precisely where to place Polaris so you lock onto the Earth’s rotation. The second is Night Sky, which lets you see the whole sky regardless of overcast; you can even point it down through the Earth to find constellations below the horizon. That made it easy to find Polaris, rough in my tripod, point the iOptron in the general direction, and then use the fine adjustments to place the star exactly where the app wanted it.

Back in the studio, I pulled the footage into LRTimelapse Pro, which is the only app I’d reach for on this kind of work. It does a great job of collecting data and telling you your settings and how they change in between shots. On this static sequence, the interval was around 40 seconds, aperture at f/2, shutter holding steady since I had it on fixed settings. The software then asks you to create keyframes, which let you adjust exposure or specific images gradually across the sequence. The Wizard option spaces them evenly and you can push it up to 20, but this sequence had even exposure throughout, so I barely needed any. First frame to last looked the same, so a single keyframe would do.

From there, you save the changes to XMP and drag the sequence into Lightroom Classic. One image imports with a four-star rating—that’s how LRTimelapse passes keyframe data to Lightroom. You filter by the LRT presets (full sequence shows everything, keyframes shows the four-star frames it flagged), then develop that keyframe. On this one, I nudged exposure and highlights, watched the shadows so the noise didn’t get out of hand, and added a touch of saturation, clarity, and Dehaze to make the stars pop.

This particular sequence was the static one, no tracker, so punching into the stars revealed a little blur from the Earth’s motion. I saved those settings, let LRTimelapse read the keyframes back, ran auto transition, and it rendered the visual previews. For export, I keep things in ProRes so I can grade in post, drop the frame rate to 23.98 to match the rest of the project, and set quality to very high. Because these were filmed on our GFX100 II cameras at 100 megapixels, I kept source resolution rather than letting 16:9 crop the top and bottom. That way I can reframe in post or even build a move, a tilt up or down, without losing any apparent resolution on a 4K delivery.

The static sequence looked great, even at only five seconds. And honestly, the slight blur on the moving stars replicates the motion blur our eyes expect from normal cinema at a 180-degree shutter, so I didn’t mind it at all. I can see how useful the tracker is for super crisp stills of the sky, but here the static look held up beautifully. (I was also hanging out next to these cameras for four or five hours grabbing different angles, surrounded by desert mice, various critters, and howling coyotes. Wild night.)

Then came the problem. As I reviewed the tracker footage, the image suddenly flipped. The ball head had been holding to the tracker mostly by friction with nothing truly locking it in place, and over the long run it loosened, swung down, and came to rest at the bottom. I didn’t catch it until post.

We did get some good frames of the tracker working, and punching into those, the stars weren’t smeared at all, confirming it was doing its job even at half-speed. But even after the head swung loose, the stars still looked crisp, because we were running a relatively fast 15-second shutter with a 40-second interval. The gimbal failure barely made a visible difference.

So is the tracker necessary? We didn’t gather enough clean tracker data to build a full comparison, but the takeaway is clear. For stills, especially long exposures, it’s a genuinely useful tool. For a timelapse at a 15-second shutter or faster, I don’t think you’d see much difference with it or without. And thanks to the GFX100 II’s 100 megapixels, even the static sequences let me reframe and level the horizon without noticing any resolution loss at a 4K delivery.

It took some coordinating and a lot of walking around in the dark, but it was worth it. The biggest lesson is that while a gadget tracking the Earth’s rotation is a neat thing to have, you can capture beautiful star timelapses with just a lens, a camera, an intervalometer, and a tripod. Get your shutter speed and interval right, and you’re most of the way there. There will be more timelapse experiments ahead, so stay tuned.

#173. Factory in Bangladesh that "redefines manufacturing architecture" wins RIBA International Prize

A rug factory in Rangpur, Bangladesh, designed by Dhaka-based studio Nakshabid Architects to dismantle workplace hierarchies, has won the RIBA International Prize for 2026.

Named Green Field Factory, the project is the fifth winner of the biennial award, presented by the Royal Institute of British Architects (RIBA) to the world’s best new building outside the UK.

Nakshabid Architects was praised by the RIBA jury for designing a factory that incorporates passive design principles and prioritises the wellbeing of its 5,000 employees.

“Green Field Factory redefines manufacturing architecture in South Asia and beyond,” said RIBA president Chris Williamson.

“By putting people, wellbeing and their everyday experiences at its core and actively supporting its female workforce, it proves that thoughtful design can dismantle traditional hierarchies to create profound social and environmental change.”

It was announced as the RIBA International Prize winner at the Stirling Prize ceremony in London last night. This year’s prestigious Stirling Prize was given to Mary Duggan Architects and Ruff Architects for the Lion Green Road housing development in London.

Commissioned by rug manufacturer Karupannya Rangpur Limited, Green Field Factory is a seven-storey building surrounded by fields and small settlements.

Nakshabid Architects based the design on the traditional Bengali home, incorporating natural ventilation and biophilic design principles.

Courtyards, verandas, gardens and a monumental green facade were designed to let natural light and airflow into the building, minimising the need for mechanical systems.

Green Field Factory has one main entrance with two grand staircases for all workers, intended to challenge hierarchies in the workplace. This responds to other factories in the area that have separate entrances for factory workers and people in management roles.

Shared spaces in the factory provide areas for workers to take breaks and socialise. Other areas are designated to support workers’ families and the wider community during the day and outside of working hours, including a rooftop daycare centre, on-site medical practice, grocery shop and prayer room.

A connection to nature is provided through low-maintenance planting throughout, which also supports insects and birds, while artwork and sculptures celebrate the role of women in the workplace, family and community.

“The project demonstrates the dissolution of architecture as a topological space, with a single-pointed focus on dismantling civilisational oppression and hierarchy, for woman and man alike,” said grand jury chair Bijoy Jain.

“Through the simple gesture of two grand stairs as an equanimous shared portal, it transforms a space and symbol once reserved exclusively for the king of the region, as landlord and ruling class, and for the colonial power that pervaded the length and breadth of the country,” he continued.

“The architect and owner shared how the women and men working in the factory would bring their families with pride to show them where they worked, and the women empowered in their self-reliance to take life and familial decisions on their own.”

The RIBA International Prize is awarded biennially to a building that “demonstrates visionary, innovative thinking, and design excellence whilst making a distinct contribution for its users and within its physical context”.

Green Field Factory was selected ahead of BRAC University in Bangladesh by WOHA, Z33 art museum in Belgium by Francesca Torzo Architetto and the renovation of Royale Belge in Belgium by Caruso St John Architects, Bovenbouw Architectuur and DDS+.

Alongside the International Prize, RIBA awarded this year’s International Emerging Architect Award to Maker Architecten for its YIMBY residential project in Kortrijk, Belgium.

The project revamped 18 plots across a 1920’s garden city neighbourhood, utilising reclaimed materials for new facades and creating communal green space.

In 2024, Peris + Toral Arquitectes won the RIBA International Prize for an “inclusive and sustainable” social housing project in Barcelona.

#174. New Abu Dhabi cultural district announced ahead of the emirate’s inaugural Frieze fair

Frieze Abu Dhabi will take place in the Saadiyat Cultural District, home to the Louvre Abu Dhabi, Zayed National Museum and the Guggenheim Abu Dhabi, due to open in December ©️Department of Culture and Tourism, Abu Dhabi

In a few weeks, the Frieze juggernaut moves to the next edition in its eight-fair portfolio: Frieze Abu Dhabi. The first edition of the fair is set to open in the United Arab Emirates on 19 November.

Abu Dhabi has already been a visible presence at Frieze London this week. On Thursday, Aldar, the leading Abu Dhabi real-estate development company and the official fair partner of Frieze Abu Dhabi, announced its new “creative neighbourhood” called Noma. Its gold logo also adorned the place settings on Thursday night’s Collectors’ Dinner in the Frieze London tent.

Concrete plans on Noma have yet to be released, but Abu Dhabi has been making a concerted push to attract creative talent to the city over the past few years. In an interview with The Art Newspaper in 2021, the Department of Culture and Tourism’s (DCT) chairman Mohamed Khalifa Al Mubarak spoke about plans for developing artist-friendly cultural districts. “In Abu Dhabi there has been a very clear and conscious decision to invest in culture, and investing in culture does not just mean buildings,” he said then. “We’re investing in infrastructure, both soft and hard—whether it’s institutions, music programmes, or school curricula.” (Al Mubarak is also chairman of Aldar.)

Districts that support exhibition and studio spaces have been successful means of anchoring artistic communities across the Gulf region. Alserkal Avenue in Dubai is the most notable example, with most of the UAE’s major galleries now long-term residents in the pedestrianised district. Riyadh has invested in own post-industrial zone, Jax, which hosts artist studios as well as the Diriyah Biennale spaces, and Abu Dhabi’s cherished Salama bint Hamdan Al Nahyan Foundation has also recently launched Miza, a creative district centred around its Warehouse421 arts space, in the port area of the city.

The name Noma is derived, New York-style, from its location: North of Manarat Al Saadiyat. Manara is the multi-purpose exhibition site that has hosted Abu Dhabi Art since 2011. When Frieze Abu Dhabi sets up shop there next month, it will bring 88 galleries, with a focus on the Swana region (South-west Asia and North Africa).

There will be elements familiar to Frieze aficionados: Frieze Sculpture installs public works along the beach at Mamsha, on Saadiyat’s northern edge; a Focus section; and Frieze Masters, curated by Marika Sardar. The fair is also drawing on decades of artistic activity in the UAE, with the Abu Dhabi-based collective Dirwaza Curatorial Lab putting the work of two Emirati artists into cross-generational dialogue (Mohammed Kazem and Alia Zaal), and by using the Global Futures section to show artists with well-established profiles in the country, such as Abdullah Al Saadi and Ala Younis.

It is unclear whether the current geopolitical unrest will affect the fair. US President Donald Trump continues to make incendiary claims about a resumption of the war with Iran, though it is impossible to know how seriously to take these. And the closure of Saudi Arabia’s airspace this week—due to a conflict that the UAE is currently not a part of—has also made some gallerists nervous. But Frieze has underlined that the organisation and DCT are “fully committed to Frieze Abu Dhabi, and preparations are well advanced for the opening on 19 November”.

“We are in close and regular contact with our exhibitors, and will be as flexible as we sensibly can be for any gallery affected by travel advisories outside their control,” says a spokesperson for Frieze. “As with every Frieze fair, the safety of participants is the primary consideration in all our planning, and we are working closely with DCT and the relevant authorities.”

• Frieze Abu Dhabi, Manarat Al Saadiyat, 19-22 November

Taking over the longstanding Abu Dhabi Art, the Frieze brand has lured international dealerships alongside a strong showing of regional names

Announcement was made at yesterday's preview of Abu Dhabi Art 2021, where cultural leaders were keen to emphasise their commitment to the emirate following its strict lockdown

The evolution of Abu Dhabi’s art ecosystem has been “many years in the making”
