#175. From Spotlight to Soft-light: New Lighting by Coil + Drift

While the concentrated light of a spotlight compels us to take center stage, the soft glow of a shaded lamp invites us to decompress and settle in. Through his new collections Touch and Strut, Coil + Drift founder John Sorensen-Jolink explores how different lighting can affect a room and its inhabitants. Presented together in Lookout, a new exhibition at Colony in New York, contrasts intentional illumination with atmospheric glow.

As a contemporary dancer turned designer, Sorensen-Jolink understands the significance of light. Whether guiding focus, capturing movement, or establishing an ambiance, lighting shifts people’s experience of a space. He explores this relationship in Touch and Strut, working with a specialized team of in-house artisans to translate his understanding of movement and space into sculptural lighting.

Touch reimagines the spotlight as a domestic object, inspired by Sorensen-Jolink’s early encounters with theatrical lighting. Growing up in a home renovated by a theater worker, he was surrounded by dimly lit interiors, where recessed and track lighting cast concentrated pools of light. Though initially resistant to this dominant, impersonal light source, Sorensen-Jolink returns to the spotlight with a hands-on approach in Touch.

Constructed primarily from brass or steel, Touch features adjustable, cylindrical shades and slender stems that allow users to pivot the beams, while wooden accents emphasize tactility. Rather than remaining fixed, Touch allows light to shift in response to the room, balancing mechanical precision with the intimacy of human touch.

“When you’re in a pool of light, you’re on, you’re performing,” Sorensen-Jolink explains. “When you step out, you can sort of disappear.”

While Touch fosters focus, Strut introduces a quiet ambiance intended to support the everyday rhythm of a home. Inspired by the exposed wooden frameworks of fire lookout towers across the Catskill and Rocky Mountains, the collection translates this quiet utility into wooden lighting fixtures with subtle metal detailing and intentional use of negative space. Elongated linen shades, inspired in part by Sorensen-Jolink’s collection of vintage cloth-shaded lamps, emit an enveloping glow reminiscent of an ember or campfire.

Together, the collections embody two contrasting approaches to illumination, informed by the changing light surrounding Sorensen-Jolink’s Catskills studio. Through their distinct forms and materials, Touch and Strut balance focused illumination with softer, ambient light, introducing the natural rhythms of sun and shade into the home.

Lookout is on view until Oct. 21 at Colony Gallery in New York City.

#177. Sigma Says the Possibilities for New Lenses Are ‘Limitless’

Sigma Says the Possibilities for New Lenses Are ‘Limitless’

Sigma CEO Kazuto Yamaki chatted with Lensvid at IBC 2026, discussing Sigma’s rapidly expanding lens lineup, its latest innovations, and, most interestingly, how Sigma feels about the future of optical design.

While Yamaki and Lensvid chatted quite a bit about Sigma Aizu Primes, including that the promised 18mm T1.3 is expected to arrive in 2027, Yamaki-san was quick to dispel any notion that the Aizu Prime family may ever include a zoom lens.

“These are all obviously prime lenses,” Lensvid says, referring to the Aizu Prime lineup. “Have you thought about making lenses for the same category, which are zoom lenses?”

“We don’t believe it belongs in the same category,” Yamaki responded. “But last year, we also launched the Cine AF zoom lenses. These lenses are very popular.”

As Lensvid notes, Sigma has been releasing many lenses lately. The company was incredibly prolific last year, launching not only the Sigma BF camera, but nearly 10 photo lenses and as many Aizu Prime cinema lenses. The company launched about as many photo lenses as the year before, too.

“Do you think that it’s possible to continue releasing at this rate of like, 10 new lenses every year?” Lensvid asked.

“I believe that the ideas for lenses is unlimited — limitless,” Yamaki continued.

Sigma’s CEO added that with new and improved technology and better materials, it’s not only possible to create all-new lenses but also to improve existing ones, leaving the pool of potential new optics very deep indeed.

“You have a lot more options to go, I think,” Yamaki said.

Another interesting question related to artificial intelligence and how Sigma may use it to design lenses.

Yamaki was clear: using AI to design lenses is, at least for now, a waste of time and resources.

“We don’t use AI yet [to develop lens designs] because the technology, or knowledge, required to make a high-quality lens are not yet available on the internet,” Yamaki said. “All technology and knowledge are proprietary to us.”

Basically, it’s not possible to train an AI that would actually be useful, unless perhaps Sigma wanted to do it internally. Which, for now, it doesn’t. There is an extremely important human element to not only optical manufacturing but also the core design workflow.

As Sony Alpha Rumors notes, there are a lot of interesting parts of the discussion, which is seen in full above, including discussions on the new Sigma 20-60mm f/2.8-4 DG Contemporary and how Sigma utilizes assistive robotics to keep its manufacturing costs down.

Sigma has had yet another fantastic year in 2026, releasing many incredible lenses. There’s little doubt 2027 will be another success for the company.

#179. CMF Speaker S review: this little milk carton sounds better than it has any right to

Clever design and unique multi-speaker performance make Speaker S a novel little speaker. Its good audio quality also makes these budget speakers worth the money.

Why you can trust Creative Bloq Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

Drivers: 45mm full-range + 2 passive radiators

Connectivity: Bluetooth 6.0, NFC, USB-C audio

Features: Custom EQ, Stereo Mode, Auracast Party Mode, Wide Soundstage

Colours: Orange, dark grey, white, turquoise

I've got two CMF Speaker S models on my desk, one black and one reddish-orange, and when they arrived, I was pretty sure I'd be keeping the black one. Black goes with everything, doesn't it? But the more I see that orange milk carton sitting there, the more I like it, and now I'm not so sure. It's a silly thing to get hung up on with a Bluetooth speaker, perhaps, but that's part of the appeal of CMF's little box of tricks; it makes you care about what is essentially a small plastic box that plays music.

CMF is Nothing's more affordable sibling brand, and it has a knack for making everyday tech look a bit different. Previously, I've been impressed with CMF Headphone Pro, a budget version of the excellent Nothing Headphone (1) Pro. The Speaker S is a pint-sized milk carton with a square body, tapered shoulders, and a pinched top, and it looks fantastic. The larger Speaker M looks more like a two-pint milk carton but retains the same approach, with an extra speaker.

The shape also serves a purpose, which is always nice to see: the top doubles as a handle (it has a slight soft give), and the little circular hole lets you hang it from a hook in your room, clip it to a bag, or dangle it inside a tent when you're off camping. At 334g, it won't weigh you down, and with IP68 dust and water resistance, you don't have to fuss over it as much as some of your other gadgets.

Then there's the front button, a chunky cross-shaped toggle that could easily have been a boring round switch, but isn't. It turns smoothly for volume and presses in with a soft, satisfying clump, and I keep finding myself fiddling with it. There's thought behind how it works, not just how it looks, too: a single press plays or pauses, a double press skips forward, a triple press goes back a track, and a long press toggles Ultra Bass. It's the kind of physical control I enjoyed on Nothing's headphones, where standard buttons are swapped for toggles and paddles and do enough that you don't have to keep reaching for your phone. Same here with Speaker S.

All very nice, but a speaker has to play music, and I was genuinely surprised when I first pressed play. I ran through tracks from The Postal Service, The Jayhawks, and Failure, and the sound coming out of this tiny milk carton had much more weight than I expected. The music has decent body, the bass has some punch, and it doesn't immediately fall apart into the thin, tinny sound you get from cheap little Bluetooth speakers. Given the size, I found myself turning it up and wondering how CMF had managed to squeeze quite so much sound out of it.

The hardware is fairly straightforward: a single 45mm full-range driver, two passive radiators, and 10W RMS output, but the radiators add some extra oomph to the low end. The Nothing X app also offers EQ tweaks, including presets for more bass, treble, and voice, so you can fiddle if the default sound isn't quite right for you.

I'm not going to pretend this is a miniature hi-fi system, and anyone who spends their weekends arguing about speaker placement and the finer points of instrumental separation will find things to pick at. But for music while I'm working, listening around the house or sticking something on while cooking, the Speaker S sounds really good for the money.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

Take it outside, though, and things change a bit. The sound can spread out and lose some of that focus, becoming more diffuse than it does indoors. It's not terrible, and I don't expect much more from something this small, but it's worth knowing if you're planning to use it as the soundtrack to a garden party or a weekend at a festival. Personally, I'd take that trade-off for something I can sling in a bag without thinking about it, rather than lugging around some hefty Bose monster that takes up half the space I've got for everything else.

With that said, Nothing / CMF has a workaround. You can connect multiple speakers (including the larger CMF Speaker L using Auracast Party Mode to spread music around a space, or pair two Speaker S models in Stereo Mode. I tried two together in Stereo Mode and Wide Soundstage Mode, and the result was much more spacious than I expected from a pair of these little things. The Postal Service's bleepy 'Such Great Heights' felt like it was bouncing around the room. The sound filled the space with a rounder, more spread-out feel, and it made a real difference compared with listening to a single unit on its own. So that's the caveat: Speaker S sound is full and wraparound if you buy two or more.

I'm sure anyone who takes their speakers seriously will have a field day moving them around, trying different positions and working out how to get the best sound from a pair. There's something appealing about placing two small speakers where they work best, rather than relying on one big box to do everything.

And at $59 / £49 each, you don't really need to spend a fortune to try it. Two will set you back $118 / £98, still a reasonable price for a stereo setup, while Party Mode gives you another option if you want to spread the sound outdoors and hook up even more speakers. I'd definitely opt for at least two Speaker S, see how you get on, and add more later if you fancy it (or if you're huge Pink Floyd fan and what the full experience).

The boxy, compact design makes it easy to use multiple speakers, hooked and hung around the room. And it means I keep coming back to the design because it's what makes the Speaker S stand out. Plenty of small Bluetooth speakers do a decent job, but most are black cylinders or little fabric-covered bricks, and you forget what they look like about five minutes after you buy one. CMF Speaker S doesn't want to be forgotten, and like other Nothing devices, it wants to start a conversation.

And you can mess around with it too, which is even better. The front panels and knobs can be swapped out, so you can change the colour scheme, and Nothing has released official design files for 3D printing your own parts. If you've got a printer, you can try making something that suits your desk, your room, or whatever odd colour combination you've decided you need this week. (For example, my black and orange Speaker S also have different shaped buttons.) I'd love to see what people come up with, especially if they push the milk-carton idea in stranger directions.

The rest of the spec is pretty good for the price, too. Nothing claims up to 18 hours of battery life, and you get Bluetooth 6.0, NFC pairing, USB-C audio and the ability to connect two devices at once. Battery life depends on how loudly you play music and how you use it, of course, but it's enough to make it useful beyond sitting on a shelf looking pretty.

For $59 / £49, I reckon CMF is onto something. The Speaker S looks great, sounds better than its size suggests and has enough practical touches to make it a genuinely useful little speaker, whether you're listening at your desk, taking it away for the weekend or hanging it up in the garden. It won't satisfy anyone looking for huge bass or the last word in audio detail, and the sound loses a little focus outdoors, but those are reasonable compromises for something this small and affordable.

What I like is that the design hasn't been left at the level of a novelty. The handle and hanging hole make sense, the cross-shaped control is a joy to use, and the removable panels and 3D-printable parts give you a reason to keep playing with it long after you've unboxed it. Add a second speaker, and you get a surprisingly good little stereo setup, too.

I started out thinking the black model was the one for me, but that orange one is winning me over by the day; and, since it sounds best as a pair, I don't really feel forced to decide. It sounds daft to say a Bluetooth speaker has a bit of personality, but this one does, and at $59 / £49 I can forgive it for not sounding like a much bigger, much more expensive speaker. Speaker S is a fun little thing that also plays music well and can be expanded to play music really well, which is pretty unique and very Nothing by design.

#180. Process as Practice: Building with Reclaimed Materials on Tarkwa Bay, Lagos

On Tarkwa Bay, off the coast of Lagos, the transformation of an abandoned building offers a way to consider how architecture might emerge from the materials, relationships and conditions already present in a place.

On Tarkwa Bay, off the coast of Lagos, the transformation of an abandoned building offers a way to consider how architecture might emerge from the materials, relationships and conditions already present in a place.

Architecture is often encountered at the end, when the uncertainties of making have been resolved into a building, a surface, a space. Less visible are the conditions that allow these outcomes to exist, the movement of materials, the availability of labour, the knowledge held by people and places, and the negotiations through which an idea becomes possible. On Tarkwa Bay, an island off the coast of Lagos accessible only by boat, these conditions are difficult to separate from the act of building itself.

Less visible are the conditions that allow these outcomes to exist, the movement of materials, the availability of labour, the knowledge held by people and places, and the negotiations through which an idea becomes possible. On Tarkwa Bay, an island off the coast of Lagos accessible only by boat, these conditions are difficult to separate from the act of building itself.

The crossing from the Lagos mainland introduces a different relationship to access. People, tools and materials move across water; some resources are readily available, others less so. Materials move across water; reclaimed elements carry histories from elsewhere; salt and sun alter the behaviour of surfaces; and the availability of local artisans influences how work unfolds. These are not necessarily prohibitions; rather, they make visible the dependencies that building elsewhere can allow us to overlook.

Hungarian graphic designer MolnÃ¡r PÃ©ter returns with PLAY 2 WIN Vol. 2, a 17-piece poster design series mixing 1980s tech and print grit.

The house always writes the rules. As Hungarian graphic designer MolnÃ¡r PÃ©ter moves through the final stretch of his forties, he treats his accumulated memories and false starts as what he calls little mood preserves. PLAY 2 WIN Vol. 2 (expanded to 12 + 5 days with its October 2025 bonus track) twists the familiar "pay to win" clichÃ© into a raw daily diary about surviving inside rigged systems. There's no rigid brief holding these pieces together. Instead, every sheet carries a recurring oval globe stamp reading "USER MANUAL FOR WHOLE DAMN LIFE," a custom P2W katakana mark, and fluorescent supermarket price stickers counting down the days left in the year.

Every sheet feels lived-in. MolnÃ¡r wraps several compositions under glossy, crinkled polyethylene film so the ink looks like a forgotten record sleeve pulled from a discount bin. In "NOW FINE LESS NEXT," a four-by-four modular stencil grid splits diagonally between cobalt blue and crimson to honor the 1982 Landsat-D mission and NASA's NSSC-1 onboard computer â reminding us that NASA landed on the moon with less RAM than a modern smart fridge. That same fondness for 1980s hardware drives "RANDOM BACKWARD," where a massive black "82" and an orange data-matrix strip frame the button layout of Sony's 1982 CDP-101 Compact Disc player beneath a weathered "*319 DAYS LEFT" tag.

#182. Objects with Narratives presents collectible design that looks "found rather than fabricated"

Belgian gallery Objects with Narratives has curated a texture-heavy exhibition at PAD London called What Remains?, featuring pieces from Ben Storms and Paul Cocksedge.

What Remains? marks the second show that Brussels platform Objects with Narratives has presented at design fair PAD London, which takes place annually in Mayfair’s Berkley Square.

The emerging Brussels gallery’s exhibition brings together a series of textured pieces united by amorphous shapes and patinated surfaces.

“Every piece was crafted in the present, yet many carry a sense of the past, as though found rather than fabricated,” said Objects with Narratives.

Among the exhibitors is Belgian designer Ben Storms, who is known for his rough-hewn furniture that looks like jumbo pillows. Storms is presenting his most recent design, a cushion-like coffee table called Ex Hale, crafted from veiny red Mexican onyx decorated with mosaic veneer.

To create the piece, the designer used a hydroforming technique to blow up two pieces of metal sheet that were welded together and 3D-scanned to form a cushion shape.

After this, Storms used a CNC machine to mill the same shape from a block of stone.

“Ex Hale plays with our common notions of materiality,” said the gallery. “The hard stone looks soft instead, an impression that is further enhanced by the delicate surface treatment.”

Also on display is Critical Mass, a handmade Corten steel standing shelf by British designer Paul Cocksedge.

A trio of metal components were arranged to support three metal shelves, forming a piece that looks familiar to What Nelson Sees, a weathering steel installation by Cocksedge that was placed in Trafalgar Square for last year’s London Design Festival.

“The Critical Mass series holds an energy, something on the edge of collapse or explosion,” said Objects with Narratives.

Belgian designer Sofie Middernacht is showing a steel credenza, bench and duo of stools clad in gleaming crimson resin.

Middernacht works with discarded industrial materials to create her furniture, which is purposefully formed like archaeological artefacts.

Venezuelan artist Jojo Corväiá is presenting a trio of glazed vessels crafted from volcanic clay, a material central to his practice.

A host of other materials feature in the show, from shaggy mohair and wool lamps by Belgian practice KRJST Studio to lighting by Danish designer Karl Monies formed from patchwork slabs of copper.

“What Remains? asks what gives an object the sense that it might outlive the moment of its making: the material, the craft, or simply the possibility that some objects belong to no single time at all,” Objects with Narratives concluded.Objects with Narratives was founded by Nik and Robbe Vandewyngaerde and Oskar Eryatmaz, who opened their first permanent brick-and-mortar gallery inside a historic 1920s fur atelier in Brussels in 2023.

PAD London 2026 takes place from 14 to 19 October 2026 at Berkeley Square, London W1J 6EN, UK. See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world.

#183. A 1908 Japanese Prison Finds New Life as a Luxury Hotel

Constructed in 1908 by government architect Keijiro Yamashita, the landmark Nara Prison is the only complex among Japan’s monumental “Five Great Prisons of Meiji” to survive almost entirely intact. More than a century later, Hoshino Resorts has transformed the former prison into Hoshinoya Nara Prison, , a 48-suite luxury hotel that preserves the building’s distinctive architecture while introducing an entirely new purpose.

Though the converted prison-hotel model isn’t anything new, Hoshinoya Nara Prison approaches adaptive reuse as an exercise in cultural preservation. With support from conservation specialists at Yasui Architects & Engineers, lead architect Rie Azuma (Azuma Environmental Architectural Research Institute) carried out a considered renovation that’s both deeply respectful of the site’s history and resolutely contemporary.

The Nara Prison complex relies on the conventional Haviland System—a radial layout in which five wings extend from a central guardhouse. Rather than masking this rigid institutional typology, Azuma and her team embraced its structural geometry, preserving the original circulation routes and emphasizing the architectural rhythm of the long corridors and brick arches.

“We aim to preserve the memory of how [Japanese people] of the time engaged with unfamiliar Western culture, while creating a space where modern guests can enjoy a comfortable stay,” Azuma explains. Despite this rigid geometry, the resulting interiors balance the building’s imposing architecture with the warmth and comfort expected of a contemporary hotel.

The primary design challenge was converting the narrow, isolated detention cells into expansive luxury suites. Azuma’s team solved this by connecting former cells to create larger accommodations while retaining elements of the original architecture. For signature suites such as The 11-Cell Deluxe, the team brought together 11 original blocks into a single footprint. The resulting suite includes an expansive living area and a separate dressing lounge.

Throughout the interiors, material choices balance historical preservation with contemporary structural requirements. Exposed steel seismic reinforcements—installed to fortify the century-old brickwork—create a compelling dialogue alongside restored plaster ceiling moldings and warm timber paneling.

While the sharp metallic lines stand in stark, graphic contrast against the rugged, hand-laid brick walls, celebrating the physical weight of the original construction, the wooden inserts introduce tactile warmth and soften the otherwise austere material palette.

The interior concept draws directly from the Meiji era’s spirit of global integration. In a first for the Hoshinoya brand, European furnishings appear throughout the property, reflecting the Western influences that shaped Japanese architecture and culture during the period. Contemporary artworks complement the historic interiors, set within the building’s preserved architectural volumes. In the main lounge, an open atrium and exposed structural beams are complemented by a series of arches extending from the windows, creating an inviting atmosphere for quiet reflection and relaxation.

Lighting designer Masanobu Takeishi used subtle indirect illumination and handcrafted ceramic fixtures, thrown by local artisans, to soften the building’s severity and introduce depth and spatial richness. In the courtyard, lighting inspired by distant moonlight creates a similarly restrained atmosphere after dark.

Outdoors, landscape architect Hiroki Hasegawa imagined the expansive grounds through an “outside within” concept, introducing geometrically arranged walkways, private decks, and carefully maintained planting areas to offer guests serene outdoor spaces within the former prison walls.

“The vast, open spaces that once served security purposes have been preserved as much as possible, while fragments of the outside world—carefully maintained landscapes—have been introduced in selected areas,” Hasegawa shares.

Beyond its architectural transformation, Hoshinoya Nara Prison in adaptive reuse and heritage preservation. Rather than treating the building’s history as a backdrop, the project incorporates it into the guest experience, allowing visitors to encounter the original architecture alongside contemporary interventions.

Through what Hoshino Resorts has dubbed the “Cycle of Heritage,” the project proposes a model in which tourism contributes to the continued preservation of significant cultural properties. Connected directly to the on-site Nara Prison Museum through a dedicated pathway, the hotel invites guests to engage with the building’s complex institutional history beyond its newly restored interiors.

#185. Building A UX ROI Case That Survives The Boardroom

Alex Williams is a seasoned full-stack developer and the former owner of Hosting Data UK. After graduating from the University of London with a Masters Degree … More about Alex ↬

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

Sooner or later, a CFO looks at your wireframes and asks what any of it actually does for the bottom line. Storyboards don’t answer that question, and the era when a 5-minute pitch could answer it ended, unfortunately, a while ago.

These days, if you want to win budget, buy-in, and backing for UX, the design has to be provably good for the business, not only for the people using it.

And proving that takes more than taping a dollar sign to a redesign. You have to understand how your organization defines value in the first place, how it measures that value, and how a credible line gets drawn between a design initiative and an outcome leadership already cares about.

Rather than scatter tips, this article follows one worked example the whole way through. Meridian is a mid-size B2B SaaS company, and it is entirely made up — that label matters, so it gets repeated where it counts. Its onboarding redesign carries the same figures from goal-setting through cost accounting, causal testing, and the final ROI number, because a framework only becomes tangible when the numbers connect. Every step is one you can rerun inside your own organization.

Companies now want clarity on what every dollar buys, and “delightful user experiences” stopped clearing that bar some time ago. I still remember a former colleague celebrating a $1 million redesign he’d gotten greenlit mostly on the strength of a couple of three.js tricks. Try that pitch in front of a finance team today and see how far the particles get you.

Executives don’t hate UX, they just hate vagueness. A pitch built on “users will find it easier” loses, every time, to the department promising 12% more sales in Q3. The difference is the one between a streamlined checkout flow that reduced cart abandonment with completed purchases up 22%, and the same work rewarded with “the QA testers like it.” One of those goes on your resume. The rest of this article is about earning the first version, with Meridian’s numbers doing the work.

Meet Image Optimization, Addy Osmani’s new practical guide to optimizing and delivering high-quality images on the web. Everything in one single 528-pages book.

Most writing about UX ROI makes a convenient assumption: that the organization already owns clean business goals and KPIs for you to hook your work onto. Real companies are messier than that. Plenty run on ambitions like “grow faster” or “improve the customer journey” that nobody ever broke into anything measurable, and an ROI case built on that ambiguity sounds impressive right up until somebody scrutinizes it.

So the first job is often to help the organization define what success even looks like. Interview stakeholders across departments — what does product consider a good quarter, where does customer success watch users struggle, where do sales deals stall — and listen for the themes that keep resurfacing across conversations, because those recurring themes are the company’s latent business objectives. A useful forcing function is the OKR model (Objectives and Key Results), which doesn’t tolerate vagueness.

At Meridian, the stated ambition was “improve the rate of new users’ adoption of the platform,” which you can neither design toward nor measure against. Interviews turned up the real shape of the problem. Trial users needed a median of 14 days to reach first value, most churned before getting there, and onboarding questions were burying the support queue. Out of that came an OKR with actual edges: reduce median time-to-first-value from 14 days to 7 with the use of a guided setup flow, and lift trial-to-paid conversion from 8% to 9.5%.

One warning about formalizing KPIs: Impose them from inside the UX team and leadership will suspect you’ve rigged the field in your own favor, so co-create them with whoever owns the outcome — though never at the price of accepting targets that set your team up for an uncomfortable situation. Meridian’s head of product agreed that setup-completion rate was a fair proxy for onboarding usability, and customer success signed off on time-to-first-value, a number already sitting on their own dashboard.

ROI has a denominator, and the denominator is where most UX teams go wrong. You can’t calculate a return without strategic financial planning, yet cost usually gets counted as designer salaries or consulting hours and nothing else. A finance team will find the rest whether or not you counted it, so count it first.

Direct costs are the visible ones. Meridian’s redesign ran $45,000 in design and research labor plus another $8,000 in tooling and participant incentives. Licenses for Figma, UserTesting, Hotjar, analytics platforms, research incentive spend — all of it belongs in the total, and that’s before the inevitable instances of vendor lock-in every UX team eventually faces. Engineering sits in the same column, because a UX redesign doesn’t stop at the mockup. Building the guided setup took two frontend sprints plus a QA pass, $38,000 worth, and the project generated about $4,000 of coordination overhead along the way in new syncs and shared dashboards.

The line item nearly everyone misses, and the one worth stealing from this article if you steal nothing else, is stakeholder time. Workshops, design reviews, and feedback sessions all pull senior people away from their primary work. A VP of Product spending four hours a week in UX reviews is a VP not spending those hours on roadmap planning or partner negotiations. Log the attendance — who came, for how long, at what seniority — and price it at fully loaded cost, meaning salary plus benefits divided by productive hours. A quarter’s worth of workshops, reviews, and interviews at Meridian priced out at $22,000.

Add it all up: $45,000 in design labor, $8,000 in tooling, $38,000 in engineering, $22,000 in stakeholder time, $4,000 in coordination. The investment is $117,000. Saying that number out loud beats saying “we spent $45K on design,” precisely because it already includes everything a finance team would have dug up on its own.

Most UX ROI pitches die right here. Conversions rose after the redesign, sure — and the CFO wants to know how you ruled out the new pricing, the seasonal traffic bump, and the marketing campaign that shipped the same week. Without a convincing answer, your entire ROI story crumbles.

After all these years, the gold standard for proving causation is still A/B testing: run the old experience against the new one on an even traffic split until the sample means something.

Onboarding happens to suit a phased rollout, which is why Meridian could do this cleanly. For eight weeks, half of new trial signups received the redesigned guided setup while half stayed on the legacy flow. Control converted to paid at 8.0%. The variant came in at 9.4%. With roughly 6,100 trials inside the window, the difference was statistically significant, but a 1.4-point gap on a single test is still the kind of result that deserves a second look before anyone builds a budget on it, which is one reason the team held back on attribution below. Where a split isn’t feasible — a change too structural, a user base too small — fall back to a time series instead. Measure steadily for weeks before the change, implement, then keep measuring against the baseline you established.

Documenting whatever else happens around the same time as your UX change is the unglamorous half of causation.

A pricing-page test from Meridian’s marketing team overlapped weeks five through eight of the rollout. The UX team noted it, confirmed it hit both cohorts evenly, and still chose to attribute only 70% of the observed lift to the redesign in the final math. There is no formula that produces that number; treat it as an illustrative assumption for this example.

The team asked how much of the lift could plausibly belong to the pricing test if it had helped one cohort slightly more than the other, settled on a ceiling of about a third, and rounded the redesign’s share down to 70%. Your figure will differ. What matters is that it is written down and argued for before the results arrive, not fitted to them afterwards. That restraint is worth money in a skeptical room. “We attribute roughly 70% of the lift to the onboarding change, with the remainder likely influenced by concurrent pricing work” survives cross-examination; claiming everything does not. Cohort analysis then backed the number up, since the lift held across acquisition channels and tenure bands, and at that point the skeptics had very little left to work with.

Leading and lagging indicators belong on the same slide, because each covers the other’s weakness. Meridian’s leading indicators moved first — setup completion climbed from 62% to 89%, median time-to-first-value dropped from 14 days to 6.5 — and the lagging trial-to-paid number followed. Mechanism first, business outcome second. Presented together, they form a causal chain that’s harder to poke holes in than either one alone.

So what did Meridian actually earn? The company sees about 40,000 trial signups a year. Lifting conversion from 8.0% to 9.4% adds roughly 560 paying customers annually, and at an average of $1,800 in annual recurring revenue per account, those customers represent about $1,008,000 in new ARR. Applying the conservative 70% attribution from the causal work trims the defensible figure to roughly $706,000.

Set that against the full $117,000 investment and the first-year ROI lands near 5:1, with payback arriving in roughly two months. There’s a second line, too. Onboarding-related support tickets dropped about 30%, some 3,600 fewer tickets a year, worth another $54,000 annually at $15 per resolved ticket. Keep it as its own line rather than folding it into one swollen headline number. The case reads as more honest that way and loses none of its force.

Three assumptions carry that result, and each belongs on the slide next to it. The 40,000 signups and the $1,800 average ARR are the prior year’s actuals held flat, so a growth or pricing change moves the outcome in either direction. The 70% attribution is the illustrative assumption from the causal work, not a measured quantity. And the two-month payback counts new ARR as it lands rather than revenue recognized net of churn, which flatters the timeline; on a net basis the payback stretches to roughly a quarter. State those three plainly and a finance team can adapt the example to its own numbers. Hide them and the whole thing starts to look like marketing math, however careful the experiment was.

What persuades in the final presentation is not sophistication. Open with the baseline: what stalled trials and support volume were already costing. Show the delta in terms leadership reads fluently, metrics like conversion rate uplift chief among them. A chart of setup completion climbing from 62% to 89% will beat a paragraph of UX jargon, and a translation like “each abandoned setup costs us 0.3 support tickets” beats the chart. Above all, keep every figure identical from the first slide to the last. A room full of finance people forgives many things, but never numbers that wobble between slides.

Budget decisions come out of coalitions. A CFO may hold the final say when adding AI to the checkout process, but marketing, product, and customer success all lean on that decision, and each means something different by “value.”

A CFO hears cost, revenue, and risk. A CMO hears conversion and acquisition cost, since UX is a lever for increasing marketing ROI. Product counts support tickets; customer success thinks in retention. The underlying numbers never change; only the framing rotates, and a CFO wants a projection, not a moodboard. Meridian’s CFO slide read “the onboarding redesign protects roughly $706,000 in new ARR a year against a $117,000 investment,” while the CMO version led with what a 9.4% trial conversion does to blended acquisition cost.

Some UX outcomes never translate cleanly into revenue, and pretending they do weakens the parts of your case that are solid.

Scores like Net Promoter Score (NPS), CSAT, and Customer Effort Score already sit inside most reporting cadences, which makes them cheap to borrow. Tie your work to their movement, and segment wherever the data allows.

Meridian could say that NPS among trial users on the redesigned onboarding was 51 against 34 for the legacy flow, which lands far harder than any blended average. Verbatim feedback from surveys, support transcripts, and app store reviews adds the emotional weight the scores lack. Internal tools deserve the same discipline, since employee experience is increasingly recognized as a business driver — a dashboard redesign that hands account managers 45 minutes a day back is a productivity gain, a satisfaction gain, and a retention lever all in one.

Brand perception resists direct measurement but leaves tracks in repeat visits, organic referrals, and social sentiment. It carries extra weight in trust-sensitive industries like finance or healthcare, and it forms fast, given that UX design influences the first impressions of a whopping 94% of customers.

Whatever you collect, systematize the collecting. Run pre- and post-surveys with consistent question sets, use structured usability testing with task-based scoring, and put the qualitative right next to the quantitative when you present.

UX loses the budget battle unless it’s mapped to company-wide objectives, so phrase the proposal in the words of this year’s board presentation.

Nobody at Meridian pitched “simplify the onboarding UI”; the pitch was a redesigned trial experience worth 1.4 points of upgrade rate, roughly $1M in annual recurring revenue before attribution. Bring evidence in both registers, since that is what social proof is for: the case, clearly labeled, plus screenshots, impact graphs, and user quotes. Find internal allies who can repeat the ROI narrative in rooms you’ll never enter, and write the playbook down, because repeatable ROI is what earns recurring investment.

This topic has been explored extensively by researchers, practitioners, and consultancies. Here’s a curated set of resources worth studying if you want to build a stronger ROI practice around UX.

A seat at the table never comes from beauty or novelty. It comes from measurable, defensible impact, which means UX leaders have to trade the artist’s posture for the strategist’s. Speak in outcomes rather than outputs. Connect pixels to profit.

When someone challenges the numbers, don’t flinch. Show the controlled experiment, the cohort analysis, and the before-and-after metrics, every figure holding steady from the first slide to the last, the way Meridian’s did, with the customer quotes and the employee-satisfaction data sitting right beside the revenue impact. Prove the work does more than delight users, and be ready to defend the ratio line by line. That’s when the CFO leans in, and that’s when design stops being optional.

#186. ‘Artist-first’ Fair Play launches to strong attendance but slow sales during London Frieze week

Crowd control: Fair Play's private view on Thursday evening attracted large numbers Donna Ford

Of all the various satellite fairs within walking distance of Frieze London this year, the inaugural Fair Play has the advantage of being the closest. Located across two floors in the repurposed church One Marylebone, the new fair boasts an “artist-first” status, cutting the galleries out of the equation by only hosting individual artist stands.

Rather, the fair acts somewhat as a gallery, with the artist playing dealer. Fair Play provides the exhibition space and white walls, gets the artists’ work in front of collectors and other audiences, and, of course, takes a 50% cut (including VAT) of any sales made. The majority of the 70 artists exhibiting were chosen by a selection committee of curators and creative directors following an open call, with an £84 application fee (including two fair tickets for all applicants) but no cost for the stand itself. For each of the chosen artists, it was up to them to sort transportation, hanging, pricing and curation of their work. Most of the artists do not have gallery representation and, for many of them, this is their first fair.

The energy on Friday morning was upbeat, and the slim corridors between the tightly placed stands were extremely busy. “Busy” was the keyword when speaking to artists at the fair so far, many of whom pointed to the apparently heaving opening the night before. According to Ryan Stanier, the fair’s founder, the private view saw more than 3,000 attendees. “It was the best opening night I’ve ever hosted,” he tells The Art Newspaper, referring to his prior role as the founder and director of The Other Art Fair.

Sales, however, seemed significantly less buzzy. Although affordable—most of the prices lie in the three- to four-figure range—red dots were scarce. The vast majority of the artists The Art Newspaper spoke to had not made any sales, although all of them were optimistic about interest and collectors returning later on. One notable exception was the London-based artist Lea Rose Kara, who sold two wall-based sculptures on the opening night: a smaller work to one of her returning collectors for £300 and a larger piece to a new collector for £3,200. Other artists were positive about alternative opportunities that may come from the fair, such as the Cornwall-based sculptor Eleanor Turnbull, who had several enquiries regarding potential commissions.

Nevertheless, staff remain steadfast about the strength of sales at the first edition. “Our ethos is to buy the piece and walk out the door with it,” said one staff member at the payment desk, with a wrapping and shipping stand located just around the corner.

#188. How Span Reimagined the Nature Museum Identity

Span gave Chicago's Nature Museum a prairie-grown identity: a Tonka wordmark, a butterfly icon, and prairie colors that bloom across the brand.

The Peggy Notebaert Nature Museum has connected Chicagoans with nature and science since 1857. After a new strategic plan, it asked Nick Adam's team at Span to evolve an identity that had barely moved in twenty years. The answer is drawn from native Illinois prairies: confident, warm, and built to speak to weekend visitors and research scientists at once. The entrance says it best: a giant vertical NATURE MUSEUM banner in milkweed cream on catalpa green, the icon's looping petals behind it, with INSPIRING NATURE CHAMPIONS running over the doors.

The wordmark is set in Tonka by CÃ©line Hurka, whose flaring stems give the name a historic, organic voice. "PEGGY NOTEBAERT" rides above stacked NATURE MUSEUM, with "OF THE CHICAGO ACADEMY OF SCIENCES" anchoring the lockup. The pairing face is Miles Newlyn's New Atten, a humanist sans named for the voice of Sir David Attenborough; the type board sets "Connections, Wonder, Nature and Inspiration" large in Compass, Columbine, Aster, and Catalpa on deep Evergreen. Best detail: the circular NATURE MUSEUM stamp, set on a curve around the butterfly icon like a field-station seal.

The palette is the real star: seven swatches named for prairie flora, each spec'd with PMS values on the system board. Catalpa and Evergreen hold the structure while Columbine pink, Aster blue, and Compass yellow do the shouting, and Milkweed cream keeps the type legible on top of it all. The icon reads as butterfly, flower, or cloud, and works three ways: a standalone mark, a lens cropping into photography, and a pattern field that the studio says "instills a sense of positive activity." Beyond the identity, Span redesigned the museum's website, signage, and store collateral, and the case study shows the system stretching across all of it. Campaign graphics stack punchy lines, "We can excite. We can inspire. We can teach." and "This is our opportunity to be bold.", over marsh photography framed by the icon. The poster trio runs from a hand cradling a skink, stamped "CONNECTING PEOPLE TO NATURE SINCE 1857," to an "URBS IN HORTO" field photography meet-up dated Friday 23 August, to a "CITY IN A GARDEN" scene by the pond. President and CEO Erin Amico frames the ambition plainly: the museum is "more than a repository of history," and the identity "now takes a transformative step forward to match the Museum's dynamic evolution." It is rare to see an institutional rebrand this willing to be loud. The prairie gave Span the excuse, and they took it.

#190. "Welcoming and inclusive" London housing wins RIBA Stirling Prize 2026

Photography by Lorenzo Zandri (unless stated otherwise)

The Lion Green Road housing in south London, designed by local studios Mary Duggan Architects with Ruff Architects, has won this year’s RIBA Stirling Prize for the UK’s best new building.

Located in Coulsdon, the high-density development commissioned by Croydon Council provides 157 homes across five blocks, which are stitched together by a series of shared green spaces.

The Royal Institute of British Architects (RIBA) named the project as winner of the prestigious prize at a ceremony in London this evening.

It is the fourth housing scheme to win the prize since its inception 30 years ago, following Accordia in Cambridge in 2008, Goldsmith Street in Norwich in 2019 and Appleby Blue Almshouse in London in 2025.

The jury hailed Mary Duggan Architects and Ruff Architects for “addressing the pressing need for national housing” and providing environmentally considerate homes with ample access to light, nature and community.

“More than a housing development, the scheme has created a welcoming and inclusive place where people can connect with one another, and with nature,” read the citation.

Lion Green Road comprises five blocks with a mix of private and socially rented homes. They are staggered across its steeply sloped site – a topographically challenging plot previously used as a car park.

The blocks have faceted, star-shaped plans, which are rotated to offer unique views across the landscape and ensure each home is dual-aspect, maximising natural light.

A trio of complementary brick types clad the buildings, helping to visually unify them while giving each its own unique aesthetic.

Shared outdoor spaces that weave through the blocks enhance this unification, giving residents opportunities to meet and engage with each other.

RIBA president Chris Williamson said the scheme demonstrates how high-density housing “can be achieved without compromising the quality of the places we create”.

“Through a consistent specification, with subtle variation in height and orientation, it offers housing at scale without uniformity,” he reflected.

“The architects have created a new kind of garden neighbourhood that balances privacy and generous views with a strong connection to nature – it’s a living landscape,” Williamson continued.

“This is thoughtful, resourceful architecture that proves that even the most challenging of sites can be transformed into truly distinctive places for people to call home.”

The RIBA Stirling Prize has been awarded annually to the UK’s best new building since 1996. Lion Green Road was chosen from a six-strong shortlist, revealed in July.

It was announced as this year’s winner at a ceremony at Old Billingsgate this evening, where RIBA also revealed the recipients of its five Special Awards.

This included the RIBA Neave Brown Award for Housing, which was won by Satish Jassal Architects for Rowan Court, a cluster of brick-clad social housing blocks in Seven Sisters.

Collaborators Samuel Chisholm Studio and Takero Shimazaki took home the RIBA Reinvention Award for Oru Sutton, a co-working space in an old department store, while Tonkin Liu Architects won the RIBA Client of the Year Award in recognition of the York Minster Centre of Excellence.

Finally, the RIBA Conservation Award was given to Architectural Thread for The Buttermarket, an arts-focused community hub in Cornwall, which also won the RIBA Stephen Lawrence Prize for emerging architectural talent.

Previous winners of the Stirling Prize include London’s Elizabeth Line in 2024, The New Library at Magdalene College in 2022 and a seaside pier in Hastings in 2017.

Last year’s award, which was won by the “hopeful and imaginative” Appleby Blue Almshouse social housing, sparked concerns about London bias, with four of the six shortlisted buildings located in the capital city.

Earlier this year, the shortlist for the 2026 Stirling Prize was a topic of conversation in our Dezeen Weekly podcast, with our journalists pondering if architecture has become too boring.

#192. Kohler Introduces Fleurette Artist Editions Collection with Aerin Lauder

Kohler unveils a new Artist Editions collaboration with AERIN founder and creative director Aerin Lauder, introducing the Fleurette Collection. Inspired by the heritage of traditional Delftware, the collection brings hand-applied floral motifs to three iconic Kohler fixtures.

Crafted in white vitreous china and rooted in the tradition of Delft tiles, the collection comprises three Kohler classics: the Memoirs Stately toilet, Memoirs Stately pedestal sink, and Caxton rectangle sink. Offered in two colorways, a traditional blue-and-white palette and a soft green-and-white option, the trio transforms functional fixtures into decorative bath forms. The green variation offers a fresh interpretation of Delftware, drawing on Lauder’s growing appreciation for the color and bringing what she describes as a garden-inspired sensibility into the home.

Lauder’s vision for the collaboration stems from the blue-and-white ceramics that filled her grandmother Estée Lauder’s home. “My grandmother taught me to appreciate beautiful objects and the stories they carry,” she says. “I wanted to create pieces that feel timeless, objects that could become part of a family’s home and be enjoyed for years to come.”

Having long admired the way Kohler elevates everyday spaces through design, Lauder was particularly drawn to the opportunity to work with its Artist Editions collection. Celebrating the intersection of art and craftsmanship for more than 40 years, the initiative combines precision manufacturing with decorative techniques executed by skilled artisans in Kohler, Wisconsin. The partnership not only reflects Lauder’s deeply personal perspective on the collection, but also underscores Kohler’s commitment to luxury design innovation.

Despite its centuries-old tradition, Lauder feels there is “something incredibly fresh about Delftware.” As bathrooms increasingly become opportunities for individual style and expression throughout the home, the collaboration between Kohler and AERIN merges heritage with enduring design, creating what Lauder describes as a “natural way to blend artistry, craftsmanship, and nostalgia, while creating something that feels modern and timeless for today’s interiors.”

When the Wicker trailer burst on the scene, it's safe to say it was met with a mixed reaction. While many were excited to see Alexander Skarsgård in all his woven wicker glory, others clutched their pearls at the saucy fantasy rom-com concept. But the film has only doubled down on the weird factor, creating the perfect poster in response.

Go to any second-hand bookshop, and you'll find an array of raunchy romance novels all with the same book cover design – a female protagonist in the throes of intimate ecstasy, with a strapping hunk by her side. Only this time, he's made of Wicker.

The unconventional film poster features lead actress Olivia Colman draped in the arms of her sentient wicker basket lover. From her enraptured expression to Skarsgård's protective embrace, the design wouldn't look out of place among a lineup of old-school romantasy book covers (so long as you don't notice he's made of wood...)

While the design is clearly a pastiche of these stereotypically schlocky novels, the poster itself is oddly beautiful. With rich jewel tones and elegant portraiture, the design has a timeless feel, only enhanced by its intricate gold script typography.

"Dressing a wicker husband movie up like a paperback romance is elite packaging" one fan on X wrote. "Homage to the 80's-90's bodice ripper mass market paperback covers. Loveee ittt!!!!" another praised, while the best comment by far was the simple sentiment, calling the design "Fifty Shades of Hay".

For more Wicker news, check out IKEA's cheeky homage to the film or take a look at Alexander Skarsgård's wood(en suit).

#194. An artist’s poetic rumination on the political promise of Opec

A scene from Sanaz Sohrabi's documentary An Incomplete Calendar (2026) © Sanaz Sohrabi

The new film An Incomplete Calendar, by the Iranian Canadian artist and film-maker Sanaz Sohrabi, thoughtfully employs archival footage and ephemera about the Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (Opec), reframing the oil cartel as both an agent of anti-imperialist solidarity and an unlikely vehicle for peace through cultural exchange.

Shown at the Vancouver International Film Festival earlier this month after winning a prize for the best debut feature this past March at the Cinéma du Réel festival in Paris, with a plethora of upcoming festival screenings, the film is especially timely in the midst of US and Israel’s war with Iran. In it, Sohrabi subverts the typical talking-heads documentary format by using poetic voiceovers—her own as well as those of the writer and curator Murtaza Vali, scholar Laleh Khalili, journalist Layla Maghribi, professor Leonardo Montaño Salas and others—as she visually centres archival materials.

“Over the course of six years, I gathered the archives for this film while I was working on my trilogy about the colonial history of extraction in Iran and West Asia,” Sohrabi said in a statement. “I collected a repository of archives without realising I was piecing together remnants and fragments of the Third World’s political calendar of independence and economic sovereignty. I layered rarely seen anticolonial magazines, stamps, newsreels and ephemera—found in flea markets, bookshops, online exchanges and mailed across continents—to shape the film’s narrative and visual structure.”

A scene from Sanaz Sohrabi's documentary An Incomplete Calendar (2026) © Sanaz Sohrabi

The film documents a key moment when political decolonisation in the 1950s empowered newly independent Asian and African nations to pursue economic sovereignty. Its timeline spans Pan-Arabism and the Arab-Israeli wars of 1967 and 1973. Archival footage from British Petroleum conveys both the mid-century optimism that began with the creation of Opec in Baghdad in 1960 and its poignant denouement, when the war between Iran and Iraq (with Ronald Regan’s administration funding both sides) began in 1980.

Footage of the Iranian Prime Minister Mohammed Mossadegh’s historic 1951 visit to Cairo before he was overthrown in a CIA-backed coup after nationalising the oil industry is of particular interest, as is footage of Egyptian President Gamal Abdel Nasser after he nationalised the Suez Canal Company (the joint British-French enterprise that operated the commercial waterway). While relations were never quite the same between Egypt and Iran when the Shah came to power, that mid-century moment (a voiceover from an Egyptian woman speaks of her relative’s pride at living on the newly named Mossadegh Street in Cairo) serves as a memento of rare Shiah-Sunni solidarity, as war now rages between Yemen and Saudi Arabia, Iran is bombed by the US and Israel, and Iran in turn bombs US allies in the region. Sohrabi began her project six years ago, researching and filming in Tehran, Cairo, Beirut and Caracas; she had no way of knowing just how timely her documentary would be.

A scene from Sanaz Sohrabi's documentary An Incomplete Calendar (2026) © Sanaz Sohrabi

Beyond its archival value, the film—which Sohrabi says was inspired by Mona Damluji’s 2017 book Pipeline Cinema: The Cultural Infrastructure of Oil Extraction in Iran and Iraq, on the history of BP films made in the region—offers a unique cultural perspective. Sohrabi rediscovered a little-known 1980 vinyl, Rhymes and Songs for Opec, a recording by the Central University of Venezuela’s concert choir commemorating the organisation’s 20th anniversary, and makes it the film’s starting point. Through interviews with former choir members, we learn that the choirmaster taught songs from Algeria, Iraq, Oman and many other Opec countries, in Arabic dialects, Farsi and even Yoruba.

Scenes from Tehran’s Museum of Contemporary Art—designed by Kamran Diba under the patronage of Empress Farah and opened in 1977—offer haunting images of art and conditions before and after the 1979 revolution. Unearthed from the BP archive is an unforgettable clip of a Japanese artist who creates his own petroleum-based installation, featuring a fountain of oil that melds Zen and Persian features.

A scene from Sanaz Sohrabi's documentary An Incomplete Calendar (2026) © Sanaz Sohrabi

Those scenes are juxtaposed with footage from the Aula Magna auditorium at the Universidad Central de Venezuela in Caracas, a Unesco World Heritage site where Alexander Calder’s monumental commission Floating Clouds (1953) still has pride of place. Here, the film-maker appears reading Farsi poems to an empty auditorium, as an anonymous viewer stands opposite with a mirror, reflecting poetry into the suspended sculpture.

This image of cultural exchange in the midst of ongoing war and horror is juxtaposed with footage of a cut-out image of the Iranian Oil Minister Mohammed Javad Tondguyan—who was captured and held hostage in Iraq at the beginning of the war in 1980—speaking at an Opec meeting earlier that year. An Incomplete Calendar ends at the moment in 1980 when “third world” secular solidarity among Opec members was superseded by political Islam, revolution and war. Yet the scenes filmed inside the Caracas auditorium suggest the phantom possibility of another way.

#197. Production Type Unveils the Ciel Typeface

LÃ©a Bruneau's Ciel typeface for Production Type knots ornamental capitals into dense monospaced squares, to be seen before read.

Ciel opens with appearance, and the foundry's own copy says the outlines overspill the linguistic task. Look at the four wireframe capitals that spell it out: C, I, E, L traced in glowing red strokes over a dark maroon field, threaded through with pink construction lines like scaffolding left in place. The strokes never fill in, they lace and double back, so the letterforms read as embroidery and circuitry at the same instant. Every glyph is confined in the same square box, and inside that constraint the complexity proliferates. This is type that insists on being looked at first and read second, the signifier deliberately dominating the signified.

The bones come from British copperplate pointed-nib calligraphy, but the stance is restrained rather than florid: Ciel leans with a tightly controlled slant, carving one sharp toccata word after another. The family ships in five weights, ExtraLight through ExtraBold, and the register shifts dramatically across them. The text-capable faces oscillate between control and exuberance, whispering in weightless hairlines at one end and asserting themselves in saturated initials at the other. The figures carry the same treatment, numerals drawn in saturated red with their construction nodes still visible, ornament rendered as structure rather than decoration.

Ciel's ornamental layer runs thick in three styles of interwoven capitals, each interlace acting as a morpheme in itself, expressive before it is functional. The base styles sustain headlines, short paragraphs, and sober editorial settings, while the initials demand to dominate space: commanding drop caps, titles, posters, book covers, even architectural inscriptions. Art direction for the release came from Bruneau herself with Charly Derouault. The industry noticed: Ciel took Best of Show in Graphic plus Gold at the European Design Awards 2026, an Award of Excellence from Communication Arts 2026, a STA100 2026 win, and a Type Directors Club 2026 finalist spot. "With Ciel, I wanted to discover where the process of complicating initially simple letters would take me," says Bruneau. The family is available now in static OTF, TTF, WOFF, and WOFF2.

#198. Frank Lloyd Wright's only planetarium restored in Florida

Photography by Florida Southern College

Campus architects at Florida Southern College have updated the only planetarium designed by American architect Frank Lloyd Wright as part of a decades-long restoration project at the school, which was masterplanned by Wright.

The restoration included interior and exterior updates of the building, known simply as the Planetarium. The structure, which sits at one end of the Polk County Science Building, has been largely closed since 2004, when the projection system stopped working.

The renovation was guided by Jeff Baker, resident campus architect and a principal at MCWB Architects. Baker has worked on Wright projects at Florida Southern College (FSC) for twenty years and said the Planetarium has long been a goal.

“Since the outset of these overall restoration efforts, the college was always looking for an opportunity to restore the Planetarium, knowing full well its potential to excite and inspire audiences of all ages as they get a glimpse into the heavens and the great genius of Frank Lloyd Wright,” Baker told Dezeen.

Work on the exterior began in 2021. The team replaced the roof, flashings, failed stucco on upper portions of the facade and replaced over 280 hand-cast “textile” tiles that line the building’s perimeter.

The team then moved inside starting in 2023, where “decades of interventions since Wright’s death had dramatically altered the room”, according to Baker.

The team updated the Planetarium’s technology and audio, repainting the walls from a deep blue, and paring down or removing insertions such as a computer closet built in the 1980s.

It also included working with local craftsmen to restore the original Wright-designed seating made of plywood and colored vinyl upholstery, and repositioning it to its rightful orientation.

“The removal of the old computer closet retrieved the space as it was designed,” said Baker. “This removal allowed us to restore and reinstate all the seating in its original circular form, which we learned is a very rare survival in planetariums throughout the country.”

Other updates included reinstating the original paint and plaster, and restoring the floor in a “Cherokee Red” finish.

It is one of thirteen Wright buildings built between 1938 and 1958, which the university has been updating since 2007.

Previous restoration work included updating the Waterdome, Wright’s largest built fountain, the Esplanades, monolithic covered walkways that traverse the campus and the towering Annie Pfieffer Chapel.

Baker said, like working on other buildings on campus, Wright’s “elemental” architecture proved to be the most challenging aspect of the project, as there are “no ‘poche’ spaces to hide modern building systems”.

“Frank Lloyd Wright spent his life conceiving architecture as a synthesis of art and structure,” he said.

“At Florida Southern College, this is manifested in buildings that are elemental – the concrete floors are the ceilings for the rooms below, the concrete ceiling is also the roof above.”

“We believe we were able to devise methods to insert these systems in sensitive ways that meet the needs of the college yet allowed us to retrieve Wright’s vision for the space.”

The team completed the ongoing work through grants from institutions such as the J Paul Getty Foundation, which supported the preparation of the original Campus Heritage Plan in 2007.

The college has used the plan as a guide to update Wright’s buildings.

It is the only college Wright master-planned. FSC president Ludd Spivey commissioned the architect in 1938 and, deemed a National Historic Landmark in 2012, it is the largest single-site collection of Frank Lloyd Wright architecture in the world.

The Planetarium is now open to the campus and public for tours and screenings.

Dezeen recently rounded up six other Frank Lloyd Wright preservation projects across the US, including recent updates to the famed Falling Water house in Pennsylvania.

Photography by Florida Southern College

#200. Alfonso Verduzco Translates Mexican Architecture Into ALMA Acoustic Panels

“A passionate Mexican risk-taker” is how Mexican-born designer Alfonso Verduzco describes his creative point of view. Now practicing in Scottsdale, Arizona, Verduzco is still deeply influenced by his background, upbringing, and the art, culture, and traditions of his homeland.

“I want to honor the richness of Mexico, its materials, craftsmanship, architecture, and cultural history, and translate those influences into a new language of sophistication and innovation,” he says. “I never want to interpret those references literally; I want to understand their essence and reimagine them in a contemporary way.”

Looking back, Verduzco recalls growing up in Mexico surrounded by artisan communities, which he visited with his family. “I remember seeing objects being made by hand and developing an appreciation for craftsmanship long before I understood it as design.”

His training in Italy and visits to factories like Poliform, B&B Italia, and Minotti reinforced that appreciation. Masters like Antonio Citterio and Piero Lissoni also had a lasting impact. “It made me want to represent my own Mexican heritage with that same level of pride, elegance, and global relevance.”

Once introduced to high-end furniture, craftsmanship, and manufacturing, Verduzco immediately “felt connected to that world,” he says, “and knew this was the path I wanted to follow.”

But the road was not exactly linear. Verduzco earned a degree in accounting in Mexico before moving to the United States at age 18, without speaking English. He began taking various design courses before finding his way to architecture at the University of Colorado in Boulder.

“This country has given me so much, but Mexico is where my roots are, and I think starting over made me even more aware of how important those roots are to me,” he says. “Today, they are an essential part of my identity as a designer and something I want to represent with pride through my work.

Alfonso Verduzco joins us for today’s Friday Five. We spent five minutes with him discussing the inspiration behind ALMA, an acoustic wall panel collection he designed in collaboration with WVH.

Launched at NeoCon earlier this year, ALMA was inspired by the material, architectural, and cultural heritage of Mexico, translated into contemporary surfaces using natural materials, including volcanic stone, copper, obsidian, and wood veneer.

“When I started ALMA, I wanted to challenge the idea of what an acoustic panel could be,” Verduzco says. “Yes, it had to perform, but I also wanted it to create an emotional and sensory connection with the person experiencing it. I began looking at materials, places, and architectural details from Mexico that have stayed with me throughout my life and sought to reinterpret them abstractly without losing their essence.”

ALMA was conceived as a family of nine designs, each with its own story and identity, reflecting a cultural, architectural, material, or historical reference from Mexico.

The first three designs of the line—SENDERO, SAGRADO, and REFLEJO—reflect Verduzco’s own journey. “Mexico gave me the roots and the story,” he says. “My education and career in the United States, together with my training and exposure to design in Italy, gave me a different perspective through which to interpret them. Bringing those worlds together into something that can now be experienced in interiors here and internationally has been incredibly meaningful to me.”

Even at the highest level of design, the human hand, the material, and the attention to detail are what give an object its soul.

Below, Verduzco describes his distinct and vivid sources of inspiration for the ALMA collection, which won a Best of NeoCon award and a MetropolisLikes2026 recognition.

“SENDERO (meaning pathway in Spanish) was inspired by the historic streets of Mexico, where large volcanic stones have been shaped over generations by rain, footsteps, horses, and carts.

“I’ve always been fascinated by how every stone develops its own character and carries a sense of time and history. I wanted to capture that feeling in an abstract way, translating the irregular rhythm of those streets into the composition of the panel and creating a contrast between the warmth of natural wood veneer and the raw presence of solid volcanic stone.”

“SAGRADO (sacred in Spanish) was inspired by the monumental wooden doors found in historic Mexican cathedrals—particularly the decorative iron and copper nails that have aged alongside the wood for generations.

“I was drawn to the contrast between the metal, its natural patina over time, and the character of the surrounding wood. I abstracted those details using solid end-grain larch treated with the Shou Sugi Ban technique, paired with copper elements that reinterpret the original metalwork in a contemporary way.”

“REFLEJO (reflection in Spanish) celebrates Mexican obsidian, a volcanic glass valued for centuries for its natural beauty and later used in jewelry for its deep black color and reflective qualities.

“I was intrigued by the idea of taking something we normally experience at the scale of a precious object and translating that feeling into an architectural surface. By combining real Mexican obsidian with the beautiful grain of a gray maple wood veneer, the design reimagines the wall almost as a piece of jewelry, allowing light, reflection, and material contrast to become part of the experience.”

A 25-plus-year veteran of the interior design industry, Danine Alati began her career at commercial design publication Contract, where she spent 11 years before moving into luxury lifestyle media and working on titles including Hamptons and Art Basel. Based in Brooklyn with her family, she has contributed to AD PRO, DuJour, Galerie, and aspire, among other design and lifestyle publications.

#202. WHEN

In an Australian first, WHEN provides at-home egg count testing and access to the country’s leading fertility experts — prompting a conversation about how and when people can access their own fertility information. They came to us to conceive a brand that could balance credibility and compassion in equal measure. One that felt just as comfortable in a trusted doctor’s office as the shiny shelves of a global beauty store.

The conversation about fertility for people with ovaries has traditionally centred around the biological clock’s looming countdown. But with all that focus on the fear-inducing countdown, there’s not a lot of helpful talk — about how fertility works, the proactive steps we can take to improve it, or why the biological clock is an outdated trope. That’s where WHEN comes in — a fertility medtech company on a mission to ensure no one with ovaries is left wondering about them.

Traditionally, brands in the fertility space are designed to build trust in their medical expertise. But this narrow focus has resulted in a category that feels overly clinical and sometimes cold, losing sight of the real people at the heart of it all. We saw an opportunity to create something that balanced the two — trust and credibility, with warmth and humanity. A direct-to-consumer lifestyle brand built on deep medical experience that felt equally at home in a retail environment.

Fertility is, understandably, incredibly personal and seldom discussed. To get to the heart of the issue, our friends at VML conducted a series of focus groups, one-on-one interviews and stakeholder research. Because in failing to talk about it, we’re failing to give people the information they need at the right time. People are proactive about pap smears, mammograms, skin checks, sexual health tests—all considered lead indicators that look ahead to impact the future. But fertility is measured as a lag indicator, only measured once it’s more difficult to affect the outcome.

Without jumping through costly medical hoops, there is no accessible way for people to know what’s happening inside their very own bodies without a referral. The medical industry is not set up to provide this kind of information proactively, which can make people feel blocked. And when it comes to fertility, information is power.

Given WHEN is the first of its kind in Australia, care needed to be taken to communicate the importance and impact of its service. Credible medical expertise was a leading reason to believe. But we also knew people needed to hear the real stories behind the brand to build trust in something so new. Striking the balance was critical.

The result is a visual and verbal system that blends emotion with science, expression with information. Designed to showcase fertility stories, expert advice and the endless questions we ask ourselves, the brand moves seamlessly from packaging to print, retail stores to social media.

The WHEN wordmark sits at the heart of the visual identity. Clear and confident, it anchors the brand as a dependable figure in the health and medical space. Paired with an organic cell shape that reacts to the world around it, the wordmark and logoform are a perfect foil to the other. Together, they represent standing strong amid the ever-changing nature of life.

WHEN’s typeface is ABC Diatype. It’s used for everything — from wordmark to body copy. Chosen for its modernity and scientific edge, it brings calm and clarity to everything we say. Paired with a colour palette of lemon and neutrals, the identity feels light and warm against an industry so often cold and clinical.

An important first touchpoint was the at-home testing kit — the Egg Count Check. The kit is split into three sections: Prepare, Collect, and Send. We designed the packaging experience to follow the same logical structure, ensuring the steps were simple to follow and easy to use.

Inspired by the sleek aesthetic of our favourite tech brands, the kit’s box takes a rigid form with special attention paid to premium print finishes. We also created a custom instruction booklet to guide the user through the process, designed and illustrated in-house.

Our primary photography style uses intimate portraits and close crops to focus on the subject’s internal thoughts and feelings. We aim to capture moments that feel like a natural extension of everyday life, empowering and relatable in their familiarity. As a secondary style, we splice natural textures and fluid forms with our portraits, like fragments of memory telling the story of a person’s inner world.

To further enhance this sense of intimacy, a series of icons were developed to capture the different states of mind one might feel around this sensitive and personal topic. Following the same visual language as the logo, these icons add flexibility and expression to the brand, especially when used with the intimate portraiture.

The brand name itself is a question — when? But it’s also a statement of intent. We worked with copywriter Amy Scott to develop a verbal concept exploring the idea of an inner monologue, giving voice to the questions we ask ourselves but perhaps never verbalise. The brand speaks as an empathetic expert, both insightful and inclusive. By creating space for open conversation and asking the questions people ask themselves, we show no matter where they’re at in their fertility journey, they’re not alone.

WHEN doesn’t only set to change fertility testing, but to also facilitate an aspirational platform that aims to drive community and empowering conversation around fertility. The brand was crafted to grow into a multidimensional platform for fertility information access and support. We helped design the first step of this journey through WHEN Matters — a curated blog for sharing real fertility stories and credible medical expertise to ensure no one with ovaries was left feeling alone on their journey.

I love the whole concept of this brand, Kudos 👏
