#205. Frieze London Diary: A dinner dance with a twist, Barbie gets the blues and Warhol’s feline showstoppers

Mind the china: Holly Blakey and her dancers mesmerise guests at the Frieze Collectors’ Dinner

Art world glitterati descended on the Frieze London tent on Thursday evening for the lavish Collectors’ Dinner attended by gallerists, patrons and (some) journalists. Guests including the director of London’s Delfina Foundation, Aaron Cezar, and Ed Behrens, the editor of Apollo magazine, joined a throng of luminaries who dined on delectable dishes such as chicken, potato and minestra nera (leafy green brassica), along with coffee fudge and chocolate truffle. (Yum—thanks, Sessions Arts Club, for the menu.)

Tongues wagged about hot topics of the day—does anyone actually like the Tate Britain 90s art show?—while quaffing Fortnum’s wines. Attendees lapped up a top-notch performance from the UK choreographer Holly Blakey, whose troupe of brilliant dancers wound in and out of transfixed diners. One guest said he almost choked on his petits fours when Blakey’s crew built a human tower that collapsed—on purpose.

Tschabalala Self waxes lyrical about Bronzino

Always one of the hottest tickets of Frieze week, Unexpected Views at the National Gallery, in which eight leading contemporary artists deliver a ten-minute talk in front of their favourite paintings, celebrated its tenth anniversary with a stellar lineup. Tschabalala Self, whose monumental Lady in Blue currently occupies Trafalgar Square’s Fourth Plinth, chose Bronzino’s An Allegory with Venus and Cupid (around 1545). Yinka Shonibare, meanwhile, talked in front of Thomas Gainsborough’s Mr and Mrs Andrews (around 1750), which shares a gallery with his own subversive life-size sculpture that presents the aristocratic couple decapitated and with their clothes remade in Dutch wax fabric.

Feeling blue: Joy Gregory’s Explosive Barbie at 1-54 Courtesy of the artist and Whitechapel Gallery.

Barbie is shedding her girly pink image for something altogether more subversive at Frieze London this week. Helen Chadwick’s photopiece Birth of Barbie (1993), on Richard Saltoun Gallery’s stand, finds the iconic dolly upside down, coloured deep scarlet and emerging out of labial folds of red meat, an image rendered all the more disconcerting by the fact that Chadwick used this image as her Christmas card for that year. Meanwhile, over at 1-54 on the Whitechapel Editions stand, Joy Gregory’s Explosive Barbie (2025) shows our favourite blonde having a very bad hair day, her splayed locks rendered in silhouette against a cyanotype blue background. Being a Barbie Girl in a Barbie World just got a whole lot less fantastic…

Feline groovy: Grayson Perry joins Andy Warhol’s kitty pals Photo: Silke Lohmann

Cats are all the rage at Frieze Masters; we’re talking mainly about the moggies on show at Shapero Modern gallery by none other than the Pop art maestro Andy Warhol. The 16 offset lithographs from the series 25 Cats Name(d) Sam and One Blue Pussy (around 1954) are stopping fairgoers in their tracks. The lettering was done by Warhol’s mother, Julia Warhola, who apparently is also responsible for the title’s missing “d”. Grayson Perry clearly thought they were purrrfect.

John Banting was one of the most flamboyant and hedonistic figures of the 1920s and 1930s, but died in obscurity. Now, he is being spotlit this week with a solo show, Livid Cosmoramas, at John Swarbrooke Fine Art, as well as a new biography by Hugh St Claire. At the exhibition opening one veteran art journalist, no slouch in the hedonism stakes herself, revealed that she had taken the ultimate fangirl plunge of having his distinctive 1932 woodcut Siamese triplets tattooed into her leg. Devotion indeed.

Maria Kreyn at the Swiss Churchphoto: Gareth Harris

A talking point show on the Frieze art trail this week is at the Swiss Church in Covent Garden. The exhibition of works by US artist Maria Kreyn (The Dream Logic, until 19 October), organised by the Ministry of Nomads Art Foundation, is a swirl of absorbing storm paintings that draw on art historical giants such as JMW Turner. Kreyn tells us what inspired one of the head-spinning pieces. “I grew up doodling under a piano while my mom practised. It’s one of my most vivid childhood memories— that space, and the feeling and the sounds. The second concerto is a reference mainly to all of the Rachmaninoff I’ve heard her play over the years. The piano felt like the whole sky, and the whole sky now feels musical,” she says. Other works by Kreyn hang in a London landmark building—her depictions of Shakespearean scenes are dotted around Theatre Royal Drury Lane (the artist was commissioned by none other than the musicals supremo Andrew Lloyd Webber).

Jim Amaral, Flowered Ears Nº 13, 14 y 15 (1978)photo: Diego Amaral/Artist’s Archive. Courtesy of LAMB

The spotlight falls on the US-born, Bogotá-based artist Jim Amaral at Frieze Masters whose fantastical drawings on show at LAMB gallery explore the body, desire, and the subconscious. The fair presentation centres on Invisible Flowers (1979–80)—ink and watercolour drawings that “merge human reproductive anatomy with imaginary plants”, says the gallery. Amaral’s back story is explored meanwhile in a parallel show at LAMB’s gallery in Mayfair (Jim Amaral: A Study of Five Decades, until 21 November). Jim and his wife Olga met as students at Cranbrook in Michigan around 1954 when their romance apparently began “over a tango”. When she returned to Colombia and he left for naval service in the Philippines, they exchanged letters, doodles, and photographs for two years. The Love Letter drawings feature in the Mayfair show, tracing his works on paper from the 1960s to the 2010s. Oh l’amour.

Mark Chambers explains why the crisp retro pixels are not what they seem.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

"Nothing says polished retro graphics like nice crisp pixels being blasted across the screen at an accelerated pace." That's how Mark Chambers, Lead Artist at Auroch Digital, sums up the appeal of Warhammer 40,000: Boltgun 2, and it's hard to argue once you see the game in motion.

This sequel picks up directly where the original Boltgun left off. This time you can play as Ultramarine Sternguard Veteran Malum Caedo or the swifter, flame-wielding Sister of Battle Nyra Veyrath, fighting through a branching campaign that stretches from the towering heights of a hive city to the dense mangrove swamps of a jungle world. Expect new weapons, new locations and new foes, including the bloodthirsty Bloodletters and their daemonic Juggernauts.

For artists, the real draw is how it all looks. Boltgun 2 is a 'boomer shooter', but its sprites are far from hand-placed relics of the 1990s. Characters begin life as 3D models, are captured from eight camera directions, and are then converted into sprite sheets packed with normal, ambient occlusion and emission data, before being projected onto billboarded planes in the game world.

It's a clever balancing act: crisp, chunky pixels on the surface, modern rendering underneath, and the sprawling detail of the Warhammer 40,000 universe squeezed into silhouettes that read instantly at speed. I spoke to Chambers about how the team pulled it off, and where retro game art limitations end and modern polish begins.

Warhammer 40,000: Boltgun 2 is out now for PC, PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S (with a Nintendo Switch 2 version still to come).

Mark Chambers: Pixel art at its best does a lot with very little, which was certainly the case in the times of boomer shooters. Working within those confines resulted in a unique art style, and we captured that look by using crisp, uniformly spaced pixels, showing an authentic, unfiltered version of our sprites but with the added bonus of a bit of modern sharpening and polish.

MC: Considering that shader technology has developed vastly from what it once was, we had to be very careful with how we applied modern techniques. Things like reflection, liquid and transparency are used sparingly so as not to lose the retro feel.

MC: Warhammer 40k features characters with considerable amounts of detail. One of the challenges we faced when creating enemies for Boltgun 2 was converting things down into a pixel art format while still making them recognisable at lower resolutions.

Step one is sourcing good references. We're in the unique situation of working with an IP that has countless amazing examples of concept art and established designs, so we're able to pick and choose candidates from a wide selection. We look for things like recognisable shapes and strong silhouettes that would read well to players in-game.

Our animation style uses the same ideas of style over realism, and poses and gestures are often exaggerated to sell strong, recognisable silhouettes. We also purposely reduce the number of frames to include only the most important angles, which is also a nice callback to how characters were animated back in the day.

MC: We begin by building 3D models and then the process of pixelisation occurs. We use a custom rendering setup that captures assets from 8 x camera directions, and a script converts the output to a compressed 2d sprite sheet composed of several different materials (spread across a number of channels).

As a final step, our rendered character gets projected onto a billboarding plane for players to marvel and blast away at.

MC: We use a fairly similar workflow to conventional game art pipelines, and we try to emphasise parts like weaponry, armour detail and skin patterns. Anything that's too high in detail is converted into an impression of the object rather than an accurate portrayal (stuff like chainmail, hair, etc.), which would end up looking too noisy. Specific resolution settings enable us to find the right balance of pixels, and enemies often have custom settings that capture exactly the right amount of detail.

MC: We use Normal and AO maps to reflect surface detail and essentially 'fake' the look of 3d onto 2d sprites (a key component in the look of our game). Glowing emission and reflection masks are available too, and we even have something called an SDF layer that enables cool status effects and overlays where needed.

MC: We use a 'hand-painted' technique to artificially bump values like shadows and lighting (also known as Ambient Occlusion), which helps with the readability of assets in-game.

A favourite technique is applying edge highlights to really make models 'pop'. Our painting style probably shares a lot in common with how real-world Warhammer 40,000 models are painted (with the added benefit of CTRL Z)

MC: Pixel art is an impressive medium which requires a lot of effort and skill. Nothing says polished retro graphics like nice, crisp pixels being blasted across the screen at an accelerated pace, and there's an appeal to games that lean more into strong visual styles over realism. A world of '3d pixels' gives us that aesthetic, and the concept can be applied to great effect.

MC: We've worked hard to develop a pipeline that captures the idea of a 'polished retro' boomer shooter, especially for characters. There were many challenges involved in the process, from exploring how best to use pixel art in a 3D setting to balancing performance, translating high levels of Warhammer 40,000 detail, and ensuring a consistent look across all areas of the game.

MC: Modern Render engines give us the flexibility to quickly experiment with different pixel resolutions in order to find that sweet spot of consistency, while still looking retro. Back in the day, artists had to ‘bake’ pixels in by hand, ensure everything was balanced, and manually make changes if needed. There's also the massive benefit of being able to capture sprites from 3D models now.

#207. Google Go North: Editorial Design by Underline Studio

Underline Studio pairs with VICE and Google Canada on Go North, an editorial design book celebrating Canadian tech startups and founders.

Tech reports usually end up gathering dust in a desk drawer. When Google Canada wanted to document the country's startup boom across the Toronto-Waterloo corridor, Montreal, and Vancouver, they didn't print a dry corporate whitepaper. Instead, they tapped Toronto-based Underline Studio for their fifth major collaboration together, working alongside VICE on the stories. Underline shaped the book's content structure, built the grid, and art directed original photography with Daniel Ehrenworth and Paul Weeks to capture pioneers like Geoffrey Hinton, Shopify, Hootsuite, and Thalmic Labs.

The physical book makes a strong first impression. Stacked on a table, the matte black softcover carries the words "GO NORTH" down the right edge in white contour lines that twist like topographic terrain waves, while tiny spine imprints line up cleanly across the stack. Open the cover and the editorial design immediately sets up a rhythm between ink-heavy dark pages and bright white reading spreads. On the table of contents, a black left-hand page uses thin gold rules and numbers to index ten chapters â covering Artificial Intelligence, Clean Tech, Coding Camps, Digital Health, Fintech, Hardware, and Software as a Service, right across from a stark white title sheet.

The pacing never goes flat. For Google Canada engineering director Steven Woods's opening letter, "Lightning in a bottle," a moody architectural shot of the glowing Google lobby sign sits opposite two crisp columns of serif copy dropped halfway down the page. Turn a few leaves and the light shifts completely. Ehrenworth and Weeks shot the hardware and founder portraits in warm, saturated studio light, so a cool violet reflection of Interaxon's Muse brain-sensing headband plays directly off a full-bleed portrait of Bridgit founders Lauren Lake and Mallorie Brodie. It's a smart, unhurried print object that gives software and hardware builders real permanence on paper.

#208. Apple consolidates smart-home capabilities in HomeView dashboard

Technology company Apple has released a screen that consolidates the functions of its app products and its home-management software into one device.

HomeView is a seven-inch display meant to function as a centralised location for home controls, signalling a step forward in Apple‘s home integration and smart home services.

The screens come in two versions. One sits on its own, standing on a base with an integrated speaker, while the other is wall-mounted.

HomeView works similarly to other Apple touchscreen products, with a home screen, apps, widgets and a built-in front-facing camera. It has many of the same functions, including FaceTime video calling.

The product creates a physical dashboard for the Apple Home app, which was released in 2022 to control integrated functions such as smart locks, appliances, cameras and thermostats.

HomeView uses face recognition for up to six people per device in a household with personalised settings for each user, instead of the app sitting on personalised devices.

The product also includes an intercom system that can connect multiple devices within one household.

The tabletop version of the device has a distinct form, with a case and a thick base made from recycled aluminium. Its rounded base and movable screen evoke the design of the 2002 iMac G4 desktop computer.

Apple emphasised the device’s potential as decor, calling it “the perfect addition to a kitchen counter, nightstand, or side table.”

It comes in four colour options: silver, starlight, rose pink, and space grey.

The company also noted the integration of its next-generation AI, called Siri AI.

“HomeView features Siri AI, an entirely new version of Siri powered by the next generation of Apple Intelligence and advanced Apple silicon,” said Apple.

“Siri AI is a profoundly more capable and conversational assistant with personal context understanding and onscreen awareness.”

The release also included a lineup of updated home products such as cameras, locks and thermostats.

HomeView comes after a slate of recent releases from Apple, including the brand’s first foldable smartphone.

#209. 262 Fifth Avenue Pairs Sculptural Architecture With Serene Interiors

At 262 Fifth Avenue, the elevator shafts, major MEP risers, and service infrastructure sit outside the perimeter of the apartments. Architecture studio Meganom developed this exo-core arrangement for the 860-foot NoMad tower in collaboration with structural engineers at WSP and MEP engineers at GEA, leaving its 26 full-floor and duplex residences free of interior columns. Moving these systems outside the apartments creates cleaner, more open interiors.

“Architecture is part of our everyday lives, and we should treat it as such,” says Boris Kuzinez, founder of Five Points Development Group, who worked closely with the design teams throughout the project. “At its core, architecture is about protecting and shaping the environments where people live.”

For Meganom founder Yury Grigoryan, that philosophy extends to the building’s exterior. “We are trying to find human significance and expressiveness in simple forms,” he says. The facade comprises more than 220,000 sculptural anodized aluminum brick elements, whose textured surfaces capture and reflect daylight as the sun moves across the city. At the crown, a 70-foot oculus frames a 24-karat gold inverted arch, created in collaboration with Florentine gold-leaf atelier Giusto Manetti Battiloro, whose restoration work includes Florence Cathedral, Big Ben, and Rockefeller Center’s Prometheus statue.

For the interiors, Meganom turned to Copenhagen-based Norm Architects, marking the first Manhattan luxury residential project for both studios. The separated core allows for full-floor customization and unobstructed city views, with floor-to-ceiling windows reaching up to 20 feet. The building also follows Passive House principles, incorporating triple-filtered fresh air and radiant floor heating by Rehau.

Norm Architects approached the interiors through three guiding concepts: Sanctuary in the Sky, Soft Elegance, and Sculptural Balance. “From the beginning, we approached the project as a sanctuary in the sky—but ultimately also as ‘just’ a home,” says partner Peter Eland. The studio envisioned the residences as a retreat from the intensity of the streets below, while maintaining a connection to the city through carefully framed views.

Natural light plays a central role in that relationship, moving across walls, floors, and other surfaces throughout the day to create shifting patterns of light and shadow. A tone-on-tone palette emphasizes the inherent qualities of the materials, while geometric forms, sculptural details, and subtle metallic accents reference the building’s aluminum facade.

That restrained approach carries through to the material selections. Sustainably sourced oak flooring by Listone Giordano establishes a warm foundation, while Trapattoni Marmi’s sculptural Grigio Alpi stonework brings a more substantial presence to the kitchens and bathrooms, complemented by minimalist fixtures from Ceadesign. Molteni&C produced the kitchens and wardrobes, while Perugini Making finished the staircase handrails in leather. Custom doors by Lualdi incorporate acoustic insulation without interrupting the interiors’ clean lines, and glare-free lighting by Flos, integrated with Lutron controls, provides illumination without drawing attention away from the architecture.

Meganom’s structural decisions create the openness and flexibility that Norm Architects builds upon, while the interiors introduce warmth and intimacy to a building of considerable scale. Together, the two studios demonstrate how architecture and interior design can work toward the same goal: creating a sense of calm high above the city without losing its connection to the streets below.

Leo Lei is the founder and editor of Leibal, a publication dedicated to minimalist design, architecture, and interiors. Through his writing and curatorial eye, he highlights thoughtful contemporary work from around the world.

#212. Sprawling contemporary art centre Large opens on island near Paris

An exterior view of Large, created from materials including Corten steel, aluminum and glassPhoto: Nicolas Trouillard

The French capital's newest contemporary art centre opens this Saturday (17 October) on the Ile Séguin, in Greater Paris's western reaches. Dubbed simply Large (or “le Large”), it is the latest philanthropic venture from the Emerige real estate group, and takes centre-stage in the wider Pointe des Arts development. Instead of a private museum in the vein of the Cartier and Louis Vuitton foundations, Large is a non-profit, without a dedicated collection, emphatically focused on public access and on promoting the French art scene.

The Pointe des Arts complex has been designed by the Spanish architecture firm, RCR Arquitectes, in collaboration with the Paris-based CALQ design agency. The three buildings combine Corten steel—the kind that rusts on purpose—with cladding scales of copper-coloured aluminum and glass. Together they house an eight-screen cinema, retail space, office space and Large.

Located at the core of the development, Large is a wedge of a building six stories tall, comprising 2,500 sq m of exhibition space. Its director Paula Aisemberg says art will greet visitors from the moment they enter.

The inaugural exhibition riffs on the island’s automotive history as the site of car-maker Renault's primary manufacturing plant for the better part of the 20th century. Entitled Imaginary Engine and curated by Cecilia Alemani, the show will put works from Renault's own collection, the Fonds Renault pour l’Art et la Culture in conversation with 17 new commissions from contemporary artists.

Exhibition view of Imaginary Engine at Large. In the foreground: Romuald Jandolo, Estafard (2026). In the background: Julio Le Parc, Peintures en frise (1971-74)

© Adagp, Paris, 2026. Photo: Aurélien Mole

Since the turn of the century the founding president of the Emerige Group Laurent Dumas has been working to foster connections with the national art scene, through commissions, acquisitions for his private collection and the annual Révélations Emerige prize, which he founded in 2014, for young, unrepresented artists under 35.

Aisemberg emphasises that this focus on artists living and working in the country, regardless of their nationality, is what will set Large apart too: “The French art scene is particularly riveting. We want to support it, promote it and make it accessible to the wider public, be that the international art crowd that doesn't necessarily know it that well, or the local public that doesn't always have access to it.”

The île Séguin sits between the Porte de Saint-Cloud and the Pont de Sèvres, at the point where the Seine river exits central Paris to the south-west and, looping back on itself, flows towards the Bois de Boulogne and St Denis beyond. For the best part of the 20th century, from 1919 to 1992, the island was owned by Renault. From the moment that historic plant shuttered, the Hauts-de-Seine department trained its sights on transforming the island into a cultural destination. Several false starts ensued. The collector François Pinault’s plans for a museum were thwarted by red tape. The subsequent R4 art city project—which Jean Nouvel was supposed to design—was sold by its embattled backer, the Swiss art dealer Yves Bouvier, before it could be built.

Installation view of Imaginary Engine at Large. In the foreground: Bertrand Lavier, R23-F1 (2026). At the back: Jean Tinguely, Requiem pour une feuille morte (1967).

© Adagp, Paris, 2026. Photo: Aurélien Mole

Dumas, by contrast, has brought his plans to fruition. Speaking to the Fondation du Collège de France in 2018, two years into the Pointe des Arts project, he said that as a developer, the île Séguin was “a dream becoming reality” and one of his most beautiful challenges.

He has long spoken of dreaming up and building the city of tomorrow, which, in this instance, is quite literally the plan. Boulogne-Billancourt mayor Pierre-Christophe Baguet has described the island’s redevelopment the “jewel in the crown” of the Vallée de la Culture initiative the Hauts-de-Seine department launched in 2008. As Baguet noted, the Pointe des Arts complements a string of local institutions, from Jean Dubuffet’s 1988 Tour aux Figures on the Île Saint-Germain just upstream from the île Séguin to the Cité de la Céramique in Sèvres, the Manufacture Nationale, the Musée des Années 30, the Albert Kahn Museum and Gardens, and the Musée Belmondo in Boulogne-Billancourt. And it sets the scene for the forthcoming Musée du Grand Siècle in the Caserne Sully, in Saint-Cloud.

This departmental cultural strategy is part of the wider metropolitan Grand Paris plan for 2050. Combining urban renewal with significant infrastructure and transport investment, the idea is to make the suburbs of the capital more accessible and more attractive, thereby easing congestion on every level. One of the new metro stations of the forthcoming Grand Paris express network, scheduled to open in 2027, will be at Pont de Sèvres, putting the island just minutes from La Défense and half an hour from Orly airport. Other ideas about river and cable-car access are floating around in a way that chimes quite beautifully with Large's name, as well as the very Modernist ideals of speed and mechanical beauty that suffuse its first exhibition.

#214. Schemata Architects restores guesthouse nestled in ancient Irish rainforest

Japanese studio Schemata Architects has renovated a guesthouse in Dromgarriff Rainforest, Ireland, connecting two existing stone buildings with a timber- and steel-framed yoga studio.

Named Linden House, the building is one of five guesthouses spread across the 39-hectare woodland in Glengarriff, which is one of Ireland’s last temperate rainforests and a protected ecological area.

After the site was purchased in 2022, its owners began to conserve and rewild the forest, funded partly by the transformation of its existing guesthouses into a wellness retreat.

Schemata Architects was tasked with redesigning one of these guesthouses, connecting two stone-and-slate buildings overlooking Bantry Bay with a new yoga space shared by its 10 bedrooms.

“The existing buildings consisted of two structures connected by a passageway,” Schemata Architects founder Jo Nagasaka told Dezeen.

“We envisioned extending this passage toward the south and transforming it into a yoga facility for the retreat centre,” he added.

The social spaces of Linden House occupy the ground floor of the longer western volume, which steps down into a large living area overlooking the bay through a fully-glazed gable end.

Three of the guesthouse’s ensuite bedrooms occupy the northern end of this longer volume, with a further three tucked beneath timber-framed gable ceilings on its first floor.

The remaining four bedrooms occupy the smaller eastern wing, the largest of which has a double-height seating area with a matching glazed gable end facing the bay.

Connecting the two wings is the yoga studio. It is framed by the exposed stone walls of the buildings on either side and sheltered by a timber- and steel-framed sawtooth roof that incorporates skylights.

“The two buildings are set at an angle to one another, and by connecting them while embracing this twisted relationship we were able to create a distinctive spatial experience and form,” Nagasaka explained.

“The most distinctive element is the hybrid sawtooth roof, which integrates daylighting and power generation,” he added.

“The north-facing surfaces bring in indirect daylight, while solar panels are installed on the south-facing surfaces to generate electricity from direct sunlight.”

A desire for the new finishes to echo the guesthouse’s original materials led to the studio’s use of timber in the studio, the pale oak finishes in the bedrooms and living spaces, and minimalist white tiles in the bathrooms.

“For the new timber elements, we chose oak, the same species of tree that is native to the surrounding forest, wherever possible,” Nagasaka said.

“In doing so, we sought to create a connection between the architecture and the natural resources and character of the site.”

Linden House marks the beginning of Schemata Architects’ involvement with the site, with long-term plans including the possible reconstruction of a hotel that once stood on the site.

Other projects recently completed by Schemata Architects include a store for perfume company Le Labo in Tokyo with board-marked concrete walls and an office in Fujisawa City fronted by a series of oversized corrugated metal shutters.

#216. Getting More From Less: Rethinking Structure Through Form

What happens when structure is treated not as something added to architecture, but as something the architecture itself provides?

What happens when structure is treated not as something added to architecture, but as something the architecture itself provides?

Throughout architectural history, form has provided structure. Arches, trusses, and other structural geometries used the arrangement of material to achieve strength, often allowing individual elements to serve multiple functions. Today, however, building envelopes often rely on a hierarchy of separate elements: a primary frame carries loads, secondary supports hold panels in place, brackets connect the pieces, and additional layers provide enclosure or finish. Together, these components require added material, weight, fabrication steps, and on-site coordination.

Some of the most significant advances in architecture emerge from eliminating unnecessary or redundant components. Reducing secondary structures, simplifying connections, and assigning multiple functions to individual elements can result in more efficient building systems. BŌK Modern approaches these complexities by revisiting that older principle through modern engineering and fabrication: simplifying a system by asking one component to do the work of several. By folding and forming metal to create strength through geometry, their idea remains on looking for opportunities to reduce supporting structure while getting more performance from the material itself.

Moscone Convention Center: Reducing the Supporting Structure

At the Moscone Convention Center, BŌK Modern reconsidered the secondary structure typically required to support large facade systems. A conventional solution would have relied on cantilever field welded steel HSS supports and Z-girts behind the architectural panels. Instead, the practice developed an integrated assembly in which formed aluminum panels took on 68% more structural loading capability than the conventional approach, reducing the required structural steel support behind it by 83%.

The shift toward an integrated assembly affected the project well beyond material quantities. Sections of the facade could be assembled at ground level and lifted into position, reducing work at height and changing the installation sequence. Compared to the conventional cantilever support and Z-girt system, this integrated approach required half the labor. The efficiencies were interconnected: eliminating structural components also reduced the work needed to fabricate, connect, and install them. At Moscone, simplification became not only an aesthetic decision, but a strategy for reducing cost, labor, material, and construction complexity.

1500 Mission: Making the Material Do More

The 1500 Mission Canopy applied the same principle in a different way. Rather than relying on a conventional system of steel trusses, aluminum cladding, and welded connections back to the façade, BŌK Modern employed modular triangular trusses made from formed aluminum sheets. The solution applied one of the simplest structural principles—the truss—through contemporary materials and fabrication technologies. Brake-forming aluminum sheets into triangular panels allowed the geometry of the formed aluminum to give relatively lightweight material the rigidity necessary to support itself and other canopy components.

Bolt-On Balcony: Consolidating the Assembly

BŌK Modern's Bolt-On Balcony applies this simplification strategy to an assembly made up of numerous individual parts. A conventional balcony might require a perimeter frame, joists, wall supports, tie rods, anchor forks, railing posts, front-cladding supports, and a separate finished floor. Instead of accepting each component as necessary, the design examined which of those functions could be combined.

The resulting formed-sheet design incorporates several roles into a single assembly, including the structural floor, finished surface, and patented Plate Truss™ technology. This system creates an integrated truss supported by two vertical attachment points at the facade. Those points connect to existing structural elements, removing the need for steel cantilevers, extensive welding, and the rod-and-fork suspension systems of the conventional approach.

Bolted construction eliminates the need for field welding, avoiding the risk of damaging nearby finishes during the final stages of construction. Its comparatively lightweight design can often be lifted into place with equipment such as a forklift rather than a crane, further simplifying logistics. Less structure is valuable not simply because there is less of it, but because eliminating unnecessary components can reduce material, connections, fabrication, welding, labor, and coordination while creating a cleaner architectural result. #217. Amazon Rethinks the Kindle From the Inside Out

For a device designed to disappear into the reading experience, even the smallest physical details matter. How it feels in your hand, how light hits the screen, and how you turn a page can all influence whether you’re absorbed in a book or distracted by the technology holding it. With its newly redesigned Kindle lineup, Amazon is reconsidering those details from the inside out. The refresh encompasses the Kindle, Kindle Paperwhite, and Kindle Colorsoft, introducing thinner profiles, new materials, a more cohesive design language, and an expanded collection of accessories.

“As we approach Kindle’s 20th year, we’ve been thinking about how we continue to make a product people already love meaningfully better,” says Chris Green, VP of design at Amazon. “Using learnings from our most recent Kindle Scribe refresh, we redesigned this new lineup from the ground up, introducing a consistent design language with flush-front displays and edge-to-edge color plus new colors and aluminum housing.”

Central to that redesign is a new reverse-stack display construction, which Amazon describes as a first for the e-reader category. By rethinking how the display, front light, and touch layers are assembled, the team was able to create a completely flush reading surface, eliminating the raised borders found on earlier devices. The result is a cleaner, more continuous surface that also contributes to thinner, lighter hardware. But reducing weight was only part of the challenge.

“When you’re holding something in your hand and reading for hours, it’s not just how much it weighs; it’s how that weight sits in your hand,” Green explains. “The closer the device can get to your hand’s natural density, the more it stops feeling like a thing you’re holding and starts feeling like a natural extension of you.”

This new design language extends across the family, but each model addresses a slightly different reading experience. The six-inch Kindle remains the most portable, now with the option of a matte aluminum housing made from 80% recycled aluminum. The Kindle Paperwhite introduces a thinner, lighter body, while retaining its adjustable warm light.

For the Kindle Colorsoft, the emphasis shifts toward bringing color to the reading experience without sacrificing the qualities that distinguish an e-reader from a tablet. Its redesigned display incorporates nitride LEDs to enhance brightness and color, an oxide backplane to improve contrast, and an ultra-thin optical coating for greater clarity. The goal is to make illustrated books, comics, and other visual content feel more natural on a paper-like screen.

While the technical changes are largely invisible, the new color palette certainly isn’t. “Customers are telling and showing us that they want their Kindle to express who they are through color,” Green says. “Two years ago, we introduced a matcha-colored Kindle, and it was a success we couldn’t ignore.”

Across the lineup, Amazon has introduced Ube, Seaglass Green, Alpine Sky, Fig, and Graphite—a palette Green says was drawn from café and dessert culture.

The redesign also introduces a new collection of accessories, including the Kindle Click, a compact Bluetooth remote that lets readers turn pages. A magnetic Page-Turn Cover incorporates physical buttons directly into the case, while a charging dock allows compatible devices to remain upright while charging. Additionally, new covers in knit fabric, plant-based leather, and pebbled leather complement the new devices.

Nearly two decades after the original Kindle debuted, Amazon’s latest redesign illustrates how much room remains for refinement in an established product. The most significant changes aren’t necessarily the ones that immediately catch the eye, but those that make the technology feel less like something you’re holding and more like an extension of the reading experience.

The new Kindle is available now at amazon.com, starting at $149.99. The Kindle Paperwhite and Kindle Colorsoft will be available October 28, starting at $199.99 and $289.99, respectively.

The controversy shows brands need to be prepared to give up some control.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

If you've not met Buck the sheep yet, where have you been? Kiwibank's comely green-woolled ewe mascot has made New Zealand's state-owned bank a global household name, and not in a way it intended.

The original campaign centred on a video in which the AI-animated sheep was shown drinking a flat white and going for a sheer, urging viewers not to follow the flock but to choose a bank that was "born to buck the system". There was barely a bleat about it outside of New Zealand – until one user declared in an all-caps post on X that they wished to have carnal intercourse with the alluring ovine.

In two shakes of a lamb's tail, Buck was elevated to digital bombshell status, and non-official lewd AI-generated images of her began circulating on furry forums. A lot of old memes about New Zealanders resurfaced too. The fervor might have blown over in a few days, but Kiwibank went on a legal blitz issuing takedown requests, which reminded everyone that, far from bucking the system, it is the system.

Should it have accepted that in 2026, brands can sometimes benefit from surrendering a little control?

Buck's a great example of a brand mascot escaping its creator's control and being reinterpreted by the internet. The attempt to regain control generated a classic Streisand effect.

As reported by the Spinoff, the bank filed a series of copyright claims against the unauthorised use of Buck’s image (US courts have previously ruled that AI art can't be copyrighted, but Kiwibank says Buck was created by artists, with AI only used to animate the character). Its clampdown led to accusations of censorship, amplifying the story and shifting the discussion from the campaign to questions around free speech.

Mascots are big in branding in 2026. Even AI companies have realised they can help humanise their brands. Meta has Jolly, OpenAI has its Dots. But the public increasingly treats brand characters as open-source cultural assets available for remixing rather than intellectual property. The US White House has set the example, regularly turning a blind eye to copyright law to post AI-generated videos of Super Mario.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

Once a mascot becomes popular, audiences feel a sense of ownership. If the narrative takes an unexpected direction, brands tend to assume they need to correct or remove the narrative. But some have shown that accepting, or joining, the new story is also an option.

The Grimace Shake trend took McDonald's by surprise back in 2023. Social media creators began posting horror-style videos in which Grimace appeared terrifying and the milkshake caused an agonising death. Rather than trying to suppress it, McDonald's occasionally acknowledged it with playful responses. It benefited from massive visibility, younger audiences felt they were driving the conversation, and the brand remained part of the joke rather than the target.

I have received so many questions about the Grimace Trend and how McDonald's handled it. I shared on LinkedIn but here is an insider view from the social media team of what happened : - if you think we planted the grimace shake trend, thank you. So much. But you think way too highly of us. This was a level of genius creativity and organic fun that I could never dream about or plan for - it was all from the fans, and the fans only, and the initial spark came from Austin Frazier. Our "only responsibility" in helping the trend happen was giving the "tools" to play with, reintroducing Grimace, the shake and going all in in letting the character take over our accounts. With a particular tone of voice, attitude, "way of typinggg" and taking badly cropped and blurry selfies. - if you think we would never acknowledge the trend, well, I thought so too at first, so I won't blame you. Honestly, I think my very first text to the team and agencies was "not sure we should jump in". It took us a bit of time to process what was happening. The campaign was already wildly successful, both on a social and business standpoint, so why would we take the "risk" to jump in? But hours of watching, reading the comments, trying to learn and genuinely understand helped us see what this was about : brilliant creativity, unfiltered fun, peak absurdist gen z humor, just the way a new generation of creators and consumers play with brands. I've seen videos which levels of production and craft made me smile silently in admiration and wonder. I've seen fan arts that made us send dozen of emails and texts to friends and colleagues saying "omg did you see that"? We then discussed what was the right thing to do about the trend : saying nothing felt disconnected, encouraging it felt self-serving, so we just decided to show our fans that we see them and their creativity in a sweet, candid and genuine way, as grimace would. The same way you would respectfully and gently nod at someone, without repeating what they said to show you agree with them and stealing their thunder. I must also say thank you to our leadership, PR and legal teams for being open, seeking to understand and trust the teams. Was there a lot of questions, sentiment analysis tools, listening dashboards and emails? More than I can count. Was there doubt? Immense doubt. Did we still move forward and get full support up to our top leadership? Sure did. A one of a kind campaign : - Billions in reach, millions in engagements, millions of mentions - Top trend at least 8 different days on twitter - Top 3 hashtags on tiktok and trend on snapchat for multiple days - and more importantly, so many internal teams, agencies and fans genuinely loving grimace and having fun Thank you, Grimace. We miss youuu.July 12, 2023

Duolingo understood the power of this earlier than most. When users turned its mascot Duo into an obsessive, threatening owl, the company embraced the characterisation, and the joke became one of the most successful social media mascot strategies of the past decade. Duo evolved from a language-learning mascot into an internet meme machine and the start of a story worthy of a soap opera, complete with faked death.

Other examples include Reddit's Snoo, who's seen as belonging as much to the community as the company, and GitHub's Octocat, which has become an creation platform in its own right, spawning hundreds of unofficial variants that have largely been encouraged.

Brands need to distinguish between genuinely harmful content on the one hand and fan art and undesired but harmless remixing on the other. Aabuse, harassment, hate speech or scams have to be addressed. Japan has been taking diplomatic steps to try to get the White House to stop using Nintendo characters out of a real fear that the US government's copyright theft could harm the company's reputation and business because people could think it's an approved collaboration.

But trying to eliminate jokes, memes, or parodies from ordinary people is often unwinnable. The internet often interprets suppression as evidence that a joke is worth repeating, and a legal response can transform a niche joke into a national news story.

In contrast, a humorous response can often diffuse a situation. Back in 2016, Kellogg's Frosties made a perfectly elegant response to furries who had been creating Tony the Tiger porn: "let’s keep things gr-r-reat – & family-friendly if you could. Cubs could be watching", it wrote on X.

I’m all for showing your stripes, feathers, etc. But let’s keep things gr-r-reat – & family-friendly if you could. Cubs could be watching 🙂January 28, 2016

Today, the ubiquity of AI-generated imagery makes it even harder to keep control. If the brand itself used AI like Kiwibank did, audiences might be more likely to consider a mascot as fair game. The smartest strategy might be to accept that the attention has value, leave room for audience creativity and to try to remain part of the conversation after control has inevitably been lost.

#219. Fieldwork Facility Unveils V&A East Storehouse Wayfinding

V&A East Storehouse wayfinding by Fieldwork Facility treats the museum like software: a low-carbon, programmable system built for updates.

The system's face is Spiller Mono, a bespoke monospace cut of the V&A's brand typeface commissioned from Commercial Type. Monospace carries the memory of early computers and code editors, and Fieldwork Facility turns that memory into the building's native language: letterforms set on modular tiles that shuffle like a departure board. One wall spells out the welcome manifesto in mixed media, physical letter tiles, dot-matrix rails and marker-pen highlighter bars in yellow, pink and green. Another asks visitors "WHAT WOULD YOU DO WITH THE V&A COLLECTION" in flip-board capitals. Nothing about it feels like standard museum graphics; it reads like a machine you can read. The studio calls the effect programmable in an analogue way, and the project picked up a Dezeen Awards 2026 regional showcase spot.

The monospace setting is doing real systems work. Fixed character widths tile every message to a strict grid, so labels, directory totems and interpretation panels snap together from interchangeable parts instead of being printed one-off. The directory totems stack level numbers, destination names and pictograms in a dense code-editor rhythm, while oversized painted numerals give each floor a glyph-sized landmark. The type behaves like components in an interface: fixed, swappable, endlessly re-typeset. It is a visual language the studio calls atypical for a museum, and that is exactly the point.

The material story is just as considered. The signage is built as a bricolage of low-carbon and recycled materials, assembled in a modular language that sits comfortably against the building's industrial architecture. Every unit is designed for disassembly, so components separate cleanly for reuse or material recovery when a display moves on. The whole scheme was briefed to be updatable and reusable from the start, closing material loops instead of designing for the skip. Production partner Standard8 fabricated the system, with interpretation hardware by IDK and Solved Workshop, large print guides by Calverts Co-op and type design by Commercial Type.

Wayfinding and interpretation by Fieldwork Facility, with creative direction and strategy by Robin Howie and design by Tilia Bertrand-Shelton, Imogen Ayres and Lan LÃª. See more from Fieldwork Facility.

#220. In pictures: boundary-pushing works in Frieze London’s Focus section

Jayeeta Chatterjee, The Infinite Weft (2026) David Owens

As is so often the case, the Focus section, for solo stands by galleries that are less than 12 years old, is the most vibrant and dynamic section at this year’s Frieze London. Where risk seems somewhat absent elsewhere, Focus retains the capacity for surprise and discovery, and the six stands that have been selected here reflect the section’s material and intellectual breadth.

Through large textile pieces and a group of woodcut prints, Chatterjee, who is based in Bengaluru but grew up in West Bengal, explores women’s labour both in the materials she uses and in her imagery. Chatterjee combines the printmaking in which she trained with a traditional but now disappearing quilting technique called nakshi kantha. She prints her figurative designs depicting women at work (including on textile production) onto used saris owned by the people she depicts. Chatterjee’s work also documents the women’s lives through photography and audio, and in the midst of The Infinite Weft (2026) what initially appear to be decorative patterns suddenly come into focus as waveforms: evocations of Chatterjee’s conversations with her subjects.

Isaiah Davis, Undertow (2026) David Owens

Davis shows three pieces, all of which address the Black body, and how its vulnerabilities are mediated by our social and political environment. He deliberately plays with the loaded materiality and the expressive potential of his medium: welded steel. The centrepiece of the stand is Undertow (2026), a sculpture with triangulated I-beams on wheels, which bear words—“Token gets spent”—and names: Don, Jeff and Sean (Trump, Epstein and Coombs, or P-Diddy). From the wheeled object emerges a chain which is fixed to the wall, its form resembling (for me, at least) a rib-cage. As well as evoking slavery the sculptures also take on broader meanings, resembling fetish objects and reliquaries: in Vesselhood (2026), a penis appears through a rectangular aperture, while Gayer Secrets (2026) is part chastity belt, part sacred heart.

Amanda Moström, Bikini Bottom David Owens

Amanda Moström sources her objects through markets and then repurposes them, via the application of goat hide, for presentation in a more rarefied market: the art fair. Her installation, which will change each day, includes an array of objects transformed by the animal skins from ordinariness—an umbrella, a tissue box, an office chair—into sensuality. In a found photo album a woman poses, often undressed, whether for personal gratification or more complicated motivations. But care is another subject of Moström’s work, and she transforms these humdrum things to a new potency or significance, whose value she tests by placing them in the fair. Her glitter ball, its mirrored tesserae occasionally interrupted by goat-hide swatches, projects a constellation onto the stand’s wall.

Yuli Serfaty, Who’s a Good Girl? (2026) David Owens

Among the creepiest of the stands at this year’s fair, Yuli Serfaty’s installation is called Who’s a Good Girl?. Two sculptures represent a headless hybrid being with multiple breasts—part dog, part human, part digital being. A CGI video at the centre shows a training environment in which the being at first barely functions, before developing agency that allows her to escape the drones that surveil her through tricking the system with glitches. Serfaty’s references are broad and fascinating—everything from feminist technoscience to the sculpture of Louise Bourgeois and the Capitoline Wolf in Rome—and her work here is laden with metaphors for our age, including the climate catastrophe and AI autonomy.

Ella Fleck, training material (2026) David Owens

“I’ve never seen such a nice cock before… Nice to meet you, Antonio.” From a speaker that rumbles the floor of Ella Fleck’s installation comes this and similar utterances from OnlyFans, the online subscription service that is a magnet for pornographers. Fleck embedded herself as a “chatter” for a company that manages OnlyFans creators’ communications, including the “chatter scripts” voiced through the floor. Screens feature data that document more chats, as well as the construction of fake chatter identities for the smutty interactions, and the enterprise’s ultimate goal: cash. The floor, meanwhile, is partly recycled from data-centre architecture. The result is an almost journalistic sculptural enquiry into the alienated, hallucinated interaction that passes as intimacy for swaths of contemporary society.

Tom Hardwick-Allan, Engine of Sickness and Light (2026) David Owens

Tom Hardwick-Allan’s multi-part work is intricate in form and meaning. On the wall appears to be a thin cross-section of an ancient tree, actually formed from nine interlocking sections of plywood, whose principal image is a baby in a womb. Up close, though, it teems with imagery that relates to Hardwick-Allan’s cornucopian enquiry: his interest in imprinting (the formation of perception and social understanding) in humans and animals, numerology, alchemy and augury. He thinks of his activities as expanded printmaking, and as if to embody this, he also shows a “staircase”—more like an edifice—of printed matter: his own book collection, wrapped in cloudily translucent glassine paper and manipulated with blobs and stains of oil and iron paste.

#221. Ashton

Ashton was the first restaurant chain in Canada to specialize in poutine – it’s been serving the iconic dish since 1969. However, as the decades passed, both Ashton’s image and its restaurants remained frozen in time. In 2022, Émily Adam and Jean-Christophe Lirette took over the reins from Ashton Leblond, with a vision of expanding the 23 locations of this beloved Quebec brand.

The new owners faced some major challenges: stagnant sales figures, outdated restaurants, an aging clientele and the need to recruit younger workers. It quickly became clear that Ashton’s brand image and experience needed to be revitalized.

LG2 reimagined Ashton’s entire brand experience at one of its flagship restaurants. Numerous elements were redesigned to simplify the brand as a whole and turn it into an exportable entity.

The experience was updated with a perfect blend of modernity and traditions rooted in Ashton’s history. In tribute to snack bar culture, all the classic codes of diners were integrated with a modern twist. A customized typographic signature emphasizing the generous, indulgent nature of Ashton dishes was created, and the chain’s signature red colour was updated. A touch of nostalgia can be felt in the new brand merchandise, which features illustrations reminiscent of one of Ashton’s earliest logos.

The colours are rich, curved edges are prominent and the triple red line – inspired by the chain’s iconic neon lighting – runs through every touchpoint in the graphic system, from the new packaging to the stripes on socks.

To create an atmosphere as comforting as its food, the design concept was completely overhauled. This transformation can be seen from the outer shell to the interior details: the pervasive curves, neon lighting and red tin roof are all reminiscent of Ashton’s original 1969 food truck.

A monochrome red border runs through the dining room where the famous banquettes are still featured prominently in the centre. This easily reproducible layout will be extended to the chain’s other restaurants over the next few years.

The numbers speak for themselves. Within 30 days of launch:

35% increase in traffic at the first renovated location 34% increase in sales at the first renovated location 40% increase in visits to the Ashton website

Ashton found the perfect recipe for securing the loyalty of diehard fans while attracting new foodies on the hunt for a retro yet contemporary experience.

LG2 elsewhere on ID: Aliments Faita et Forgione.

Very good evolution of the brand. Took the core and simplified it. Less is more. In this case more attractive to customers. But what does Adidas say about the 3 stripes? ;)

I’m concerned about the recent decline in quality from LG2. Their design solutions have been growing increasingly weak and generic, with a focus on blending in rather than standing out. This troubling trend undermines the core elements that build a strong, distinctive brand image. It almost seems like the wordmark was hastily created and delivered to the client on the same day.

#223. "Radically simple" Resonance pavilion takes centre stage at Tallinn Architecture Biennale

Limestone and plywood make up the temporary pavilion at the heart of this year’s Tallinn Architecture Biennale, designed by Shanghai- and Tokyo-based studio Aru Ma- Architects.

Named Resonance, the pavilion was the winning entry of a competition hosted by the 2026 Tallinn Architecture Biennale (TAB) for its central pavilion, which sits outside the Estonian Museum of Architecture.

Resonance was designed from a palette of what Aru Ma- Architects called “ordinary materials” and is intended as a comment on how luxury can be achieved with limited resources.

It responds to this year’s curatorial theme at the TAB, How Much?, which invites discourse about the role of money in architecture.

This is also the focus of the festival’s main exhibition, developed by this year’s curator, Estonian architecture practice Stuudio Täna.

“The pavilion uses standard construction materials in unexpected ways, elevating them into something new and unique,” said Stuudio Täna architect Kertu Johanna Jõeste.

“A spatially intriguing visual is accomplished with radically simple techniques and materials, aligning the pavilion very well with the topics of TAB 2026.”

The pavilion takes the form of a square inward-facing courtyard, intended to offer respite from its busy surroundings on a traffic island.

It is built from a palette of rebar, rope, limestone and plywood, offering a deliberately pared-back, timeless aesthetic, while ensuring the structure can be easily demounted at the end of the festival.

According to Aru Ma- Architects, its structure is “a carefully balanced tensile structure”, with a limestone core as a ballast.

“The project transforms strict economic and material constraints into an immersive architectural environment shaped by light, wind, sound, and gravity,” the studio said.

TAB is an international architecture and urban planning festival, which has taken place in the Estonian capital every two years since 2011. This year’s edition takes place from 9 September to 30 November 2026.

Previous central pavilions at the event include the Fungible Non-Fungible Pavilion, which had a puzzle-like structure partly designed by the public, and a bus shelter built from reclaimed materials.

The 2026 edition of Tallinn Architecture Biennale runs from 9 September to 30 November. For more events, talks and installations in architecture and design, visit the Dezeen Events Guide.

#224. Falconry Takes Flight Inside Dubai’s N53 Cigar Lounge

Cigar lounges have traditionally favored the atmosphere of a private club, with dark woods, leather furnishings, and an emphasis on exclusivity. For N53, located more than 300 feet above Dubai, Bergman Design House took a different approach, creating an interior that draws on regional heritage while responding to its distinctly contemporary architectural setting.

Photography by Vigo Jansons; courtesy of One&Only One Za’abeel and Bergman Design House

Set within The Link, which connects the two towers at One Za’abeel, this new cigar lounge needed to highlight its unique architectural setting.

“Within this modern architectural envelope (One Za’abeel development), N53 introduces a layered interior language, one that blends contemporary luxury with heritage craftsmanship, creating a timeless counterpoint to the building’s striking modernity,” says Marie Soliman, co-founder of Bergman Design House.

Photography by Vigo Jansons; courtesy of One&Only One Za’abeel and Bergman Design House

Conceived as an open-plan lounge, N53 is carefully zoned to encourage both privacy and social interaction. Seating clusters are arranged around a cigar display, retail area, and custom bar, while a private VIP area features a locked humidor. The lounge also offers a collection of 90 premium cigars and a selection of rare spirits, including Hakushu 18-Year-Old Japanese single malt whisky.

Photography by Vigo Jansons; courtesy of One&Only One Za’abeel and Bergman Design House

Falconry, a longstanding tradition in the region, became a central reference for the interior’s design narrative. Recognized as a symbol of power and precision throughout the Middle East, the ancient sport is interpreted here through a contemporary lens. Bespoke marquetry artwork pays tribute to the practice, introducing a cultural reference that complements the contemporary space.

Photography by Vigo Jansons; courtesy of One&Only One Za’abeel and Bergman Design House

Warm shades of tobacco leaf, caramel, and cognac are complemented by deep charcoals on the ceiling and underfoot. Hints of slate blue and amber round out the color palette. Rich woods, Cipollino marble, leather, and brushed metals introduce contrasting textures, while accessories include Elie Bleu cigar pieces and cigar cutters made from Damascus steel.

Photography by Vigo Jansons; courtesy of One&Only One Za’abeel and Bergman Design House

Lighting plays an equally important role in shaping the atmosphere. A metal mesh installation forms a cloud-like piece that seems to float overhead, while Murano glass floor lights add an artisanal touch. Together with the rich materials, intimate seating arrangements, and acoustic softness, these elements create an environment designed to encourage guests to linger.

Photography by Vigo Jansons; courtesy of One&Only One Za’abeel and Bergman Design House

Rather than compete with the striking architecture of The Link, N53 introduces a more intimate scale, using materials, craftsmanship, and regional references to create a counterpoint to the city beyond its windows.

#225. Bastét: Inside Wedge's New Oral Care Branding

Wedge puts toothpaste on the beauty counter with this oral care branding for BastÃ©t: a carved-serif wordmark, one green badge, zero clichÃ©s.

The first thing you notice is what is missing. No red, white and blue. No open smile. Instead: an unlined aluminium tube, cool and industrial, printed in off-black; a palette of silver, black and off-white; and exactly one accent, a small green hexagonal badge stamped with nHA. Wedge, the MontrÃ©al and Los Angeles studio, built the whole brand world for BastÃ©t, from naming and strategy to visual identity, packaging and guidelines. The brief from the founders was simple: make a premium, high-performance oral care company that earns its place on the beauty counter. The answer treats brushing as a ritual of renewal, where rigor meets pleasure.

The wordmark is drawn, not typeset. Wedge took its forms from the stone-carved lettering on the facade of the Grande Galerie de l'Ãvolution at the Paris Natural History Museum, completed in 1889: unusual terminals, narrow joins, sharp apertures, a monumentality meant to signal trust and rigor. The brand's primary typeface extends the idea. Daubenton, by Olivier Dolbeau of the Velvetyne foundry, is a high-contrast serif in the Didot lineage, all strong vertical stress and crisp, unbracketed serifs. For everything small, the system drops to Nimbus Sans in Regular and Condensed, neutral enough to set a bilingual ingredients list at tiny sizes. French and English share every panel: a fully branded face, a side panel per language for story, instructions and ingredients, and a bilingual front of pack. Saying everything twice forces the edit down to what is actually worth saying.

Materially, the system splits in two. The box is built for the retail shelf; the tube is built for the beauty counter. That tube is unlined aluminium, and it shows: the metal catches the light and dents softly, closer to an artist's paint tube than anything in the dental aisle. The green badge carries the ingredient story alone. nHA, nano hydroxyapatite, is the hero, a mineral found naturally in human teeth that supports enamel protection, so the hierarchy stays blunt: the name, then the proof. Wedge kept a few category conventions on purpose. The No List stays, and so do the brushing instructions, because with nHA the method is part of the performance: spit, don't rinse. The art direction stages the feeling of clean instead of the literal smile: still lifes in the spirit of Irving Penn's Clinique years, a tube balanced on a suede shoe, a silk-gloved hand heavy with jewels, the day's bag spilled across pink silk. Morning and evening, four minutes at a time.

#227. I pushed Nvidia’s RTX Spark to its limits in our favourite creative laptop

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

This is a review of the ASUS ProArt P14 rather than of the RTX Spark platform as a whole, but despite that the new PC chips seem to show a lot of promise. The P14 throws up some excellent scores in testing, is well built and beautifully thin and light, and will last all day on a charge. It suffers from the problem all first-gen hardware has, app compatibility, and also from the high prices plaguing all laptops; but there is definite promise here, and at least one of those problems can be fixed with a few software patches.

Why you can trust Creative Bloq Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

Laptops with new processors in them are always exciting, as we find out how well they can perform in creative apps. Nvidia’s RTX Spark combines a Grace CPU - in this case 20 Arm cores, though an 18-core version is also available - with a big GPU from the Blackwell generation (aka the GeForce 5000-series). Given how well the Arm-based Snapdragon CPUs have performed in the past, and how we’ve lamented that they’re not being paired with the kind of GPUs that could make creative apps sing, this would appear to be the answer to our prayers.

However, Nvidia isn’t aiming its new system directly at creatives, nor at gamers, but squarely at AI development, particularly the running of agents. Happily, this has the side effect of making RTX Spark machines useful for creative purposes, especially as AI tools are creeping into our apps (see our initial Blender testing), and there are other things to like about them too, including excellent battery life and bright OLED screens.

RTX Spark laptops run Windows 11, so software compatibility shouldn’t be too much of a problem. Let’s see how this one stacks up and if it's heading to the best laptops for game development list.

Nvidia Blackwell RTX GPU (6,144 CUDA cores)

1x USB 3.2 Gen 2 Type-A, 3x USB4, 1x HDMI 2.1, 1x 3.5mm audio

• Lightweight metal shell• Bright, punchy screen

As the smaller of the two ProArt laptops available at the launch of the RTX Spark chips, (the other being the P16) the ProArt P14 is a compact and lightweight machine, the sort of thing dished out to remote workers the world over. It’s got a very nicely engineered shell, with speakers either side of the keyboard and ProArt branding rather than ASUS logos everywhere.

Place it next to a MacBook Pro 14, and it becomes clear who this new laptop is aimed at. ASUS is targeting a professional demographic here, with a metal finish that feels great under your fingers and a low-profile, lightweight build. It has a lighter, magnesium-esque look about it rather than Apple’s Space Grey, and the keyboard feels like it has slightly more depth than the Mac’s, for a satisfying feeling while typing.

The OLED touchscreen is magnificently bright, as we’ve come to expect from ASUS devices, and the colours are punchy. Having a 120hz maximum refresh rate means everything feels very smooth, and the colour response displaying 97% of the DCI-P3 colour gamut using the display’s built-in profile, along with 100% of sRGB and 94% of Adobe RGB. It puts out a maximum SDR brightness of 640 nits, which is excellent, and over all it’s a good choice for colour grading or print design, as long as 14 inches corner to corner is big enough for you.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

With a trio of USB4 ports and a full-size HDMI, the ProArt P14 is made to connect to all kinds of peripherals and monitors. You’ll be able to dump camera footage onto its SSD through the SD card slot or via a cable connection, though a 1TB SSD is the only build to order option here apart from boosting the RAM from 24GB to 32GB. The RTX Spark platform uses a unified memory architecture, where one RAM pool is shared between the CPU and GPU, rather than having two allocations as is the norm with Nvidia GPUs paired with AMD or Intel CPUs. This means you’ll need to calculate your RAM needs when you buy, and it supports up to 128GB of the currently very expensive stuff. More is, of course, always better.

The fan in the ProArt P14 came on when it was updating software and not being pushed remotely hard (we’d locked it into Performance mode to get the best results from testing, which might have something to do with it), and it’s possible software support could be as big an issue for the new platform as cooling is. The Windows on Arm ecosystem is larger now than when the first Snapdragon chips launched, but not perfect, and Microsoft’s Prism translation layer, which allows older apps to run on the new chips, has an overhead in terms of processor cycles and can slow things down. It’s better to run optimised software, and there is a lot of it out there, especially if you’re using it for AI work, where the apps are all fairly new.

If you don’t like the fans you can put it in Whisper mode, which is where we found the best battery life. It’ll go all day (8.5 hours) if you’re just editing text documents, watching videos and browsing the web, and if you leave it playing a video you can get more than 11 hours out of it. Naturally it drops more quickly when you’re making it work harder, and some of our AI benchmarks took several percent off the battery in about 15 minutes.

We test every one of our laptops using the same benchmarking software suite to give you a thorough overview of its suitability for creatives of all disciplines and levels. This includes:

• Geekbench: Tests the CPU for single-core and multi-core power, and the GPU for the system's potential for gaming, image processing, or video editing. Geekbench AI tests the CPU and GPU on a variety of AI-powered and AI-boosted tasks.• Cinebench: Tests the CPU and GPU's ability to run Cinema 4D and Redshift.• UL Procyon: Uses UL Solutions' Procyon software suite to test the system's ability for AI image generation in Stable Diffusion, its Microsoft Office performance and its battery life in a looping video test.• Topaz Video AI: We use Topaz Video AI to test the system's ability to upscale video and convert video to slow-motion.• PugetBench for Creators: We use the PugetBench for Creators benchmarking suite to test the system's ability to run several key tasks in Photoshop and Adobe Premiere Pro, as well as its performance when encoding/transcoding video.• ON1 Resize AI: Tests the system's ability to resize 5 photos to 200% in a batch process. We take the total time taken to resize the images and divide by 5.

• Good for AI use• Holds up in games and creative apps

For the N1X, Nvidia has created a 20-core CPU on what it calls its Grace microarchitecture. Grace has been around for a bit as a server platform, but this is the first time we’ve seen it in a consumer product. In this configuration, you get ten Cortex-X925 cores - for high single-threaded performance - along with ten more Cortex-A725 cores that are a bit more power efficient but still potent enough to make up the majority of the cores in Google’s Tensor G5 smartphone chip.

This is then joined by a Blackwell GPU with 6,144 CUDA cores, a figure that sits somewhere between the laptop versions of the RTX 5070 and 5080 GPUs. This all sits on the NVLink-C2C interconnect, which has 600 GB/s of bidirectional bandwidth, enough to keep all the bits talking to each other more quickly than a standard PCIe connection. The whole SoC has a TGP of 85W, rather less than some RTX 5080-equipped gaming laptops which can go as high as 175W, and pointing toward quieter operation and a longer battery life.

In tests, it pays off. While gaming isn’t the ProArt 14’s forte, it can manage 60FPS in Cyberpunk 2077 (ray-tracing ultra) at the screen’s native resolution if you enable Nvidia tricks like DLSS and frame-gen, something that puts it in the same ballpark as an RTX 5070 laptop GPU. The new GPU in the Spark wasn’t supported in Cinebench at the time of our testing, and that was also true of many of our other standard tests. Adobe is already trotting out optimised versions of its apps for the architecture, with betas of Photoshop and Premiere available that will take advantage of its potential. In the 32GB configuration we’ve got here, 12GB is allocated to the GPU by default, but you can change this in the ProArt Creator Hub.

As Nvidia is pushing the AI capabilities of the Spark so hard, it made sense to try some AI benchmarks. Creative Bloq has been running Geekbench AI for a while now, but we also turned to MLPerf to get a tokens per second figure, running the Llama 3.1 8 Billion Instruction LLM benchmark on a few different computers using the most appropriate framework for the processor.

The obvious winner here is the RTX 5080 desktop card, which has a TGP of 350W so jolly well should be better than laptops running at 85W or less. The ProArt P14 slots in nicely as the best laptop in this test, producing more than twice the tokens per second of Apple’s M5 (the vanilla non-Max or Ultra version), and this workout also proves Nvidia’s claims that the system’s performance is the same whether it’s plugged in or running on battery: with only two points’ difference between the scores, the difference is negligible.

In Topaz Video AI, the P14 sits with the lower-end gaming laptops, coming up just behind the RTX 5050-equipped Lenovo LOQ 15i Gen 10 and ASUS TUF Gaming A16. This could be explained by the software not being optimised for the RTX Spark. In ON1 Resize, which uses machine learning to up-res image files, it sits just behind the Acer Predator Triton (RTX 5070).

The prices of some of the new RTX Spark laptops are enough to make you gasp. Not only do they have a new SoC architecture inside them, but often a lot of RAM too. The ASUS ProArt P14 starts at £2,699.99 or $2,599 for the version with 24GB of RAM, and hops up to £3,199.99/$3,099.99 if you choose the 32GB upgrade. That’s MacBook Pro money, and you can get a 14in M5 model with 32GB of RAM for less.

This is a laptop, and indeed a whole platform, designed around the emergent field of the locally-run AI agent. Nvidia thinks it’s going to change the way we interact with our PCs, and for some it will be important to be in on this from the start. For anyone looking for something to edit video on, then while this is a fine laptop, it’s too new and expensive for many creative uses that don’t involve AI.

Good for AI, but you can get more creative punch for less.

Terribly expensive, especially if you add more RAM.

With this MacBook Pro, Apple has squeezed the kind of power you’d expect from a desktop Mac Pro in a tower case into a 14-inch laptop, and backed it up with plenty of RAM. It’s extremely expensive, but is probably the best professional laptop you can get right now.

While it may be a gaming laptop, there's no denying that the 2026 Razer Blade 18 is one of the most powerful portable machines you can buy, and that means it can blitz through creative work as easily as it can render spaceships. The price is high, but the speed is higher.

A phenomenal laptop that makes more sense for productivity and creative apps than it does for the gamers it’s ostensibly aimed at. However, it does this at an enormous price.

Ian Evenden has been a journalist for over 20 years, starting in the days of QuarkXpress 4 and Photoshop 5. He now mainly works in Creative Cloud and Google Docs, but can always find a use for a powerful laptop or two. When not sweating over page layout or photo editing, you can find him peering at the stars or growing vegetables.
