#229. ‘I like to take time to understand the work and its maker’: collector Helen Sunderland-Cohen on what she has bought and why

Helen Sunderland-Cohen is the custodian of the Sunderland Collection of rare historical maps, atlases and globes, which was established by her father, alongside the Ex Carta collection of fictional maps Courtesy Oculi Mundi

The London-based lawyer, Helen Sunderland-Cohen, oversees not one but three collections. She is the custodian of the Sunderland Collection of rare historical maps, atlases and globes that her father, Neil, originated; the founder, in 2024, of the Ex Carta collection of fictional maps; and an intuitive collector of contemporary art that she lives with in her central London home. Her personal collection includes recent paintings by Nick Goss, abstract work by Prunella Clough, and a wooden painted mask by Yinka Shonibare.

In 2021, the entire Sunderland Collection became available digitally on the site Oculi Mundi. Meanwhile, gems from Ex Carta are currently on view at the Zurich Central Library in an exhibition called Fantastical Maps from Legendary Stories (until 5 December) and in the Warburg Institute’s Night Maps, which opens in London on 21 October.

Sutherland-Cohen is a fan of Ali Kazim, whose works include Untitled (The Bird Hunter Series XIV) (2026) Courtesy the artist and Cristea Roberts Gallery, London; © Ali Kazim

The Art Newspaper: What was the first work you ever bought?

Helen Sunderland-Cohen:The first “serious” work was a lovely photograph from the 1970s, by the feminist artist Alexis Hunter. It is a self-portrait of her reflected in a mirror.

An exquisite watercolour from the Bird Hunter Series, by Pakistani artist Ali Kazim.

How different is it to buy work for the Sunderland Collection or Ex Carta, and work that you personally like and want to live with?

It is completely different. My own art collection is very eclectic and personal; it is mostly Modern and contemporary visual arts. There are loose themes but a lot is simply work from artists I admire, or that resonates for personal reasons. I am fascinated by both meaning and process. The map collections are quite specific: the Sunderland Collection focuses on world maps and celestial cartography up to around 1700; and Ex Carta focuses on literary or worldbuilding cartography, and ideally from first editions. The common denominator among the three is quality.

How quickly do you decide to buy a work of art?

I rarely buy spontaneously. I like to take time to understand the work and its maker. If possible, I try to meet them in person (trickier with the maps!). I also like to look: it is important to put things in context and train the eye.

What do you regret not buying when you had the chance?

Objects that I did not realise were for sale until afterwards. It can be hard keeping up, even with the magic of the internet.

If you could have any work from any museum in the world, what would it be?

I would rather they stay where they are, unless the museum is doing a terrible job at conservation. It is also great to lend objects rather than have them sit at home or in storage: it is exciting to see other people experience them and hear new perspectives.

Alexis Hunter’s 2018 exhibition Sexual Warfare at Goldsmiths Centre for Contemporary Art in south London. The first work that Sutherland-Cohen purchased was by the artist © Alexis Hunter

Which exhibition are you most looking forward to seeing in London this month?

The degree show at the City & Guilds of London Art School, where I am a trustee, happens in June and has such great energy. In October in London, I will be trying to catch the Richard Dadd at the Royal Academy of Arts, Henry Moore at Kew Gardens and Ana Mendieta at Tate Modern.

Where do you like to eat and drink during Frieze London?

At the fair itself, Jikoni—their food is wonderful. Outside the fair, I love the food and vibes at Claro London. For a degustation, it’s Restaurant St. Barts. For somewhere small and chill, Cloth Fair or Doppo. And finally for old-school fish, Wiltons.

The one I am really looking forward to is for The Soothsayer’s Chorus, an exhibition co-curated by the formidable yet humble curator Beth Greenacre and consultant Bettina Prentice. It is at Pink Floyd’s former recording studio near King’s Cross.

What is your least favourite thing about art fairs?

Entitled people who take themselves too seriously or those who are not there for the art!

Where do you go in London to get away from it all?

My home. It is very peaceful and we have big trees outside; I like to listen to the birds.

What tip would you give to someone visiting London for the first time?

Spend time on the river. And don’t worry if you cannot see everything in one go.

• Fantastical Maps from Legendary Stories, Zentralbibliothek Zürich, until 5 December

•  Night Maps, The Warburg Institute, London, 21 October-17 April 2027

#230. "People need to be able to afford to adapt to climate change" says architect founder of Shaded

London-based architectural designer Aimée Daniels has invented an awning system that sold out multiple times this summer. In this interview, she argues the UK needs to get on board with the power of shading.

Self-described “clean-tech startup” Shaded sells simple and colourful external awnings that can be easily installed on or removed from sash windows and retail at £89.

“It’s a detachable awning for sash windows,” Daniels told Dezeen. “It’s sort of an alternative to air conditioning.”

Daniels, who is originally from New York and grew up with the comforts of air conditioning, founded Shaded in 2023 after struggling with UK temperatures that reached 40 degrees the previous summer.

The product’s success was a great validation that there is an appetite for affordable passive cooling products that also look good

Concerned by the lack of shading across UK homes and privy to the benefits of shading techniques through her ten years in architecture, Daniels became dedicated to retrofitting buildings.

“I guess the 40-degree weather of summer 2022 put me in an inventive mood, initially in response to my own discomfort and the lack of accessible, sustainable solutions available to deal with it,” she said.

“The idea for the awning came through a combination of doing passive design at work, and knowing about the principles and how shade is so effective,” she said.

With the UK’s summers continuing to break temperature records ever since, Shaded has become extremely popular and gained significant attention online, with the awning system selling out three times since being launched earlier this year.

“I had doubts and launched the product with the goal of breaking even,” Daniels admitted. “The product’s success was a great validation that there is an appetite for affordable passive cooling products that also look good.”

The UK seems to be the only European country that hasn’t clocked on to shading windows as a first line of defence

Daniels conceived Shaded as a more affordable and sustainable alternative for cooling Britain’s homes than air conditioning, which is also becoming much more popular among those who can afford it.

“[Passive solutions] should be the first thing people do, at the very least, before bringing in mechanical cooling,” she said. “I think that making that more accessible is a big component of how to promote it and get people to buy in.”

External shading systems can be highly effective, reducing room temperatures by several degrees Celsius. But despite their widespread use across other temperate climates, awnings remain fairly uncommon in the UK, especially on residential buildings.

Much more common, says Daniels, are blinds and curtains, which can contribute to overheating.

“The UK seems to be the only European country that hasn’t clocked on to shading windows as a first line of defence,” she said.

Affordability is a major factor in this lack of adoption, Daniels suggests.

“Right now, it’s actually really hard to choose passive cooling for reasons like costs being too high,” Daniels said. “Installation is a big driver of cost,” she continued. “The fact that you have to fix something externally to the facade means that you probably need to put up scaffolding, et cetera. It requires specialist help.

It’s completely temporary and doesn’t interact with the building fabric at all. It leaves zero trace

In contrast, Shaded’s awnings are clipped on from the inside – reducing installation costs to zero.

Even in the case that someone might be able to afford to install a traditional, permanent awning, Daniels says, the route to gaining planning permission can be costly.

In addition to this, the lack of a blanket policy for the installation of awnings in the UK can make the process convoluted, with existing regulations often specifying limitations for buildings that are rented, listed or located within a conservation area, Daniels explains.

“Permanent awnings are drilled into facades, becoming a material component of a building, and their cassettes have a year-round presence,” she said.

In the London Borough of Islington, for example, planning permission is required for awnings on front elevations of flats, multiple-occupation houses and properties within a conservation area.

Meanwhile, London’s Westminster City Council, in collaboration with property investment company Grosvenor, has recently given blanket consent for awnings and other retrofit measures on listed buildings in Belgravia’s Eaton Square.

Daniels’ second design marker was therefore meeting regulatory requirements.

“I went around in circles a lot around figuring out what I have to do to meet regulations,” she said. “[Typically], if you wanted to install external shading you’d have to put a planning application in.”

“You might have to submit drawings, and that all costs money and time – on top of the fact that the existing products are expensive,” she added.

Daniels’ awning offers a temporary, “zero-trace” alternative, meaning that it side-steps the bureaucracy of installing a permanent one.

“It’s completely temporary and doesn’t interact with the building fabric at all. It leaves zero trace,” she said.

Following the success of her first product, Daniels has plans to create a new range of awnings that cater to more window types, alongside the creation of other affordable passive solutions.

“We need to adapt our built environment to temperatures,” Daniels said. “My motivation is making sure the mass of people can actually afford to do it.”

“Why can certain people adapt to climate change and not others? People need to be able to afford to adapt to climate change,” she added.

#231. Rethinking Data Visualisation: A UX Approach To Dashboards That Actually Drives Decisions

Meriem Benhabiles is a Designer specialising in User Experience, with over five years working in-house, agency-side, and independently. Her background in … More about Meriem ↬

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

In organisations today, data has never been more available. Dashboards and performance decks exist for almost every function — sales, product, marketing, operations — and the tools to build them have never been more accessible. And yet, in weekly standups and quarterly reviews, the same thing happens constantly: someone shares the numbers, the room nods, and the meeting ends without a decision or clear direction.

When that happens, the data usually takes the blame. The numbers weren’t granular enough, the dataset wasn’t complete, we need more information before we can act. But the data is almost never the problem. The reality is that nobody designed it to deliver insights. The chart was built from what was available, not from the question that needed answering. The audience was assumed rather than understood, and what should actually change as a result of seeing this data — that question — was never asked at all.

Data visualisation and UX are solving the same underlying problem: both are trying to move the right information to the right person in a way that changes something. The vocabulary is different, but the underlying challenge is identical, and the moment you start treating them as complementary disciplines is the moment dashboards stop being a passive collection of charts and start doing something functional.

For designers who work with data, analysts who present to non-technical audiences, and marketers who need their numbers to do more than sit in a slide, this read is for you.

In 1973, the statistician Francis Anscombe (PDF) published a paper that made a quiet but clarifying point. He constructed four datasets that are statistically identical: same mean, same variance, same correlation coefficient, and same regression line. Run the numbers on any of them, and they are identical. Plot them, and they could not be more different.

Anscombe’s lesson to statisticians was about diagnosis: visualisation reveals the operational truth that raw numbers conceal.

But visualisation isn’t just diagnostic; it is also communicative. The form you choose is where understanding either emerges or gets lost in the noise. Does your audience walk away with numbers, or with a story they’ll quote and talk about?

One of the most striking examples is Visual Capitalist’s History of Pandemics. Instead of burying the reader in a massive data table of casualty counts, it maps the death toll of major historical pandemics using a proportional bubble layout on a single timeline.

Before your brain reads a single number, your visual system grasps the sheer scale of the Black Death relative to everything else on the page. The right visualisation does not just plot the data but makes the story impossible to miss.

Edward Tufte codified a foundational principle for the craft with his data-ink ratio: every mark on a chart should serve the data, not decorate it. It remains a widely used framework in data visualisation, anchored in the assumption that clarity and visual hygiene are the goal.

For a chart in isolation, that holds. But a chart is never read in isolation: it’s read by a person, in a specific context, under specific pressure. Strip a chart down to its cleanest form, and you might be removing the exact layer of context a decision-maker needs. Simplicity isn’t the goal in itself; appropriate complexity is.

Data is a message, and the right amount of signal depends entirely on who’s receiving it.

Which leads to the core principle of data UX: roughly 80% of the work that determines whether a dashboard succeeds happens before you ever draw a chart.

That dependency is the thread the rest of this piece pulls on.

Meet Smashing Workshops on front-end, design & UX, with practical takeaways, live sessions, video recordings and a friendly Q&A. With Brad Frost, Stéph Walter and so many others.

The high-leverage 80% almost never happens on screen. It happens upstream: before a tool is opened, before a dataset is pulled, before a single design choice is made. It comes down to three questions, and once they become habitual, they change what you notice, what you ask, and what you push back on at the outset of every project.

Most data-heavy projects start backward: teams pull whatever metrics their internal analytics tools already track and build visualisations around them, while the question the data was supposed to answer either gets assumed or never gets asked. This happens simply because we anchor on the data in front of us as the boundary of what’s possible.

Defining a goal first sounds obvious, but in practice, it rarely happens with the necessary clarity. “Show me how the product is performing” is not a goal; “Identify which features drive retention among users who signed up in Q1” is, as it includes three things the first doesn’t: a metric, a population, and an implied action. That specificity is what converts an open-ended exploration into a constrained, answerable design problem. Which one you start from determines everything that follows: what you include, what comparisons matter, and what you leave out entirely.

Starting with available data produces a dashboard that answers no particular question, because it was never built for one — every number is present, none of them pointed anywhere. Starting with the operational question does the reverse: every element on the screen earns its place, because each one is there to help answer it.

For example, consider a UX team trying to fix a leaky checkout flow for an e-commerce website. A data-first approach pulls everything available, from clicks to scroll depth and device types, yielding a massive dashboard that leaves everyone asking, “Okay, but what do we actually change?” A context-first approach starts with a constraint: “At which step of the checkout do users drop off?” By filtering out 90% of the noise, the team builds a simple funnel chart, instantly spots a bottleneck on the payment screen, and knows exactly what to redesign.

Designing for an audience comes down to two things: accountability and familiarity.

Familiarity is about data literacy. Do they read charts instinctively, or does a complex visualisation create friction? Handing a dense, multi-layered dashboard to a Head of Sales and a senior analyst is like giving the same map to someone who navigates by landmarks and someone who reads grid coordinates. The data is accurate, but it is only functional for one of them.

Accountability dictates how that complexity must be presented. A chart showing a 12% decline carries vastly different weight for the executive responsible for that number versus the analyst simply reporting it. Understanding your audience means grasping this relationship; data is never processed neutrally when your performance is on the line.

Together, familiarity and accountability decide one practical thing: how much you can put in front of someone.

In data visualisation, simplicity is not a fixed virtue — the right level of it is contingent on who is reading, and what they need to do.

An analyst relies on a high-density environment to conduct diagnostic discovery. By isolating individual behaviour nodes and mapping out raw user flows, they interrogate the data at its atomic level to uncover the hidden insights and underperforming spend that will shape future campaigns.

An executive, by contrast, requires a highly synthesised translation of that data to immediately identify what is driving commercial growth. Tailoring a dashboard to your audience means adjusting the density dial, delivering maximum signal with appropriate complexity for the specific brain in the room.

Most data projects operate on the comfortable assumption that if a chart is accurate and clear, the insight will take care of itself. In reality, information and insight are entirely different states. Information is what the data shows, whereas insight is the specific decision, shift in understanding, or course correction someone makes as a result of seeing it. If the intended business change isn’t defined before the design begins, a dashboard will default to passive reporting rather than driving action.

Marketing and engineering teams experience the danger of this gap whenever a core business metric suddenly plummets.

A dashboard built for information simply sounds the alarm, showing a chart that tracks a sharp 15% drop in booking rates. Because the data lacks depth, leadership defaults to panic: they immediately call the UX design team, assuming the app is broken or the checkout flow is flawed. Because the data doesn’t pinpoint the core of the problem, it triggers a costly, misplaced fire drill.

A dashboard built for insight isolates the variables required to make an informed decision. Instead of a single, flat booking metric, the visualisation maps the drop against traffic sources and campaign launches — instantly revealing that while app performance and core user conversion are perfectly stable, the sitewide rate was artificially diluted by a massive influx of low-intent click traffic from a newly scaled campaign. The team doesn’t waste time redesigning a functioning app; they get the exact insight needed to pause the underperforming marketing campaign and adjust their acquisition strategy.

Every visualisation implies a next step, even if that step is “nothing needs to change right now.” The question is whether the design makes that implication clear enough for the viewer to recognise it.

My aha moment in data visualisation happened during a project for a client-facing B2B SaaS platform focused on enterprise talent management and competency tracking in Pegasystems skills. The platform captured a massive footprint of daily telemetry, and the brief arrived open-ended: “We have an immense archive of user activity, now we need to present it to enterprise teams.”

We could very easily have charted everything that was captured, but we wouldn’t be doing end users any favours if they just ended up looking at a data graveyard. My responsibility immediately moved beyond pure interface craftsmanship; it became about architecting a highly practical tool for real people who would open this dashboard routinely and need it to tell them an honest, immediate story about their workflows.

The client believed this massive pool of data could help their users perform better, and wanted an interface that finally enabled that growth. Translating that broad ambition into tangible visualisations required defining the practical mechanics of performance. What variables indicate advancement vs passive usage? What does “perform better” actually mean? How do you measure it?

An obvious candidate was time spent by product. Every platform tracks it. It is easy to show, and it feels meaningful. But time spent is a proxy; it tells you someone was there, not whether they got anything out of it.

The more meaningful signals were competency scores by area, certification completion rates, and historical performance trajectories. Integrating time-spent data alongside these performance metrics added a useful layer of interpretation, helping us surface which modules users were underutilising and whether that directly correlated with lagging scores. Time spent became a supporting signal in the larger story.

The second question was about the appropriate level of granularity. An identical metric carries completely different weight depending on who is looking at it. An individual contributor tracking their own completion rate needs to know if they are pacing correctly, whereas a manager reviewing a team aggregate needs to know precisely who requires immediate support. This distinction shaped every subsequent data-exposure and filtering decision. Defining that structural story early determined exactly what to show, and to whom.

The most straightforward approach to this design would have been predictable: use the same charts, but offer an individual view and an aggregated team view. Far too many dashboards rely on this shortcut, subtly tweaking the scale of identical data visualisations and labelling it “personalisation.”

An authentic analysis of the audience reveals a much deeper rift. Frontline team leads and individual contributors required distinct narrative structures and design principles.

Having used e-learning platforms myself, I remember the frustration of opening a tool without a clear sense of my current standing, core strengths, or slipping metrics. That personal experience directly guided the individual contributor workspace; it needed to act as a highly tailored, self-directed mirror that was granular, honest, and personal.

Conversely, the manager’s interface had to bypass individual milestones initially to provide a macro pulse check on team vulnerabilities. It was designed around a different operational reality: how is the group progressing, and where are the consistent gaps? The view prioritised the aggregate picture first, while retaining an intuitive path to drill down into tactical day-to-day coordination when needed.

Our insight strategy was locked in during the early conceptual phase, long before wireframing a single chart. We intentionally abandoned the idea of building a dense, passive data log and focused on pacing the narrative arc.

For individual contributors, the core value was self-direction, ensuring they could glance at the interface on a Monday morning and immediately derive a clear priority list for the week ahead.

For managers, the goal was to fundamentally shift the timing of operational conversations, providing them with the necessary baseline to intervene before a skill gap evolved into a critical project failure. The visualisations needed to surface the exact moments when a human check-in would be useful, shifting their workflow from reactive post-mortems to proactive guidance.

The comparison tool was the highlight nobody had asked for. A manager dashboard and an individual dashboard are easy to anticipate. What is harder to land is: what if a manager wants to compare two specific team members against the same metrics, side by side? That view came from a design assumption, and it turned out to be the feature that resonated most.

The decisions that mattered most in this project weren’t in the initial brief — capturing data they hadn’t thought to request, and structuring it to answer questions they had not previously known how to articulate, which is the core differentiator of a user-centric data strategy.

The choice of visualisation layout must follow the geometric nature of the data itself. For this project, the core design problem was enabling an individual user to answer a specific question at a single glance: across eight distinct competency areas, where are my relative strengths and gaps?

To solve this, we mapped the data using a radar chart. By organising multiple variables across axes radiating from a central point using polar coordinates, the interface connects the data points to form a single, unified shape. An even, balanced polygon instantly signals well-rounded proficiency, while a sharply skewed shape draws the eye immediately to an outlier area.

While a traditional linear bar chart would have forced the viewer to scan eight individual bars and mentally calculate the variance, a concentric, radial layout segments the data layers to make progress tracking and skill gaps immediately readable. When all dimensions share an identical scale and scoring method, the radar chart is not an unconventional aesthetic choice — it is the most functional tool for multi-dimensional analysis.

The colour system was the other decision made early, and I mean early. During the branding exercise, each of the three products was assigned a colour. That colour did not stay in the brand guidelines. It was built into the data model from the beginning, running consistently across every chart, every filter, every breakdown. By the time a user landed on the dashboard for the first time, the mental model was already in place. They had not been taught the language. They already knew it.

The shift from passive information to active insight showed up first in how the dashboard was actually used. Following the deployment of the personalised dashboards and side-by-side team comparison tools, weekly active engagement on the platform’s analytics features rose noticeably, per internally reported figures. Managers were no longer opening the tool once a month to pull static reports. They were using it every Monday morning to actively plan their week.

Revenue and user growth also moved in the right direction over the following two quarters, though — as with most single-project outcomes — it’s hard to isolate the dashboard’s exact contribution from everything else that changed at the same time. The client reported churn across the platform falling to one of its lowest points on record. The clearest evidence of impact came from qualitative feedback. Managers reported that instead of using data to dissect a ‘bad’ month after the fact, the visualisations allowed them to instantly spot slipping performance and schedule a quick supportive catch-up before it turned into a real gap.

Data design reaches its full potential when visual presentation is treated as an upstream architectural choice rather than a downstream formatting step. Bringing structured UX thinking to data turns visualisations into active decision-making engines, ensuring every chart, report, and metric directly serves a human purpose:

The next time you are tasked with creating a data visualisation — whether it is an enterprise dashboard, an executive report, or a public-facing infographic — step away from the design canvas and BI tools. Focus your initial effort on the human decisions behind the screen. Only then will your data stop being a passive log of the past and start driving the direction of the future.

#232. The Dinner Ladies

The Dinner Ladies needed a recipe for a rebrand that would not only pay respect to their unique origin story but bring their visual and verbal identity up to speed with their growth as Australia’s tastiest frozen meal service. We joined forces to cook them up a fresh look and feel that reflects their homely meals and anti-“mumsy” attitude, extending all the way from their website through to their packaging. Now whack the oven on, because Australia’s hottest frozen meal service has arrived.

Since it all began with two determined women in a Sydney-side backyard shed in 2007, The Dinner Ladies have been filling the freezers, bellies and hearts of thousands of busy Australian families with their ready-to-heat comfort meals. Born from a deep understanding of dinner time chaos, and the desire to bring some ease back into this routine, The Dinner Ladies’ commitment to delivering meals worthy of mum’s tick of approval remains unwavering.

The market for pre-prepared meal delivery is an oversaturated landscape steeped in clichés and same-same messaging that claims to be the most healthy, convenient or delicious dinnertime solution. They not only lack a distinct personality but also relatability to their customer — time-poor people who just want simple, genuinely good, homemade meals that help take the pressure off when it’s needed most. This is where The Dinner Ladies shine. A flavour-stacked service that takes care of dinner, so you can focus on doing life.

The brand had become known and loved for their unexpected, no nonsense and slightly audacious approach. This was not only refreshingly real but a reflection of both their wholesome offering and the founding ladies. However, over seventeen years of brand iterations their look had become diluted, lost its attitudinal punch, and needed a big serve of reinvigoration. Our vision was to bring back the best from their history and turn up the heat across the board to let the nation know they mean (meal delivery) business.

We fully immersed ourselves in The Dinner Ladies story, from taking a deep dive through past website designs and hand drawn logos on a napkin, to visiting the shed where it all began and the factory where it now thrives. This helped us draw out the strongest existing brand elements, like their early trad-tattoo-esque illustrations and counter-“mumsy” stereotype, and turn them into a modern evolution. Driven by “Food from the Heart,” each component of the visual identity communicates the brand essence and no-BS confidence of a service that truly helps take the stress out of dinnertime.

The first step was the refinement of the logo. By decoupling the heart and the script, we gave it flexibility, made it easier to read at every touchpoint and allowed it to scale as needed. The custom heart logo was designed by us and then, alongside the wordmark, handed to illustrator Jake Foreman to redraw and personalise with his iconic texture and gritty stipple.

The Dinner Ladies’ existing red already had distinct brand attribution in the category so we just refined it with a bright and modern twist. The secondary palette supports our hero red with a balance of warm, approachable and slightly retro hues. When united, the system unlocks a number of interesting and vibrant combinations that are particularly useful across hard-working digital applications.

We used the typeface Denim by Displaay Type Foundry to show off the brand’s confident personality yet retain practicality. Denim Wide’s used in headings and call-to-action applications to command attention, while its regular cut counterpart rounds out the system with a friendly, clean and legible option for subheadings and body copy. With its subtle details, the typeface can be an attention-grabbing hero element that showcases the bold tone of voice but also work alongside more expressive moments.

The tone of voice needed to capture the brand’s joyful, cheeky yet comforting personality, while steering clear of any patronising “mumsy” tropes and stereotypes. We worked with copywriter Cat Wall to develop a verbal identity that balanced the empathetic caregiver with the charmingly rebellious tone of the ladies themselves. In a category saturated with over-sincerity and fake friendliness, the tone offers a refreshing sprinkle of irreverence with a straight-forward, bull-free reflection of the audience and their needs.

The photography celebrates the authentic messiness of real life dinnertime. A reflection of the brand’s tell-it-like-it-is attitude, the shoot didn’t shy away from capturing raw moments — the remnants of a great dish alongside a new one being served or a bolognese-faced baby — mixed with the joy of sharing generous, mouth-watering food.

With Alana Dimou behind the lens, Jerrie-Joy Redman-Lloyd on styling, Oriana De Luca on wardrobe, Gavin Anesbury with a hair and makeup brush in hand, and Michaela Le on production, the brand came to life. Warm, natural lighting, combined with quirky styling choices, pops of colour or pattern and intentional (and encouraged) chaos set a homely and inviting scene with a pinch of rebellion.

Illustration has always been a major piece of The Dinner Ladies’ brand so we wanted to bring it across to the rebrand. The original illustrations’ punk and rough-around-the-edges flair drew us to references of traditional trad tattoos.

Collaborating further with illustrator Jake Foreman, we crafted a suite of illustrations that served as both personality-rich storytelling pieces and functional devices. While the small scenes and spots speak to specific offerings of the brand, the hero illustration speaks to the love behind every Dinner Ladies dish and the comforting shared experiences created around the table.

These illustrations are supported by our suite of type-furniture elements that not only support the main design elements but add character to any layout.

As a product that’s often shoved into the freezer and then reached for in a rush, legibility and easy differentiation were priorities for designing the packaging. A simple colour-coded system helps to distinguish between protein groups at a glance, making it quick and effortless to find the crowd-pleasing meal that’s ready to save the day.

The Dinner Ladies now have a brand that not only celebrates their seventeen year legacy but gives them the tools for future decades of success. The flexible design system and punchy tone of voice pays tribute to their tenacious past, the founding ladies behind the service and their wholesome mission put joy back into dinner time. Now The Dinner Ladies can stand loud and proud with a brand that reflects their readiness to dish up delicious dinners to an entire nation.

#234. Product Design: MaPC your PC games on your Mac

Discover MaPC, a new Mac app from the team behind Abduzeedo that brings Windows games from Steam, Epic Games and GOG to Apple Silicon Macs.

Gaming on Apple Silicon has always felt like an exercise in compromise. For years, running Windows titles meant wrestling with terminal flags, compatibility layers and configuration files that felt alien to macOS. We built MaPC to remove that friction. Born from the same design principles behind Calmaria and Abduzeedo, it lets you connect your Steam, Epic Games or GOG account, install a game and press Play. No Wine setup and no tinkering.

Every screen in MaPC was designed as a real Mac app. Itâs built with SwiftUI, with no Electron wrapper or web container, and it respects system typography, keyboard shortcuts, light and dark mode, and window behavior. Game pages take their colors from each gameâs cover art, so every title gets its own ambient palette. You can switch between an editorial Magazine layout and structured glass Panels to choose how your library looks.

Under the surface, MaPC handles the technical setup for you. Games that use DirectX 9, 10 and 11 run through open-source translation layers (Wine, DXVK and MoltenVK), set up automatically. Per-game settings let you adjust the graphics backend and launch options and switch on Retina rendering or a performance HUD when you want more control. We publish the source of every engine we build.

MaPC is free. Supporters can unlock optional extras: save backups to iCloud Drive or any folder, playtime stats, game shortcuts and a menu bar launcher.

MaPC is in public beta for Apple Silicon Macs running macOS 15 or later. Not every game runs yet. Games with kernel-level anti-cheat canât run on macOS, so check the list of limits before you download. Get MaPC at mapc.games, and explore more of our design work here on Abduzeedo.

#236. Jonas Hejduk's blurry furnishings are deliberately low resolution

Designer Jonas Hejduk has released a collection of rugs and benches that have ambiguously pixellated aesthetics.

Hejduk‘s focus on deliberately compressed, low-resolution versions of popular furnishings were informed by his childhood fixation with video game graphics.

“Youngsters like myself were already caught in the spiral logic of infinite growth, trained never to tolerate technological stagnation,” Hejduk told Dezeen.

Stools and rugs are among the French designer’s output, each of which were named using computer filename formats.

In the case of the designer’s rugs, the filename, initial file size and post-processing size are woven onto the surface of the piece.

Made from digitally woven wool and cotton jacquard, the designer described the Traditional-rug-1.jpeg as “poetic and gently ironic”.

“Once a symbol of prestige and early global exchange, the Persian rug gradually shifted into a standardised archetype of mass culture and uniformity,” Hejduk told Dezeen.

“Here, it is reduced to its own thumbnail – an enigmatic blurry image of troubled origins, copied and pasted too many times.”

Hejduk’s Tiger skin rug is part of a wider collection called Crash.jpeg, in which the designer explored the contemporary obsession with digital clarity and technological advancement.

“By embracing the ambiguity of the poor image, the collection presents works that are deliberately difficult to photograph and rendered anachronistic to the eyes of social media algorithms: high-definition designs are deliberately sabotaged down to lower resolutions,” said Hejduk.

Similarly, Hejduk’s Log-texture-1.jpeg bench recalls the nostalgia of logs as resting places in 1990s video games.

The benches were wrapped in a blurry bark skin with cut-through textures at either end, tacked together with traditional nailhead trim.

Like many of the designer’s works, the logs act like an optical illusion, contrasting with their surroundings in a jarring way owing to their not-finished-loading appearance.

“Visually, it ‘has no business being there’, and yet, its digital nature conveys an authenticity that brings a smile, far removed from what AI offers in our daily lives,” the designer continued.

In addition to rugs and benches, Hejduk produces similarly blurry ceramics, garments, bed sheets and wallpapers.

“These pieces of furniture are not just ‘designer jokes about 3D’, but objects of mourning and resistance,” said Hejduk.

“Through the physicality of craft and raw materials, they serve as tangible reminders of the unfulfilled promises of digital modernity, all while rejecting the sanitised present that tech oligarchs attempt to impose on us.”

Other products on Dezeen created in rejection of AI include a shirt that prevents the wearer from being picked up by AI video surveillance and a font that cannot be read by AI software.

British singer Lily Allen is gunning for a Grammy, and her For Your Consideration (FYC) ad is perhaps the most nonchalant pledge ever. Creating a disarmingly raunchy (yet surprisingly classy) poster design, the artist once again proves the power of her offbeat branding for the West End Girl album.

Praised for her candid lyrics and immersive tour performances, Lily's West End Girl era has embraced chaos and the clumsiness of love and sex. Her strikingly lewd poster is yet another example of why the album's raw approach to music has earned her a shot at this year's Grammys.

The design features the polka-dot-patterned novelty USB flash drive butt plug that became the unexpected star of the singer's cheeky album campaign. Immediately contrasting the domestic connotation of polka dots with the sexualised object, the poster embodies the themes of the album with a wonderfully unserious playfulness.

The FYC phase of the Grammys is a chance for artists to promote their work in hopes that voting members will cast ballots in their favour. Lily's casual and provocative approach to this historically professional artist pitch is a wonderfully refreshing subversion of the rules, once again proving the artist isn't afraid to challenge convention and taboo.

#239. Apex

Auto racing’s seen an explosion of flimsy “fashion wheel” brands that pretend to be high-performance. Apex is different — engineering elite racing wheels at an unmatched price point. But when we met them, customers were completely unaware of the difference. Working closely with their CEO, Eddy Pintacsi, we developed a new category vision and brand, positioning them as the category leader they are, and injecting some much-needed truth into the wheel industry.

We started by naming the problem that Apex solves, calling it The Great Knowledge Void. A state of play where any wheel brand can make performance claims — true or not — just to make a buck. And the worst part? Customers have no way to know the difference. We went on to tell a story of how Apex is fixing this problem with their core ethos: “Real performance.” A pledge to show customers the truth — or die trying. End of story.

The identity is loud and urgent. To stop people from buying bogus wheels. The arching curves and high-contrast colors catch the eyes on the track — where it matters. And we worked with Apex to weave the same sense of urgency into how they talk about their testing standards. So that the entire industry would get with the program.

Altogether, the rebrand, POV, and messaging proves that Apex stands alone in its category. We call this a “Category of One” brand. Because when you risk everything on the track, there’s only one thing you can trust — Real Performance.

#240. Tate Modern exhibition explores Pictorialism and the birth of soft-focus photography

Luo Bonian’s Drawing Water from a Well (1932) Courtesy Luo Bonian Art Foundation and Three Shadows +3 Gallery

“This is probably our first ever revisionist photography exhibition,” says Charmaine Toh, the Tate’s senior curator of international art photography. “In the past we’ve celebrated certain movements or certain themes. But this time we wanted to do something different.” Toh is talking about Light and Magic, Tate Modern’s new show about Pictorialism, the salon-based photography movement that is perhaps most strongly associated with soft-focus, deliberately artful Edwardian pictures, and which sought to establish photography as an art form on a par with painting or sculpture.

But Toh is keen to get a different perspective across. “Pictorialism used to be seen as very old fashioned and a narrow kind of practice,” she says. “It supposedly ended in the 1920s and 30s, and was confined to Europe and North America. But there were people making work into the 1950s and 60s, all over the world, who are using the word Pictorialism. So, what is all this work being made after Pictorialism had supposedly stopped in all the photography textbooks you pick up?”

It is a subject that would appear to be close to Toh’s heart; this is her first major exhibition since being appointed to Tate in 2024, and she wrote her PhD thesis on the Pictorialist movement in her home city of Singapore. This was part of the ongoing Pictorialist movement that persisted into the decades after the Second World War, and was supported by a network of international clubs and exhibitions that provided a focus for photographers to disseminate their work.

US photographer Paul Strand’s Miss Thomson, New Mexico (around 1922) Wilson Centre for Photography; © Paul Strand Archive; Aperture Foundation

Toh defines Pictorialism as “fundamentally, a desire for photography to be accepted as fine art”, and the pioneers of the style were the smoky, atmospheric pictures by the likes of Alfred Stieglitz, Clarence Hudson White and Henry Peach Robinson. These were photographers in the late 19th and early 20th century who sought to manipulate the visual elements as a direct response to the idea that photography was an objective record of its subject.

Hence the early Pictorialists seemed to emulate the more subjective forms of art: Aestheticism, Impressionismand the like. Toh has included in the exhibition studies by the French Pictorialist Robert Demachy that are dead ringers for Edgar Degas’s paintings of ballet dancers (apart from the black-and-white colour scheme), and pictures by the Chinese photographer Luo Bonian that resemble traditional ink drawings. Toh has also highlighted another strand of Pictoralism: its interest in dance, and particularly kinetic, near-abstract figure studies that offered another way to counter static documentary observation.

The curator is at pains to point out that Pictorialism was a far wider phenomenon than its early style tropes might suggest. “That’s just where they started from,” Toh says. “I think this idea of style is a red herring that we tend to blindly follow because it’s just easier for us as curators and historians because we’re trained to think that way. But fundamentally, it was a desire for photography to be accepted as fine art. The contribution of Pictorialism was the networks that were set up.”

A photograph (title unknown) by Shigeru Onishi (around 1950s) Tate; © Estate of Shigeru Onishi

Clubs like the Linked Ring in London, the Photo-Club de Paris, Photo-Secession and the Vienna Camera Club were, Toh says, crucial organisations that gave hundreds of photographers an outlet through their international exhibitions. Even someone like the Soviet Constructivist Aleksandr Rodchenko would send pictures to club shows through the Moscow-based All-Union Society for Cultural Relations with Foreign Countries.

“And this happened not just in the centres like London and San Francisco,” Toh says. “In Singapore, it was a point of pride for them to have an international exhibition. They thought: look, we might be a British colony, but we’ve got an international exhibition and we’re going to judge the British works that are being sent to us. And that happened in Brazil. It happened in Australia.”

It may perhaps be a slight curatorial indulgence, but in the end Toh says she wants to reclaim Pictorialism’s place as a vital 20th-century artistic movement alongside, but not superseded by, Modernism. “The relationship between Modernism and Pictorialism is something that I’ve been very interested in,” she says. “It is as though Modernism needed Pictorialism to be what it wasn’t.” She adds that Modernist photography defined itself as “clear, sharp, about being in the city, about modernity”, while Pictorialism in contrast was defined as “non-Modern”.

“It was a strategy as to how to position Modernism,” Toh says. “I call it the curse of the avant-garde: we believe so strongly in the rule of the avant-garde, in its linearity, that we then struggle to fit things that don’t match the avant-garde into that story.” She adds: “The works I look at are outside of North America and Europe, and they don’t fall in the avant-garde story. That becomes an exclusion—and very important for me personally.”

Light and Magic: The Birth of Art Photography, Tate Modern, until 21 February 2027

#241. Properly Studio Unveils the Axi Rebrand

Properly rebuilt Axi's brand, website and trading app in four months. The Axi rebrand keeps the signature red and adds a custom typeface.

Four months. That is the timeline Properly took to rebuild the brand, a 150-page website and the trading platform UI of Axi, the global online trading provider. Most rebrands this size ship a logo and a landing page and call it a system. This one treats the whole company as the canvas: brand, site and product rebuilt together so the app reads as the same brand as the billboard.

The visual premise is restraint with one loud color. Properly kept Axi's logo and signature red, then built everything else around it: off-white fields, slate gradients, dark rock photography. The red never fills a background. It shows up as a dot on a chart, a corner tick, a single word set against black. That discipline is what makes the system scale across a hundred-plus markets without splintering into local versions.

The type move is the spine of the project. Axi's old face, Caros Soft, is out; a custom grotesque called Axi Saans is in, and the before/after frames make the shift obvious: tighter apertures, squarer curves, a more mechanical rhythm at large sizes. It carries headlines, UI labels and the app onboarding in one voice. Set white against the signature red, it is doing the job type is supposed to do in a rebrand: make the company sound like itself.

The grid discipline shows up clearest on the product pages. Cards for CFDs, Perpetual Futures and shares sit on a strict modular grid, each cell holding one fact: max leverage, product range, trading platform. One weight, one size step, generous margins. It reads like a data table that learned manners.

Where the system gets interesting is the 3D layer. Axi trades forex, shares, indices and commodities, and each category got its own dimension: chrome tiles with brand logos embossed, metallic lockpads and checkmarks, gold and copper bars for commodities. These were rendered through generative workflows instead of weeks of traditional 3D work per asset, and in motion each category reads at a glance.

The same asset logic drives the campaign side. Regional personas, built through a custom AI workflow and refined by hand, step from a banner into an animation into a new market without a reshoot. A phone render over dark rock, an onboarding card, a help chat tile: everything repeats the same red ticks, the same corner radius, the same card logic, so the system holds from the 150-page website down to a watchlist row.

#242. Why Your Website Should Never Stop Changing

Pierre Burgy is the co-founder and CEO of Strapi, the leading open-source headless CMS, and co-founder of Fimo, a product incubated at Strapi that keeps … More about Pierre ↬

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

This article has been kindly supported by our dear friends at Fimo, the infrastructure that keeps a website improving after launch. It runs over your real code, lets your team edit anything visually, and puts agents to work on content, accessibility, and the maintenance you never get to. Incubated at Strapi. Thank you!

Every website is at its best the day it ships. The final branch merges, the site goes live exactly as designed, and it is briefly perfect. It will never be this good again.

Not because anything breaks. The site keeps working. But the market moves, the messaging shifts, a competitor launches something, and the careful thing you built slowly stops matching the company it represents. A year later, it is a period piece. Not broken, just behind. Every team knows this decay, and almost everyone treats it as a law of nature.

It doesn’t have to be that way. A website could keep improving after launch instead of drifting away from its best day, quietly optimizing itself while the team that built it works on something else.

Picture it working: while you sleep, an agent catches that last week’s design-system change never propagated to the pricing page, and fixes it. Another finds a set of images shipped uncompressed in a rushed release and optimizes them. A third flags an accessibility regression a new component introduced, and either fixes it or leaves it for you to check. You wake up to a site that is measurably better than the one you left, and a short list of the few decisions the agents wanted your eyes on. That is the version worth wanting.

And the moment you take that promise seriously, you run into a problem that has nothing to do with the technology:

The obvious move, once you have capable agents, is to hand them the whole site. Let them write, edit, optimize, and publish, and get out of the way. It sounds like the natural endpoint, and it is the first thing most people picture when they hear “autonomous website.”

It is also the thing almost nobody wants once it is real in front of them.

We learned this the way you learn most things worth knowing: by building the opposite first. Building Fimo, an autonomous website platform, we set out to make websites fully autonomous, assumed that was the goal, and then watched what people actually did with it. What they did was hesitate. Not because they distrusted the agents, but because a website has no single owner. Different parts belong to different people, and each one wants a different amount of autonomy. So the question was never whether to trust the agents. It was where to draw the line, and for whom.

Once you ask it that way, the work splits cleanly into three kinds.

Start with the largest pile, because it is bigger than people expect. Most of what keeps a website healthy is rule-bound, repetitive, and completely joyless. Keeping accessibility compliant as pages change. Propagating a design-system update once a token moves. Catching a broken meta tag, an unoptimized image, a link that rotted when a URL changed three sprints ago.

None of this is where anyone’s talent lives. Nobody was hired because of their gift for spotting a missing alt attribute. This is the work you are actively relieved to hand off, and it is the work agents are best at, because it is defined by rules rather than taste. An agent that quietly keeps this layer correct across a whole site, unattended, is not a threat to anyone’s job. It is the tedious eighty percent finally taken care of.

Naming how much of the maintenance load actually lives in this pile is what makes the whole idea of an autonomous site feel less like a leap. You are not handing over judgment. You are handing over chores.

At the other end sits the work you would not delegate at any price. It is a small pile, but it is the reason you exist.

An agent can check a new page against every rule you have given it. It can confirm the contrast passes, the heading order is right, the tokens are correct, the copy matches the style guide. What it cannot do is decide what the page should feel like, or whether the thing you are shipping is, in the taste sense, good. That judgment is exactly what you were hired for, and no amount of capability moves it off your desk.

This is the part people reach for first when they resist autonomy, and they are right to protect it. The mistake is thinking the whole site is made of this kind of work. Almost none of it is. But that small part matters more than all the rest, which is why automating everything feels so wrong.

Between the chores and the untouchable sits the part no product can settle for you, because the line runs through different places for different people.

Notice what is happening there. It isn’t that one of them is cautious and the other reckless. It is that the same task carries different amounts of judgment for each of them. For one person it is a decision; for the other it is a chore. There is no default a product could ship that would be right for both, because “right” is a function of where your value sits, not of the task itself.

This is why the control has to be per-task and per-person, and why we stopped trying to find the setting that would work for everyone. There isn’t one. There is only the line each person draws, and the tools to draw it precisely.

Once you accept that the line is personal, a toggle between “approve” and “delegate” stops being enough. Where the line sits depends on what the agent is actually doing, so the real unit of control is the agent itself.

This is where it stopped being a settings problem, and it is the shape Fimo took. You don’t pick from a fixed menu of behaviors. You compose the agents, deciding what each one is even allowed to touch. You can build one from scratch, or take one close to your needs and shape it to your own line: an accessibility agent you trust to run unattended, a content agent you keep close to anything brand-facing.

And they don’t stay fixed. They learn from their tasks and from what you teach them, so the boundary you set last month isn’t the one you’re stuck with. What you had to approve then, you can delegate now, not because you lowered your guard but because the agent earned it. The line is not a setting you configure once. It moves as trust is earned, in the direction of less work for you.

None of this means flipping a site to autonomous on day one. In practice it goes the other way. You delegate a little, watch how it does, and loosen.

And you can actually watch. Every agent’s runs, its history, its logs, and a before-and-after of what it changed are there to inspect. Trust doesn’t grow because you got used to the idea; it grows because you can see what happened and compare. The first time an agent quietly fixes something you would have missed, and you can see exactly what it did, the next delegation gets easier.

Deadlines keep you from becoming the bottleneck on what you have already handed over. If you don’t weigh in, the agent proceeds. You set the terms once, and you stop being the thing the whole site waits on.

The worry people voice first is that an agent will change something on their site without them. Turn it around: the real risk is a site that never changes at all. A frozen site doesn’t stay safe. It just falls behind, slowly, in a way nobody notices until it represents a company that no longer exists.

The point of autonomy was never to remove you from your website. It was to remove the decay.

The point of autonomy is to keep the launch-day version from being the best version, and to let you spend your judgment on the handful of things that actually deserve it, while the rest takes care of itself. Draw the line where your value is. Let the agents hold everything on the other side of it. And let the line move as they prove they can.

#243. Behnaz Farahi creates Ocean of Dreams video installation for MIT Future Fest

Photography by MIT Media Lab (unless stated otherwise)

US-based designer Behnaz Farahi and the Critical Matter Group at the MIT Media Lab have projected sounds and video of the ocean alongside crowd-sourced messages into a public square for the university’s inaugural Future Fest symposium.

Called Ocean of Dreams, the installation was projected from the top of the MIT Museum down onto Kendall Plaza, a central square for the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT).

Farahi, who leads MIT Media Lab’s Critical Matter Group, mounted two Panasonic 30,000-lumen laser projectors and loaded an aerial view of the tides coming in and out for a hyper-realistic depiction of the ocean.

In the video, underneath the lapping waves, were words and phrases in dozens of languages collected from more than 400 international participants. Phrases such as “end to all wars” and “end poverty” were included to represent a hopeful vision of the future.

“Ocean of Dreams approaches hope not as passive optimism, but as a form of agency, the capacity to imagine that things could be otherwise,” said Farahi.

“At a time when the future feels increasingly uncertain and shaped by anxiety, I wanted to create a space where people could reclaim the act of imagining it. Perhaps one of the most radical things we can do right now is imagine.”

The footage was derived from the work of photographer Jan Erik Waider, while ocean sounds were mixed with ambient tracks from musician Justin Boreta.

In total, the projection surface covered around 2,850 square feet (264 square metres) and passersby could walk directly through the projection.

For Farahi, the installation represented a “way of thinking” beyond simply “designing objects”.

“From that perspective, we can also think about designing the future: not predicting it, but actively imagining and shaping the kinds of futures we want to live in,” said Farahi.

“For me, design is ultimately a way of asking: what could be otherwise, and how might we help bring that possibility into being. That is also how I think about Ocean of Dreams, as a space for collectively imagining and designing possible futures.”

It was the centerpoint of Future Fest, which brought together MIT scholars and outside thinkers to talk about evolving technologies. For the inaugural year, the festival focused on issues surrounding the ocean and included talks and open labs.

MIT Museum director Michael John Gorman, who led the event’s organisation, commented on the quick turnaround by Farahi, her students, and colleagues.

“She and her students pulled that together in three weeks just for this,” he told Dezeen.

Gorman said this shows the university’s attitude toward the event, which came together to support the festival.

Other recent sensory installations include Aesop’s suspension of paper books to create temporary perfumeries and an immersive kaleidoscopic installation in a New York skyscraper.

Future Fest took place from 30 September to 4 October in Cambridge, Massachusetts. For more events in architecture and design, visit Dezeen Events Guide.

Italian Brain Rot may be dumb nonsense for kids, but it could have profound effects on our creative work as a whole

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

If you’ve got kids under 12, you’ve probably heard them chanting “Tung tung tung sahur” around the house recently, asked what it means, and tumbled into an internet rabbit hole. If not, let me explain.

Tung tung tung sahur is one of many characters who've emerged from an internet culture called Italian brain rot, which emerged in early 2025 and has since taken over online spaces and physical playgrounds across the world.

These absurd, AI-generated creatures are have Italian-sounding names and are typically a mashup of two things that would never normally go together.

For instance, Ballerina Cappuccina is a dancer with a coffee cup for a head. Tralalero Tralala is a three-legged shark who wears Nikes on his, er, feet. Bombardiro Crocodilo is a crocodile crossed with a wartime bomber plane. You get the picture.

It's utter nonsense, but like a lot of utter nonsense, it's become big business. There are trading cards, a Panini sticker album, toys, Fortnite skins and a Roblox game called Steal a Brainrot.

And here's where things get relevant for anyone who's passed puberty. The latter has sparked a court case that could change what copyright means for anyone who uses generative AI in their work.

The subject of the case is Tung Tung Tung Sahur: a grinning wooden figure carrying a bat. It’s essentially an anthropomorphic rendering of the kentongan, a wooden drum beaten to wake Muslims for their pre-dawn meal, or sahur, during Ramadan in south-east Asia.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

The character was created by an Indonesian teenager, known as Noxa, using OpenAI's image generator. It became a global sensation, and now Noxa is represented by a French agency that specialises in this kind of thing, called Mementum (see what they did there?).

In September 2025, Mementum sent a cease and desist letter to the owners of Do Big Studios, the company behind Steal a Brainrot, over its use of the character. Do Big initially pulled the character, tried to negotiate a settlement, but when that failed they sued Mementum in a California federal court.

Do Big Studios' position seems watertight. In the US, copyright only protects work made by humans. A 2025 report by the US Copyright Office stated that you cannot copyright purely AI-generated material. There's some grey area, though: the same report said that work with sufficient human creative input might be protected, but would have to be considered on a case by case basis.

So how much human input went into Tung Tung Tung Sahur? Well, the character was literally generated about 15 minutes using seven prompts, starting with “draw a pentungan sahur with a face and legs”. Can me an old fuddy-duddy, but that doesn't sound like a lot of human input to me. But I'm not a legal expert, so we'll just have to see what the legal experts make of it.

And let me clear: the stakes are serious. If the court decides that a handful of prompts isn’t enough "human input" to protect creative work, that has big implications for how you make things for clients.

For example, if you create a logo, character or illustration for them partly or wholly using AI, that work might be unprotected. Which means, at the extreme, that the clients' rivals could copy it freely without any comeback. Which would beg the question what exactly the client is paying you for.

On the other hand, if the court finds that Tung Tung Tung Sahur is copyright-protected, that poses a lot of questions for clients employing freelancers and agencies who spend a lot of time painstakingly creating everything by hand. The idea that the client could make similar work themselves, just by a typing a few prompts, and still have it protected in law would make that option seem much more tempting.

Whatever the court decides, then, an entire profession of adults is about to be profoundly affected. Not bad for a teenager typing a few prompts into an AI bot.

Tom May is an award-winning journalist specialising in art, design, photography and technology. He is the author of the books The 50 Greatest Designers (Arcturus) and Great TED Talks: Creativity (Pavilion). Tom was previously editor of Professional Photography magazine, associate editor at Creative Bloq, and deputy editor at net magazine.

#247. Champ

Designed by Jesús López, Hermosillo, Mexico.

Located in the heart of the Mexican city of Hermosillo, Sonora, you will find Champ, a small boutique hotel. The street on which it is located is Campodónico, the surname of recognized waltz composer Rodolfo Campodónico, born in Hermosillo in 1866. He garnered a lot of recognition for his work during the early 20th century and his nickname was “Champ,” and that is from where the hotel took its name.

Champ celebrates the desert, the city, the local spirit and Sonoran traditions. Using imagery from old postcards and photos found in basements and thrift shops, its aim is to be as cozy and comfortable as possible for its guests.

The muted color palette was inspired by the arid northern Mexican region, where the vastness of the land and the sky reign supreme. A retro typography was chosen, since the old house where Champ is located was built in the 1970s.

#248. Not just bricks and mortar: how can gallerists operate without a permanent space?

Bolanle Contemporary, founded by Bolanle Tajudeen, has exhibited at No.9 Cork Street and Sadie Coles HQ, and is the only nomadic gallery at Frieze London this week Photo: Toby Bo Fan

When Bolanle Tajudeen announced her gallery in 2023, she was not sure what that meant. “I’ve just always wanted one, so I announced it, and I didn’t really have a plan,” she says. The curator and arts educator, known for her online art school, Black Blossoms, hoped to support emerging and mid-career artists through curatorial projects, rather than simply establishing a conventional commercial space. Thus, Bolanle Contemporary was born, without a permanent home or an immediate roster of artists. Three years on, it has exhibited with Frieze’s No.9 Cork Street and Sadie Coles HQ, as well as at fairs in London and Miami Beach.

Bolanle Contemporary held a solo presentation by Osman Yousefzada at No. 9 Cork Street last April Damian Griffiths

This year, Bolanle Contemporary is the only nomadic gallery to show at Frieze London. This comes after the fair formally removed galleries needing to have a physical space from its requirements for its contemporary art fairs earlier this year, starting with Frieze Seoul.

“Some of the most exciting galleries working today are operating without permanent spaces, or through a combination of temporary exhibitions, collaborations and fairs,” says Kristell Chadé, the executive director of fairs at Frieze. “We want our eligibility criteria to recognise the quality of a gallery’s programme rather than prescribe a single way in which it must operate.”

Eva Langret, Frieze’s director of Europe, the Middle East and Africa, notes that, even before starting her gallery, Tajudeen had “been part of London’s art scene for many years, creating opportunities for artists and practices that might otherwise go unseen”. At the fair, Bolanle Contemporary is taking part in Artist-to-Artist, a curated programme that sees established international artists select emerging ones for solo presentations. The New York-based Dominican artist Firelei Báez chose the Dominican American Eilen Itzel do Espírito Santo, “which feels like a fitting reflection of that spirit”, Langret says. Do Espírito Santo graduated with an MFA in painting from the Slade School of Fine Art in 2024, and is showing abstract paintings, prints, drawings and sculptures.

For Tajudeen, not having a physical space was never an act of defiance but one of necessity, she says, noting that it is “the biggest overheads [for a gallery] alongside participating in all of the international fairs”. She adds: “My goal is to have one eventually, but I don’t think the market right now is in a place where I can take that on.” Emerging and established galleries alike have felt this tension, with some of the industry’s biggest names having to close spaces in prime locations to stay afloat. Stephen Friedman Gallery, for example, closed its Tribeca space late last year before entering administration and closing its Cork Street flagship in February.

Yet for many gallerists this changing landscape presents an opportunity to reconsider what a gallery is and does. While forgoing a permanent physical space can mean missing out on organic connections generated by foot traffic, or relying on unconventional venues that might impose constraints on the artist’s work, on the other hand, it means that everything “does not always have to happen in the same building”, Chadé says, adding that she has noticed many galleries’ “willingness to think differently about how they support artists and create meaningful encounters with their work”.

In 2024 Artsy described the nomadic gallery model as part of a post-pandemic phenomenon driven by soaring real estate prices, a stronger relationship with technology globally and, sometimes, ethical reasons. But for some galleries, it is an integral part of their practice. One of these is Superposition Gallery, founded by the artist, curator and writer Storm Ascher in 2018, and primarily showing in temporary spaces in Los Angeles, New York and Miami. This includes exhibiting at Frieze Los Angeles over the past two years, making it one of the few nomadic galleries to have participated in Frieze’s contemporary art fairs before the criteria changed.

Superposition presented work by Helina Metaferia at this year’s Expo Chicago Courtesy of Superposition Gallery

Ascher explains that while a gallery’s “credibility is often measured by square footage”, Superposition is prospering regardless, having exhibited February James and Greg Ito at Frieze Los Angeles; the Philadelphia Museum of Art acquired a piece by Helina Metaferia from its 2026 stand at Expo Chicago; and at this year’s Armory Show, its artist Zoë Pulley won the fair’s inaugural Bronx Museum Acquisition Prize. “Without a permanent space, the fair is where Superposition physically comes to life, so I treat every booth as its own exhibition,” Ascher says. “I design it around the artist’s world rather than a neutral backdrop, and the response from collectors and institutions has been remarkable.”

Superposition also involves the locals of a fair, giving opportunities to those who might not engage with art in this way. “When we brought Alex Anderson to the Seattle Art Fair, [taking place earlier this year] in his hometown, the presentation carried on outside the fair with dinners and gatherings for the community that raised him,” Ascher says. “That kind of connection is our foundation.” She references criticism of the 1893 Chicago World’s Fair, an international exposition showcasing a range of human achievement from technology to fine art, where the committee was accused of purposefully excluding African Americans, as inspiration for this aspect of her approach. “[Journalist and activist] Ida B. Wells and [the abolitionist] Frederick Douglass handed out a pamphlet protesting that Black Americans had been left out,” she says. “So we build trust by showing up fully.”

Tajudeen describes Bolanle Contemporary as operating with an “artist-first” approach. For Tajudeen, this means helping the artist secure institutional placements, press coverage and introductions to curators, as well as developing broader networks both nationally and internationally. It also allows Bolanle Contemporary to direct more resources to exhibitions. “I really care about curating installations that are memorable and museum-worthy,” Tajudeen says, adding that she is particularly committed to solo and two-person shows. “Group shows are great marketing for the gallery, whereas solo shows are great marketing for the artists.”

At the Minor Attractions fair in 2024, Bolanle Contemporary exhibited Djofray Makumbu Courtesy of the artist and Bolanle Contemporary

For the 2025 edition of the alternative art fair Minor Attractions (which for the past three years has offered luxury hotel rooms as gallery spaces), Bolanle Contemporary transformed its room at The Mandrake Hotel into a traditional Jamaican wake. The presentation by the artist Ramone K. Anderson took the form of a shrine-like memorial inspired by Jamaican Nine-Night (a community vigil that runs in the days leading up to a formal farewell) with a stereo, hanging clothes, shelves of collectables and CDs. It was awarded the WYN Exhibitor Prize for best domestic booth presentation.

Tajudeen also points out that her gallery’s show with the British-Congolese artist Djofray Makumbu at Minor Attractions the year before saw the re-creation of a classic Congolese living room, complete with a nostalgic 1970s television, alongside videos and music from the country. “We tried to create [unique experiential exhibitions]—which we developed with the artist—without it being too like set design or gimmicky,” she says.

Tajudeen emphasises her distaste for the term “nomadic”, explaining that it does not encapsulate all that her gallery does. “The art world is all about words, and I think nomadic is a really ugly one; it’s not sexy,” she says. Instead, she calls Bolanle Contemporary “a contemporary art gallery with an international exhibition programme”. She adds: “Words that feel a bit more sophisticated could help more people in the arts move to this new way of running galleries without a fixed location.”

But, regardless of semantics, Frieze’s decision to alter its rules suggests that perceptions of what constitutes a gallery are changing. For Ascher, removing the requirement for real estate “lowers the barrier for young dealers, makes room for artists who’ve been shut out, and draws in collectors who want a relationship with the work, not just an asset”, she says. “A gallery can be wherever its people are, and the art world is richer for it.”

Several new fairs are debuting in the UK capital this year, while another changes venue

From the National Gallery to the Wallace Collection, a wave of museum shows suggests the intergenerational hang is here to stay, despite lingering reservations

The fair’s Presents section for younger galleries, often among its most vibrant sectors, features bold stands organised by ambitious dealers who understand the costs of doing business

After the gallery’s shock collapse, many of its artists are present at the fair under different representation
