#249. Omar Gandhi designs house and studio with "striking silhouette" for furniture maker

Omar Gandhi Architects has collaborated with furniture maker Brodye Chappell to build a house and workshop with a corrugated metal facade on Prince Edward Island, Canada.

Located in the agricultural area of Marshfield, just outside Charlottetown, the two-part property touches lightly on its surroundings.

“The intent was to create somewhat of a line in the dirt on the top of the agrarian landscape,” Omar Gandhi Architects (OGA) founder Omar Gandhi told Dezeen.

“There was an ambition to create a minimal response, and a striking silhouette in the farmstead landscape.”

The client – proprietor of Brodye Chappell Builds and Chappell Custom Homes – provided ongoing design input, crafted the interior millwork and furniture and led the piecemeal construction on evenings and weekends, leveraging help from friends, colleagues and tradespeople on the island.

Omar Gandhi, who has offices in Nova Scotia, Ontario and Germany, designed the building’s form and exterior palette.

Settled along the property line, the spaces look out to Chappell’s parents’ horse farm.

“The architecture borrows from rural vernacular building forms – elongated rooflines, agricultural profiles – then abstracts them into something leaner and more contemporary,” OGA said.

“A gable roof pairs with a hyper‑extended hip, producing a familiar silhouette sharpened into new form.”

Light-grey corrugated metal runs down the slope of the roof and along the exterior walls, shielding the spaces from summer sun, rainy shoulder seasons and winter snowfall.

Broken by vertical stripes of glass and black detailing, the metallic finish reflects the surrounding sky and helps the house blend into its surroundings, where it sits just above the grassy fields.

On one end, the primary suite opens to a small porch underneath the slope of the hip roof, while on the other, the workshop dissolves into wooden slats that fold open as a concealed garage door.

The shared family spaces are on one edge of the courtyard, while the workshop is on the other.

“The interior palette is warm and bright with wood, crafted pieces and a collection of art and fixtures from friends and colleagues,” Gandhi said.

“The garage is quite raw – concrete floors, exposed structure and enough wall space for tools and materials.”

While walls and delicate pendant lights give the house a soft finish, the workshop is outfitted with skateboards and a glass garage door.

“The Chappell Residence is a home built slowly, with intention,” the studio said.

“Rooted in land, labour and family connection, it stands as a place lived in and made by hand – an architecture where work and life form one continuous narrative.”

Other homes OGA recently completed in Nova Scotia include a Corten-steel cabin, a coastal cedar house and a cascading cedar lake property.

#251. Branding: Gunnersbury Park Museum Identity by Wiedemann Lampe

Wiedemann Lampe gave Gunnersbury Park Museum identity a centenary refresh, building it around playful icons and confident yellow wayfinding.

The brief had real tension. Gunnersbury is 72 hectares of Grade II listed parkland in West London, once home to royalty and Rothschilds, now a free space that belongs to everyone: picnickers, dog walkers, Park Runners, wedding parties. More than a million people visit each year, yet many regulars had no idea the museum existed. The new identity had to read as a civic institution and a playground at once. Wiedemann Lampe answered with a system built on icons: hand-drawn birds, hands, suns, eyes and vases that fill the shapes of a tree and a museum, a folk-art emblem for a place that holds many different lives.

A condensed grotesque does the naming. GUNNERSBURY sets in white, PARK & MUSEUM in a warm yellow, stacked tight on a deep parkland green. The brand architecture splits cleanly: the park takes green, the museum takes purple, each with its own icon, while the master lockup keeps the yellow pair. It is a sensible hierarchy that still reads as one family.

Type gets playful at the edges. Headlines arch across cafe bags and posters: WANDER AND UNWIND, DISCOVER AND DELIGHT. The centenary banner hides its best detail in plain sight, with the two zeroes of GUNNERSBURY 100 drawn as yellow circles filled with the icon set. A quiet serif sets the tagline, Discover, Play, Enjoy, and leaves the shouting to the grotesque.

The wayfinding is where the system earns its keep. Yellow fingerpost arms point to the Meadows, the Cafe, the Sports Hub and Kew Bridge Station, each carrying its small icon, and the same marks get painted large on the park paths, turning a walk into a treasure trail. Welcome boards, interpretation panels and pond signs repeat the deep green and yellow across the whole estate.

Collateral plays the full range. A green cafe bag arches FOR ALL LIFE'S RICH FLAVOURS over tone-on-tone icons, a kraft cup wears the eye and curl marks at billboard scale, and a sticker sheet of birds, kites, vases and magnifiers puts the whole system in children's hands. The wedding book, staff uniforms and apparel all speak the same language.

The Brazilian-born artist talks about her work and influences.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Isabella Nalin Fais is a vis dev and concept artist currently living in Paris. Growing up in Brazil has influenced her art to be colourful and expressive. She always tries to include storytelling in pieces to create a connection, sometimes mixing 3D with 2D techniques.

We caught up with her to learn more about her career and cartoon characters. If you need to upgrade your own setup for digital art, see our guides to the best drawing tablets and the best laptops for drawing.

I grew up in the south of Brazil, where the weather is pretty hot. I remember being surrounded by nature and vibrant colours, and that translated to the way I pick colours when I paint.

Animated films and cartoons always had a major influence in my art. Especially the old ones, like Winnie the Pooh, and stop-motion movies like Coraline. I always try to paint in a way that you could relate to the character as if you’re watching a movie.

Besides that, having an interest in musical instruments influences me to think of brushstrokes as if they have a rhythm so the read of a piece feels like a flow.

My first paid commission was an illustration for a stream pack, for Twitch. It was a lo-fi bedroom at night, pretty cosy. It was not the most technically impressive work, but people liked it because of the purple mood and colours I used. It was years ago, so today the quality would hopefully be better, but everything has its own time.

If I could talk to my younger self, I would advise her to be confident while making mistakes. When you’re starting, sometimes it’s easy to be frustrated with results, but it’s the failure that makes you a better artist. Enjoying the process and then moving on to the next piece is the best thing to do to improve.

I really identify with my latest project, Pepo. It’s a world-building project about a little duck who leaves home to seek his dreams. It reminds me of the innocence of being young and ambitious without knowing where it will lead you, even when you’re scared. I left home at a young age to study animation and it feels somewhat similar to that.

My next step is to keep growing and improving, especially making more room for plain air painting. I want to work on the readability and simplification of my pieces as well as keep working to make my moods and storytelling sharper than ever.

The goal is to be able to communicate feelings through my art, hopefully to a point I can help animated movies or game productions to bond with the audience with meaningful stories.

You can see more of Isabella’s work on her ArtStation profile. .

An advert for the high-speed rail service features a picture of the Impressionist painting, which depicts the boisterous entertainment centre at the top of Montmartre, just beyond a sliding train door.

For British art afficados, there are plenty of reasons to travel to Orsay, but Dance at the Moulin de la Galette is not one of them. “Why wouldn’t you?”, Eurostar asks in its advert. They needed a design system that not only spoke to all of those use cases, but stood out as its own brand.

Just because its implementation would often be behind-the-scenes doesn’t mean the identity of the brand has to hide in the shadows. We helped them craft something with a bit of a digital edge — something that could live in the dark mode world, but had some really beautiful color and animation to make spending time with it that much more pleasant.

Since launch, LiveKit has been named the “Fastest Growing WEBRTC Stack” and has been featured as one of GitHub’s Top 10 Fastest Growing Repos in Q3 2021 and Q2 2022. s pretending to be circles. But if you’ve ever met a real , you’ll know that they’ve got a lot more going for them. Dressed in SVG, they fit into a wider range of crowds than a humble
wearing HTML/CSS can. has a strict no .html policy.

The tag is not as static as its name suggests. Any embedded JavaScript unfortunately won’t run if you load an SVG file with an tag, but CSS animations work perfectly fine. Many of the SVG attributes do have CSS property counterparts, and the geometry properties have been supported across the major browsers since 2024. Some attributes that you might want to animate, like viewBox, don’t have equivalents yet.

Besides JavaScript and CSS, there’s another way to animate SVGs: Synchronized Multimedia Integration Language (SMIL). Despite its quirks, it’s still worth learning. Like CSS animations, SMIL animations also work in tags and can fully animate everything in an SVG, without JavaScript.

If you’ve never heard of SMIL or need a refresher, check out Andy Clarke’s well-named article. Then we’ll look at a way to plan an animation and make SMIL markup more manageable.

SMIL has a problem: it gets bloated quickly. Unlike CSS and JavaScript, where you can list multiple properties in each keyframe and easily reuse animations, each SMIL tag can only target one element and only one property of that element at a time. A property can be animated through a list of values. But it is still one tag, one element, one property. The shortest way you can write a color and opacity change that will run is the following:

That’s not bad, but consider that it needs to be repeated for every element included in the animation. A SMIL animation can quickly get longer than its CSS equivalent.

To make things easier when starting a new animation, let’s plan all of the elements and properties we want to animate, and create a list of descriptive IDs for each tag.

Meet Smashing Workshops on front-end, design & UX, with practical takeaways, live sessions, video recordings and a friendly Q&A. With Brad Frost, Stéph Walter and so many others.

I like to plan my animations using what’s called a timing chart. A timing chart is effectively a line segment; some choose horizontal lines, others prefer vertical, which is a great analogy for animation as a whole because line segments can run parallel, overlap, and follow each other with or without a gap. Just like animations.

For now, we’re only interested in when animations start and stop. When drawing our charts, we’ll forget about the in-between lines and instead draw a line for each component animation, marking the beginning and end. I like to annotate timing with a circle and a bar. You can draw your chart using whatever, and it doesn’t have to be exactly to scale, as long as the relative timing between all the little animations that make up the whole is clear. Besides, adding labels for the durations is an easy cheat to get around drawing to scale.

Here is a demo of how I typically set up a timing chart with more than one animation:

See the Pen [colorAndOpacityChange [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/01a016dc-399c-7652-b172-4cd4663746b9) by Johan Grobler.

The important thing to note is that the timing chart lines are arranged according to how the animations are arranged in time. One piece of the animation follows the next piece, which is followed by a subsequent piece, and so forth. It visualizes how the animation’s parts run together and cascade over time.

A big part of SMIL is synchronization. It’s even in the name, after all. And there are multiple ways to specify when an animation should start (here’s a test case to check what your browser supports). One of the most useful ways is with a syncbase value, which is a SMIL tag’s ID followed by either .begin or .end, with an optional positive or negative offset.

Let’s piggyback off the previous animation example that includes changes in color and opacity. If we want the opacity animation to start 300 milliseconds before the color animation finishes, we could do arithmetic. Alternatively, the second animation can use the syncbase value colorChange.end - 300ms. This way, the relative timing between the two animations becomes explicit.

Using syncbase values, the beginning of an animation is positioned in time relative to the .begin or .end of some other animation. A positive offset moves the start to the right (forwards in time), and a negative offset to the left (backwards in time).

See the Pen [syncbase.end [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/emgwwGJ) by Johan Grobler.

Something with negative offsets is that they can specify a time before the document has loaded or when a click happens. Computers can’t predict the future (at least not yet). The best they can do is jump the animation to where it would have been had the computer peeked into the future to preemptively start the animation. The second animation only runs from start to finish if there is enough room, so to speak.

See the Pen [syncbase.begin [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/xbgooXq) by Johan Grobler.

Syncbase values don’t only allow you to connect animations from .end to .begin. Elect a primary animation; the animation that first comes to mind is usually the best representation of the group. All secondary animations can be set with begin="primary.begin". I’ve only used the ID #primary for emphasis. That way, all the other animations begin relative to that starting point. Stacking animations like this reduces maintenance if, say, we later want the whole group to start at a different time.

Let’s put the idea to work and build a loading indicator (or spinner). Then we’re going to explore how changing the relative timing between the parts changes the effect of the whole animation:

Browsers have wide support for the prefers-reduced-motion media feature and Val Head explains this in depth in another article. We definitely want to respect this user preference as we consider moving things around. In fact, consider it non-negotiable.

There are various approaches to adhering to a user’s prefers-reduced-motion setting when it comes to SMIL. Each with its pros and cons. Evaluating early on what’s going to work best for your use case could save you a partial rewrite down the line.

For example, we could consider using a element instead of a plain because supports multiple elements that can be used as fallbacks in a media attribute for reduced motion preferences.

Or one SVG file with an inline CSS @media query that uses display: none to swap between versions. That said, it’s an approach that might cause trouble in various environments. But browsers are continuously changing, and this might not be an issue in the future.

You might also consider a CSS background-image instead because we can wrap that style in a media query — @media (prefers-reduced-motion) — that sets a static image as the fallback for reduced motion preferences.

There are even more options we can turn to! For example, SVG’s element can also be used to swap things out for motion preferences.

Or, if we prefer everything bundled together, we can use JavaScript .matchMedia() and the handy SMIL DOM interface to control which animations start instead of completely switching out files.

For this, I’m avoiding any motion and sticking to opacity animations, which tend to cause less trouble. For a non-interactive animation like this, we can load it in an tag. When we add motion, we can go the route to show the most appropriate version of our animation.

We’re going to do our own version of the classic three-dot spinner:

See the Pen [StaticDots [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/01a016e5-c44d-75b3-bbb2-3eca2f83932d) by Johan Grobler.

SVG wizards might be able to do everything directly in a text editor. I recommend using a graphic editor like Inkscape if you’re having trouble visualizing how the markup will be rendered. Once again, Andy Clarke has a great article about his process for optimizing and structuring his own drawings.

Note: There’s a gotcha with Inkscape. Setting what you would expect to be an element’s ID via the Layers window actually sets the value of a metadata attribute used internally by Inkscape. Use Inkscape’s object properties or XML editor window to set the true element’s ID. Your mileage may vary with a different editor. Also, in Inkscape, remember to save the file as optimized SVG when the drawing is done to strip away unneeded metadata.

OK, so we’re sticking with the opacity animation idea. The dots are going to fade in and out. We’ll use separate tags for those. Six tags in total.

Our naming scheme is going to be straightforward: we’ll call them #fadeIn and #fadeOut, and to differentiate between each pair of tags, we’ll postfix the tag’s ID with either Left, Middle or Right. Try to follow a convention that makes sense to you when coming up with your own IDs.

The fade-in tag for the dot on the left:

And the fade-out for the middle dot:

We have an infinite number of ways in which we could space these six animations in time. Let’s look at a couple of choice examples alongside their timing charts to see how changing the arrangement of the parts impacts the visual effect of the whole animation.

To narrow our choices a bit, all of the tags will use the same dur value, and none of the syncbase values will have offsets.

For someone coming from a culture that reads from left to right, the dots appearing on screen along the same pattern would feel natural. Let’s also start with all the dots fading out together at the end:

See the Pen [dotsVersion1 [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/01a016ec-0b1b-731e-bf44-2dd45b7c075f) by Johan Grobler.

Syncbase values stagger the fade-ins and restart the loop when the dots have disappeared:

Since all the fade-outs end at the same time, it is an arbitrary choice which one we use to restart the loop. We’ll consider #fadeOutLeft as the primary animation here and also synchronize the other fade-outs to it with the syncbase value fadeOutLeft.begin. Later, if we want to move the fade-outs in time, all we do is change when #fadeOutLeft starts.

Instead of a group fade-out, we could stagger them just like the fade-ins:

Without adding an offset, there are a couple of points in time we could start #fadeOutLeft at. If it starts on fadeInRight.end:

See the Pen [dotsVersion2 [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/01a016ef-1be0-7359-a8ce-1d45194ed50a) by Johan Grobler.

The visual effect is subtly changed by moving up a spot and starting #fadeOutLeft on fadeInMiddle.end instead:

See the Pen [dotsVersion3 [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/01a016ef-f4d9-745b-a89f-2ff35d898589) by Johan Grobler.

We can see from the charts that we could try moving up a spot further to fadeInLeft.end:

See the Pen [dotsVersion4 [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/01a016f1-07f8-732a-966d-c295618c60d7) by Johan Grobler.

How about starting the sequence with a fade-out:

See the Pen [dotsVersion5 [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/01a016f1-b6a5-7078-a73c-217459f53e20) by Johan Grobler.

You might prefer to start with the dot in the middle:

See the Pen [centerFirstDots [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/01a016f2-5f78-70a2-a948-f030c147fbe3) by Johan Grobler.

As you iterate on your animation, timing charts are a great way to keep track of your work, and they make visual comparison between versions possible. And by drawing a timing chart, you might even see a pattern in the timing between the parts of the animations that you might otherwise have missed.

As you animate more elements and properties, it gets harder to keep track of what starts when. To see how timing charts can help you make sense of things, let’s build on the basic spinner:

See the Pen [staticDotsWithClipPaths [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/01a016f4-f99c-7779-b526-1265ecf5619b) by Johan Grobler.

I’ve added a for each dot to the drawing. We’ll move those into to a tag and remove the fill="white". As the animation runs, the rectangles are going to move over the dots for a different approach to animating the stroke than by animating stroke-dashoffset.

We only need a single for all three dots, but it adds structure to the document, and it’s good practice to wrap it, and similar tags, in a tag:

Remember to set the clip path for the s. Either with CSS or using the clip-path attribute:

Because the dots now have a stroke added, to leave their size unchanged, we need to compensate by subtracting half the value of stroke-width from r:

That’s all the changes the graphics need. Have a look at the animated version with its timing chart, then we’ll look in more detail at the changes that have been made to the animation:

See the Pen [clipPathDots [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/01a016f8-73b0-707a-b21a-7aa07fb194b2) by Johan Grobler.

There’s a new animation, #moveClipPathLeft, that starts the whole sequence, and to tweak the animation’s rhythm a bit, there’s a 1s delay between when the fade-outs end and the loop restarts:

You could use s to move the rectangles instead, but we need to move them back to their starting positions at the end for a smooth restart of the animation. You’ll need to take into account which tags can animate and set which data types if you do decide to animate the transform attribute instead of translating the rectangles with the y attribute.

To change things up, the for the middle dot moves down:

We’re also using the fill-opacity property instead of the opacity property for the fade-ins, and they’ve been synchronized to start once a dot’s clipping has finished moving:

The fade-outs still use the normal opacity property, so both the fill and stroke fade out together. Because this arrangement is set up to use a group fade-out at the end, there are a few places the markup could be optimized. One of them is dropping the fill="freeze" to automatically reset the dot’s opacity back to its starting value once the tag finishes running:

For the tags that did use fill="freeze", we’ll use tags to reset those properties back to their starting values. I’ve simplified the chart a little by lumping those tags together. Because these tags don’t have a duration over which they act, on the chart I’ve drawn the start and end markers over each other.

To reset the fill-opacity on the left dot:

If you use fill="freeze" with the fade-outs, you’ll need an extra for each dot to reset the middle dot’s opacity:

The last thing we need to do is move the clipping rectangles back to their starting positions. For the right :

That’s just one of the possible timing variations, and most of what you’ll need to try some of the others, as we did with the basic spinner, is already in place. You might want to have a try at coming up with a couple of your own alternate timings.

To sum things up, we know that balancing the different stages of an animation can be difficult at best, and untenable at worst. Any time we get into multi-step animations that exceed one or two steps, it’s a form of orchestration. You’re almost building a Rube Goldberg machine of markup. And using a timing chart is a strategy I use that I hope will help you in your projects as well. They are outlines of what to expect and when, allowing you to map things out in a way that not only helps plan your code, but also makes future updates and maintenance a lot more bearable than going into it without a plan.

While a timing chart can’t reduce the complexity of the markup, it can give a good overview of what should happen when. Timing charts are definitely not limited to SMIL animations. Unfortunately, syncbase values are, and they can still help even if you’re going to use a different approach to implementing your animation.

I highly recommend checking out Andy’s other articles on Smashing Magazine. There’s even more stuff on combining CSS and SVG.

Yosra Emad wrote a great article on creating animations with multiple steps in CSS, and you might want to try drawing a few timing charts as you read through it.

When you’re ready to start adding those in-between lines to your timing chart, Nash Vail’s article on easing dives deep into the details of easing curves.

You might also be interested in tests for your browser’s SVG implementation to see what is supported.

#258. Recycled-plastic plinths hold furniture at "secret" Barragán house in Mexico City

Photography by Juan Hernandez (unless stated otherwise)

For Design Week Mexico 2026, design studio 2×1 displayed works by French and Mexican designers on plinths in the gardens of Casa Ortega, a rarely opened private residence designed by local architect Luis Barragán in the 1940s.

The Creative Immersions France-Mexico 2026 exhibition featured furniture and design objects by over 30 designers.

It was the result of three years of residency programs in which French designers travel across different regions of Mexico to work with local artisans, craftsmen and studios.

The pieces, which include an assortment of furniture, bags, vessels and more, were displayed across a system created by Paris- and Mexico City-based studio 2×1.

The studio worked with Mexican materials company New Fibers to create dark-red plinths made of Polyroca, a plastic panel made of recycled post-industrial laminated cardboard waste.

The team also created more extensive display units made of industrial metal structures and fabric awnings.

The works included a 2026 stool by French designer Fanny Serouart and Taller Maya, a group that connects Mayan artisans with global markets, and vessels created by French designer Matali Crasset and Mexican studio And Jacob.

Other collaborations presented include a bright yellow metal chair by Paris-based design group Hall Haus and Mexico City-based studio Neko Design, created in 2024.

The works were distributed in the corners and open verandas of the gardens of Casa Jardín Ortega (Casa Ortega), Luis Barragán’s personal residence that predated the more famed Casa Luis Barragán, which sits just next door in the San Miguel Chapultepec neighbourhood.

Designed between 1942 and 1947, Casa Ortega was a house for the architect in his 40s. He experimented with different motifs and structures in the house that he would later implement in Casa Luis Barragán, but it is distinguished by its expansive gardens.

Its caretakers consider it “Barragán’s best-kept secret”.

Local silversmith Alfredo Ortega Rojas purchased the property in 1947 after Barragán moved out, giving the house its name.

Today, Casa Ortega is privately owned and stewarded by Ortega’s descendants and family, including local architect José Manuel Bárcena.

The family keeps Casa Ortega relatively restricted to visitors, as it is currently inhabited. For Design Week Mexico 2026, however, it is hosting tours and has opened the gardens for the Creative Immersions exhibition.

Supported by a group that includes the French Embassy in Mexico, the Creative Immersions residencies focus on “200 years of cultural, intellectual, artistic, and economic exchange” between Mexico and France, with the intent to blend traditional and contemporary design.

Creative Immersions France-Mexico 2026 was curated by C Cúbica Arquitectos, whose co-founder Andrea Cesarman organises Design Week Mexico and was a founding member of the event eighteen years ago.

Dezeen previously rounded up eleven designers that used surprising sustainable materials at Design Week Mexico 2025 and ten noteworthy exhibitions from the week in 2023.

The Creative Immersions France-Mexico 2026 exhibition is on show at Casa Ortega from 5 to 25 October. For more events, talks and installations in architecture and design, visit the Dezeen Events Guide.

Photography by Juan Hernandez (unless stated otherwise)

#259. Studio Marcus Kraft Unveils Klangwelt Toggenburg Rebrand

Studio Marcus Kraft built the Klangwelt Toggenburg rebrand around a dynamic typeface whose letters expand and scatter like sound in the Alps.

The key visual says everything in one frame: the wordmark set huge in white over the Toggenburg valley, its letters breaking into repeating fragments that drift apart like overtones. Studio Marcus Kraft calls it typographic resonance, and the metaphor holds across the whole system. Sound frequencies, harmonics, the contour lines of the terrain, all of it lands in how the letters behave. The palette stays out of the way: black type on white paper, photography carrying the greens and rock greys of the valley. The work picked up Silver at the 2026 European Design Awards, ADC Switzerland Silver and a TDC Tokyo Certificate.

The face introduces itself in the specimen: "Hello. I am the custom font of Klangwelt Toggenburg. My name is Klangwelt Regular." Font engineering came from David Jonathan Ross, and the construction shows. A compact grotesque with tight apertures, set large enough that stroke ends read as physical mass. The modular trick is the repeating letter elements: fragments of K, g and y detach and scatter, so headlines can stretch, compress and dissolve while staying legible. The same logic drives the wordmark, the wayfinding discs on the Klangweg trail and the animated trailers. Layout principles, grids included, are codified in the design manual.

Everything physical sits on white. The stationery suite, letterheads, cards and envelopes, runs the scattered wordmark across uncoated stock with an even, catalog-like light. Two bound volumes make up the design manual, its table of contents reading like a syllabus: values, wordmark, brand architecture, typography, grid, color, materiality. The Programm '25 brochure pairs the broken-apart headlines with full-bleed valley photography, and the steel wayfinding discs carry the system out onto the trail itself. A new website by vitamin 2, animation by Miriam Palopoli and a sonic logo by Christian Zehnder complete the rollout, which began with the Klangweg reopening in 2024 ahead of the Klanghaus opening in 2025.

#262. Andy Matthews Studio designs Dulwich cricket pavilion to be antithesis of "off-the-shelf generic designs"

Architecture practice Andy Matthews Studio has unveiled a black, contemporary cricket pavilion on Dulwich Common, south London.

Built for Streatham & Marlborough Cricket Club, the pavilion stands alongside Dulwich Common overlooking the club’s main pitch.

The mono-pitch main form was designed to be a contemporary expression of a traditional cricket pavilion, while demonstrating the quality of facilities possible for community sports clubs.

“The concept was to create a contemporary interpretation of a traditional cricket pavilion and club room space allowing the viewing of both pitches from within whilst meeting the [England and Wales Cricket Board] ECB requirements for modern cricket facilities,” Andy Matthews Studio founder Andy Matthews told Dezeen.

“Community clubs often end up with rudimentary, unimaginative buildings, or adapted shipping containers, due to limited budgets available,” he continued.

“Despite budget constraints, the project proposes the idea that clubs and community groups can achieve, and deserve, site-specific generous light-filled spaces rather than off-the-shelf generic design.”

While traditional cricket pavilions have simple pitched roof forms and are predominantly white, the Dulwich pavilion has a distinct mono pitch roof and is clad in black, Japanese burnt larch cladding, which contrasts with a white clock.

“We took that traditional cricket pavilion form – a pitched roof – and twisted it by splitting it in two and extending the roof form to create the canopies that define the entrances and public areas while providing solar shading and little gathering spots,” said Matthews.

“And there’s the inversion of colour – the black cladding with the white clock face,” he continued.

“The black blends into the broad expanses of sky and landscape, giving the impression that it’s been there a long while, part of nature just like the old willow tree.”

The building was designed to be compact and is 100 square meters smaller than the structure it replaced. Its main, mono-pitch form contains a multipurpose hall that is enclosed on two sides with full-height, sliding glass doors.

This glazing gives the clubroom views of both the main pitch and the secondary pitch, while a large canopy overhangs the doors to create a protected outside area to watch matches.

While it was created with match days in mind, it was also designed to be a flexible space that could be rented to provide income for the club.

“A community building has to work for the whole community, so we designed the pavilion as a robust, adaptable setting for pretty much all of life, seven days a week,” said Matthews.

“The clubroom is generous and flexible, so it can hold the big occasions – christenings, birthdays, weddings, wakes – as comfortably as everyday activities like yoga classes, forest school, writing groups, and community meetings,” he continued.

“That versatility also makes the building financially sustainable. The revenue it generates pays for its upkeep, so the club shouldn’t need to fundraise again.”

Alongside the main space are a pair of changing rooms that are accessed directly from the pitch. Each of these spaces contains a toilet, showers and a bench that has direct views of the pitch to allow players to observe the game while preparing to play.

The other, smaller, mono-pitched volume contains the bar and kitchen for the clubroom, as well as the toilets.

Overall, Matthews hopes that the pavilion goes beyond being a functional, traditional pavilion.

“The pavilion brings a calm but joyful response to the site rather than simply meeting a functional brief for minimum space requirements,” he said.

“This contemporary response is designed to appeal to a wider and more diverse audience than might normally be associated with cricket in the UK,” Matthews continued.

“The building is conceived as a modest, almost agricultural building within a landscape. Externally clad in dark-stained timber and crowned with a black corrugated sheet metal roof, the building is made of mass timber to speed up construction and reduce carbon impact.”

#263. Comment | The Bayeux Tapestry should prompt a conversation about the environmental war we are living through

The Bayeux Tapestry is displayed in a 70m-long display case at the British Museum

The once-in-a-lifetime loan of the Bayeux Tapestry to the British Museum might prove highly frustrating in 40 for years for those wanting to celebrate the millennium of the Norman invasion. The timing is, on the face of it, quite arbitrary, down to the determination of certain individuals—including, laudably, Emmanuel Macron—but also more prosaically because the museum in Bayeux is closed for renovation.

Perhaps this is all the better. The return of the object itself to England at any time is an event worth celebrating, unencumbered by meaningless anniversaries or cultural diplomacy. Shuffling down the 70m-long display case, it is impossible not to become absorbed by the story that the embroidery tells, but also the often-bizarre way that it is told. The shapes and colours of trees, horses, waves, architecture, the famous comet and a whole bestiary of animals, real and imaginary, braided in wool died with woad and madder on bleached linen, are often so strange that the world described seems far more exotic than 11th-century France and Britain.

Part of this absorption is the way that the story unfolds with such narrative brilliance. The premises are laid out by Harold's ill-fated envoy to France, then his duplicity on return, unleashing the second chapter, the building up of French forces and the invasion. The culmination of the action is in truth not the grisly death of Harold, but rather the great scene of tumbling horses, in which the spinning, helpless horses symbolise the utter defeat of the English and the world turned upside down.

It is this scene that sticks most in my mind. The horses become the symbol for the bouleversement, as the French might say, of the invasion, the feeling of time itself coming out of joint, of catastrophic upheaval. And it is this upheaval and change, bringing with it a flavour of the apocalypse, that lends the Bayeux exhibition significance at this juncture in history.

The week that the exhibition opened, the United Nations made the grave announcement from Nairobi that we have failed the limit of 1.5ºC of warming, the figure set by the Paris Agreement in 2015, and which now looks to be surpassed by some margin. The government report from earlier this year, Global Biodiversity Loss, Ecosystem Collapse and UK National Security, warned that the collapse of ecosystems around the world would have a catastrophic effect on life on Britain, let alone those far more vulnerable nations around the world—food shortages, mass migration, the collapse of civil society and devastating war. So stark are the findings from the joint intelligence committee that only a heavily redacted version of the report has been published to date. It seems highly likely that the world of 2066 will be entirely different from the one that we currently inhabit, far more so than ours is from the world of 1066, when the Normans conquered England.

As guardian spaces of human culture, museums should be planning for this future and at the very least commissioning resilience plans. Three years ago, a report was written in the wake of a climate conference at Tate Modern, which laid out much important groundwork. And yet the situation has deteriorated more rapidly than any could have imagined, as the recent UN announcement makes clear. Beyond the basic need to decarbonise and be sustainable, there are the security and civil society impacts laid out in the joint intelligence committee report, from which no institution—especially museums whose revenue is based on mass tourism and who care for objects in climate-controlled conditions—can afford to disregard.

The British Museum itself might consider commissioning a ‘Bayeux Report’ to commemorate the historic loan and project the role of the museum in a changing world over the next 40 years—especially now we know that decarbonising and achieving net zero by 2050 is unlikely to be enough to stop passing into the ‘catastrophic’ realms of warming above 1.5ºC. On a practical level, such a report would offer steering for how museums can physically cope with climate extremes—not just of fire and flood, but also of the likely end of mass tourism, or its replacement with mass climate migration, the breakdown of civil society, economic insecurity, and the need to foster cooperation and mutual support in such a catastrophically upturned world. It would, in short, be a report on museums as beacons of human endeavour and hope during wartime.

There is also an ethical obligation for such strategic projection. Earlier this year, in response to criticism of the postponement of a planned lecture due to possible protest and disruption, the British Museum published its first coherent statement of moral positioning on current debates. The director, Nicholas Cullinan, wrote: “Museums exist to facilitate learning, inquiry and debate. They are not merely buildings that house objects; they are civic spaces where histories can be examined and contested through evidence, scholarship and discussion.” Difficult times require difficult conversations, Cullinan stated, and it is the task of the museum to enable those conversations without fear of “cancellation” or physical intimidation. These words signal a dramatic policy change. Rather than doing all it can to keep out of the newspapers, as past institutional leaders have urged, the museum has entered a new era of direct public statement and engagement.

By initiating a “difficult conversation” on the subject of climate change now, in this pivotal Bayeux year, the British Museum could create bridges that in the future will prove of vital importance, especially in light of its highly damaging sponsorship deal with BP—reputation enhancement in return for a sum of money that amounts to around three hours of corporate profit during the bombing of Iran earlier this year.

Commissioning a ‘Bayeux Report’ would be just one aspect of such a conversation. A more immediate opportunity exists in the form of the People’s Emergency Briefing, the powerfully effective and entertaining documentary film that is currently being screened in venues around the UK (although has yet to be shown in any museum). The genius of the film is that it records ‘ordinary’ people’s responses to the sober laying-out of the facts on climate change and nature loss by eight experts, including the Lancaster University professor Mike Berners-Lee. The film gives viewers a language for discussing an otherwise extremely worrying and difficult topic.

Few other museums could mount an exhibition as stunning as that of the Bayeux Tapestry at the British Museum. Those lucky enough to visit the exhibition will experience world heritage at its most important, brilliantly and powerfully displayed.

The British Museum, along with the Musée du Louvre in Paris and the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York, the Berlin museums, and institutions such as the Iraq Museum in Baghdad, which has been so well supported by the British Museum, are the institutions that preserve and interpret this world heritage. The British Museum has taken a leading role in many international initiatives in response to war and disaster. The commissioning of a ‘Bayeux Report’, alongside screenings of the People’s Emergency Briefing and other climate events, could connect this engagement to the environmental war that is now raging around our shared planet, and create a powerful legacy for a remarkable exhibition.

#265. Bát Tràng Museum

Designed by M — N Associates, Ho Chi Minh City.

The Bát Tràng Museum stands as the first private museum authorized by the government within Bát Tràng Village, founded by National Artist Vũ Đức Thắng. Originally named “Hồn Đất Việt” — translated as “Viet’s Ceramic Soul” — this museum embodies his remarkable legacy. Vũ Đức Thắng gained widespread recognition for his spectacular creation of 12 remarkably genuine pottery boots, earning the Guinness Record in 2013. His artistic skills include a collection of modern artworks highlighted by two unique techniques: color-changing ceramic glaze and intricate three-dimensional sculpting. These methods display his mastery and creativity in ceramic art.

We carefully researched and studied to include his unique artistic techniques and style in creating a new look for the museum. This involved giving the museum a new name and creating a unique custom typeface MN Vũ Thắng with “pottery-shoes-soul” inktrap touches. We wanted to echo his process and masterpieces into the content system.

The brand’s visual system was created to resonate with the beauty of the various unique artworks while systematizing them into an archive through a new, clean photography style. A deliberate pottery silhouette canvas was employed for buttons and patterns across different applications, maintaining a unique and relative aesthetic. This design approach bonded to a grid system inspired by the 3-parts floor plan layout of the museum, ensuring consistency and structure throughout the brand’s visual elements.

We simplified the color palette, emphasizing the vividness and authenticity of the artwork, especially the rich colors and textures of the ceramic glaze. This focused approach highlights the authentic essence of each piece, elevating their visual impact while preserving their nature.

Collaboratively, we aimed to assemble the Bát Tràng Museum towards a more contemporary style while preserving its rich heritage.

#266. How KIND Reimagined the Osland Rebrand

KIND's Osland rebrand grows from biology: circular forms inspired by trout roe, DNA and the fish itself, set in coral reds and marine blues.

The mark is a circle that behaves like a living thing: an open arc crossed by a second curve, trailed by a scatter of dots like roe drifting from a single egg mass. KIND repeats the same circle at every scale, as the mark itself, as a dotted field marching across folder covers, and as the curve of the fjord-side facility seen from the air. Coral and warm reds carry the biology, deep marine blue carries the water, and a quiet sand-and-grey register keeps the system clinical instead of romantic. Osland has bred trout since 1963 and keeps Norway's oldest pedigree trout broodstock, so the identity had to speak science and scale at once. It took Gold in Rebranding Projects at the 2026 European Design Awards.

The wordmark is a lowercase grotesque with an engineered calm, set small and tight wherever it appears, osland, in the same weight as the body copy, never shouting. It shares the frame with the mark rather than competing with it. On the cards it is blind-embossed, so it reads as texture before it reads as type. The editorial voice follows the same discipline: short declarative lines like Strong Genes. and Superior Guidance., and the project's central idea stated as a wordplay, From becomes Form, turning deep inherited expertise into future value.

Production discipline is where the system earns its keep. Cards in Osland Coral, Sand, Grey, Dark Blue and Breeze carry the wordmark embossed without ink, so the stock does the talking. Folder covers run the roe-dot pattern as a field of fine debossed points. Trout roe boxes stack the mark in a hard grid across packaging, and signage scales the circle up to architectural size on concrete. The same language fills the website, where coral macro photography of roe opens the story of how life takes form, from egg to fjord, micro to macro. KIND worked from the inside out, sharpening the business strategy and the market role before drawing a single lockup, and the result reads as one organism across every touchpoint.

#267. New EU Guidelines For AI Labelling

Vitaly Friedman loves beautiful content and doesn’t like to give in easily. When he is not writing, he’s most probably running front-end & UX … More about Vitaly ↬

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

There’s been a lot of confusion and panic this week about “huge fines”, “drastic measures” and “sweeping new AI rules” in the EU. In reality, it’s a lot more narrow — and a lot more sensible. And mostly it’s about making AI more obvious when it actually needs to be obvious — especially for AI-generated content.

Starting from Aug 2, 2026, AI labelling is a legal requirement for any company that serves EU citizens. And similar to European Accessibility Act, it’s not limited to EU companies. It affects any company worldwide with EU operations as long as their AI output is used by people in the EU. Let’s see what exactly it means for us.

The goal of AI labelling is to help everyone exposed to AI content to recognize, in a clear and distinguishable way, that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated.

According to Article 50(4) of the AI Act, AI labelling applies to:

Both providers (who build or supply the AI system) and deployers (who use it) carry legal obligations. Similar to GDPR and EAA, a company doesn’t escape Article 50 just because it licensed an external AI tool from a third party.

However, it doesn’t mean that all AI-generated content must be explicitly labelled.

Beyond the use cases above, pretty much everything else — the vast majority of AI-assisted work — simply isn’t covered by new transparency rules. Most notably, the disclosure obligation does not apply where the AI-generated text has been reviewed and edited by a human, with a named person or entity taking editorial responsibility for it.

Some confusion circles around what exactly “public interest” means, where it starts and where it ends. On its own, it refers to health, safety, environment, economy, finances, politics, science, or culture. If AI-generated product claims touch upon them, the disclosure rule applies.

Some law firms recommend labelling realistic AI-generated illustrations or photos as a precaution for advertising, marketing and other commercial content. AI-generated product illustrations, photos, or posters do need a disclosure, as long as they resemble a real person, place, object, or event.

But at which point does edited AI content stop being AI content? When a form is pre-filled with AI, but then a user edits it, is it still AI? EU Commission’s guidance is a little fuzzy. Small assistive edits — spellcheck, grammar, formatting, cropping, colour correction, and AI-generated translation — don’t count as AI generation.

AI-generated summaries, composite imagery, substantive rewrites, or adding and removing elements from a photo are considered AI generation. In practice, fine-tuning a sentence a person wrote is fine, but generating the sentence on its own requires a disclosure.

“A human skimmed it before publishing” doesn’t qualify as editorial review. The Commission is explicit that it needs to be substantive, with a named person responsible for the editorial control.

In other words, the fine line lies between intentional manual intervention and automated generation. The latter always has to be disclosed (exception: closed B2B environments).

As part of the Code of Practice, the European Commission has published an EU AI icon set. It’s a specific “AI” mark (similar to the AI label in Carbon Design System) — not the generic ✨ sparkle that many products use to signal AI. The signal must be “clear and distinguishable”.

The sparkle might be too ambiguous to signal AI clearly. Mostly because it’s often used to mean “AI-powered feature”, rather than “this specific content was generated by AI”. That’s the kind of signal EU guidelines are trying to rule out.

The Commission is explicit: using an icon “does not establish legal compliance by itself.” A barely visible icon, a note buried in the footer, or a label that flashes for a second are all not compliant.

The icon should be clearly visible, with a plain language label and accessible to assistive technologies. A safe bet is to pair any icon with plain text (“AI-generated”) — and it needs to persist when being reshared or downloaded.

In fact, the EU Commission also published Code of Practice on marking and labelling of AI content.

It might feel like a yet another regulation coming from the EU, but in reality there are plenty of other similar regulations that emerged recently worldwide:

All of these are signs of upcoming AI regulation that looks more like a pattern, rather than a coincidence. So if you’re shipping anything AI this year, it’s probably a good idea to have a conversation about what exactly is going to be AI-labelled, and what not.

One final note is that new EU AI transparency rules are much broader than US laws on AI disclosure, where certain state laws require disclosures for synthetic human performers, political advertising or specific AI applications.

None of this really deserves panic or confusion. It’s about a fairly simple idea that has been emerging worldwide at almost the same time:

If anything, it will help people distinguish between AI slop and not AI — and everybody can only benefit from that.

#270. Ten homes from the mid-century "time capsule" Studley Park

Riverside Modern is a book documenting the mid-century modern homes of Studley Park in Melbourne. In this roundup, its author Jake Taylor selects 10 standout residences from the architectural enclave.

Published by Thames and Hudson, Riverside Modern was written by architect Taylor with his collaborator, the photographer Jack Lovel, to celebrate the architecturally distinct neighbourhood in the suburb of Kew.

The book tells the story of Studley Park, where almost 100 experimental mid-century homes were built between the 1940s and 1970s as a contemporary vision for Australian life, and captures them today in their present, lived-in state.

“The streets of Studley Park showcase the energy and desire post-world war two to define a new image for Australia through the detached family home, a constant theme of modern Australian society,” Taylor told Dezeen.

“The diversity and breadth of mid-century styles and architects is profound; nearly all the key Melbourne mid-century architects have projects in this area, often working side-by-side,” he explained.

“The density of mid-century houses was truly something I had never seen before. Areas such as Yarra Street were fully developed in a 15-year window, with no houses pre-dating this era, and importantly very few afterwards, allowing it to be a rare time capsule of this period of design.”

Among the featured homes are Pettigrew House, one of Melbourne’s earliest modernist buildings, and Guss House, a modernist glass box by local studio McGlashan Everist.

Taylor decided to write the book after researching the area extensively during the Covid-19 pandemic and later creating a self-guided walking tour, which quickly became popular.

“By chance, I was living near Kew for most of 2020 and stumbled into the amazing concentration of mid-century houses in the area and was blown away,” he continued. “The constant demand and energy for the tours led to the idea of exploring a potential book on the area.”

The homes were all photographed without styling to present readers with an “honest look” at them, which Taylor hopes will offer a guide in developing residential design that stands the test of time.

“Modestly scaled mid-century houses have sadly been regularly demolished in high quantities across parts of Melbourne and Australia,” said Taylor.

“The houses in Studley Park up until recently did not have any limited heritage overlays, but yet the majority of these houses have not only survived but thrived,” he continued.

“This is largely thanks to the innovative and very site-sensitive methods at the heart of these projects that have allowed the homes to age and feel an integrated part of the riverside setting. A characteristic that we should all strive for in contemporary houses.”

Read on for 10 of the author’s favourites from the book:

Pettigrew House, 1946, by Robin Boyd, Kevin Pethebridge and Frank Bell

“Boyd, Pethebridge and Bell all served together in world war two and then created a joint practice soon after returning, with this being one of their first projects.

“Pettigrew House was designed in two phases initially to comply with post-war labour and supply shortages. Robin Boyd went on to become a world-renowned architect, writer and design leader.

“The home was renovated very sensitively in 2018 by Flack Studio.”

“Bell House was designed by Russian-born, German-trained architect Anatol Kagan.

“Kagan is the most prolific of any architect in the area, with the neighbourhood around Yarravale Road known as ‘Kaganville’ due to the tight concentration of his houses.

“Bell House, which is Kagan’s earliest project in Studley Park, skillfully lifts the living areas of the house into the tree canopies to tame a wedge-shaped corner lot. It was renovated in 2019 by Kennedy Nolan.”

“Geoffrey Danne’s own family home, Danne House was the first to be completed on Yarra Street, the most iconic of all streets in Studley Park, and built a year before the street formalised.

“The home was positioned so the rear door of the upper living opened onto the backyard, but due to the steep slope of the site, this initially created a dramatic two-storey carport below to link the house to the street below.

“The house underwent significant updates in the 1970s, which included filling in the carport. The home is now owned by Bryant Alsop, who renovated the interiors in 2022. This process revealed much of the original charm of the house.”

“Designed by architect Ernest Milston as his own family home, Milston House is situated in the southern half of Studley Park around numerous other architects’ own houses, including those of Don Fulton, Peter and Dione McIntyre and John Kenny.

“The lightweight house with butterfly roof form sits below the streetscape nestled in an Edna Walling-designed garden. The site continues to fall away to the rear to allow the living spaces of the home to have views that float out in the riverside, heavily-vegetated landscape beyond.”

Williams House, 1958, by Peter and Dione McIntyre

“The rectangular plan of this house wraps around a large central courtyard that allows all the rooms to have dual aspect views.

“The sloping site prompts the living spaces to elevate upwards towards the street. This creates a carport, entry and storage areas below. The elevation is accentuated by the living room window that reaches forward into the canopy of the beautiful Golden Elm tree in the front garden.

“The home has been owned by architect Albert Mo and his family for two the last two decades. They have recently completed a sensitive renovation that improves the home’s link to the rear yard through the addition of an extra storey at the back that connects to an added pool terrace via a bridge.”

“The glass box modernist form of the Guss House, as it propels itself towards Yarra Street, is one of the most iconic architectural moments in Studley Park.

“The house was designed around a huge eucalyptus tree situated in the central courtyard. The flat-roofed design, which, through glass and a steel frame, adheres to a gridded layout and manages to also blend seamlessly into the heavily vegetated riverside site.

“The home underwent small interior updates by Australian architect Maggie Edmond in 2019.”

N Fink Residence, 1963, by Moore & Hammond

“N Fink Residence is located on Carnsworth Avenue, one of the quietest cul-de-sacs with the very quiet Studley Park.

“The sloping nature of this site propels the house dramatically above the street below. The late modernist palette features a reinforced concrete structure that frees up expansive views from the main living spaces, while allowing for the driveway to swoop in under the cantilevered end of the main form.

“The garden was originally designed by landscape architect Gordon Ford and has been recently updated sympathetically. The house was renovated by Jackson Clements Burrows Architects in 2014.”

“The full career of both modernism in Studley Park and Robin Boyd’s career can be traced across his projects in Studley Park.

“Purves House was one of his final projects in his career and showcases a much more mature design palette when compared to his earlier post-war modern projects. Designed for the Purves art family, the home was intended to be both a home and gallery space.

“The interconnected living spaces around the central timber staircase showcase the home’s energy and natural potential as an events space. The large picture windows dramatically puncture the exterior, but act as part of the balance of the interior walls that were intended to be filled by the who’s who of Australian modern artworks.”

Molesworth Townhouses, 1969, by Graeme Gunn

“Developed by renowned Merchant Builders, Molesworth Townhouses was designed as six concrete block townhouses clustered around a medieval-inspired bluestone cobble driveway.

“The landscape by landscape architect Ellis Stones now engulfs the stark concrete forms of the homes, and with the natural patina of the material, they have come to feel integral to the sweeping corner site.

“Located on Yarra Boulevard, this project is one of the rare projects in the area to be in the public spotlight, with most others hidden away on side streets.”

“Positioned on a narrow corner site, this design lunges up confidently to nestle into the mature trees of the site as a late modernist treehouse.

“The textured palette of rough-sawn timber, brick and stone extends across the whole home to create a warm and emotive series of both interior and exterior spaces.

“The ground level opens onto and is surrounded by a series of curated exterior spaces that allow the house to activate the full extent of the site.”

#271. Ancient shipwreck found off Turkey may be the world’s oldest

An underwater archaeologist approaches one of the clay containers, which were found lying on a slope

Archaeologists in Turkey have discovered what they believe may be the remains of the world’s oldest known shipwreck. About 30 ceramic storage jars, or amphorae, were found near the small island of Kekova off Turkey’s south-west coast, said Hakan Öniz, a professor of archaeology at Akdeniz University who lead the excavation by the Mediterranean Archaeology Association. They are believed to belong to a vessel that sank some 4,500 years ago, when Bronze Age communities were building far-reaching trade networks across the eastern Mediterranean.

Some of the clay containers, lying on a slope in clear waters at depths of between 25 and 40 metres, still contain the residue of the goods they carried. The jars’ distinctive shape and clay are characteristic of pottery produced in the Jordan Valley during the Early Bronze Age, providing new clues as to the movement of goods between the Levant, Egypt and the Aegean Sea, Öniz told The Art Newspaper. The wooden ship, which may have been 10 metres long, that carried the amphorae has long since disappeared, likely eaten away by Teredo navalis, a wood-boring mollusc common in the Mediterranean.

“This wreck has become the first scientific evidence in the world that maritime routes existed and were used during that period,” he said. While historical sources indicated seaborne commerce occured in the eastern Mediterranean at the time, the Kekova wreck provides rare physical proof, he said.

The site was first identified in 2022 during a survey of the Kekova area, where strong currents can run against the wind through a narrow passage, creating turbulent conditions for ships.

Öniz’s team initially thought the flat-bottomed jars featuring two side handles, which resemble traditional Turkish water jugs, were from the Ottoman period. “To us, it was just another wreck, one of 434,” he says, referring to the number of shipwrecks documented along the coast. The breakthrough came when Öniz encountered similar, far older pottery in a publication on Egyptian archaeology. “I thought, ‘By God.’”

An artefact being removed from the seabed

Öniz consulted with Karin Sowada, an Egyptologist at Macquarie University in Australia, who examined the finds and confirmed their resemblance to imported Levantine amphorae, he said. Similar examples have been found in Egypt and at sites associated with Troy and Minoan Crete.

Preliminary finds, published in the Journal of Maritime Archaeology in July, date the finds to around 2700-2400 BCE. This would make the Kekova wreck older than the current holder of the title for the oldest shipwreck ever discovered: a vessel believed to be 4,200 years old that was found in 1975 off the Greek island of Dokos in the Aegean.

The amphorae “shed light on the deep-rooted history of trade along the Anatolian coast,” Mehmet Nuri Ersoy, Turkey’s culture minister, said in a social media post. “These containers, believed to have been used to transport olive oil or wine, bear important traces of trade and cultural interaction in the eastern Mediterranean.”

Tree resin, dried meat or dried fish are other possibilities for the cargo. Researchers are using X-ray fluorescence and X-ray diffraction to analyse the pottery’s material and contents, Öniz said.

One perforated ceramic vessel, bearing nine symbols that may represent spiritual beliefs, may have been used by the sailors as a churn. Öniz said the ship may have carried a handful of goats to make butter or cheese during the long voyage before they were consumed for meat.

Such glimpses of life aboard an ancient trading vessel remind Öniz of the people who never returned home. “You wonder what the captain was feeling as the ship went down, what the sailors went through trying to reach the shore [and] their families waiting for them in port,” he said.

#272. Norfolk Coast

The Norfolk Coast is one of the UK’s best-loved and most at-risk tourist destinations. Designated an Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty, the region is also home to Sites of Special Scientific Interest, National Nature Reserves, Marine Conservation Zones, a Biosphere Reserve and Heritage Coast. A collection of protected landscapes, united through their biodiversity and fragility. Lantern was appointed to bring these organisations together and better define and promote their common goals to preserve, restore and enhance the local life, landscapes and wildlife of the Norfolk Coast.

We helped to define this unique destination’s strategic positioning, whilst delivering a new visual and verbal identity to promote the responsible exploration of the region, ensuring it’s here for everyone, forever.

Hiking, cycling and kayaking through protected landscapes

To fully understand what makes Norfolk so special and distinct, we embarked on a four-day immersion trip as a team. We hiked, cycled, bird watched, and conducted several interviews with local families and visitors.

It was important for us to discover the genuine essence of Norfolk and what it means for the local community and stakeholders who call it home, as well as identifying the key areas that require greater protection.

Norfolk’s coastal landscapes, seascapes and communities have rhythms like a heartbeat. They move across millennia, change with the seasons, and even differ day to day. Waterways widen and wander. Wildlife migrates and hibernates. Farmland flourishes and lies fallow. This is a living coast in perpetual motion. This is a living coast in perpetual motion. Often wild yet sometimes serene.

Our new strategy celebrates this wild, natural backdrop and all that defines it; land and sea, nature and community, they all live together in gentle harmony. And like every living thing, this delicate place deserves to be respected and protected.

Inspired by the sweeping landscapes of Norfolk’s coast and creeks we brought together the N and C of the brand name creating a unique symbol, paired with a visual language that’s full of energy and alive with nature.

Reflected through the interplay of type, image and illustration, we put the audience deep into the experience. To further reflect the landscape we directed an off-season photoshoot, encouraging sustainable exploration throughout the year.

A suite of illustrations capture key essences from our findings and strategy along with unique wildlife and nature found in Norfolk. We utilise these within patches and stamps reflecting the positive adventures we want to encourage people to experience.

#274. Inside the Craft of ADC: Living Brand Identity by CLEVER°FRANKE

CLEVERÂ°FRANKE built ADC a living brand identity: generative patterns from mathematical symbols, refined by an AI model and human feedback.

The system starts with the raw material of ADCâs business: mathematical operators. Plus signs, crosses, dots, dashes, triangles and diamonds cluster and merge according to proximity and density, forming compositions that read as organic even though they are entirely computational. A quadtree structures the space beneath the surface, so every output shares the same rhythm while no two outputs look alike. The logo itself grows out of the same shape language, set only in black or white so it holds its ground against the patterns moving around it. The work took Gold in Brand Identity, Complete Systems at the 2026 European Design Awards.

The typeface is Ease by Studio Feixen, chosen because it sits between structure and expression: neither rounded nor straight. The studio calls it a nod to the latent space of AI models, the in-between territory where meaning takes shape. Quirky yet refined, technically credible and warm, it sets report covers and headlines in the same voice as the patterns behind them. The wordmark and the type specimen read as one continuous system, not a logo dropped on top of decoration.

The palette breaks deliberately from dark tech aesthetics: violet #A187FF, pink #FF9BFC, teal #2BEBCB, green #58EB81, yellow #FFF347 and gold #E5C574, with black and white reserved for the logo. These are not static swatches. The colors shift across the generative patterns, so a finance report and a conference slide feel related without looking identical. Under the hood sits a generative tool driven by more than 50 parameters, fed by a custom AI model trained on more than 100 data points about ADCâs work, values and people. A web tool puts it in everyoneâs hands: describe a project and it places the input in ADCâs embedding space, then offers three pattern variations drawn from nearby concepts. Pick a favorite and the choice feeds back into the model, refining future outputs. A brand vitality dashboard tracks it all live: 87 patterns generated this month, 1,232 in total, a diversity score of 0.91.

#275. Armadillo furniture is clad in reused shingles to resemble "friendly monsters"

Photography by Penguins Egg, courtesy of Gallery Fumi.

Designers Lukas Wegwerth and Corinna Dehn have unveiled their Armadillo furniture pieces, clad in facade shingles from buildings in Germany’s Vogelsberg region, at the Companions exhibition at London’s Galleri Fumi.

The Companions show features six new Armadillo pieces – two cabinets, a sideboard, a birdhouse, a dining table and a stand-alone screen – as well as some older furniture in the series.

All are all clad in wooden shingles in reference to Vogelsberg’s traditional architecture.

The designers became fascinated with the material after renovating Wegwerth‘s grandmother’s house in the region, which was clad in weathered wooden shingles from the 1800s.

“What differentiates a shingle from a piece of wood is very minimal, yet the shingle becomes a system component created from chunks of wood that cannot be used for much else, apart from firewood,” Wegwerth and Dehn told Dezeen.

“A shingled facade is a very vital entity, it’s a habitat for wild bees and other insects that live in the rain shadow. Visually, it can create an equally vivid and animated appearance.”

The shingles used in the Armadillo series came from a variety of different sources – some from Wegwerth’s grandmother’s house, some from a construction site in a neighbouring village and some from an older project by the artists where they created shingles to clad mobile houses.

Wegwerth and Dehn cleaned, brushed and sanded the old shingles to use them in the project, before preparing them in different ways to create a variety of surface designs.

“The shingles are treated with wood stains in various colours, applied in a very wet stage so the colours can blend into each other, similarly to water colours,” the duo explained.

“Other pieces were finished using linseed oil paints. For some pieces, the shingles were ebonised through a process involving successive baths of tannins, rust and slaked lime, which gradually darken the wood.”

Organic, playful shapes were used to create the furniture designs, which resemble woodland forest creatures clad in scales. Their friendly appearance gave the exhibition its name, Companions.

“Some of the pieces of the Armadillo series are inspired by elements of vernacular architecture like the timber frame house we renovate, others are more organic and animate, like friendly monsters – companions,” the artists said.

However, these shapes add an extra challenge for the artists when it comes to covering the pieces in shingles, with vertically curved areas needing slim shingles and horizontally curved areas calling for short or curved shingles.

“The shapes and sizes of shingles need to be very manyfold and made specifically for a certain spot on the furniture to make it work,” Wegwerth and Dehn said.

“Going from more flat areas to more complex shapes, the shingles can go from rather big to pretty small, just like you can observe them in the shell of an armadillo or the scale on a fish,” they continued.

This process means that the artists themselves were unsure of what the pieces would look like until they were completely finished.

“The thickness of the shingle coat varies depending on the complexity of the shingled area,” Wegwerth and Dehn said. “As a result, the final silhouettes and tonal values only emerge gradually during the process.”

Previous designs shown at Gallery Fumi include rubber furniture that resembles ancient ruins and furniture made from cardboard boxes.

Companions will be on display at Gallery Fumi from 6 October to 21 November 2026. See Dezeen Events Guide for an up-to-date list of architecture and design events taking place around the world.
