#276. Building Tactile UX: Honoring Intentional Design With Lottie

With over 14 years of experience and deep expertise in API development, third-party tool integration, and scalable software solutions, Alexey specializes in … More about Alexey ↬

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

This article has been kindly supported by our dear friends at Isadora Agency who help enterprise brands and market leaders navigate digital, evolve profitably, and launch unforgettable websites, products, and campaigns. Thank you!

When front-end developers and UX engineers are tasked with building a web interface that feels tactile, bouncy, or destructive, the industry instinct is almost always the same: reach for a physics engine. Frameworks like Matter.js, Cannon.js, or custom WebGL solutions have become the gold standard for creating immersive, gamified websites.

When our team at Isadora Agency set out to build Stress Release, a digital stress-relief squeeze toy designed to let burnt-out creatives smash, stretch, and distort animated UI characters, we initially explored that route. The goal was to build a highly tactile experience where every click yielded a satisfying, squishy reaction.

But as we began prototyping, we realized something crucial: Physics engines produce plausible motion, but in our case, the animators produced intentional motion.

We didn’t need our characters to act like realistic rubber balls bouncing uncontrollably around a canvas. We needed them to react in very specific, highly designed ways. So, we scrapped the physics engine entirely.

In this article, we’ll break down how we built a real-time stress-relief squeeze toy without a single line of WebGL or Matter.js, relying entirely on programmatic Lottie state controls, DOM manipulation, and distance-based math.

Our core requirement for Stress Release was absolute deterministic control. Our animators had crafted bespoke .json Lottie files that required exact, frame-by-frame sequencing.

For instance, our ‘mega squeeze’ reaction required a precise 181-frame build-up followed by a specific release sequence. To honor this design, we needed an architecture that wouldn’t overwrite the animators’ crafted keyframes with algorithmic approximations.

The tighter the click-feedback loop (click → squish → score), the more you need deterministic frame control. By choosing programmatic state control using Lottie’s native API, we ensured that the interaction layer acted as a flawless trigger for the animation layer.

Because our architecture relied on Lottie and the standard DOM, rendering is handled directly by the Lottie runtime, which plays the JSON-based vector animations as SVGs internally. We selected elements directly by ID and CSS class, driving their behavior using a combination of Lottie animation segments, CSS transforms, and click-event math.

To achieve a deeply satisfying “tactile feel” upon hitting a character, we used radial input mapping. The first step was converting the click from page coordinates into the character’s local coordinate space.

Every click was measured against the character’s center point, then translated into score, feedback intensity, and explosion placement:

Then we calculate the straight-line distance from the center of the click using the Pythagorean theorem:

That single number drives everything: the score, the feedback intensity, and where the explosion animation appears:

The result is a concentric zone system — a perfect circle of scoring rings around the character’s center, similar to a dartboard. The visual complexity of the Lottie SVG is completely irrelevant to hit detection; the hitbox is always a clean circle. Critically, the explosion Lottie animation is repositioned to (a, b) — the same vector used for scoring, so it always appears exactly where the player clicked. This spatial accuracy creates the tactile “I hit that” sensation entirely through math and DOM positioning.

Because the experience used DOM-managed SVG elements, desktop clicks and mobile taps could be handled directly through native event listeners. This avoided extra raycasting or coordinate remapping layers, while keeping the interaction model aligned with how the animations were rendered.

Since the game requires a visual reaction at a specific point, Lottie handles all the squish and bounce feelings internally through its animation curves. Each character has a defined set of animation sections (idle loops, reaction frames, and end states) stored as frame ranges. When a click lands, we jump directly to the exact segment that matches the current game state:

On every click, we advance through the play order and fire the next segment:

When the segment completes, control returns to the idle loop:

And for the mega squeeze build-up, the bar loops on a specific frame range until triggered:

Another major factor in our architectural decision was responsive behavior. Because we built Stress Release in the DOM, we bypassed the complexities of scaling bounding boxes and collision vectors across different devices.

We handled responsive resizing entirely through CSS variables. By recalculating CSS custom properties on every resize, the layout simply reacts to the updated variables, and the Lottie SVGs scale naturally inside their containers without losing their state:

While this architecture gave us total control over the art direction, it introduced a different challenge: file size.

Lottie JSON files can be heavy. We had 21 different character animations, plus multiple explosion variants that all needed to load. To ensure the experience remained fluid — especially on mobile devices — we implemented a few aggressive optimization strategies:

When determining the stack for a gamified web experience, it is critical to let the design requirements dictate the technology.

Because our interactions required bespoke, highly controlled visual reactions, we opted for programmatic state control over emergent simulation. This decision empowered the animators to dictate the exact feel of the experience, leaving the code to do what it does best: listen, calculate, and trigger.

By mapping Lottie’s native timeline capabilities to the DOM, you can deliver incredibly rich, tactile user experiences while maintaining absolute control over the art direction.

#278. Revealed: How Vincent van Gogh’s brother Theo gave Monet his first exhibition in London

Left: Claude Monet (1899) and right: Theo van Gogh (1889) Paul Nadar (photo © Aguttes) and Van Gogh Museum, Amsterdam (Vincent van Gogh Foundation)

Adventures with Van Gogh is a weekly blog by Martin Bailey, The Art Newspaper's long-standing correspondent and expert on the Dutch painter. Published on Fridays, stories range from newsy items about this most intriguing artist, to scholarly pieces based on meticulous investigations and discoveries.

Explore all of Martin’s adventures with Van Gogh here.

A new book on the correspondence of Claude Monet includes a letter reporting on the artist’s solo show in London, organised by the art dealer Theo van Gogh, Vincent’s brother. This missive is included in Claude Monet: A Life in Letters, published by Thames & Hudson last week.

Monet wrote to Alice Hoschedé, his companion and later wife, on 3 May 1889: “I received a letter from [Theo] Van Gogh, in which he enclosed a letter from his London gallery… Nothing sold, but the exhibition was very well received by the public with praise from all the English newspapers.”

Claude Monet’s Self-portrait with a Beret (1886) Private collection (photograph ©Roy Fox Fine Art)

Monet added with pride that the critics wrote that he was “currently the true hero of art”. We have tracked down the original source. It was the unnamed critic of The Echo, a London evening newspaper, who began his review by saying that “M. Claude Monet is the art-hero of the hour”.

The start of The Echo’s review of Monet’s London show The Echo, London, 15 April 1889

The London exhibition had been masterminded by Theo, the manager of the Boussod & Valadon gallery (formerly known as Goupil) in Boulevard Montmartre in Paris. He had got to know Monet and in 1887 began to seriously sell his work.

In February 1889, Theo had held a Monet exhibition at his Paris gallery and he quickly arranged to send a larger group of paintings to their London branch. It was then located at 116-117 New Bond Street.

Impressionism was novel for most London art lovers in 1889 and visitors needed to be advised on how to appreciate these avant-garde works. The unusual display arrangements at the Monet exhibition were explained by the critic of the Manchester City News: “There are twenty [paintings] on the walls, and against each wall is a chair, where, upon your entrance, you are requested to seat yourself. Then you look at the pictures on the walls opposite you, and so round the room, till you grow thoughtful and half persuaded to be a Monetite.” The loose brushwork of Impressionism was best appreciated from a little distance.

Today the conventional wisdom is that British critics came late to appreciate Impressionism. The art historian Frances Fowle, in an essay on Monet’s late 19th-century reception in the UK, wrote that “national press reviews of the Goupil exhibition were generally unfavourable or simply baffled”. However, our analysis of more than a dozen newspaper reviews in April-May 1889 reveals a rather different story: the critics were nearly all positive and enthusiastic.

Theo must have been particularly delighted with The Scotsman’s comment on the Monet show: “The managers of the Goupil Gallery have done a service to all connoisseurs”. The World described Monet as “one of the most vividly faithful landscapists living”. The Saturday Review commented that he had “a very remarkable and original talent”. And The Echo ended its review: “Monet is so young and fresh, so clever—brutally clever” (unfortunately they got his age wrong, he was then 48).

Despite the critics’ enthusiasm, no paintings were actually sold in London. Fowle was quite correct in her essay that British buyers of Monet were few and far between until the 1920s. After Theo’s efforts in 1889, Monet’s second solo show in London did not take place until 1936, a decade after his death.

Theo had had much better luck in Paris. He held two exhibitions in June 1888 and February 1889 and altogether he sold more than than 60 works by Monet between 1887-90.

Theo’s relationship with Monet was business, but what did Vincent think about his art? Vincent was in Arles during Monet’s exhibitions at his brother’s Paris gallery, but he had seen his work earlier while he had been living in Paris, before his move to Provence. Vincent became a great admirer, referring to Monet in more than 30 of his letters.

Monet’s Bend in the Epte River near Giverny (1888) Philadelphia Museum of Art (William L. Elkins Collection, E1924-3-16)

Among the Monet paintings Vincent singled out for praise was Bend in the Epte River near Giverny (1888), which he never saw, but was described to him by Theo in June 1888, when it was in Theo’s Paris exhibition. Writing (in English) to his Australian artist friend John Russell, Vincent reported that it was “a landscape with red sunset and a group of dark fir trees by the seaside”.

Extract from Vincent van Gogh’s letter to John Russell, 17 June 1888 Van Gogh Museum, Amsterdam (Vincent van Gogh Foundation)

The admiration was mutual. When Monet visited the exhibition of the Indépendants in April 1890, he told Theo that Vincent’s pictures were “the best in the exhibition” (there were nearly 900 works on show). Among Vincent’s ten paintings were two of his Sunflowers (August 1888), a motif which Monet had tackled seven years earlier.

Monet’s Bouquet of Sunflowers (1881) and Van Gogh’s Sunflowers (August 1888) Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York and Neue Pinakothek, Munich

And a year after Van Gogh’s suicide, Monet made a telling comment to the French critic Octave Mirbeau: “How could a man who has loved flowers and light so much and has rendered them so well, how could he have managed to be so unhappy?”

With the centenary of Monet’s death in Giverny on 6 December, he will be much in the news this autumn. The artist is now being celebrated with two exhibitions in Paris: Monet, Painting Time at the Musée de l'Orangerie (until 25 January 2027) and Histories of Landscape: From Monet to Hockney (1890-2026) at the Musée Marmottan Monet (until 31 January). The Musée de l'Orangerie show will then travel to London, to Tate Modern (25 February-27 June 2027).

A fragment of Van Gogh’s copied-out text (autumn 1876) from Jules Breton’s poem Crépuscule Christie’s

On 13 October Christie’s in New York sold a four-line fragment of a poem by Jules Breton that had been copied out by Van Gogh. It went for $23,040. The tiny fragment (only 1.7cm high) had been cut from Van Gogh’s six pages of poems and text that he wrote in the visitors’ book of Annie Slade-Jones, his landlady when he was staying in Isleworth, in west London, in the autumn of 1876.

The seller of the fragment was the Jim Irsay collection, amassed by the US businessman who died last year. Another Van Gogh fragment from the same Breton poem was sold some years ago by the Pennsylvania-based Raab Collection.

Martin Bailey is a leading Van Gogh specialist and special correspondent for The Art Newspaper. He has curated exhibitions at the Barbican Art Gallery, Compton Verney/National Gallery of Scotland and Tate Britain.

Martin has written a number of bestselling books on Van Gogh’s years in France: The Sunflowers Are Mine: The Story of Van Gogh's Masterpiece (Frances Lincoln 2013, UK and US), Studio of the South: Van Gogh in Provence (Frances Lincoln 2016, UK and US), Starry Night: Van Gogh at the Asylum (White Lion Publishing 2018, UK and US) and Van Gogh’s Finale: Auvers and the Artist’s Rise to Fame (Frances Lincoln 2021, UK and US). The Sunflowers are Mine (2024, UK and US) and Van Gogh’s Finale (2024, UK and US) are also now available in a more compact paperback format.

His other recent books include Living with Vincent van Gogh: The Homes & Landscapes that shaped the Artist (White Lion Publishing 2019, UK and US), which provides an overview of the artist’s life. The Illustrated Provence Letters of Van Gogh has been reissued (Batsford 2021, UK and US). My Friend Van Gogh/Emile Bernard provides the first English translation of Bernard’s writings on Van Gogh (David Zwirner Books 2023, UKand US).

To contact Martin Bailey, please email vangogh@theartnewspaper.com

Please note that he does not undertake authentications.

#279. NASA-backed research project creates 3D-printed cookies from plastic

Photography by Russell Bailey of Southern Illinois University Carbondale.

Led by Southern Illinois University Carbondale associate professor Lahiru Jayakody, the researchers created µBites by using yeast to turn polyethylene terephthalate (PET) plastic, which is commonly used for drink bottles, into edible ingredients.

The project also aims to tackle plastic pollution, using specialised microbes to transform plastic into a useful, edible product.

“We were trying to develop technologies for plastic upcycling to make more valuable products,” said Jayakody. “We thought, why not focus on making food? Because plastic is carbon and food is carbon.”

To make µBites, PET plastic, discarded corn plant stalks and leaves, and other biomass were put through a process developed at Southern Illinois University Carbondale called oxidative hydrothermal dissolution, which uses water and oxygen at high temperature and pressure to break down the tough material into microbe-accessible pieces.

These pieces were fed to specially designed yeasts, which were programmed to transform them into new food ingredients, creating an edible mixture of proteins, vitamins and flavourings.

In the future, they hope to develop µBites to the point where yeast creates all the main ingredients, as well as enhanced flavouring and additives.

Currently, they can create vanilla flavouring from plant biomass using baker’s yeast, and another yeast strain can turn ethylene glycol in PET into beta-carotene, which the body turns into vitamin A.

The researchers plan to have µBites ready for public consumption in the coming years, intending to use them for extreme environments like submarines or colonies on the moon or Mars.

“Global food demand is expected to rise 35 to 56 per cent by the year 2050, and about 30 per cent of the world population will be at risk of hunger in the future,” he continued. “The way to address that, I believe, is by using microbes.”

Earlier this year, NASA updated plans for a permanent moon base, announcing that living and working on the moon will become reality after 2032.

Photography by Russell Bailey of Southern Illinois University Carbondale.

#282. Nescau Display: Type Design by Plau Design

Plau Design teams up with FutureBrand SÃ£o Paulo on Nescau Display, a custom type design system weaving lightning bolts into 36 styles.

Every kid in Brazil knows that yellow lightning bolt. For over 90 years, NestlÃ©'s Nescau has sat on kitchen tables across the country, tied to childhood sports, skate parks, and morning chocolate milk. When FutureBrand SÃ£o Paulo set out to evolve the brand's visual identity, they brought in type foundry Plau Design â led on the project by Carlos Mignot, Rodrigo Saiani, and Lu Leitenperger â to redraw the core logotype and build a custom sans serif family from scratch. The brief was simple. Make the letters carry the voltage.

The details hide inside the glyphs. Instead of treating the lightning bolt as a separate sticker, Plau carved those sharp diagonal cuts directly into the anatomy of the type design. You can spot the notched bolt angles slicing through the crossbar of the uppercase G, the tail of the Q, the leg of the R, and the lowercase k, while the exclamation mark turns into a full lightning bolt. It could've felt too aggressive. To keep the voice warm, the team gave the bowls and terminals an open, almost smiling curve that softens all those sharp corners.

That gives art directors 36 styles to play with. #283. Wheeler Kearns Architects staggers brown-metal house on Lake Michigan shore

US studio Wheeler Kearns Architects has completed a brown-metal and limestone house organised around a courtyard on the shore of Lake Michigan, in Michigan, USA.

Known as Timber Lane Retreat, the 2026 house is composed of three volumes – two two-story gabled forms that align with a central courtyard and an offset single-story box with a flat roof.

A glazed corridor runs between the different volumes, connecting the spaces and creating a sightline from the street to the water.

The varying forms and connecting elements open and close the house to the exterior.

“This home is really a response to the tension between openness and shelter,” Wheeler Kearns Architects told Dezeen.

“The site offered a spectacular lake view but also demanded privacy, wind resistance and a sensitivity to the neighboring street.”

“Every decision – the courtyard, the staggered plan, the material palette – came from balancing those competing demands,” the team continued. “The result is a home that feels open and expansive, but also grounded and quiet.”

Closest to the street, the first gabled mass holds the garage and mudroom below an exercise room and sauna. The offset box contains the communal spaces with a kitchen, dining and living spaces that look out onto the patio and lake beyond through floor-to-ceiling sliding glass.

On the waterfront, the largest form is anchored to the patio with a screened porch.

Two guest suites hold the edge of the property, while the entire upper level comprises the private, primary suite and a study.

“Most clients building on a lake instinctively want the house oriented parallel to the water – one long, panoramic view,” the studio said.

“What we’ve found, and what this project really demonstrates, is that staggering the spaces along the shoreline actually exposes more of the home to the lake, creating varied and intimate views from different rooms rather than one singular experience.”

The internal garden courtyard sits on the northeast side of the site, protected on three sides by the house.

“It’s an unexpected space that offers a transition between the neighborhood street and an expansive lake view,” the studio said. “It draws natural light and air deep into each of the three structures.”

The gable roofs help the structure fit into its context, while the standing-seam roof and dark bronze metal box rib elevate the form with a clean, contemporary expression.

To contrast the colour and texture of the metal, the shorter mass is clad in light-toned limestone.

“We wanted the exterior to feel rooted in the region,” the studio said.

“The limestone is quarried regionally, and paired with recyclable metal cladding, it’s a palette built to last.”

Inside, character-grade domestic wood on the floors and ceilings adds warmth to the space.

It has intentional gaps between boards so sound can be absorbed via black insulation to manage the acoustics of the space.

Founded in Chicago in 1987, Wheeler Kearns works across multiple design sectors. In recent years, the small studio has built another gabled house overlooking Lake Michigan, a low-lying house in a ravine and a penthouse for art collectors – both near Chicago.

#284. US-Italian curator Francesco Bonami appointed artistic director of Moscow's GES-2 House of Culture

Francesco Bonami © GES-2 House of Culture

The Italian curator Francesco Bonami, who is also a US citizen, has been appointed the artistic director of GES-2 House of Culture in Moscow. The move comes as Russia’s official relations with Europe continue to deteriorate over the ongoing invasion of Ukraine.

The institution—which was opened in 2021 by the billionaire Leonid Mikhelson’s V-A-C Foundation inside an early-20th century power plant opposite the Kremlin—announced the appointment this week. Teresa Iarocci Mavica, the Italian-born co-founder of V-A-C Foundation, stepped down as the head of GES-2 a month after it opened. Alisa Prudnikova, a curator and the founder of the Ural Industrial Biennial of Contemporary Art, has overseen programming at GES-2 since 2022 and will stay on until December whereafter she will continue as an independent project curator.

Bonami, who started out as an artist, has previously served as an editor of Flash Art magazine, as well as the artistic director of the 50th Venice Biennale in 2003, the co-curator of Manifesta 3 (2000) and of the Whitney Biennial (2010). He was a senior curator at the Museum of Contemporary Art, Chicago for nearly a decade. In 2024, he was the curator of Maurizio Cattelan’s first solo gallery exhibition in 20 years, at Gagosian in New York.

GES-2 House of Culture in Moscow © GES-2 House of Culture

Bonami has collaborated with the V-A-C Foundation since 2010. In 2024 he was the co-curator, with Zelfira Tregulova, the former director of the State Tretyakov Gallery, of Square and Space: From Malevich to GES-2—which explored “the important role played by Russian art” in artistic innovation of the 20th century, according to a release. He told Artnews at the time: “Sanctions are economic, not cultural. To sanction culture is a white crime that kills people’s souls.” Meanwhile, Ukrainian art historians have been working to establish Malevich’s identity as a Ukrainian artist at international institutions.

While Europe at large has widely condemned Russia on the cultural stage—the European Union pulled €2m Venice Biennale funding over Russia's participation earlier this year—Italy has been more open. The Biennale’s president, Pietrangelo Buttafuoco, continues to defend his decision to allow Russia back into the international exhibition. Museum exchanges between Russia and EU countries and the UK were suspended after the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Mikhelson has not been personally sanctioned by the EU or US since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. However the UK, Canada, Australia, New Zealand and Ukraine did impose personal sanctions on him after the invasion. Mikhelson’s daughter Victoria, to whom he transferred ownership of GES-2 in 2023, has not been personally sanctioned by any country but Ukraine.

Bonami did not respond to a request for comment from The Art Newspaper about his appointment. In GES-2’s press release he is quoted as saying that his role as artistic director is to “catalyse artistic energy” and “search for the best projects,” adding: “My experience should help with this.”

In an interview with Moskva 24 television channel, the cultural commentator Eugenia Smurygina emphasised Bonami’s US citizenship. “The artistic director of GES-2 will be an American, an ethnic Italian,” she said. “Isn’t this interesting, in 2026?”

A statement from the GES-2 team sent to The Art Newspaper on 15 October said: “GES-2’s international outlook is integral to its identity, independent of any individual appointment. Francesco Bonami’s appointment reflects this commitment to dialogue and exchange, including the possibility of exhibitions involving artists and cultural practitioners from any country who are open to such engagement.”

Update: This article was updated to make clear that Leonid Mikhelson was sanctioned by the UK, Canada, Australia, New Zealand and Ukraine in 2022

#286. How Baseline Can Help You Ship Less JavaScript

Jad is an independent JavaScript & Web Performance consultant and educator who has trained developers worldwide through online platforms, in-person … More about Jad ↬

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

Most of us install a dependency once and never look at it again. It does its job, the tests pass, and we move on. But the web platform keeps moving too, and a surprising number of the libraries sitting in your package.json today are now built into the browser.

In a typical mid-sized JavaScript app, you can often find somewhere between 60KB and 90KB (minified and gzipped) of dependencies that the platform can now handle on its own. Date and number formatting, HTTP requests, modals, tooltips, deep cloning, grouping arrays: these were all real gaps a few years ago. A lot of them aren’t gaps anymore.

The reason those libraries stick around isn’t laziness. It’s that most teams don’t re-audit their dependencies on a Baseline cadence, or are simply not aware of how fast browsers are shipping these days. You check npm audit for security, but is this library still doing something the browser can’t? is a question that rarely gets asked. So the libraries stay.

In this article, we’ll run that audit together. Instead of going through dependencies one by one, we’ll work in clusters, because the wins tend to come in groups. We’ll do the bundle math, build a small decision framework you can reuse, and stay honest about the cases where the platform still falls short. By the end, you’ll have a repeatable process you can run on your own package.json.

Before we start deleting things, let’s quickly recap what Baseline is. Feel free to skip this section if you’re already familiar.

Baseline is a project from the WebDX Community Group that tells you, in plain terms, how safe a web feature is to use across the major browsers (Chrome, Edge, Firefox, and Safari). A feature can be in one of three states:

That 30-month gap between “Newly” and “Widely” matters a lot for this audit. A feature that’s Widely available is something you can usually drop a library for today. A feature that’s only Newly available is something you can drop a library for if you check your audience first, or if you’re comfortable with a small feature check. We’ll treat those two cases differently throughout.

You can look any feature up on webstatus.dev, on MDN (every reference page shows a Baseline badge near the top), or programmatically with the web-features npm package. We’ll use all three later when we run the audit on a real project.

Meet “TypeScript in 50 Lessons”, our shiny new guide to TypeScript. With detailed code walkthroughs, hands-on examples and common gotchas. For developers who know enough JavaScript to be dangerous.

It’s tempting to read “the browser does this now” and start ripping libraries out. Let’s not do that. A swap that looks free on paper can quietly break things for a chunk of your users, or cost you a feature you were relying on without realizing it.

So before dropping any library, ask three questions. We’ll reuse these in every cluster below.

1. Is the replacement Baseline-safe for my audience?

Not “is it Baseline” in the abstract, but “is it safe for the people who actually use my app.” If the native feature is Widely available, this is usually a yes. If it’s only Newly available, check your analytics or your browserslist config and see what share of your users would miss out. A B2B dashboard where everyone’s on the latest browser is a very different situation from a public-facing site with a long tail of old Android devices.

Dropping a library isn’t always free. Sometimes the native feature isn’t supported widely enough yet, so you’d reach for a polyfill. If that polyfill is heavier than the library you’re removing, you’ve made your bundle bigger, unless you load it conditionally. We’ll see exactly this with Temporal later.

3. Does the platform feature cover my real use case?

Libraries often do more than the platform feature they resemble. axios isn’t just fetch with automatic JSON parsing; it has interceptors, request cancellation, and retries. If you’re using those, a straight swap to fetch will leave you reimplementing them. Check what you actually use before assuming it’s a drop-in replacement.

Keep these three in mind. Every cluster below is really just these questions applied to a different corner of your dependencies.

This is the cluster where you’ll usually find the most KBs sitting on top of features that are already Widely available. The browser ships a whole family of formatting tools under the Intl namespace, and a lot of small, popular libraries became unnecessary.

Here are the usual suspects and what replaces them:

timeago.js exists to turn a timestamp into “3 hours ago”. Intl.RelativeTimeFormat does the same thing, and it’s Baseline Widely available.

The numeric: "auto" option is the nice touch here: it gives you “yesterday” instead of “1 day ago” where the language has a word for it. You pass a number and a unit, and you get a localized string back.

You may be wondering about the one thing timeago.js does that this snippet doesn’t: it picks the unit for you. Given a date, timeago.js decides whether to say “seconds” or “days.” Intl.RelativeTimeFormat expects you to do that part. It’s a few lines of arithmetic (work out the difference, find the largest unit that fits), and once you’ve written that helper, you don’t need the library anymore.

Intl.NumberFormat covers most of what number-formatting libraries do: thousands separators, currency, percentages, and compact notation.

And Intl.ListFormat, Widely available, handles the “join an array into a sentence” problem, including the Oxford comma, which is the kind of thing people write fiddly helper functions for:

humanize-duration turns a number of milliseconds into “1 hour, 30 minutes”. The platform equivalent is Intl.DurationFormat:

One thing to keep in mind is that Intl.DurationFormat is Baseline Newly available at the time of writing, not Widely available. It landed in all the major engines in March 2025, and it’s on track to become Widely available in 2027. So this one fails question 1 for broad-audience apps unless you check your traffic first or add a fallback. For an internal tool on modern browsers, it’s fine today. For a public site with old devices, give it another year or guard it with a feature check.

If your app uses the full set (humanize-duration, timeago.js, pluralize, numeral), that’s roughly 14 KB gzipped of dependencies, most of it replaceable right now with Widely available APIs. The internationalization cluster is usually the easiest win in the whole audit.

This cluster is more nuanced, so it’s a good one to slow down on.

The browser HTTP libraries people reach for are axios (17 KB gz) and superagent (19 KB gz). For most requests, fetch plus AbortController covers what you need, and both are Widely available.

The one extra line (res.json()) is fetch being explicit where axios was implicit. That’s the pattern across this whole cluster: fetch does less for you by default, and you decide whether you want the things it leaves out.

axios has a timeout option. fetch has AbortSignal.timeout():

This is where question 3 does most of the work, so let’s be specific about the gaps:

I personally heavily rely on interceptors in my interactive online courses, such as Learn JavaScript, and I have solved that for years using a custom class on top of fetch. I’ve shipped this to millions of users and have seen lots of success with it.

None of these are hard to rebuild, and most apps only use one or two of them. But this is exactly the kind of cluster where you shouldn’t do a blind find-and-replace. Look at how you actually use your HTTP client first. If it’s plain GETs and POSTs, dropping axios for a thin fetch wrapper saves you about 17 KB gzipped.

This cluster has some of the most satisfying swaps, because the platform features don’t just match the libraries, they’re often more accessible than what teams ship by hand.

The libraries here are modal dialogs (something like a11y-dialog, 1.8 KB gz), tooltip and popover libraries (tippy.js, 14 KB gz, which bundles Popper for positioning), focus-trap (6.6 KB gz), and body-scroll-lock (1.3 KB gz). They get replaced by three platform features: the

element, the Popover API, and CSS anchor positioning.

A huge amount of modal-related code exists to solve accessibility problems: trapping focus inside the modal, closing on Escape, restoring focus to the previous element when the dialog is closed, and rendering above everything else. The

element, Widely available, does all of that for you.

Calling showModal() does the work that focus-trap was installed for: focus moves into the dialog, the rest of the page becomes inert so you can’t tab out of it, Escape closes it, and focus returns to the element that opened it. The dialog renders in the browser’s Top layer, so you don’t fight z-index. You also get a ::backdrop pseudo-element to style the overlay.

That single element can replace your modal library and focus-trap. The one piece it doesn’t handle on its own is locking the background from scrolling, which is what body-scroll-lock was for. That’s now one line of CSS:

If you’re wondering why we’re using dialog:modal instead of dialog[open], it’s because the open attribute is set as soon as you call show(), but the dialog isn’t actually modal so you don’t want to lock scrolling yet. The :modal pseudo-class is only true when the dialog is actually modal, which is the case when you call showModal().

So three libraries collapse into one element and one CSS rule.

For things that aren’t full modals (dropdown menus, tooltips, the small floating panels that tippy.js handles), the Popover API gives you light-dismiss behavior, top-layer rendering, and Escape-to-close with no JavaScript at all:

Clicking the button toggles the popover. Clicking outside it closes it. It’s Baseline Newly available (since January 2025).

The other half of what a tooltip library does is positioning: keeping the floating element pinned to its trigger and flipping it when it would overflow the viewport. That’s what Popper (bundled inside tippy.js) handles, and it’s now a CSS feature called anchor positioning. Here it pins the same #menu popover directly under its trigger button:

Anchor positioning is the newest feature in this article. It became Baseline Newly available in January 2026, when Firefox 147 shipped it (Chrome had it since version 125, and Safari since version 26). Because it’s this fresh, it’s squarely a question-1 feature: great for modern audiences, but check your traffic, and note that some of the more advanced parts (like position-try fallbacks) have uneven support across versions. Keep a sensible fallback for older browsers.

Between

, the Popover API, and anchor positioning, the UI primitives cluster (tooltip library, modal library, focus-trap, body-scroll-lock) adds up to roughly 24 KB gzipped, and you come out the other side with better accessibility defaults than most hand-rolled solutions.

Lodash is rarely imported whole anymore, but its individual functions show up everywhere, either as the full lodash package (25 KB gz) or as standalone installs like lodash.clonedeep and lodash.groupby. Several of the most common ones now have direct platform equivalents.

lodash.groupby reorganizes an array into an object keyed by some property. Object.groupBy does exactly that:

There’s also Map.groupBy for when you want a Map instead of a plain object (handy if your keys aren’t strings). Both are Baseline Newly available, since March 2024, and on track to become Widely available in late 2026.

lodash.clonedeep makes a deep copy of an object. structuredClone is the platform version, and it’s Widely available:

structuredClone handles the tricky cases that trip up JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(...)): it clones Date, Map, Set, ArrayBuffer, and circular references correctly. The limit to know about (question 3 again) is that it can’t clone functions, DOM nodes, or class instances; it throws on functions and drops the prototype on class instances. For plain data, which is what most people deep-clone, it’s a clean replacement.

If you’ve ever pulled in a Lodash helper for union, intersection, or difference, the Set object now has these built in. They’re Baseline Newly available, since June 2024:

The full set of methods is union, intersection, difference, symmetricDifference, isSubsetOf, isSupersetOf, and isDisjointFrom.

Not all of Lodash has moved into the platform. debounce and throttle still have no native equivalent, and they’re genuinely useful, so cherry-picking lodash.debounce is reasonable. The point of this cluster isn’t “delete Lodash,” it’s “stop shipping the parts the browser already has.” Dropping lodash.clonedeep and lodash.groupby alone is about 8 KB gzipped, and if you were importing the full lodash for a handful of functions, replacing the platform-covered ones can let you drop it entirely.

Every cluster so far has ended in “go ahead, drop it.” This one is the opposite, and that’s why it’s worth including: it shows the framework telling you to wait.

Temporal is the long-awaited replacement for JavaScript’s Date, and it’s a genuinely better API: immutable objects, sane time zone handling, and no more month indexes starting at zero. It reached TC39 Stage 4 in March 2026 and is part of the ES2026 specification. Firefox shipped it in version 139 (in 2025), and Chrome shipped it in version 144 (January 2026). Safari hasn’t shipped it in a stable release yet; it’s in Safari Technology Preview, with stable support expected later in 2026.

If Temporal is news to you, check out the Temporal Cheatsheet for a quick overview of the API and a comparison to Date.

However, Temporal is not Baseline. It’s still in limited availability, because Safari users don’t have it. To use it across all browsers today, you need a polyfill, and this is where the math turns against you.

The official @js-temporal/polyfill is about 44 KB gzipped. There’s a smaller polyfill that internally does not depend on BigInt and it weighs 19 KB gzipped. A lightweight date library like dayjs is about 3 KB gzipped. So if you swap dayjs for Temporal plus its polyfill right now, you’re not saving 3 KB, you’re adding roughly 41 KB to your bundle, unless you are able to load the polyfill conditionally.

The verdict is generally clear: keep dayjs (or date-fns) for now. The moment to revisit is when Safari ships Temporal in a stable release and it reaches Baseline. At that point you can use Temporal natively and conditionally load the polyfill for users on older browsers. This is a feature to write down and check again in a few months, not one to act on today.

The clusters above are a starting map, but your dependencies are your own. Here’s a repeatable process you can run this quarter.

Start by listing what actually ships to users:

For a quick per-package number, Bundlephobia gives you the minified and gzipped size of any npm package. For the real picture (what each dependency costs in your actual bundle, after tree-shaking and deduplication), run a bundle analyzer against your build. npx source-map-explorer works on most bundles, and npx vite-bundle-visualizer works for Vite projects.

For each candidate, find the platform feature that would replace it and check its Baseline status. The quickest way is webstatus.dev or the Baseline badge on the feature’s MDN page.

For each library with a platform replacement, go back to the framework: Is it Baseline-safe for your audience? What does the swap cost? Does the feature cover how you actually use the library? Most of your decisions will fall out of question 1 (check the feature’s status against your browserslist) and question 3 (check your own usage).

For Widely available features, swap and move on. For Newly available ones, either confirm your audience is on modern browsers or guard the new code with a quick feature check and keep a fallback:

That way you ship less code to the users who can run it, without breaking the ones who can’t.

Add the clusters up, and the picture is concrete. The internationalization cluster is around 14 KB gzipped, HTTP is around 17 KB, the UI primitives are around 24 KB, and the Lodash utilities are 8 KB or more depending on how much of the library you were shipping. For a typical mid-sized app, that’s somewhere between 60 KB and 90 KB gzipped of dependencies you can hand back to the platform, and more if you were shipping the full lodash or several of these libraries at once. (The uncompressed numbers are two to three times larger, which is what you’ll see in a bundle analyzer before gzip.)

I’ve chosen relatively lean packages for most of these features, but some individual packages could still be heavy. Your dialog package, for instance, could alone weigh as much as 50KB gzipped depending on what you’re using.

A few features are worth keeping an eye on over the next year, because they’ll open up further swaps:

None of this is a one-time cleanup. The platform ships new features constantly, and the gap between “you need a library for this” and “the browser does this” keeps closing. The habit worth building is small: once a quarter, run the audit. List your dependencies, check what’s now Baseline, and hand back what you can.

Pick one cluster from this article, open your package.json, and see how much of it the browser already does for you.

#287. Editorial Design: Word's Eye by Crtomir Just

Crtomir Just creates an expressive editorial design for literary festival Word's Eye, using lenticular prints and kinetic eye graphics.

Slovenian graphic designer Ärtomir Just developed the visual identity, campaign assets, exhibition design, and promotional poster series for Word's Eye, an annual national gathering celebrating youth literature in Murska Sobota. Translating the event's name into a literal graphic motif, Just constructs an abstract eye illustration that inspects featured literary works across print and digital media channels. High-contrast monochromatic typography pairs with distorted circular pupil geometries, creating strong visual tension across print and digital formats. Rather than relying on traditional bookish imagery, the system uses bold graphic forms to capture the raw curiosities of young writers.

The underlying layout framework balances expressive eyeball illustrations with a disciplined architectural grid. Just places heavy sans-serif logotypes and event schedules at the margins, allowing the central eye pupil graphic to shift position across different poster iterations. This variable placement gives the promotional series dynamic rhythm when displayed together in gallery spaces or public street walls. This clear structural cohesion across the editorial design ensures that whether rendered as static print announcements or animated social media clips where the pupil rotates, event details remain immediately readable to passersby.

Production craft elevates the physical poster series into interactive public art. Just utilized custom lenticular printing techniques for the outdoor display posters, causing the printed eye graphic to track viewers as they walk past the exhibition frames in physical space. On digital platforms, short motion loops extend the lenticular effect through subtle frame shifts and iris dilations. By combining physical print technology with digital motion discipline, the project demonstrates how event-driven editorial design can transform standard promotional posters into engaging, responsive visual experiences.

#288. De Kooning sets European record but still falls flat at muted Sotheby’s Contemporary Evening Sale

Willem de Kooning’s Untitled (1977) sold for £9.8m after fees, setting a record for the artist at auction in Europe

“Don’t panic, it’s okay,” auctioneer Tom Eddison told the sale room as an alarm briefly interrupted the start of Sotheby’s London’s Contemporary Evening Sale on Thursday. The disruption was quickly dealt with, but the art market warning delivered by the auction results may prove harder to brush aside.

The sale, held at Sotheby’s New Bond Street premises on Thursday (15 October), brought in £36.9m at hammer, below its £39.5m low estimate. Including fees, the total reached £45.9m, slightly below last October’s £47.6m.

The top lot of the evening was Willem de Kooning’s 1977 oil on canvas Untitled. Eddison opened the bid for the guaranteed work at £7m, below the presale low estimate of £8m. (Sale price includes fees, presale estimates do not.) The work hammered at £8.2m and sold for £9.8m after fees, setting a record for the artist at auction in Europe. The amount paid is two and a half times what the work sold for at Sotheby’s New York in 2015.

Of the 34 lots offered after three were withdrawn, six went unsold. The sell-through rate was 82%, with approximately 30% of the lots hammering above their respective presale low estimate.

The results reflect the overall cautious mood of the market for contemporary art, which has also been observed at Frieze London, said Thomas Stauffer, the co-founder of the Zurich-based Gerber & Stauffer Fine Arts and president of the Swiss Art Market Association. Stauffer is in town for the art week.

“Collectors are not willing to take big risks,” Stauffer said, noting that many are on the fence and put their limits “conservatively low”, unwilling to go above high estimates in most cases.

The fact that works by Lynette Yiadom-Boakye (presale estimates £600,000 to £900,000) and Jadé Fadojutimi (£350,000 to £450,000), whose prices were off the charts a couple of years ago, went unsold is “concerning” for the ultra-contemporary segment, the dealer and advisor said. “The price hikes have been proven to be unhealthy, and people are no longer willing to pay fantasy prices for young artists.”

A 2021 walled sculpture, I Who Was Awestruck at the Shape of the Secret I Found in the Cosmos, by Yayoi Kusama, who died recently, was hammered at £250,000, a quarter of the presale low estimate of £1m. It sold for £320,000 after fees. “It’s more than a little scratch; that result does not go down well in auction database history,” Stauffer commented. He questioned the presale valuation and called the consignor's consent to sell substantially below that figure as “mysterious”.

It was not all bad news. The second most valuable lot of the night was Gerhard Richter’s 1992 Abstraktes Bild, which debuted at Documenta and was shown last year at the artist’s major retrospective at Fondation Louis Vuitton in Paris. The work sold for £5.4m (£6.7m with fees), slightly below the presale low estimate of £6m. But this is well above its previous sale price of £3.6m achieved in a 2011 Christie’s London sale.

Gerhard Richter’s Abstraktes Bild (1992) sold for £5.4m (£6.7m with fees),

Trailing behind in third place was Mark Rothko’s Untitled guaranteed Colour Field painting executed in 1969. The painting sold for £3m (£3.8m) to an online bidder, meeting the presale low estimate. The work, which has been in the same collection for more than three decades, last sold for $264,000 (approximately £148,104 based on the historical exchange rate) at a 1992 Christie’s sale. A 1964 Rothko painting, which had a $9.9m to $16m (£7.5m to £12.3m) estimate, was withdrawn from Sotheby’s Hong Kong evening sale last month.

Mark Rothko, Untitled (1969) sold for £3m (£3.8m) to an online bidder, meeting the presale low estimate

David Hockney's iPad drawing 10th – 22nd June 2021, Water Lilies in the Pond with Pots of Flowers attracted active bidding. The drawing made a hammer price of £1.5 million (£1.9m with fees)—three times its £450,000 presale low estimate and setting an auction record for any iPad work by the artist.

Another Hockney work, an acrylic and paper collage titled Henry Reading (1985), sold for £2.3m (£2.8m after fees), above the presale low estimate of £2.2m. It was a guaranteed work and fresh to the auction market.

David Hockney, Henry Reading sold for £2.3m (£2.8m after fees), above the presale low estimate of £2.2m

Michael Andrews’ small acrylic on paper painting Butterfly Fish (1978) also sparked interest among bidders, who drove the bids to nearly five times above the presale high estimate of £120,000, reaching a hammer price of £550,000. The fresh-to-auction work sold for £704,000 after fees, setting an artist record for a work on paper.

Other notable results included George Baselitz’s figurative painting P.D. Idol (1964). Bidding for the guaranteed work was intense and it sold for £1.9m (£2.4m after fees), nearly double the presale low estimate of £1m. The result was slightly above its previous sale price of £1.8m achieved at Phillips London in 2018.

The house noted that Thursday’s sale result has brought the total auction sales across all categories at Sotheby’s London in 2026 to $1bn, with £598m ($793m) generated from Modern and contemporary auctions, the highest year-to-date total since 2015.

#289. OMA to convert Houston coffee plant into music school with instrument-informed architecture

Architecture studio OMA has broken ground on the Frank Liu Jr Academy for Music and Arts charter school in Houston, a pre-K through eighth-grade institution housed in a former coffee plant.

The three-storey Frank Liu Jr Academy for Music and Arts (FLAMA) building will be organised around Montessori learning principles, according to the team, and will integrate instrument forms into spaces, such as a curved stair that “recalls the form of a French horn”.

Located along the Buffalo Bayou East corridor in Houston’s second ward, FLAMA will be housed within the city’s historic 1930s JA Folger & Co coffee plant, a 250,000-square-foot complex that contains multiple warehouse buildings.

“Like fine-tuning an instrument, our design recalibrates the existing industrial structure into an open, connected, and expressive environment for learning,” said OMA partner Jason Long.

“FLAMA will be a new learning environment that builds on the character of the existing building while giving it a new life for the community.”

According to the studio, learning spaces will ascend in age from the bottom to top floors. Each floor will contain two central spaces for gathering, with classrooms, practice rooms, and academic programs organised around them to create “neighbourhoods” of learning.

Beyond the expansive main stair, the form of instruments will also be integrated into spaces such as the double-height cafetorium, which will feature a large circular opening informed by the round body of a banjo.

An F-shaped opening will also connect two library commons, calling to the forte symbol and the f-hole of a string instrument.

Montirossi’s principles of “prioritising openness, independence, and collective learning” shaped much of the design strategy, according to the team, and the renderings show expansive, colourful spaces throughout, including a roof terrace with an enormous yellow roof.

According to local reports, commercial, retail and apartment buildings are also slated to be located at the former coffee plant, which is being developed by local firm Lovett Commercial.

FLAMA is expected to open in 2027 and will be an open-enrollment, tuition-free public charter school.

OMA recently completed an affordable housing development in San Francisco, while OMA co-founder Elia Zenghelis passed away aged 89 earlier this month.

Previously, Lovett Commercial and OMA worked together on POST Houston.

#290. Editorial Web Design: Rambling Muse by SocioDesign

Discover the sophisticated editorial web design for Rambling Muse by SocioDesign, featuring modular grids, custom icons, and refined typography.

Commissioned by writer Clarisse Lehmann, London-based agency SocioDesign developed a comprehensive visual identity and responsive editorial web design for Rambling Muse. Having lived in New York, Geneva, Tokyo, Madrid, and London, Lehmann approached her lifestyle publication through the distinctive lens of an observant outsider. Rather than adopting the busy, advertising-heavy conventions of traditional lifestyle blogs, SocioDesign treated the digital platform with the typographic rigor and quiet sophistication of an archival literary quarterly.

The brand identity is anchored by a stylized geometric owl mark, capturing the watchful, nocturnal curiosity of the writer observing urban life. Paired with an expansive library of custom monoline illustrations, the graphic language adds warmth and narrative whimsy across category headers including Go, Linger, and Get. These delicate line drawings depict metropolitan artifactsâfrom espresso cups and cocktail glasses to iconic skyline silhouettes like Big Ben and the Eiffel Towerâgiving the publication an artisanal, handcrafted visual signature.

The chromatic system relies on restrained editorial elegance. Soft blush pink and warm porcelain tones provide a gentle, tactile background for rich charcoal typography and high-contrast photography. This palette creates visual warmth without overwhelming the reading experience, allowing editorial photography and witty cultural essays to take center stage.

The web layout employs an asymmetrical modular grid that breaks away from rigid single-column templates. SocioDesign engineered responsive content cards with varying proportionsâjuxtaposing vertical architectural photography, circular pull-quote badges, and horizontal food spreads with generous white space. A fixed, minimalist sidebar navigation anchors the reading flow on desktop, while on mobile, the layout reflows into a seamless, distraction-free reading experience with precise typographic hierarchy.

#291. Guerrilla Shading Pavilion demonstrates that "shade doesn't need to be expensive or complicated"

Architecture studio Pearce+ has created a timber pavilion in Camden, London, to draw attention to the need for shade in the UK and encourage people to build their own DIY shading.

Commissioned by Camden Inspire festival, the simple pavilion is currently situated at the site of the Camden Collective charity in north London. It was built to show how shade can easily be created.

“We wanted to show that shade can be practical, playful and beautiful,” Pearce+ founder Owen Pearce told Dezeen.

“Making shade doesn’t need to be expensive or complicated,” he continued. “A bit of ingenuity, some simple materials and a few willing hands can go a long way.”

The timber pavilion has a simple hexagonal form constructed from five prefabricated, trapezoidal sections that were assembled on site. All of the timber was reused from previous Pearce+ projects.

The slated timber walls shade a small interior space, while the structure acts as an anchor that large pieces of fabric can be attached to, creating a roof for additional shading.

Pearce+ worked with Shade The UK to develop the structure with the aim of drawing attention to the growing need to create shaded spaces in the UK.

“Shade is one of the simplest ways to make our increasingly hot environments more bearable, yet it’s remarkably overlooked in the UK,” said Pearce.

“We have surprisingly short memories when it comes to hot summers, and conversations about overheating quickly disappear when the weather cools,” he continued.

“We need to start treating shade as essential infrastructure, not a seasonal luxury. That means changing planning policy, but also empowering people to take action themselves.”

The lower sections of the pavilion were left unfinished, with visitors to the festival completing them using donated fabric to weave into the walls.

This participation was part of a wider desire to use the pavilion to encourage people to add shade to streets and public spaces themselves as part of the studio’s Guerrilla Shading initiative.

“I’d love people to adopt a can-do attitude for shading,” said Pearce. “Look around your school, garden, street or local park and ask: where could we make some shade? Who could we work with? What could we make it from?”

“And don’t wait until the next heatwave!” he continued. “Start thinking and making now, so we’re ready for next summer. Small, creative interventions can make a real difference and spark much bigger conversations.”

According to Pearce, the pavilion was designed to be disassembled and rebuilt, and he hopes to take the structure on tour – ideally to Glastonbury Festival.

“The pavilion was designed to be dismantled and reassembled, with new shade sails and contributions added wherever it goes,” said Pearce.

“It’s currently at the festival’s home of Camden Collective, but organisers Camden Unlimited are planning to take it on tour in the new year with local organisations or schools, so hopefully it will continue evolving and sparking conversations,” he continued.

“Personally, I’d love to take it to Glastonbury. Anyone who’s been there during a heatwave knows there’s precious little shade! A series of collectively made shading structures across the festival could be brilliant.”

Previously on Dezeen, architect Liz Gálvez created a pavilion Los Angeles from cord and earthen blocks to showcase the potential of urban shade.

#292. François Pinault to launch permanent display of his collection at Venice’s Palazzo Grassi

The French billionaire art collector François Pinault has announced plans to launch a permanent display of his holdings at the Palazzo Grassi gallery in Venice. In an interview in the newspaper Le Monde published on Thursday (15 October), Pinault confirmed that the new permanent exhibition will include 106 pieces by 54 artists drawn from his holdings.

The move means the prestigious temporary exhibition programme ends at the palazzo, which Pinault purchased in 2005 and opened in 2006. A show of works by the Kenyan-British artist Michael Armitage is showing at Palazzo Grassi until 10 January 2027. Temporary shows will continue at Pinault’s other Venetian venue, the Punta della Dogana.

The idea for the permanent display at Palazzo Grassi came about gradually, explains Pinault. “For 20 years, we opted for temporary exhibitions, major monographic projects, collaborative projects with artists, and dialogues between works in the collection and those from elsewhere. But in those 20 years, the collection itself has evolved considerably. It has grown, become more structured, and certain works have stood out for their power and their ability to transcend time.”

He adds: “A permanent display allows for the juxtaposition of works from different periods and generations, demonstrating how, beyond their individuality, certain questions persist. This is in no way intended to freeze the collection or offer a definitive interpretation.”

Pinault, the founder of the Kering and Artemis companies and owner of Christie's auction house, has amassed a contemporary art collection of over 10,000 works in the last 20 years. The interview in Le Monde throws light on his collecting tastes.

Minimalism and Arte Povera occupy a central place in his collection, he says. His interest in African-American art, meanwhile, has been driven by “encounters with extraordinary, almost shamanic figures like David Hammons for several decades now,” he says. “Highlighting this African-American scene invites us to stray from the well-trodden paths of Western art, to explore alternative routes.”

Studio visits are also a priority for him. “I enjoy observing the creative process, meeting artists in their studios, like the young [French artist] Louis Le Kim I recently met,” he says. “You have to behave delicately [in studios], not settle in for the afternoon.”

#294. "Pioneering conservationist" Donald Insall dies aged 100

Photography by Donald Insall Associates

Architect Donald Insall, founder of Donald Insall Associates and known for his conservation and renovation work, including on Windsor Castle, has died at the age of 100.

Insall, whose death was announced in a statement from his studio, was best known for his work in conservation, which he saw as different to preservation.

“Preservation he said is ‘what you do for marmalade’,” Donald Insall Associates said in a statement. “In the case of buildings, this means keeping them in their original state for posterity.”

Instead, Insall, whom his studio described as a “pioneering conservationist”, aimed to conserve buildings for their continued use.

“Conservation means working with old buildings, streets and towns in ways that allow them to live on usefully and delightfully for new uses when and where appropriate and for future generations,” his studio said.

Born in Bristol on 7 February 1926, Insall founded his studio, Donald Insall Associates, in 1958 and served as its chairman until 1998.

The many projects that Insall worked on include the 18th-century baroque Wotton House, Buckinghamshire, which was saved from demolition in 1957, the renovation of William Morris’s Kelmscott Manor in Oxfordshire and the conservation of the historic city centre in Chester.

After a fire devastated Windsor Castle, the royal residence in Berkshire, in 1992, Insall led the teams that restored the building.

His book Living Buildings, first printed in 2008, was reprinted in 2018 with a foreword by King Charles (then Prince of Wales) in 2018.

In it, the King stated that Insall had been “deeply involved, not just as a tireless practitioner, but in mentoring and inspiring others” in the realm of heritage and architectural conservation.

Insall started his architectural studies in 1942 at the Royal West of England Academy School of Architecture and then studied civic design at the Royal Academy Schools and later at the School of Planning in London.

After his studies, he worked for London practice Phillimore and Jenkins, which restored and designed country houses.

In 1958, he founded his own studio together with Peter Locke. Among the projects it worked on was a study of Chester, which involved visiting more than four hundred buildings in the city and led to the creation of conservation officers by local councils across England.

Insall is also known for his role in creating the English Heritage charity, for which he was a founding commissioner.

The architect believed that to get the best results when it came to conserving historic buildings, it was important was to “try to make friends” with them.

“I think that as a result of our experience over the years”, he said, “we have developed a method that we feel is a wise one. We always try to make friends with the building itself, but also with its current users, so that both their respective needs can be met.”

“We prepare a life story of the building, and from there we assess the building’s positive aspects,” Insall continued. “We also take a look at its less successful features and see how these can be helped. However, the important thing is to take a positive approach to the project.”

Recent projects by his studio include the renovation of a Grade II-listed Oxford college library and the renovation of the “deconstructed” Hardwick Old Hall ruin.

Photography by Donald Insall Associates

#295. Four Squares Cafe Is a Masterclass in Cafe Branding

Studio Moara gave Four Squares Cafe a chunky four-square wordmark, a line-drawn blob mascot, and a warm green-and-rust identity for lingering.

Most cafe identities choose between type and character. Four Squares Cafe takes both and makes them share a grid. The wordmark stacks F-O-U-R into a literal two-by-two square of fat, custom block letters, each filled with its own pattern, so the name doubles as a floor plan for the brand. Next to it sits a soft line-drawn blob of a mascot, hugging a coffee cup, drawn with one continuous wobble that undercuts the type's architectural weight. Deep green, brick rust, and golden ochre do the talking over cream and oat milk grounds, and the system reads as warm without going heavy. It is an identity built for the Saudi cafe's whole promise: coffee as a reason to connect and stay a while.

Typography is the system here. The blocky FOUR anchors signage, cards, and packaging at architectural scale, while a quieter layer of italic serif accents ("for STAYING," "for COMFORT") and small-caps microcopy ("Since 2016," "Made to be enjoyed, not rushed") gives the voice its warmth. The mascot earns its own specimen sheet: the blob pours, carries, waves, and naps across a grid of poses, which proves the character works as a repeatable drawing system instead of a one-off doodle. Nothing is decorative for its own sake; every mark carries the comfort brief.

Packaging carries the identity into the hand. White retail bags wear the mascot as a full-wrap line drawing, takeaway cups stack the blocky FOUR against cream sleeves, and a kraft carrier holds the pair for the trip home. The loyalty card keeps the same economy: a cream card stamped with the four-square mark and a promise of the eighth cup free. Out front, a cube sign and an illustrated A-frame take the mascot onto the sidewalk, so the system reads from the street all the way to the saucer.

#296. Formafantasma creates "travelling science exhibition" for Prada Group and IOC

Italian studio Formafantasma has created the displays for Ocean & Climate Village, an exhibition at Prada Group‘s Luna Rossa base in Cagliari, Sardinia, that uses “design as an educational tool” to show the importance of the ocean.

The show, which fashion conglomerate Prada Group describes as a “travelling science exhibition”, was developed by UNESCO‘s Intergovernmental Oceanographic Commission (IOC). It is supported by Prada Group as part of its educational Sea Beyond project.

Formafantasma created a lightweight, modular design for the Ocean & Climate Village, using a disassemblable and reusable aluminium-and-wood structure that allows it to be moved after it has finished its stint at the Luna Rossa base.

The base, which is used by Prada Group’s sailboat racing syndicate Luna Rossa, is located right by the ocean in Sardinia, where the exhibition will be open to the public until 15 October.

The aim of the show, which is divided into four sections – One Ocean, The Climate Engine, Biodiversity and Ocean Anomalies – was to help visitors learn about the connections between biological, climatic and geological processes to better understand the ocean’s impact on our environment.

Formafantasma worked with a craftsman from a natural history museum in Italy to create striking lifelike animals for the exhibition, including a blue crab and a turtle.

As the exhibition is open to visitors of all ages, it was important to create a design that could be understood by both children and adults.

“Sometimes the concepts [on show] are very abstract for us – I could tell you data, I could show you graphs and a number of scientific studies, but especially for lay people, it’s important to find the hooks,” senior programme officer of the IOC Francesca Santoro told Dezeen at the opening of the event.

“I guess you will always remember this because it’s beautiful; it makes [the information] look really nice,” she continued. “The idea was to use design as an educational tool and as a way to attract people’s attention.”

Formafantasma also designed the space on multiple levels to make it more engaging for kids, and created a leaflet that explains words such as CO2 and biodiversity.

The studio has previously designed a picture book about the environment for children and was appointed ecology advisor for the Serpentine Galleries earlier this year.

Ocean & Climate Village will be on display at Luna Rossa base, Cagliari, Sardinia, from 10 to 15 October 2026. See Dezeen Events Guide for an up-to-date list of architecture and design events taking place around the world.
