#298. The Bull And Bear Case For Digital Design In The Age Of AI

Andy is a design founder turned startup investor and coach. He loves speaking at conferences like Smashing Conf and is a founding member of the Adobe Design … More about Andy ↬

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

Designers have spent years saying they would do better work if the organisation got out of the way. Not always in those exact words, obviously. It usually comes out as something more reasonable: we didn’t get enough engineering time, product had already decided the solution, the roadmap was too packed, leadership only cared about this quarter’s numbers, research got cut, the experiment was never run properly, the design debt was known about, but nobody wanted to spend a sprint fixing it.

Much of this is true. Most designers have worked inside that awkward middle space between product and engineering. Product frames the problem, or at least thinks it does. Engineering decides what is feasible, or at least what is affordable. Design is expected to make the thing clearer, simpler, more coherent, more usable, and occasionally more desirable, while also being careful not to disrupt the plan too much.

That position has always been uncomfortable.

They can spot the broken onboarding flow, the confusing upgrade path, the empty state that makes users feel stupid, the feature that looks reasonable in a product review but makes no sense in real use. Seeing the problem is one thing. Getting it fixed is another.

So design often becomes an argument. You make the case. You annotate the flow. You bring the research clip. You point to the support tickets. You show the Figma prototype. You explain why the “small edge case” is actually the first-run experience for half your new users. Then everyone nods, agrees it matters, and moves on to whatever had already made it onto the roadmap.

This is one reason AI is more interesting for design than the usual “will it replace designers?” debate suggests. The real change is not that designers can make more screens. Nobody needs more screens. The interesting change is that designers may need less permission.

Once a week. Useful tips on front-end & UX. Trusted by 207.000 friendly folks.

A good designer can now move from “we should fix this” to “I fixed this, and pushed it live.” They can prototype the alternative onboarding flow, write and test clearer product copy, build a rough working version of the interaction, clean up small pieces of design debt without waiting three months for a roadmap slot, and make the better thing visible enough that it becomes harder to ignore.

That changes the politics of the work. Design has often relied on persuasion because designers lacked direct means of production. AI weakens that dependency. Not everywhere, and not for everything. Complex products still have architecture, infrastructure, data models, permissions, security, compliance, legacy systems, and all the other unglamorous reasons software is hard. But the boundary is moving.

In this version of the future, designers become less permission-dependent: less reliant on product to bless the problem, less reliant on engineering to make every small improvement real, less trapped in the role of internal critic, taste-provider, or Figma operator. More able to make, test, repair, and ship.

The best designers start to look less like traditional product designers and more like hybrid product leaders. They still care about interaction, hierarchy, language, flow, brand and craft, but they also understand the commercial shape of the problem. They can make trade-offs. They can prototype in code, or close enough to code. They can use AI to explore options quickly, then use judgment to throw most of them away. They can sit with a founder or PM and move from a vague product concern to something tangible by the end of the day.

There may be fewer of these people, but they will be harder to ignore. The current design-org model was partly built around scarcity: scarce engineering time, slow production, expensive prototypes, handoffs between specialists, heavy coordination across teams. If AI reduces some of that scarcity, it probably reduces the need for some of the roles that grew around it. The optimistic case is not that every designer keeps their job and gets a productivity boost. That feels like wishful thinking. The more believable version is that the total number of designers goes down, but the designers who remain have more direct influence over the product.

That is not a bad outcome for the strongest designers. It may even be the thing many of them have wanted for years.

Autonomy has teeth. If AI gives designers more room to act, it also removes some of the cover. The same constraints that held good designers back have also protected weaker ones from being tested too directly.

For years, it has been easy to say: I had a better idea, but we never got the engineering time. Sometimes that was exactly what happened. Sometimes the better idea was never really more than a critique. It had not been made concrete. It had not been tested. It had not dealt with the awkward trade-offs. It sounded strong because it lived safely in opposition to the shipped thing.

If you can prototype the recommendation, the recommendation has to get better. If you can make the alternative flow, the flow has to survive contact with details. If you can test the product copy, you have to care what happens when users read it. If you can fix the small piece of design debt, you have to decide whether it was really worth fixing.

Some designers are not as strategic as they think they are. They have learned the language of strategy without the discomfort of owning outcomes. They can talk about user needs, business goals, systems thinking, and product quality, but struggle when asked to make a call. They want influence, but not the exposure that comes with it.

The profession has spent a long time arguing that design deserves more power. Fine. But more power means fewer excuses. It means the work is judged less by the elegance of the argument and more by the quality of the thing you made, tested, or changed. That is a better standard, but it will not be kind to everyone.

There is a second bear case, and it is probably the one large design teams should worry about most. Product and engineering already have more institutional power than design in most companies. They own the roadmap, the technical architecture, the sprint machinery, the metrics, and usually the language leadership understands. Design often has to translate its concerns into someone else’s terms before they count.

AI may not rebalance that power. It may hand product and engineering enough design capability to make design easier to bypass. A PM who can generate a decent flow, decent copy, and a decent prototype may not feel the same need to involve design early. An engineer who can use AI to produce a reasonable interface may decide the design system covers enough of the decision-making. A founder who can get to a polished demo in an afternoon may confuse polish with product thinking.

The problem is not that these people will suddenly become great designers. The problem is that many companies do not know the difference between great design and plausible design. Plausible design is dangerous. It looks coherent in a product review. It uses the right components. The spacing is fine. The copy is not embarrassing. The flow mostly works. Nobody in the meeting feels strongly enough to object. So it ships.

If a company already thinks design is mostly screens, prototypes, and polish, AI gives it a cheaper way to get those things.

In that world, design does not gain more agency. It gets narrowed. The remaining designers manage the design system, police component usage, review flows that have already been decided, tidy the interface, maintain brand consistency, and get pulled into high-stakes launches, executive demos, and the occasional messy cross-platform problem. Useful work, but a smaller surface area. Less shaping the product, more maintaining the furniture.

This is why the “AI will automate the boring 20%” argument feels too comforting. In some companies, perhaps that is what happens. But in large tech organisations, where design teams grew around coordination, production and process, the cut could be much deeper. Not 20%. Maybe 50%. Maybe more. Especially in places where leadership never really understood why the design team had grown so large in the first place.

The painful part is that both futures can be true at the same time. AI can make the best designers more capable and many average designers less necessary. It can give design more agency while reducing design headcount. It can help a small number of designers move closer to product leadership while pushing others into governance and clean-up work. It can free designers from waiting for permission, then reveal that some were more comfortable waiting than acting.

The designers who do well will not be the ones who merely use AI to produce more options. Options are cheap now. They will be the ones who know which option is worth pursuing, why it matters, how to test it, what to cut, where the product is lying to itself, and when “good enough” is quietly damaging the business.

They will have taste, but taste will not be enough. They will need product judgment, technical curiosity, commercial awareness and the nerve to make decisions before every variable is settled. They will need to be comfortable moving between a customer conversation, a prototype, a pricing concern, a brand question, and a messy implementation detail without insisting that all of those belong to someone else.

I’m not completely sure where we end up. I hope it is closer to the bull case: fewer permission structures, more making, more agency, better designers finally able to show what they can do without being held back by the machinery around them.

I fear it may be closer to the bear case: product and engineering absorb much of the work, companies decide plausible design is good enough, and design loses status, headcount, and strategic ground.

In reality, it will probably be some uncomfortable mix of the two. Some designers will use AI to gain more agency. Some companies will use it to need fewer designers. Some teams will produce better work because the distance between judgment and execution gets shorter. Others will ship more plausible mediocrity because nobody in the room can tell the difference.

For years, designers have said they could create more value if they were less constrained by the organisation around them. AI is about to test that claim. Some will finally get to prove it. Some will find out the constraints were doing them a favour.

#299. Gustaf Westman creates Mickey Mouse-shaped sofa and cup for Disney

Swedish designer Gustaf Westman has teamed up with media company Disney to transform its Mickey Mouse character into furniture and accessories that convey “joy and playfulness” ahead of a wider product collaboration.

Westman, who is known for his rounded, colourful designs, revealed the first three items in the Disney collaboration: a sofa, cup and a tumbler.

All have an abstract take on the recognisable Mickey Mouse character, focusing on his ears and face as well as his red shorts with white buttons, which have been turned into the base of the tumbler.

The full collection, which was inspired by Disney brand Mickey & Friends, will include apparel and accessories as well as furniture and homeware. It will be revealed at pop-up stores in Tokyo, New York and Paris.

Westman’s own designs, which span everything from crockery to furniture, often have rounded edges and cartoon-like inflated shapes.

This was something that the designer thought worked well in combination with the Disney characters.

“Collaborating with Disney felt like a very natural creative match from the start – when it came to sketching ideas and exploring how a silhouette or colour of a character could meet my own design language, there was so much overlap between these recognisable silhouettes and my signature work,” he said.

“It felt like two worlds coming together in a way that felt genuine and effortless. There’s so much joy and playfulness associated with these characters, and I wanted to capture some of that feeling in every piece.”

The designer recreated his Chunky Tumbler to look like Mickey Mouse, using the same colour palette as that of the character.

“The Mickey Tumbler is probably my favourite piece,” Westman said. “You can look at it for one second and totally understand it. “

“You see both my world and how I have taken inspiration from Mickey’s world at the same time, and that simplicity is something I’m always trying to achieve,” he continued.

In contrast, the ceramic Mickey Mouse cup and leather Mickey Mouse sofa are all black, with a more abstract, sculptural feel. The sofa will be part of a made-to-order furniture collection and will retail for €9,250.

The Disney x Gustaf Westman collection will first launch at a Paris pop-up on 30 October before moving on to the other cities.

Disney, which was founded as an animation studio in 1923, has inspired a number of designers over the years – especially its Mickey Mouse character. Interior designer Kelly Hoppen reimagined him for a “grown-up” audience, while designer Ron Arad has decorated chairs with Mickey’s oversized ears.

#300. Inside Robot Food’s Packaging Design for Postcard

Robot Food rebrands Singapore's Oasis Beauty Kitchen into Postcard with stamp-illustrated packaging design and custom-molded cleansing bars.

The brief was refreshingly blunt. When founder Hildra Grace approached Robot Food to take her sustainable Singapore beauty brand global, she asked for "less farmers market, more Sephora." Ten-step skincare routines and bathroom shelves crowded with plastic bottles have turned self-care into another daily chore. To strip away that clutter while nodding to the company's previous name, Oasis Beauty Kitchen, Senior Designer Craig and Senior Copywriter Lizzie renamed the line Postcard. It's a warm, immediate hook built around the feeling of escaping to a personal oasis. On the brand's divided manifesto cards, distressed typewriter serif copy sits beside a vertical postal rule, paired with a chunky, rounded geometric wordmark textured like a fresh rubber ink stamp on cream stock.

Every scent gets its own destination. Across the 50 ml Anywhere Fragrance range, the packaging design pairs cylindrical glass bottles and turned wood caps with textured off-white cartons anchored by perforated postage-stamp illustrations. Nothing on the shelf feels clinical. Smoked Roses frames a flame-shaped rose bud inside a crimson stamp border with wavy postmark cancellation lines printed along the side panel, while Hotel Lobby stacks vintage suitcases on a brass bellhop cart inside a royal-blue frame. Moon Bloom shifts the mood to an indigo crescent moon surrounded by botanical leaves, sitting alongside cartons for Sunlit Terrace, Hyaluronic Heaven, Rooftop Disco, and Java Jungle.

The typography keeps the travel narrative grounded without overdoing the nostalgia. On the wrap-around bottle labels, the heavy ink-stamped Postcard logo sits above a fine horizontal rule, where typewriter-style scent names meet tall condensed serifs reading Anywhere Fragrance. Even the soap skips the standard rectangular block. For the Head-to-Toe cleansing bars, Robot Food molded the terracotta and sage-green bars into an ergonomic, cloud-like curve with the wordmark deeply debossed along the lower edge â paired with punchy condensed headlines announcing a "100% chance of showers."

#301. ‘I’ve learnt I can enjoy a work without having to acquire it’: Dasha Shenkman on her approach to art collecting

Dasha Shenkman works closely with the Contemporary Art Society, to which has donated many works to public collections Courtesy Dasha Shenkman

Arts patronage runs in the family for the Canadian-born, UK-based collector Dasha Shenkman. Her late mother, Belle Shenkman, was a notable supporter of the arts and has rooms at both the Royal Academy of Arts and the Royal College of Music named after her for her philanthropy. Dasha, who previously worked as a literary agent, has for several years “supported a wide range of cultural organisations as a trustee, patron and donor”, says a press spokesperson.

She has donated dozens of works to public collections, including the Contemporary Art Society (CAS), with which she has a longstanding relationship. It is alongside CAS that Shenkman has recently launched the Dasha Shenkman Focus Fund, which helps a public institution buy a young artist’s work from Frieze London’s Focus section. “I’ve always sought to support artists during the early, pivotal moments in their career,” Shenkman says, “and I’m very glad to have developed this new fund.”

The Art Newspaper: What was the first work you ever bought?

Dasha Shenkman: A Jean Arp lithograph. I was living in Montreal and fell in love with it as soon as I saw it in a gallery called Mira Godard, one of Canada’s top art dealers. I told the gallerist I wanted to buy it but that I didn’t have the money—I had to save up for it and pay in instalments! The gallery was happy to wait for me, which isn’t so likely to happen these days.

Vassily Kandinsky’s Composition No IV (1911); Shenkman has a passion for the artist’s early works Kunstsammlung Nordrhein-Westfalen

The last work I bought was from an open call show called Hypha Curates, a pop up in a skyscraper near Euston station in London. It is a beautiful drypoint, monotype, collage and embroidery work divided into two halves. It’s called Book of Two Ways by the artist Neil Groom, who explained the background to me when I went to collect it from him. I always aim to meet the artists whose work I collect, if possible. I was delighted to support Neil, Hypha Curates and a close friend of mine, Sarah Elson, who curated the show.

How quickly do you decide to buy a work of art?

I usually make a decision pretty quickly. It’s a gut feeling and I often know where it will live and give me pleasure.

What do you regret not buying when you had the chance?

Not much, to be honest. There are plenty of works I’ve been seriously tempted to buy—I’ll see something somewhere, meet the artist, imagine living with the work—but, in the end, I’ve learnt that I can’t buy everything I like. And that I can simply enjoy a work without having to acquire it. Therapist’s fodder, there!

If you could have any work from any museum in the world, what would it be?

I would love a fresco by Fra Angelico, who created a series of frescoes and altarpieces for the Dominican convent of San Marco in Florence in the Early Renaissance period. If it had to be from a museum, I would probably go for an early [Wassily] Kandinsky or [Egon] Schiele. I get great pleasure, however, from giving works to museums. I must have donated more than 40 now and I love knowing that they’re being enjoyed by people all over the UK. I don’t have anything in storage.

Hop on: “You’ll notice so much more” if you travel around London by bus, Shenkman says Sergii Figurnyi

Which events are you most looking forward to in London this month?

I love going to the annual Unexpected Views event at the National Gallery. The director and various curators from the gallery chat with some of the most important cultural practitioners working today about a masterpiece that they particularly love.It is fascinating listening to the artists looking at the works through the lens of their own practice. The whole event is a lot of fun, sort of like speed-dating from picture to picture, dashing from room to room for the next talk. It is beautifully organised by the team at the National Gallery, and you always see and chat with people you know.

Where do you like to eat and drink during Frieze London?

Wherever I can find an available table. It gets so busy!

If you mean have I been invited to any, the answer is yes. If you mean am I hosting any, the answer is also yes. I’m hosting a party for the Distinguished Patrons of the National Gallery of Canada.

What is your least favourite thing about art fairs?

There’s always too much to see and the crowds are inescapable. But this year at Frieze London I’m looking forward to spending most of my time in the Focus section. The new Focus Fund that I’m bringing to the fair with the Contemporary Art Society is an opportunity to put my convictions into practice: both for the museum who will receive the work and for the young artist whose work will be purchased.

We’ll be buying work for Abbot Hall in Cumbria, who are custodians of a very special collection. I had been to Abbott Hall many years ago, but we all made a visit this summer and I was reminded what a wonderful place it is. I loved meeting Niall Hodson, the keeper of collections, and Will Cooper, the senior curator there. It’s a great context for this inaugural year of the fund.

Where do you go in London to get away from it all?

What tip would you give to someone visiting London for the first time?

Walk everywhere—or take the bus. You’ll notice so much more that way.

#302. Grimshaw completes rammed-earth visitor centre for Twelve Apostles in Australia

Architecture studio Grimshaw and landscape architect Aspect Studios have completed a visitor experience centre for one of Australia‘s most-visited natural landmarks, the Twelve Apostles in Victoria.

Located at the top of the site in Port Campbell National Park, the 3,300-square-metre visitor centre is designed by Grimshaw and Aspect Studios with rammed-earth walls intended to resemble a “landform rather than an autonomous object”.

It comprises two interconnected volumes, the Coastal Building and the Hinterland Building, which each extend outwards in a hugging gesture, facing the coast and the hinterland respectively.

The Hinterland Building houses a cafe and retail facilities, while the Coastal Building serves as the main public education and viewing area, crowned with a rooftop ocean lookout.

The centre was developed in collaboration with the non-profit organisation Eastern Maar Aboriginal Corporation. The organisation helped decide the building’s scale and position to respect both its site within Keerray Woorroong Country and its Traditional Owners, the Eastern Maar peoples.

Landscaped paths gently ascend to the rooftop lookout, with rest areas along the way, where visitors can pause and enjoy the views at various elevations.

“This sequence is central to a broader ambition for the precinct: to move beyond simply processing large numbers of visitors and create a slower and more connected experience of Country,” Grimshaw explained.

“The Twelve Apostles is a truly unique landscape in Australia and arguably anywhere in the world, where the power of the natural environment, the experience of Country and the enduring culture of Eastern Maar come together,” added Grimshaw managing partner Andrew Perez.

“More than simply providing a new destination from which to experience the Twelve Apostles, the project invites visitors to pause, linger and explore, creating a meaningful connection to this extraordinary landscape and the culture and history that have shaped it.”

To enhance the natural look of the building, Grimshaw used a natural material palette including rammed earth and plywood, adding warmth and tactility throughout.

As part of the project, the team also created the Welcome Garden – an outdoor events space and welcome area celebrating Eastern Maar cultural heritage – and introduced coastal scrub, grassland and woodland around the site.

A landscaped car park and access roads were added to separate buses and private vehicles, while pedestrian routes draw visitors from the parking areas into the Welcome Garden and the visitor experience centre, before dispersal to the Twelve Apostles and surrounding coastal attractions.

“The Twelve Apostles Visitor Precinct presented an opportunity to create a more considered relationship between visitors, Country and this extraordinary coastal landscape,” concluded Aspect Studios director Matthew Mackay.

Elsewhere, Grimshaw recently unveiled a trio of Auckland stations informed by Māori narratives, and released plans for a reimagined entry plaza for Allegiant Stadium in Las Vegas.

Architect: Grimshaw Design lead: Harriet Oswald Lead designer: Eduard Ross Partner in charge: Andrew Perez Landscape architect, traditional owner engagement lead, signage and wayfinding: Aspect Studios Lead designers: Matthew Mackay, Nirvana Kadric Co-design partners and heritage consultants: Eastern Maar Aboriginal Land Corporation Builder: Kane Constructions

#303. Editorial Design: Fons Hickmann Posters by Slanted

Explore Fons Hickmann Posters â Now and Then by Slanted Publishers, a masterclass in editorial design, linen binding, and typography.

Monographs dedicated to poster work often stumble into a predictable trap: they treat the book format as nothing more than a passive container for flat graphics. This survey doesn't do that. Published on the occasion of Fons Hickmann's major exhibition at the Brandenburgisches Landesmuseum fÃ¼r moderne Kunst, this volume treats the printed artifact with the exact same rigor that defines Hickmann's three decades of visual communication. Designed in close collaboration between Sven Lindhorst-Emme and Hickmann himself, the publication functions as both an archival retrospective and an active space of typographic inquiry.

At 172 pages bound in tactile grey linen with crisp hot foil embossing, the physical presence of the monograph establishes an immediate sense of weight and purpose. Turn inside, and the editorial design reveals a disciplined two-column grid system balancing bilingual German and English texts by Helene Roolf and JÃ¼rgen W. Schulz. The typography gives every essay ample breathing room, letting running heads and deliberate margins structure the reading cadence before releasing into full-bleed poster reproductions. Nothing feels rushed. The pacing oscillates between dense academic reflections and unrestrained full-page visual spreads.

What makes Hickmann's posters endure is their refusal to settle into decorative routine. Whether constructing fluid, melted letterforms for the PAN Museum or assembling stark optical-art geometry that destabilizes viewer perception, every composition operates as both an aesthetic object and a sharp political statement. Full-color offset printing on heavyweight uncoated stock ensures the ink saturation reproduces every nuanced layer of torn-paper collages and screenprinted halftones. It's a reminder that poster design remains one of the purest testing grounds for typographic invention.

For designers invested in the craft of editorial design and print production, this survey stands as an essential reference. Explore more of the publication or secure a copy directly through Slanted Publishers, and discover further work from Fons Hickmann and studio Lindhorst-Emme+Hinrichs.

#304. Ten things to have on your radar ahead of Dutch Design Week 2026

Dutch Design Week kicks off in Eindhoven this Saturday. To help you navigate the many exhibitions, installations and events taking place across the city, here are 10 of our picks.

From 17 to 25 October, Dutch Design Week will take over multiple locations across Eindhoven, the Netherlands.

Both established and emerging designers and studios will present projects based on this year’s theme of “raw”, selected to interrogate and celebrate raw, unpolished and authentic design projects.

Read on for 10 of Dezeen’s highlights to look out for during the city-wide festival:

Design Academy Eindhoven Graduation Show 2026

If you only see one thing, make it the Design Academy Eindhoven graduation show.

The school is responsible for nurturing some of the design world’s biggest and most interesting names – Sabine Marcelis, Formafantasma, Hella Jongerius, Philippe Malouin – so take this opportunity to spot tomorrow’s rising stars before they make it big.

Microstad, Professor Doctor, Dorgelolaan 2, 5611BA

Teresa van Dongen has long been fascinated with how clean energy could be used and generated in unexpected ways.

Following her experiments in bioluminescent lighting (powered by bacteria sourced from octopi and boggy World War Two bomb craters), the Dutch designer is now launching her latest project – a transparent window decal that serves as a solar-powered night light.

Among this year’s large-scale installations, Field by Isabel + Helen promises to be a standout.

The design duo is taking over Eindhoven’s Stadhuisplein with a family of towering wind turbines that passersby are encouraged to move and turn towards the wind to visualise the invisible energy flowing around us at all times.

For the Echo group show, 14 designers have transformed aluminium offcuts from the production of street lighting poles and extrusion profiles into new, useful products.

See the outcomes of their experiments in the newly minted TX Buildings.

With provocative projects, including a car that runs on waste plastic and a motorbike powered by swamp gas, Dutch designer Gijs Schalkx seeks to question our dependence on fossil fuels.

See these and some of his other dystopian transport designs in Onderweg naar een toekomst or “On the way to a future”.

As AI systems become ever more pervasive, designers are coming up with new and innovative ways to evade them.

Among them is Berlin’s Simon Weckert, who is showcasing one of the most-read projects published by Dezeen in the last few months – the Digital Camouflage shirt that scrambles the facial recognition system of surveillance cameras.

It’s worth going to see it with your own human eyes in the Punt-C warehouse, alongside projects from 14 other international designers.

Sectie-C Punt-C Industriële hotspot, Daalakkersweg 10-16 – Hal 10 5641JA

Eindhoven design collective Show Not Show is back for its third year, presenting an exhibition that recreates a high-powered boardroom inside studio complex de Kruisruimte.

Alongside existing members like Frank Penders and Lucas Zito, the 2026 edition will include work from three invited guest exhibitors – Aleksandra Adamchyk, Kilian Vos, and Pablo Octavio.

De Kruisruimte, Generaal Bothastraat 7-E 5642NJ

Rising star Teun Zwets has steadily made a name for himself at Dutch Design Week. Last year, he presented a mobile exhibition of his trademark glossy, splintered wood furniture from the back of a car trailer. The year before, he showcased his playful pieces in an exhibition arranged like a mock home.

For this year’s edition, Zwets is trying something new. He is unveiling 50 new chair designs that step away from his recognisable splintered-wood style, each designed with materials and methodologies he has never used before.

The pieces will be on display at Zwets’s wood and metal workshop.

Forward Furniture by Liv Vaisberg and Dutch Design Week

Curated by Design Biennale Rotterdam co-founder Liv Vaisberg, the Forward Furniture exhibition is returning to Dutch Design Week.

Almost 100 established and emerging designers working in and around collectible design will present three pieces each, highlighting their distinctive visual languages.

The exhibition design is based on carpets, which offer a soft touch to the show’s former factory setting.

Local Linoleum is an exhibition by designer Christien Meindetsma, whose aim is to uncover the hidden origins of materials and demystify the murky production chains of everyday objects.

Meindetsma’s show highlights how myriad issues related to industrialisation and globalisation mean that these production chains are typically largely invisible to consumers.

Dutch Design Week 2026 takes place from 17 to 25 October 2026 at various locations across Eindhoven, the Netherlands. See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world.

#305. Slow down and look: the simple complexity of Robert Ryman is revealed in Barbican exhibition

Robert Ryman in 1974; he taught himself to paint while working as a guard at MoMA Photo: Philippe De Gobert; © 2026 DACS

Known for his austere white canvases, Robert Ryman (1930-2019) spent his career testing the limits of what the discipline of painting could be. More than 30 years after his last major UK exhibition, the late American artist is the subject of Robert Ryman: The Real Thing at the Barbican. Bringing together works made from the mid-1950s through to the early 2010s, the show aims to introduce Ryman to a new generation of British audiences, while challenging the perception of an artist whose practice has often been reduced to the shorthand of “white paintings”.

“For the past decade, painting has been a prominent strand of the Barbican’s programme,” says the exhibition’s curator Wells Fray-Smith. Ryman, she adds, is “one of the most beloved painters of the 20th and 21st centuries”, yet opportunities to see his work in Britain have been scarce.

Born in Nashville, Tennessee in 1930, Ryman moved to New York in the early 1950s intending to pursue music as a jazz saxophonist. While in the city, he worked for years as a guard at the Museum of Modern Art (MoMA) and taught himself to paint. Ryman’s eventual practice departed from conventional ideas of what a painting should do. Rather than depicting an image or conveying a narrative, he became interested in the conditions of the work itself: pigment, surface, scale, light and space.

White was his dominant colour, allowing its relative neutrality to make these other elements more apparent. “The ‘seeming simplicity’ of a Ryman painting belies a vast complexity of expression, emotion, rhythm and possibility, for creating a work that appears simple is one of the most difficult artistic feats,” says Susan Dunne, a senior director at David Zwirner, which represents Ryman’s estate. “To Ryman, a painting’s presentation, its relationship to the wall and space that it occupies, is integral to the work itself. Anything but simple, Ryman’s art asks us to slow down and look carefully.”

Robert Ryman’s 12ft by 12ft Surface Veil II (around 1970) rarely travels due to its size Photo: David Heald; © 2026 Robert Ryman/DACS, London

Among the exhibition’s highlights is Untitled (Orange Painting) (1955 and 1959), which he began while working at MoMA. “Ryman considered this to be his first-ever ‘professional’ painting,” Fray-Smith says. “The piece is flaming orange with an acid-green underpainting and very surprising. Ryman often excluded the work from his own exhibitions because he found the colour ‘shocking.’”

The piece, however, proved significant to the artist. “I’ve always thought that if I ever wanted to paint a white painting it would be in the order of the way this painting was done, because this is an orange painting but there are many nuances and many oranges (and black and green),” Ryman once said about the work.

Another highlight is Surface Veil II (around 1970), a 12ft by 12ft work that rarely travels due to its size. The work was so large that Ryman laid it unstretched on the floor, drawing a square in blue chalk to paint within. When the canvas was subsequently stretched, the bars extended beyond the chalk line, leaving a narrow margin of unpainted material.

In curating the show, Fray-Smith wanted to challenge the perception of Ryman as austere or monochromatic. The exhibition also features pieces that incorporate additional materials and supports, including works on canvas, wallpaper, aluminium, Plexiglas and copper, as well as paintings from a more experimental period in the 1960s in which colour plays a role.

The installation will reinforce Ryman’s insistence on direct experience and sustained looking. In one section, the works are shown without wall texts or interpretation, with contextual information instead provided in a handout. “The gift of Ryman’s work is that it asks for us to pay attention,” Fray-Smith says. “While text and interpretation are important in introducing our audiences to Ryman and giving useful context to the work, it engages a cognitive ‘thinky’ brain that Ryman did not think was wholly necessary to have a meaningful experience with painting.” By removing these didactics, the museum hopes to inspire closer inspection of the works and their surroundings, allowing visitors to focus less on what something might mean.

To this end, Fray-Smith hopes visitors will leave with “a fresh sense of Ryman and his work”—and, crucially, with greater confidence in their own responses to art. Ryman’s achievement was not simply to make paintings with less; it was to make the act of looking itself part of the subject.

• Robert Ryman: The Real Thing, Barbican Art Gallery, London, until 28 February 2027

#306. Thinking Outside The Box: Digital Design In The AI Era

Oleksii Hrzhehorzhevskyi is a Senior Character Producer at MacPaw, specializing in character design, animation, and visual storytelling. He currently leads the … More about Oleksii ↬

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

This article has been kindly supported by our dear friends at MacPaw who not only believe that making great products requires seeing the world in a different light, but also strive to innovate and create incredible software ecosystem for users’ Macs. Thank you!

The phrase “artificial intelligence” has many excited, especially those in tech. But for those of us in creative fields like digital art and design, AI can be more concerning than it is exciting.

AI-generated art, videos, and images have flooded the internet, raising questions about whether more companies will turn to tools like OpenAI’s Dall-E, Midjourney, Leonardo.ai, and more, rather than employing human artists. What’s more, the fact that these AI models are trained on real artists’ work without their consent leaves many feeling as if they have no choice but to accept AI into their work and lives.

In a digital world increasingly dominated by faceless AI chatbots, agents, and features, it can be easy to get overwhelmed by all the technology. AI will certainly play a huge role in reshaping many industries, including design. We can’t deny this. But at the same time, humanization, empathy, and having a person at the wheel have never been more important.

Rather than viewing AI as something that replaces human creativity, we at MacPaw saw an opportunity to explore how we could make AI feel more personal and accessible — all the while keeping humans at the center of the experience. That led us to rethink how AI assistants are created.

Traditional AI assistants like Claude and ChatGPT typically take the form of a conversational textbox or webpage on screen, as this is how users have interacted with their devices. It’s comfortable and familiar. While extremely useful for a variety of tasks, interacting with these AI assistants can feel transactional and technical.

Using the same textbox format across all AI assistants does provide consistency. But we wanted to create a new, more personal and differentiated experience for users. But what format would be best? Even if we change how an AI tool looks, it still needs to be useful and intuitive to use.

As humans, it’s easier to understand and connect with things that resemble us. This is why we often find ourselves drawn to things like animals and characters: they have traits that we recognize within ourselves. Understanding this, we saw an opportunity to combine these values: utility and personality.

Enter Eney: a new proactive AI assistant. MacPaw didn’t want Eney to simply be another AI tool for users, but rather one that proactively assists within a user’s workflow. The vision was to help users connect with Eney more easily than with other AI tools, so we decided to create a character users could interact with. We wanted Eney to be expressive, friendly, and to emote as humans do. But we needed to strike an important balance: making Eney cheerful without it being overly goofy or childish.

This is where human animation and intervention played a critical role. While challenging, it was crucial because an overloaded character UI could turn users off and make navigating Eney difficult. To avoid this, the design team chose to create a select set of emotions and gestures for Eney to express, ensuring that its expressions conveyed useful information. For example, when working on a task, Eney’s figure resembles a loading icon. To do this, we worked to reduce Eney’s on-screen movement to make sure it wasn’t distracting or excessive.

After exploring a few different shapes and styles for Eney, we settled on a circular figure, as it felt the most approachable. It was simple and helped create the feeling of a calm, floating digital companion, rather than another rigid interface element on a user’s desktop. Eney’s minimal face design also plays an important role in connecting with the user. Its eyes are the main emotional connector — a key feature in showing emotions without being cartoonish.

The color choice for Eney was also important. Many AI assistants and companies use blue in their products, as it’s typically associated with intelligence. Blue is a great color, but we wanted Eney to stand out. We still wanted the color to be warm and inviting while slightly more visually stimulating, which led us to choose the color pink. Among dozens of other AI products that choose a more blue aesthetic, Eney was designed to catch a user’s eye and stand out in their mind (and on their screen).

All in all, we wanted to create a character that was present but not attention-seeking; a warm and supportive digital helper that enhances a user’s workflow rather than distracts from it. Eney’s character gives personality to otherwise invisible processes.

While those who aren’t design professionals may assume there wasn’t much significance behind Eney’s character creation, this couldn’t be further from the truth. Like many other products, all these elements — style, design, emotion, size, name, and more — were intentionally chosen, not by machines but by humans.

Even though AI has streamlined many design processes, namely enabling faster design, there are still many things it can’t do well. Even when designing Eney, while technology supported the process, human designers controlled every step and decision.

As designers, it’s more important than ever to have good judgment, artistic direction, integrity, and emotional sensitivity when working in the field. Technology like AI can help us work faster, but it can’t replace the values that inspire and shape our work.

What’s more, while anyone can easily generate something by typing a prompt into an AI image tool, there’s a true beauty and talent when intentionally crafting something through manual design.

As designers, we shouldn’t stray away from the latest tools. Rather, we should learn them and see how they could potentially help us within our creative workflows. Personally, I like to use AI tools such as Perplexity and ChatGPT for research purposes in the early stages. However, we need to remember that they’re just that: tools. At the end of the day, technology like AI cannot, and should not, replace human artistry. It should help us express our visions, not replace us entirely.

If there’s one thing to take away from this piece, it’s that curiosity helps build taste over time, and taste becomes more valuable, not less, in the AI era.

#307. BIG designs cloud-like Tirana Fountain Plaza raised above public park

Cloaked in layers of white disks, architecture studio BIG has revealed plans for a mixed-use building in Tirana containing apartments, offices, cultural spaces and water features.

Named Tirana Fountain Plaza, the cloud-like building will be raised on slim white columns over Rinia Park, designed to keep the ground level largely open as a public space.

BIG recently won the competition to design the building, which will contain offices, apartments, a hotel and cultural spaces.

Rows of perforated white disks will line the glazed facades and animate the interior spaces.

Two curved volumes wrapped in fluted glass at either end of the building will connect the upper volume to the ground.

Renders of the design show it placed at the edge of the Rinia Park on Rruga Sami Frashëri, where the Taiwan Center restaurant complex and adjacent Taiwan Pool water feature currently stand.

BIG aimed to improve the natural landscape of Rinia Park in its design for the Tirana Fountain Plaza, surrounding it with planted gardens and adding rainwater management features.

The studio will preserve the existing Taiwan Pool and capture, store and reuse the water in a closed-loop system.

BIG’s design aims to irrigate the landscape to help reduce the risk of flooding in the area and cool the surrounding park.

“Awarded first place in the international competition for Tirana Fountain Plaza, BIG’s proposal expands the landscape of Rinia Park beneath and around a new mixed-use development in the heart of Tirana,” said BIG.

“The project transforms a privately operated site into a new cultural and mixed-use destination, introducing gardens, plazas, water features, and gathering spaces that connect the park to the Lana River while preserving the historic fountain,” BIG continued.

“Selected from a shortlist including Cobe, Barozzi Veiga, l’AUC, and JDSA, the design brings architecture, landscape, and water management together as a single civic experience.”

Tirana Fountain Plaza will be situated near the Pyramid of Tirana, a former museum that was renovated into a cultural hub by MVRDV.

Elsewhere in Tirana, BIG is building the bow-tie-shaped National Theatre of Albania. In 2020, activists were arrested for protesting the demolition of the original 1930s theatre to make way for the new construction.

BIG is also working on plans to add a cluster of interfaith pavilion buildings on a hillside near Tirana.

#308. Web Design: Point of View by Anna Hodarkovskaya

Anna Hodarkovskaya designed the web design for Point of View, tracing eyewear history through scroll transitions and typographic craft.

Most digital longreads treat typography like an afterthought, dumping endless paragraphs into generic single-column templates. Point of View takes the opposite route. Researched, designed, and developed by Anna Hodarkovskaya, the project turns the history of optical lenses into an interactive exhibition. The layout opens with stark diopter scales, braille accents, and crisp technical diagrams that immediately establish the ocular theme. Nothing in this grid feels accidental. It relies on sharp scale contrasts to pace the reader, pulling the eye downward through centuries of lens experimentation without relying on decorative clutter. Itâs an exercise in discipline.

Scroll mechanics set the pace. As you move through the viewport, the page blurs and sharpens to simulate optical focal lengths and focal shifts. Early sections introduce blurred historical portraits of figures like Alexander Pushkin, Marie Antoinette, and Catherine the Great. They reveal how uncorrected vision isolated scholars before wearable optics arrived. From there, the editorial web design transitions smoothly into the eleventh-century reading stone â polished glass hemispheres monks rested on illuminated manuscripts. The layout sandwiches manuscript fragments between wireframe curvature diagrams, giving tactile weight to ancient reading tools.

The technical restraint stands out. Hodarkovskaya pairs bold grotesque display headings with delicate mono-spaced metadata, tracking the leap from Northern Italyâs thirteenth-century rivet spectacles to twentieth-century pop icons like John Lennonâs round frames. Wireframe lens vectors rotate alongside interactive timeline modules, shifting the narrative from medical utility to personal self-expression. Each chapter flows into the next through careful scroll choreography that highlights how materials evolved from horn and bone into lightweight wire and acetate. By anchoring complex historical research in clean web design, the site lets the typography do the heavy lifting.

#309. ‘Even an ugly thistle can be so beautiful’: painter Sabine Moritz on how nature informs her work

Cologne-based artist Sabine Moritz’s retrospective Lie Down in Green Pastures is at London’s Garden Museum Photo: © Albrecht Fuchs

The German painter Sabine Moritz has long worked in ways that frustrate easy categorisation. When an interviewer in 2023 asked her about a new body of gestural paintings being somewhere between abstraction and figuration, she described the act of painting itself as a landscape of sorts. “It’s like there are two banks,” she said. “Figuration on one side and abstraction on the other, and a river between. The river is obstinate. It takes time to cross.” This imagery draws out a golden thread that weaves through all her work, where ever-present attention is paid to the natural world.

As Moritz was preparing to open Lie Down in Green Pastures at the Garden Museum in London—her first large-scale museum show in the UK—she spoke about her early works, based on memories of her childhood, that brought her to the world’s attention and how her new work is not about understanding the past but how to live in the present.

The Art Newspaper: This is your first UK museum exhibition. How does that make you feel?

Sabine Moritz: I’m so proud and so happy to be doing this show, particularly in the Garden Museum, which has made clear all kinds of connections that I wasn’t really aware of until now. When the curator Emma House and I first discussed what to include, I sent over images and gave her free rein. She immediately knew she wanted the two big Institute paintings: Institute I and Institute II. I wasn’t sure. I had never shown them before because I was just never happy with them. I made them a long time ago back in 1993, while studying at the Academy of Art in Düsseldorf, and I knew exactly what I was trying to achieve with them then. But somehow I always felt I could have done better. I was essentially trying to teach myself how to paint with oils.

I made the botanical drawings around the same time, which I’ve also never shown. I kind of only recently rediscovered them. What has been amazing is seeing anew the works Emma chose—it makes me think there is a quality there that I hadn’t seen myself. Perhaps the sense of urgency or intensity I felt when making them and wanted to instil in them is discernible—even if, to my mind, they aren’t entirely successful in formal terms.

Moritz’s Institute I (1993). “I love the subversive nature of plants, the way they will always grow back, no matter how much you fight against them,” the artist says Photo: Georgios Michaloudis; © Sabine Moritz; courtesy of the artist and Pilar Corrias, London

Does the show give a thorough overview of 30 years of your practice? What are the throughlines you have picked out?

The exhibition does cover 30 years, but there are, of course, gaps. For a while I was working a lot on the idea of war—helicopters and airplanes are among the motifs I explored—none of which is included in the show.

But towards the end of that period, I came across these photos Robert Capa took while travelling through Ukraine, then a Soviet republic, in 1947 with John Steinbeck. He captured people in the fields during the harvest. I was so fascinated. Because it’s both really beautiful, seeing people at work in nature, but you also know how hard these years were. There was famine; so many men didn’t come back from the war. Among the figures was that photograph of a child, which I painted again and again. When I’m fascinated or busy with something, I tend to do many variations on it.

It is only later that I realised that that child is like an alter ego, or a second me—a figure that reminds me so much of my own childhood, or perhaps of something that all of us experienced as children. Being left to our own devices, running around outside making noise, in a state of Selbstvergessenheit—I don’t think there is a satisfactory English equivalent of this word. Literally it translates as “self-forgetfulness”, but it isn’t about forgetfulness. Rather, it is being so at one with nature and your surroundings that nothing else matters and you are able to let go, to be at peace. It is a very happy experience you can have outdoors, in nature, but also when working.

Building a garden in a landscape is kind of what art is too. I’m never dogmatic—I’ll see something growing and just look at it and consider whether to prune it, let it keep growing or suppress it. And that’s what happens often in work too.

In interviews you have often spoken about looking out the window, and in your studio now you have a huge window looking out over treetops. Is it particularly poignant for your this show to take place in a museum focused on our relationship to the natural world?

I’m not sure why looking outside is so beautiful. I find it always so calming. Whenever I’ve gone through periods of not knowing what to do in my work, I’ve simply drawn what I could see through the window. It’s also about a search for beauty. German cities are often so ugly, because of the war and of how much was destroyed and then rebuilt with a lack of funds or a misguided idea of what modern is; also, tastes have changed.

Your Institute paintings relate to the wider body of work you did early on around Neulobeda, in East Germany—a new town built in the 1960s and 70s full of concrete-slab residential blocks, where your family lived after your father’s death. He had worked as a chemist at the Central Institute of Genetic and Cultivated Plant Research in Gatersleben. How has your approach to working with memory changed?

When I was working on the Institute paintings, I had such a strong impulse to work with memory, and to go back in time—to live in that past, which of course isn’t possible, but that’s what art is for.

My main works at the time were my Lobeda line drawings. People often say they look naive or childlike; they were done purely from memory. As a counterpart, I wanted to integrate something living in this world. As a child I was always outdoors, digging in the ground, making things with plants, creating tiny worlds for tiny animals. Nowadays people talk about there not being any weeds—that all plants are beautiful. As a child I was aware of how beautiful even an ugly thistle was. I love the subversive nature of plants, the way they will always grow back, no matter how much you fight against them. They have such an energy about them. So that’s where the botanical drawings came from.

What I had never made a connection with is the fact that the institute where my father worked was for genetic plant research. There were huge gardens there. It still exists—they have one of the world’s biggest seed banks.

I still work in an associative way, but memory no longer plays such a great role in my work. I’m actually trying more to understand the present. It might be because I’m in my late 50s and there’s so much, so many images, in my mind.

Is the title of the show, Lie Down in Green Pastures, a biblical reference?

Yes absolutely. I find Psalm 23 so beautiful, and so becalming. And I thought it fitted so well, this sense of trusting in God and the idea that we are being led. In German, not in the Catholic Bible but in the Lutheran Bible, which is much more beautifully worded and poetic, the verse is “er weidet mich auf einer grünen Aue”: “he grazes me on a green pasture”. Of course, humans don’t graze, animals do. But there is, to my mind, a certain humility in that, the idea that we are a part of creation. And a sense of trust, or hope. But of course, today, often desperation too—my god, the heat this summer. I was in London recently and walked through Hyde Park with my son. Everything looked dead, the trees were suffering. We need to all think so much more about how we want to live in this world. Artists are always trying to make the world a better place and it never works.

Moritz’s Two Chrysanthemums (2014), part of an ongoing series of floral still-life paintings Photo: © Simon Vogel; © Sabine Moritz; Courtesy the artist and Pilar Corrias, London

How does the new work in the show, Melancholy of the Wind, relate to these earlier works? What connections and conversations have surprised you, when putting it all together?

For the past ten years, I’ve been making these purely abstract paintings, more recently including female figures within them. Sometimes I feel they don’t go with the older works at all, so I’m actually excited to see how it all comes together. In Melancholy of the Wind, I’ve included four female figures, and they’re in the state of Selbstvergessenheit that I mentioned, of thoughtfulness or contemplation. They’re naked in nature, but it isn’t a realistic nature, the colours are not those you would normally associate with the landscape. It is a place with a dreamlike quality, where you might relax and lose yourself, effortlessly thinking about what comes next.

• Sabine Moritz: Lie Down in Green Pastures, Garden Museum, London, until 20 December

#310. Gundry & Ducker draws on French dining culture for London restaurant Cassette

Design studio Gundry & Ducker has renovated the interiors of a Grade II-listed workshop for Cassette, a Parisian-style bistro that has recently opened in the heart of London‘s West End.

The spacious eatery is housed within a nineteenth-century gothic building, which features double-height ceilings and an expansive glass facade with intricate detailing.

Located in Covent Garden, the restaurant spans 107 square metres and accommodates 52 customers across a ground floor dining room and a basement level.

An outdoor terrace welcomes an additional 30 guests when the weather permits.

“Our brief talked about a neighbourhood restaurant in the centre of town,” Gundry & Ducker co-founder Tyeth Gundry told Dezeen.

“From there, the conversation centred on familiarity, recognition and ease – creating a neighbourhood restaurant for friends who live in different parts of the city.”

The studio intended for the design to resemble traditional Parisian establishments by incorporating familiar elements, including deep aubergine finishes, dark banquette seating and classic bentwood bistro chairs.

Alongside this, the designers combined natural fabrics, sapele wood and stainless steel with exposed brickwork to create a restrained colour palette and an overall “deliberately unfussy” interior.

“We talked a lot about colour: summer park landscapes, Parisian bistros and wine,” Gundry explained.

“Tone too was really important; we needed colours that would dim well to help us create a low-level evening setting that feels warm; the key to which is controlling reflected light,” he continued.

Taking cues from the surrounding theatre district, the studio installed a sophisticated sound system and a statement curtain with acoustic qualities that wraps around the main dining area.

“We felt that we could explore the world of theatres given the restaurant’s location in London’s West End,” Gundry said.

“By placing the curtain within gantry structures, they became theatre curtains and added some character to the space,” he continued.

“In this case, acoustics was as much part of the conversation as colour or operation. The curtains help to control reverb and talk about a softer acoustic.”

Cassette’s owners, Mark Gurney and Matt Bushnell, sourced a selection of artworks from local markets and car boot sales to add pops of colour and personality into the space.

Other restaurant interiors recently featured on Dezeen include Bétyle Studio’s design for Parisian eatery Arcane 17 and the newly opened Skywalker Grill located in the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art, Los Angeles.
